A MESSAGE from His Majesty, by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman U(her of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That, in pursuance of the Directions of an Act, pafl'ed in the 10th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " to enable the Speaker of the House of Commons to " issue his Warrants, to make out new Writs for the " Choice of Members to serve in Parliament, in the room " of such Members as shall die during the Recess of Parliament," he had issued his Warrants to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out new Writs, for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament, for the following Places; viz.for the Borough of Scarborough, in the County of York, in the room of George Manners, Esquire; for the Borough of Boroughbridge, in the County of York, in the room of James West, Esquire; for the Borough of Harwich, in the County of Essex, in the room of John Roberts, Esquire; for the County of Wilts, in the room of Edward Popltam, Esquire; for the City of Ro-ckefier, in the County of Kent, in the room of John era/t, Esquire; and for the Borough of New the County of Berks, in the' room of Richard Tonfon, Esquire.

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes: And such of the said Members, as are by Law required to deliver in to the Clerk of this House, an Account of their Qualification, and to take and lubscribe the Oath of Qualification, delivered in such Account, and took and subscribed the said Oath accordingly.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended Kng’sSpeech His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty reported, was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr.

Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I should most willingly have consulted your private Convenience, by allowing you a longer Recess from Business, if' I had not thought that some very important Parts of the Public Service required the immediate Attention of Parliament.

It is impossible that I can look with Indifference upon whatever concerns either the Commerce and Revenue of the Kingdom at large, or the private Rights and Interest of considerable Numbers among My People:

Neither can I be insensible how materially every one of thele great Objects must be interested in the Maintenance of the Credit, and Prosperity, of the East India Company. When, therefore, I received Information of the Difficulties in which that Company appear to be involved, I determined to give you an early Opportunity of informing yourselves fully of the true State of their Affairs; and of making such Provisions, for the common Benefit and Security of all the various Intorefts concerned, as you shall find belt adapted to the Exigencies of the Cafe.

I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you. That there is Reason to hope, that the War, which has so long unhappily prevailed in one Part of Europe, is now. drawing to a Conclusion: And although there was no Probability of our being involved therein, yet the Discontinuance of those Troubles will afford a fairer Prospect of the Duration of Peace; which, I trust, the Altera--tions that have happened in Europe, will not, in their Consequer.ces, affect.

I continue to receive, from Foreign Powers, the strongest Assurances of their pacific Dispositions towards

this

this Country: And it shall be My constant Endeavour to preserve the general Tranquillity, as far as is confident with the Honour of My Crown, and the intereds of My People.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

It gives Me much Satisfaction, That the Continuance of Peace has enabled Me to proceed in the Reduction of the Establishment of My Naval Forces; but you will, I am confident, agree with Me, that a considerable Strength at Sea mud be ever necessary for preserving the Reputation, and Power, of My Kingdoms.

The proper Edimates for the ensuing Year shall he laid before you; and whatever Supplies you may grant shall, on My Part, be managed with the drifted (Economy, and applied with the utmod Fidelity.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I cannot but feel the most real Concern, That the Prod pee of the late Harved has not given Us the Relief which We had hoped Tor, in respect to the Dear-ness of Corn. As far as Human Wisdom can provide for alleviating the Didrefles of the Poor, lam persuaded, your Attention will not be wanting: And you cannot gratify Me more, than by calling upon Me for My Concurrence in whatever may contribute to the true Welfare, and Happiness, of all My People.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, To return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Speech from the Throne: To acknowledge His Majesty’s great Goodness, in His condant Attention to whatever concerns either the Commerce and Revenue of His Kingdom at large, or the private Rights and intereds of copsiderable Numbers among His People: To return His Majesty our hearty Thanks, for having given us so early an Opportunity of informing ourselves fully of the true State of ^he Affairs of the East India Company; and to allure His Majesty, that, impressed with a due Sense of the great Importance of the Business, we will, without Delay, proceed to the Consideration of it, and endeavour to provide, in the most effectual Manner that the Nature of the same will admit, for the common Benefit and Security of all the great and weighty intereds recommended to our Care by His Majesty:

To allure His Majesty, That we rejoice to hear His Majesty has llealon to hope that the War, which has so long unhappily prevailed in one Part of , is

now drawing to a Conclusion; and that the favourable Prospect of the Duration of Peace, which the Probability of this Event affords us, will not be affected by the Alterations which have lately happened: That it gives us the highed Satisfaction, to find that His Majesty continues to receive from Foreign Powers the dronged Assurances of their pacific Disposition towards this Country; and that we most gratefully acknowledge His Majesty’s gracious Declaration, That it will be His condant Endeavour to preserve the general Tranquillity, as far as is confident with the Honour of His Crown, and the intereds of His People:

That His Majesty’s faithful Commons will chearfully grant such Supplies as the Services of the ensuing Year shall require: And though it mud ever be for the Intered and Reputation of this Country to have a conG-derable Strength at Sea, yet we learn with much Satisfaction, that His Majesty has been enabled, during the Course of this Year, to proceed in the Reduction of His Naval Edablishment:

With Hearts full of Gratitude, to acknowledge the paternal and affectionate Concern, which His Majesty has expressed, for the Didrefles which the Poor continue to suffer, from the Dearness of Corn: And to assure His Majesty, that a diligent Attention shall not be wanting, on our Part, to consider of the most proper Means for preventing the Encrease of the Evil, and for

alleviating the present Didrefles, as far as they are in their Nature capable of Relief; being persuaded, that we cannot render any Service more acceptable to His Majesty, than by contributing to the Happiness of all His People.

A Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Exe- Westminster cution the several Acts, passed in the Reign of His present Majesty, for paving, cleansing, lighting, and regulating, the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and other Places in the said Acts mentioned, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, since the Beginning of the Works under the Petitioners Direction, they have found it necessary to make several other Applications to Parliament, as Occasion required; and several other Acts have been passed; in the Execution whereof, the Petitioners find some further Amendments necessary to be made, which, the Petitioners conceive, would greatly facilitate the Execution of the said Acts:

And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to amend the said Acts, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

King't pointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be pre-

fcpeoch. fented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn

up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; cxz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg leave to return Your Majesty our humble Thanks, for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We acknowledge, with the warmest Gratitude, Your Majesty’s great Goodness, in Your constant Attention to whatever concerns either the Commerce and Revenue of Your Kingdom at large, or the private Rights and Interests of considerable Numbers among Your People. And we return our most dutiful Thanks to Your Majesty, for having given us an early Opportunity of informing ourselves fully of the true State of the Affairs of the East India Company: And we assure Your Majesty, that, impressed with a due Sense of the great . Importance of the Business, we will, without Delay, proceed to the Consideration of it; and endeavour to provide, in the most effectual Manner that the Nature of the same will admit, for the comnsion Benefit and Security of all the great and weighty Interests recommended to our Care by Your Majesty.

Your faithful Commons cannot but rejoice to hear that Your Majesty has Reason to hope that the War, which has so long unhappily prevailed in one Part of Europe, is now drawing to a Conclusion; and that the favourable Prospect of the Duration of Peace, which the Probability of this Event affords us, will not be affected by the Alterations which have lately happened: And we feel the highest Satisfaction, at the Assurances, winch Your Majesty continues to receive from Foreign Powers, of their pacific Dispositions towards this Country; and at the same Time we most gratefully acknowlege Your Majesty’s gracious Declaration, That it will be Your constant Endeavour to preserve the general Tranquillity, as far as is consistent with the Honour of Your Crown, and the Interests of Your People.

Your Majesty may be assured, that Your faithful Commons will chearfully grant such Supplies as the Services of the ensuing Year shall require: And although we are convinced, that it must ever be for the Interest and Reputation of this Country, to have a considerable Strength at Sea, yet we learn with much Satisfaction, that Your Majesty has been enabled, during the Course of this Year, to proceed in the Reduction of Your Naval Establishment.

Permit us to offer to Your Majesty our most humble and unfeigned Thanks, for the paternal and affectionate Concern which Your Majesty has expressed for the Distresses which the Poor continue to suffer, from the Dearness of Corn. And we allure Your Majesty, that a diligent Attention shall not be wanting, on our Part, toconsider of the most proper Means for preventing the Encrease of the Evil; and for alleviating the present Distresses, as far as they are in their Nature capable of Relief; being persuaded, that we cannot render any

Service more acceptable to Your Majesty, than by contributing to the Happir.efs of all Your People.

lyir. Onslow reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Onslow accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Corn, Grain, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, and Starch; and also, the Extraction of Low Wines and Spirits from Wheat and Wheat Flour, be prohibited for a further Time, to be limited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Importation of Wheat, Wheat Flour, Rye, Rye Meal, and Indian Corn, into this Kingdom, be allowed for a further Time, to be limited, free of Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Importation of Barley, Barley Meal, Oats, Oatmeal, and Pulse, into this Kingdom, be allowed for a Time to be limited, free of Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Importation of Rice, from any of His Majesty’s Colonies in Americinto this Kingdom, be allowed for a further Time, to be limited, free of Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion, of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Eighth Year of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to continue and amend an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for Importation of Salted Beef, Pork, Bacon, and Butter, from Ireland, for a limited Time; and for allowing the Importation of Salted Beef, Pork, Bacon, and Butter, from the Rritifk Dominions in America, for a limited Time, be continued for a further Time, to be limited.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That no Peer of" this Realm hath an)' Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to fei ve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the tdoiife shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious* the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against,

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Rejbhed, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any same before this House, or arty Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and , the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members^ giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this , House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be in-f<*rmed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting 5 and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the Hcfufe is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers of Middlesex and Westminster, do take Care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning till One in th', Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the PassageS through the Streets between Tetqple Bar and Westminster Hall, shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructkms 'be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House;

and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take Care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in WestminsterHall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen* or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent* to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put

in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading the retoi

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the lead immediately after the Riling of the House; and also from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take Care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Postmaster General,

Ordered, That when any Letter or Packet, di reded to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the feme, and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, when the House is going to Prayers, give Notice thereof to all Committees; and that all Proceedings of Committees in a Morning, after such Notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the Printing thereof; and that no Person, but such as he shall appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petitions for private Bills after the Second Day of February next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Petition of the High Sheriff, Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, at a General Meeting of the said County, upon the 12th Day of August last, in order to take into Confederation the State of their Courts of Justice, situated in the Castle of Rougemont, it was resolved. That the Courts, wherein their Assizes and Sessions are always holden, were very ruinous, inconvenient, and inadequate to the Purposes of Public Business; and that the present Courts should be intirely taken down, and others built in a better Form, upon an Estimate not exceeding £.4,000; and that Application be made to Parliament, to carry the said Resolutions into Execution; and that there is a Sum of Money, amounting to £.1,231. 13J. 2 now vetted in the Public Funds, in Trust, for the Use of the County; which the Petitioners are desirous of applying, in the first Place, towards defraying the Expence of the said Building; but the said Money, being in Trust, cannot be so applied without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, to enable the Petitioners to carry the aforesaid Resolutions into Execution, to apply the said Monies towards re-building the said Courts of Justice, and to vest the same in the County, for the Purposes aforesaid; or that the House will grant them such other Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Richard Warwick Mr. Parker, fee.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the High Sheriff, Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That an Act passed in the 9th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the more effectual Relief " of the Poor, in the County of Devon" which hath been found ineffectual to answer the Purposes for which it was intended, and would, if continued in Force, be found extremely burthensome and oppressive to the several Parishes in the said County, which were proposed to be relieved thereby: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Repeal of the said Act; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the preceding Petition is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared -to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read j and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Whitworth, a Surveyor, being examined, said. That he had surveyed that Branch of the River Trent, that runs by the Town of Newark, which is about Miles in Length; that, for Want of a sufficient Quantity of Water, at certain Times of the Year, and on Account of several Shoals, the Navigation is greatly obstructed; and that the said Branch may be easily made navigable, at the Expence of about £. 2,500.

Mr. Job Brough, being examined, said. That the making the said Branch navigable will be of great Advantage to the Town of Newark and the adjoining Counties; and be of Public Utility.

Freeholders of the said Parish of Tryfull, on Behalf of themselves and others, the Freeholders of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Manor and Parish, certain Common and Waste Lands, containing, by Estimation, 600 Acres and upwards; and the find Sir John Wrottesley, and the several Persons having Right of Common upon the said Common and Waste Lands, are desirous that the same may be inclosed, divided, and allotted, amongst the several Persons interested therein; and the said Joseph Honeyborne is desirous to have a reasonable Part or Share of the said Common and Waste Lands allotted to him, in Lieu and Satisfaction of all Vicarial Tythes or Dues, and Composition for the fame, arising and happening within the said Parish: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for inclosing, dividing, and allotting, the said Common and Waste Lands, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Farnborough A Petition of several Trustees for putting in Execu-Road. tion an Act of Parliament, made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty George the Second, intituled, "An Act for repairing and widening the Road " leading from the Well at the North West End of the " Town or Village of Farnborough, in the County of " Kent, to a Place called Riverhill, in the Parish of " Sevenoakes in the said County," was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money on the Credit thereof, which now remains due, and which, together with the Tolls authorized to be collected by virtue of the said Act, hath been applied in repairing the said Road; and that Progress hath been made in the Repairs thereof; and that, unless the Term granted by the said Act is further continued, and the Powers thereof enlarged, the Money now owing cannot be repaid, and the Road kept in good Repair: And therefore 7

praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Term, and enlarging the Powers, of the said Act, in such Manner as the House shall think fit.

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Bethnal Poor, and the several Vestrymen and Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Matthew Bethnal Green, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act passed in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for maintaining, regulating, and employing, the Poor within the said Parish, whereby , the Governors and Directors of the Poor were im(-powered to provide and furnifti a Workhouse, and to raise, by Sale of Annuities, the Sum of Two thousand Pounds, to defray the Expences thereof; and that a Workhouse was accordingly built, and furnished in a proper Manner; but, the said Sum being found infus-ficient, the further Sum of One thousand Pounds, which was rTeceffarily expended in finishing and furnishing the said Workhouse, has been advanced, and now remains due, together with a large Arrear of Interest; and that the Money collected annually by the Poors Rate?, within the said Parish, since the passing of the said Act, has not been" sufficient to pay the Annuities, and defray the Expences of maintaining and regulating the Poor; and that, although such Rates have been extended to 4 s.6 d.in the Pound, and great Frugality and

(Economy used, the said Governors and Directors are now in Debt £. 1,500, or thereabouts, on Account of the Maintenance of the Poor; and that the Petitioned have Reason to expect that the Expence of providing for the Poor will further increase, and make it impossible to discharge the above-mentioned Debts, unless Power is given to raise Money to defray it by some other Means than the Poors Rates: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Governors and Directors of the Poor of the said Parish to raise Money sufficient to discharge the Debt incurred on Account of finishing and furnishing the Workhouse, and in maintaining and regulating the Poor, within the said Parish of Saint Matthew Bethnal Green, in such Manner, and by such Ways and Means, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Mackworth, Sir Charles Whitworth, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

THE House being informed, that some of the Commissioners of the Customs attended at the Door, they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to several Acts of Parliament, N° 1. An Account of prohibited India Goods brought into Saint Hellen's Warehouses, in the Port of

London, from Michaelmas 1771 to Michaelmas 1772; also what exported during that Time; and what remained in the said Warehouses Michaelmas 1772: And also,

N° 2. An Account of prohibited East India Goods brought into Lcadenhall Warehouses, in the Port of London, from Michaelmas 1771 to Michaelmas 1772; also what exported during that Time; and what remained in the said Warehouses at Michaelmas 1772: And also,

N° 3. An Account of prohibited East India Goods Y Vol. 34.

remaining in His Majesty’s Warehouses in the Port of London, at Michaelmas 1771; what have been since brought in; what exported; as also what remained at Michaelmas 1772: And also,

N° 4. An Account of East India Goods, prohibited to be worn in this Kingdom, in the respective Warehouses in the Out Ports, at Michaelmas 1771; what have been since brought in; what exported; as also what remained at Michaelmas 1772: And also,

N° 5. An Account of prohibited East India Goods, which have been delivered out of the Warehouses at Saint Hellen's, Leadenhall, Rilliter Lane, and the Custom House, in the Port of London, since Michaelmas 1771, in order to be dyed, glazed, and refreshed; what have been returned; and what remained out at Michaelmas 1772: And also,

N° 6. An Account of Naval Stores imported from Ruftta, into the Port of London, from Michaelmas 1771 to Michaelmas 1772: And also,

N° 7. An Account of Naval Stores imported from,

Russia, into the Ports of England, commonly called the Out Ports, from Michaelmas 1771 to Michaelmas 1772:

And also,

N° 8. An Account of the Number of Ships which have been employed in the Whale Fishery, to s

Straits and the Greenland Seas, with their respective Names and Burthens; from whence they were fitted out; and at what Port in Great Britain they were discharged; also the Number of Whales, Seals, and Quantity of Blubber, imported by each Ship, in the Year 1772:

And also

N° 9. An Account of all Corn, Grain, Meal, Malt,

Flour, Bread, Biscuit, and Starch, exported from England, to any Place whatsoever, by Virtue or in Pursuance of any of the Liberties or Powers given or granted for that Purpose, by an Act passed last Session, to prohibit the Exportation thereof, continued; viz. from the 10th of October 1771, exclusive, to the 10th of October 1772, inclusive.

And then they withdrew.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, a Member present informed the Committee

That many Complaints have been made by the Judges on the Circuits, of the great Inconvenience of the Courts of Justice belonging to the said County, in the Cattle of Rougemont, contiguous to the City of Exeter — that the said Courts were presented by the Grand Jury at the last Lent Assizes, as being unfit for carrying on the Business of the County; and that it was then unani-mously resolved to apply to Parliament, for Power to re-build the said Courts. — And he added. That the Sum of f. 1,200, and upwards, is vetted in him and another Gentleman, in Trust, for the Use of the County, which might be very properly applied to the above Purpose; and that it was agreed, at the said Meeting, that a Sum not exceeding £ 4,000 should be expended in re-building the said Courts.

A Petition of William Prince, of , in the Coun- Mr. Prince’s ty of Middlesex, Starch Maker, was presented to the p.eMt"n :T" House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner ,ce' urc has for many Years been concerned in the Starch Manufactory, which, at a Time when the Scarcity of Wheat is universally deplored, is to be wished did not confilme that immense Quantity which is used in the said Manufactory; and that the Petitioner, to whom His Majesty hath granted His Royal Letters Patent, for the making of Rice Starch, for the Term of Fourteen Years, is well acquainted with Rice and its Quality, and can make it manifest that Rice would answer every Purpose intended, having used it in the Manufactory of Starch, and found it of equal Goodnefswith that manufactured from Wheat; and can be afforded Ten per Cent, cheaper than from Wheat, at the present Price thereof; yet that the high Duty usually paid for Rice, when payable, will not admit of the Petitioner, or of others, proceeding the rein, as it is a new Branch of Business, that requires additional Buildings, and very expensive Utensils must be had for the Purposes, unless they could rely upon the Discontinuance of the Duty for such a Term as would afford a luffi* cient Encouragemert to engage in that Manufactory; which, at the same Time that it would tend to alleviate, in a great Degree, the Distrefl'es now laboured undet from a Scarcity of Wheat, might like wife be of National Advantage, when the Ports were opened, by encreasing the Export of Wheat, and employing our Shipping and Navigation in a Branch of Commerce

highly

highly beneficial to Great; and therefore the

Petitioner, who is willing to wave the Benefit of his Letters Patent, for the Purpose of Relief to the industrious Poor, and for the Sake of so advantageous a Manufactory, submitstothe Consideration of the House, that Rice, imported from His Majesty’s Colonies in America, might, for the Term of Seven Years, be free of Duty, and that Rice Starch might be allowed to be so exported, as the Petitioner and others would in such same be enabled to proceed in the manufacturing of Rice Starch.

subscribed, as well on Behalf of themselves, as of the rest of the Undertakers of the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Calder, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act passed in the 10th and i ith Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for making and keeping navigable the Rivers Air and Calder, in the County of York; and that the several Works executed under the Authority of the said Act have proved very beneficial; and that since the passing of the said Act, the Trade and Commerce in the Neighbourhood of the said Rivers have been much advanced and encreased, and a greater Number of Vessels than heretofore have been employed on the said Rivers; and that Complaints have been made to the Petitioners, that Goods carried up and down the said Rivers have of late not only been longer on their Passage than heretofore, but Embezzlements more frequent; and that the Petitioners find the Inconveniencies complained of to be occasioned by Shoals, Obstructions, and other Caules, in different Parts of the said Rivers, as well below as within the Limits of the Navigation, which, by the said Act, the Petitioners are made Undertakers of; and that, by the Removal of such Impediments, and by some additional Works, the said Navigation, the Petitioners apprehend, may be greatly improved, and less liable to the Defects and Inconveniencies complained of, the Freight of Good s co n fid erably lowered, and VesselIs not only enabled to cany larger Burthens, but to perform their Passage with greater Dispatch, Safety, and Certainty; and that, in order to effectuate such good Purposes, the Petitioners are desirous, at their own Colts, and without any VOL. 34.

additional Tolls or Duties, to extend and improve the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Calder, and to render the same more convenient and useful to the Community; but Doubts have been conceived, how far the Petitioners are enabled, under the Powers of the said Act, to remove such of the said Impediments as are within the Limits of the said Navigation, or to make Cuts, or other necessary Works, to avoid them, and other Impediments in the River Air, between and the River Ouze, out of the present Limits of the said Navigation: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Petitioners to extend and make all necessary Improvements in the Navigation of the said Rivers, under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Daniel Lascelles, Sir George Savile, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Bacon, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the present State of the Corn Trade, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Wheat imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Wheat is at or above Forty-eight Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Six Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Wheat imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Wheat in this Kingdom shall be at or above Forty-eight Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence per Hundred Weight be laid upon all Wheat Flour imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Wheat in this Kingdom shall be at or above Forty-eight Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Wheat from this Kingdom, when the Price of Wheat shall be at or above Forty-four Shillings per Quarter, be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Rye imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Rye in this Kingdom is at or above Thirty-two Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that a Duty of Three Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Rye imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Rye in this Kingdom shall be at or above Thirty-two Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Rye from this Kingdom, when the Price of Rye shall be at or above Twenty-eight Shillings per Quarter, be prohibited-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Barley imparted into this Kingdom, when the Price of Barley in this Kingdom is at or above Twenty-four Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Barley imported into this Kingdom when the Price of Barley in this Kingdom shall be at or above Twenty-four Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Barley from this Kingdom, when the Price of Barley shall be at or above Twenty-two Shillings per Quarter, be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Oats imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Oats in this Kingdom is at or above Sixteen Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Oats imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Oats in this Kingdom shall be at or above Sixteen Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Exportation of Oats from this Kingdom, when the Price of Oats shall be at or above Sixteen Shillings per Quarter, be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That when the Price of Oats, of the Growth of this Kingdom, shall be under Sixteen Shillings per Quarter, a Bounty, not exceeding Two Shillings for every Quarter of Oats, be allowed upon the Exportation of Oats and Oatmeal from this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Bounties now allowed by Law, upon the Exportation of the several Species of Corn and Grain, be continued to be allowed and made payable upon all Corn and Grain which shall be exported from'this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for and upon all Wheat, W’heat Flour, Rye,

Barley, and Oats, which shall have been imported into this Kingdom, and which shall be exported again thereout, there shall be drawn back any and all such Duty and Duties as shall have been paid on the Importation of such Wheat, Wheat Flour, Rye, Barley, and Oats, into Great Britain; such Drawback to be demanded and paid under such Rules and Regulations as Drawbacks in Cafes of the like Nature are drawn back and paid.

Ordered, That the further Confident ion of the said Report be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House Supply, to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now read.

Mr. Garth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of William Prince, of Chelsea, in the County of Middlesex, Starchmaker, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: \Vhere the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, is as follows:

His Majesty’s Letters Patent, granted to Mr. William Prince, in the Year 1768, were produced; whereby it appeared, that he enjoys an exclusive Right to make Starch of Rice, for the Term of 14 Years from the Date thereof: And

Mr. Alexander Kilgore, being examined, said, That he dealt largely in Starch; was acquainted with Mr. Prince-, and had seen his Manufactory for making Starch at Chelsea — that he had had Samples of Mr. Prince’s Rice Starch, which were superior both in Texture and Colour, to any he ever saw — that he shewed it to many of his Customers, who desired to have it, in preference to any other: And

Mr. William Prince, being examined, said. That he began to make Starch of Rice in the Year 1766 — that being in Expectation, that the making of Starch of Wheat would be prohibited, and it being alledged by the Starch Makers, that there was no other Material of which it could be made; he tried several Experiments, by which he found tha^ it might be made of Rice full as well as of Wheat — that he consumed upwards of 100 Barrels of Rice before he left off yfing it; but Wheat falling in its Price, induced him to make Starch of that as formerly — and he produced Samples of both Sorts of Starch.

Being further examined, he said, he apprehended that 500 Quarters of Wheat are consumed every Week in the Starch Manufactories in London and within Twenty Miles round, which amounts to 26,000 Quarters a Year; and that about 14,000 Quarters more are annually used for the same Article in the other Parts of the Kingdom — that a Quarter of Wheat, weighing 448 Pounds, will' produce 200 Pounds of Starch, and that 448 Pounds of Rice will make 336 Pounds of Starch — that when Wheat is at £.2. 10s. per Quarter, Rice at 14^. and 6 d.per Hundred, exclusive of the Duty on Importation, and the best Starch at 56 per Ton, which is the present Price, it may be made of Rice £. 10 per Cent. cheaper than of wheat — that Rice is at this Time I4J. 6 d.per Hundred, exclusive of the Duty of 6s. and \\d. on Importation — that as the adapting a Starch Manufactory to the Use of Rice, must be attended with an Expence of about £. 500, no Starch Maker would choose to put himself to such a Charge, without an Assurance, that the Duty on Importation of Rice should be discontinued for a Term, not less than Seven Years: And the Witness declared, that if the said Duty on Importation of Rice was taken off, and Starch made therewith allowed to be exported on the same Terms that Wheaten Starch is, when it is permitted to be carried out of the Kingdom, he was willing to relinquish the exclusive Right of making Starch of Rice, granted him by the said Letters Patent: Then

John Nutt, Esquire, a Merchant, said, That the Growth of Rice, in the Provinces of Carolina and Georgia, is much encrealed within these few Years, and the last Crop much greater than that of any former Year — that as the Number of Settlers in East and West Florida encrease considerably, and Part of the Land in those Colonies is proper for the Culture of Rice, there is no Vo*. 34.

Doubt but that large Quantities of it may be imported from thence; and if used in the Starch Manufactory, the Consumption thereby occasioned might, as he appre- . hended, tend to encourage the Growth and Importation of it; and added, that about 4,000 Barrels of R ce are annually consumed in Great Britain, when the Duty of 6s. and 4 id.per Hundred is paid on the Importation.

John Clark, Esquire, a Merchant, confirmed Mr.

Nutt’s Evidence.

Mr. Cooper accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolution which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Distillery from Wheat and Wheat Flour being already prohibited by Law, to extend that Prohibition, at present, to the Distillery from Barley and Malt would not tend materially towards reducing the Price of Corn.

The House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Bacon took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Bacon reported from the Committee, That they hadcomctofeveralResolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the fame.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Bacon accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Wheat imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Wheat is at or above Forty-eight Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Six Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Wheat imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Wheat in this Kingdom shall be at or above Forty-eight Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence per hundred Weight be laid upon ali Wheat Flour imported into this Kingdom, when 3

the Price of Wheat in this Kingdom shall be at or above Forty-eight Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That the Exportation of Wheat from this Kingdom* when the Price of Wheat shall be at or above Forty-four Shillings per Quarter, be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That the Duties now payable upon Rye imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Rye in this Kingdom is at or above Thirty-two Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That a Duty of Three Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Rye imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Rye in this Kingdom shall be at or above Thirty-two Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Rye from this Kingdom, when the Price of Rye shall be at or above Twenty-eight Shillings pa Quarter, be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Barley imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Barley in this Kingdom is at or above Twenty-four Shillings pa Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Barley imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Barley in this Kingdom shall be at or above Twenty-four Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Barley from this Kingdom, when the Price of Barley shall be at or above Twenty-two Shillings per Quarter, be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Oats imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Oats in this Kingdom is at or above Eighteen Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That a Duty of Two Pence pa Quarter be laid upon all Oats imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Oats in this Kingdom shall be at or above Eighteen Shillings pa Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Oats from this Kingdom, when the Price of Oats shall be at or above Sixteen Shillings pa Quarter, be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, when the Price of Oats of the Growth of this Kingdom shall be under Sixteen Shillings pa Quarter, a Bounty, not exceeding Two Shillings for every Quarter of Oats, be allowed, upon the Exportation of Oats and Oatmeal from this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bounties now allowed by Law, upon the Exportation of the several Species of Corn and Grain, be continued to be allowed and made payable upon all Corn and Grain, which shall be exported from this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for and upon all Wheat, Wheat Flour, Rye, Barley, and Oats, which shall have been imported into this Kingdom, and which shall be exported again thereout, there shall be drawn back any and all such Duty and Duties as shall have been paid on the Importation of such Wheat, Wheat Flour, Rye, Barley, and Oats, into Great Britain; such Drawback to be demanded and paid under such Rules and Regulations as Drawbacks in Cafes, of the like Nature are drawn back and paid.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, wete, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the United Company of Merchants of East India England, trading to the East Indies, was presented to Affairs — the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Peti- Secrft Com* tioners are informed, by the Votes, that, in pursuance

of

13 Geo. III. 146 — 15'

of a Report from the Committee of Secrecy appointed to enquire into the State of the East India Company; it was ordered. That Leave be given to bring in a Rill to restrain the East India Company; for a Time to be limited, from making any Appointment of Commissioners for lupetintending and regulating the Company’s Affairs at their Pivlidencies in the East Indus \ and that the Petitioners cannot help considering i’uch a Bill as subversive of those Rights which they hold under their Charter; the original Privileges of which; and the Continuation thereof! have been purchased by their Predecessors from the Public for a valuable Consideration, and repeatedly confirmed by several Acts of Parliament; the Provisions of which the Petitioners are not in any Degree conscious of having violated; and that the Petitioners conceive it to be their undoubted legal Right to send out any Persons, whom they judge proper, to enforce and execute such Regulations, agreeable to the Power of their Charters, as the said Company shall think necessary for the good Government of their several Settlements in India, or for correcting such Abul'cs as may have prevailed therein; and that the present State of Affairs in India appears to the Petitioners to be such, as requires many new Orders and Regulations to be speedily sent out; as well for restraining exorbitant and unnecessary Expences, as for correcting other Abuses; and it has been found, Upon Examination; that Savings riiay be made in the several Settlements and Presidencies of the Company, to the Amount of many Hundred Thousand Pounds; and that, under thele Circumstances, the Petitioners have thought it necessary to chuse certain Commissioners, who appeared to thent to be qualified for so important aTruft; and to grant them a Commission, with extraordinary Powers, for carrying into Effect such Regulations, and enforcing such Savings, as have been, or shall be, deemed necessary and expedient; and reprei'enting to the House; that the Grounds of the Calculation of Expences, upon which (according to the Report of the Secret Committee) the present Bill proceeds to restrain the Petitioners in the Eiertife of their legal Rights, Appears to the Petitioners to be incomplete and erroneous; and they are confident; if their Affairs had been examined in a public Mahner, agreeable to the Genius of this happy Constitution, whereby the Petitioners (as well as the particular Pecfons who are so deeply affected by the present Bill, should it pass into a Law) might have an Opportunity of attending to their several I nterefts, that the Members of the Committee would have made a Report very different from that which has appeared} and that, as the Expences of the Commission are intended to be defrayed from a Part of the Savings pro*-posed to be made thereby, such Expences, the Petitioners apprehend, cannot in any Degree injure the Creditors of the said Company *, but, on the contrary, fnuft tend to their Advantage, more ei'pecially as the Petitioners are determined to proportion them, with the most exact CEconomy, to the present Circumstances of their Affairs; and that the Petitioners intreat the House to consider the dangerous Cdniequences of such x Bill to the Credit of the Company, which, by preventing them from taking the necessary Steps for the Arrangement of their Affairs, may deprive them of the Means of fulfilling their Engagements to the Public-: The Petitioners therefore claim the Benefit of the Law of the Land, and the public Faith of the Nation, for the "free Enjoyment and Exercise of the Rights and Powers which they hold under their Charter; and pray. That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill, as tending to restrain or suspend what appears to them to be the legal Operation of those Rights and Powers.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: — And,

Mr. George Box, Clerk to the said Commissioners, being examined* said. That many Inconveniencies arise from the Acts not being reduced into One; as Persons frequently look into wrong Acts, and regulate their Conduct by such Clauses as are repealed or varied: That many Doybts have arise n in regard to the placing of Signs, as the Words in the Act that requires them to be " fixed on the Fronts of Houses" are liable to many Interpretations; and that under those Words many Signs have been improperly placed t

That t he Penalty upon breaking Lamps is inadequate to the Damage; and that Persons evade the Punishment upon causing Nuisances, as the Acts require Six Hoiirs Notice to be given for removing the m} and it is common to remove them within that Time, upon such Notice being given, and immediately replace them;

And that the said Acts are in many other Respects defective.

Mr. David Forrejier, Surveyor of the Pavements, and Mr. John Marquand, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence*

Mr. Pownall reported from the Committee appointed to examine the several Laws now in being, relative to the Assize of Bread, and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had examined the same accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him tore-port to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; vh.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if the Magistrates were by Law permitted (when and where they shall think fit to set an Assize on Bread) to introduce again, under certain Regulations and Restrictions, the old Standard Bread, made of Flour, which is the whole Produce of the Wheat (the said Flour weighing, on an Average, Three Fourths of the Weight of the Wheat whereof it is made) it would tend to prevent many Inconveniencies, which have arisen in the Assize and Making of Bread for Sale.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Columnscakulated for theWheaten Bread, in the now repealed Tables of the Act of the Eighth of Queen Arne, intituled, "An Act to regulate the Price and

Assize of Bread," wo.uld be the proper Assize for the hud Standard Wheaten Bread; and that the Twelve Penny Loaf of this Standard Wheaten Bread, containing the whole Flour of the Wheat (the said Flour weighing, on an Average, Three Fourths of the Weight of the said Wheat) would, upon a Medium, contain One Pound of Bread in Eight mote than the Twelve Penny Loaf of the present Wheaten Bread, made under the Act of the Thirty-first of the Second.

Ordered, That the further Confederation of the said Report be adjourned till Friday the 2 2d Day of January next.

Ordered, That such a Humber of Copies of the said Report, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The said Report is preserved amongst the other Papets of this Session.

%"he Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to reveral Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Tardebigg A Petition of the Right honourable Other Lewis inclosure. Earl of Plymouth, and the humble Petition of George Boulton, William Callow, James Moor, William Lucas, and William Sheward, and of the several other Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselvesand others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, an Act passed, for dividing and inclosing certain Commons, Commonable Grounds, and Wade, called Redditch Common and Web-heath, situate in that Part of the Manor of Tardebigg, which lies in the County of Worcester, an-J for other Purposes therein mentioned; and that the Commissioners thereby appointed gave Notice, pursuant to the said Act, of the Time and Place of their First Meeting; but for Want of a sufficient Number of Commissioners, no Meeting could be had, nor any regular Adjournment made to another Day; and that the said Commissioners did, pursuant to further Notice given for that Purpose, meet on Monday the 8th Day of July, at the Place appointed by such Notice, and proceeded in the Execution of the said Act; and have, by their Award duly executed, caused the said Lands to be divided and allotted, agreeable to the Directions of the said Act; and that, the First Meeting of the Commissioners not being held within Two Months next after the passing the said Act, as thereby directed, a Doubt hath arilen, whether the Award so made and executed by the said Commissioners is binding upon the Parties: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for obviating all such Doubts, and for confirming and establishing the Award and Proceedings of the said Commissioners, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Dowdeswelland Mr. Ward do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Everthorpe A Petition of Christophe Bethett, Esquire, Lord of lndoiurc. the Manor of Everthorpe, in the Parish of North Cave, in the East Riding of the County of York, and also the most considerable Owner of and in the several Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, Pastures, and other Open or uninclosed Grounds, within the Township or Lordship of Everthorpe aforesaid, Sir George Montgomery Metham, Knight, Robert Burton, Esquire, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Proprietors of, or otherwise interested in, the said Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, Pastures, and Grounds, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, within the Township or Lordship of Everthorpe aforesaid, there are several Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, Pastures, and other Open or Uninclosed Grounds, which are computed to contain in the Whole about Five hundred Acres; and that the said Common Fields, Common Meadows, Pastures, and Grounds, in their present Situation, are capable of very little Improvement; and that, if the same were inclosed, and specific Shares thereof allotted to the several Proprietors, it would be a Benefit to all Parties interested therein, and to the Public in general: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting, the Purposes above mentioned, subject to such Regulations as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Dowdeswell and Sir William Codrington do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That the said Estimates do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Mr* Dowdeswell presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for obviating Doubts touching the Validity of the Proceedings of the Commissioners appointed by an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for dividing and inclosing certain Lands therein mentioned, in that Part of the Manor of Tardebigg., which lies in the County of Worcester: And the same was received} and read the First Time,

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Right honourable Sackville Earl of Thanet, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a considerable Part of the Canal Navigation from Leeds to Liverpool is now completed, and made navigable for Boats and other Vessels, and particularly such Part thereof as lies between Skipton and Shipley, in the County of York; and that the Land Owners and Inhabitants, at and near* Leeds, Bradford, Bingley, Keighley, Silfden, and other Places, lying contiguous to

the said Canal, have Occasion for large Quantities of Lime and Lime Stone, and are frequently in great Want thereof, and that the Petitioner is seised and possessed of certain Land* ind Premisses, lying near Skipton Castle, in which are great Plenty of Lime Stone Rocks and#Quarries; and that a Cut, or Canal, for the Navigation of Boat^ and other Vessels, may be conveniently madf from the same to the Leeds and' Liverpool Canal, ancf to communicate therewith in a certain Close in Skipton aforesaid, called the Hobble-end; and that 'the same will open a short, easy, and commodious. Communication, from the said Great Canal, to the said Lime Stone Rocks, and render the Conveyance of Lime and Lime Stone to the said Towns and Places less expensive, and tend greatly to the Improvement of the adjacent kands, and be of general Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Navigation, in a Close called the end Close in Skipton, to the said Lime Stone Rocks near Skipton Castle aforesaid, in such Manner, and with such Powers and Provisions, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House Shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it Shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Lord George , Mr. Mack-

worth, &c.: And they are to meet upon Friday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there is, within the Township of Skipton, in the County of York, a certain Open Un-inclosed Field, commonly called Skipton Ings, containing 100 Statute Acres, or thereabouts; and also a certain large Tract, or Parcel, of Common and Waste Ground, called Rumblefmoor; and several other Parcels of Common and Waste Grounds, containing in the Whole 729 Acres, or thereabouts; and within the Township or Hamlet of Stir ton with in the

Parish of Skipton aforesaid, and adjoining to the Township of Skipton, there are several other Parcels of Common, Common of Pasture, and Waste Grounds, containing, by Estimation, 50 Acres, or thereabouts; and within the Manor or Lordship of Silfden, in the Parish of Kild-wick, in the said County, adjoining to the said Town-Ship of Skipton, there are several other large Tracts of Moor, or Parcels of Common and Waste Grounds, containing together 1600 Acres, or thereabouts; and 9

that the said Open Field, Open Commons, and Waste Grounds, are not, in their present Situation, capable of Improvement, nor can be 'occupied to such Advantage as they might be, if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Parts thereof allotted to the Petitioners, and others interested therein: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing the said Open Field, Commons, and Common of Pasture, and Waste Grounds, under such Rules, Regulations, and Provisoes, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Lord George Cavendish, Sir Anthony Abdy, and Lord John Cavendish, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of Ptolemy Humfrey, Clerk, John Clerk, and Catharina Dorothea his Wife, and Richard Jennens, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner Ptolemy Humfrey is Rector and Incumbent of the Parish Church of Thorp Mandeville, in the County of Northampton, and, by virtue of the last Will of his late Father Nathaniel Humfrey, Doctor of Laws, deceased, is seised of the Advowson of the said Rectory for his Life, with divers Remainders over. Remainder to the Heirs of the Body of the said Nathaniel Humfrey; and that the said Ptolemy Humfrey, in Right of his said Rectory, is seised of all the Glebe Lands belonging to the said Rectory, and all the Great and Small Tithes arising within the Parish of Thorp Mandeville; A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, and Common- West India alty, of the Society of Merchants Venturers of the City Colonies, of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was presented to

the House, and read; Setting forth, That many Owners of Estates in His Majesty’s Colonies in the West Indies, particulary in the Ceded Islands, are in great Want of Money, to complete and carry on the Cultivation and Improvement of such Estates, and, from a Variety of Causes, cannot be sufficiently supplied by His Majesty’s Subjects; by Reason whereof, the Adventurers are in great Danger of loling great Sums of Money, which will tend not only to the Injury of the present Lenders, but to the Ruin of the Adventurers, and most probably of the Islands themselves, the Success whereof depends upon a Supply of Money; and that, from the Want of a sufficient Number of Real Securities, amongst the Subjects of Foreign States, adequate to the Sums which such Subjects have to lend, the Rate of Interest for Money on Inch Securities amongst them is miich lower than in England-, and the Adventurers in the Ceded Islands, as well as in the other Colonies, might be easily and amply supplied, if they were enabled, by Law, to make a Real Security of such their Estates to Foreigners; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the Danish Island of Santa Croix is a striking Example, not only of the Fitness, but of the Efficacy, of such a Measure 1 And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to encourage the Subjects of Foreign States to lend Money, upon the Security of Estates in His Majesty’s Colonies in the West Indies, and to render the Securities made to such Aliens effectual for recovering Payment of the Money so to be lent.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider farther of the Propriety of encouraging the Subjects of Foreign States to lend Money upon Estates in His Majesty’s Colonies in the West Indies.

John Horton, Esquire, being examined-, said, That, pursuanf to the Directions of the said Act, a Wcrk-house was built, and furnished in a proper Manner; but the Sum of £. 2,000, which the Parish were authorized to raise for those Purposes, being found. insufficient td complete the same, a further Sum of £.1,000 was borrowed, which was expended in finishing and furnifiling the said Workhouse; and yet remains due, with a large Arrear of Interest.

Mr. May, Vestry Clerk of the said Parish, being examined, said, That of late Years the Rates have not produced Money enough to pay the Annuities charged thereon, and to defray the Expences of maintaining the Poor, though such Rates have been extended to 4 (sd. in the Pound; but on the contrary, by Reason of the great Increase in the Number of People claiming Relief, and of the very high Price of Provisions, the Governors and Directors have incurred Debts from Time to Time on Account of the Poor, including the Money so advanced on Account of the Workhouse, amounting to the Sum of £. 3,187. i8r.; for which some of the said Governors and Directors were under a Necessity of giving their Personal Securities, iii order to prevent a Distress falling upon the Poor, which must otherwise inevitably have happened: — That, as it is necessary to raise a sufficient Sum of Money to discharge the above Debts and Interest, the Parish are de-lirous of having a Power to borrow about £. 4,000 by way of Annuities, in order to have some Money in Hand to go on with for the Relief of the Poor, in Hopes of avoiding the Necessity of increasing the Rates.

David Wilmot, Esquire, John Horton, Esquire, Mr.

James Marciron, and Mr. John White, confirmed Mr.

May's Evidence.

Glass A Petition of the honourable Charles the

Ranald Macdonald, and Samuel Chollett, was prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, having great Reason to believe that considerable Improvements may be made in the Glass Manufactory of this Country, and particularly in the Manufactory of large Plates, have formed themselves into a Society, for the Purpose of establishing a Work of that Kind, under the Name of " The British Call Plate Glass Manufacturers j" and have already engaged several Persons of Skill and Knowledge in the Business; but, in regard to . the great Expence which will attend the Undertaking, the Petitioners are advised, they cannot establish nor carry on the fame, to a sufficient Extent, nor on a permanent Foundation, or with Safety, unless formed into a Company, and authorized by Parliament to make proper Rules, Ordinances, and Bye Laws, and are invested with such Powers, Rights, and Privileges, as may tend to the effectual establishing, conducting, and improving, the said Manufactory: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for incorporating the Petitioners and their Successors, under the Name of " The Governor and Company of British " Call Plate Glass Manufacturersand for veiling them with such Powers and Authorities, for the better and more effectual establishing, directing, managing, and carrying on, the said Manufactory, in such Manner as in the said Bill is intended to be set forth, or as the Parliament shall think meet and convenient.

That the River Bure, commonly called the North , runs from the Town of Aylsham to the Town of Great Yarmouth, in the said County; and that such Part as runs by, and fr«in the Town of Coltishall, to the said Town of Great Yarmouth, hath been navigable for several Years; and that, by a Survey which has been made of the said River from Coltishall to Aylsham, and of the Lands and Grounds adjoining thereto, it appears that the Navigation is capable of being extended up to Aylsham aforesaid, although in some Parts of the River there are Shallows and other Obstructions, the Removal whereof would be attended with great Expence, which, the Petitioners are informed, will be avoided, and the Navigation made shorter and more beneficial to the Public, if proper Cuts or Canals were made from the said River, over the Lands adjoining, at such Places as shall be found proper and necessary; and that the making and extending the Navigation of the said River, from Coltishall to Aylsham Bridge, will be of public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave maybe given to bring in a Bill for extending the said Navigation by and from Coltishall aforesaid, to Aylsham Bridge aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Council of th6 Town of Greenock, in the County of Renfrew, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the present Harbours in the Town of Greenock, belonging to the said Town, are too small and shallow to accommodate the Shipping resorting thereto; and that the Inhabitants of the said Town, and the Shipping belonging and resorting thereto, are, in certain Seasons of the Year, at a great Loss, and have much Difficulty in getting fresh and wholesome Water; and that the Streets of the said Town are not properly paved, lighted, and watched; and that, the Town of Greenock being only a Burgh of Barony, it would tend greatly to the Ease, Advantage, and Convenience, of the Inhabitants, if the Jurisdiction of the Magistrates was extended; and that, if there were new Quays and Piers built, and a new Harbour made in the said Town, and the present Harbours deepened, cleansed, and made more commodious, and Water brought into the Town from the Springs in the Neighbourhood, and the Streets were properly paVed, lighted, and watched, and the Jurisdiction of the Magistrates extended, the said I^conveniencies would be removed, would greatly pqjmote the Increase of the Trade of the said Town, and be of considerable Advantage to the Inhabitants thereof: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for budding new Quays and Piers, and making a new Harbour, in the said Town; and for keeping, cleansing, and making more commodious, the present Harbours; and for bringing Water into the said Town; and for paving, lighting, watching, and cleansing, the Streets of the fame; and for levying certain Rates and Duties, for defraying the Expence of the Operations aforesaid; and for extending the Jurisdiction of the said Magistrates, and their Successors in Office, according to Justice.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Lord Frederick

Campbell, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

That great Progress has been made in repairing the said Road; and that the Sum of 5,980/. has been borrowed on the Credit thereof, which now remains due, with a large Arrear of Interest; and that the said Sum, together with the Tolls collected, have been laid out according to the Directions of the said Acts; but, by reason of many heavy Carriages passing thereon, with narrow Wheels, several of which Carriages are by the said former Acts exempted from paying the Tolls thereby granted, and the Tolls annually received upon the said Road not raising a sufficient Fund to answer the Purposes of the said Road, the same is still in many Parts thereof, in a ruinous Condition, and cannot be completed, and kept in Repair, unless greater and other Tolls be granted, and the said former Acts be repealed, and reduced into One, and the Terms and Powers therein granted further continued, amended, and made more effectual, and the said Trustees be enabled to borrow a further Sum of Money, to complete the Repairs of the said Road; and that the completing the Repairs of the said Road, and keeping the same in Repair, will tend greatly to the Improvement of the Landed Estates in the Neighbourhood, and the Increase of Trade and Commerce in the County of Durham, and the Town and County of the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, and Parts adjacent, and the Commercial Interest of the Kingdom in general: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repealing and reducing the said Two several Atts of Parliament into One, and for the further continuing, explaining, amending, and enlarging, the Terms and Powers thereby granted; and for the more effectual repairing, and keeping in Repair, the said Read, and for other the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and by such Means, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of what may be necessary for the Buildings, Re-buildings, and Repairs, of Ships of War, in His Majesty’s and the Merchants Yards, and other Extra Works, over and above what are proposed to be done upon the Heads of Wear and Tear, and Ordinary, in the Year 1773, be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Bradshaw took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Bradshaw reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Monday Morning next,

Mr. Bradshaw also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.
