To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Samuel Shergold, being examined, said. That the Town of

Brighthelmstone is become a public Place of Resort for the Benefit of Bathing in the Sea; and that the Pavements of the several Streets in the said Town are, by Reason of the great Number of Carriages which pal's and repass through the fame, become very ruinous; and

that the said Town is ill cleansed and lighted, and rendered narrow and incommodious by Projections and other Annoyances; and that if the same were properly lighted, paved, and cleansed, and the Annoyances therein removed, and prevented for the future, it would lend greatly to the Benefit and Health of the Inhabitants of Bright helmstone aforesaid, and all Persons resorting thereto; and if a Market was established in some

convenient Part Of the said Town, bhder proper Regulations, for the Sale of all Sorts of Provisions, it would also tend to the Benefit of the Inhabitants thereof; that there is a Place called ‘The Bartholomew, which is a*fpd* ciouSi and he thinks a well-adapted, Place for that Purpose:

That great Part of the said Town having been destroyed by the breaking in of the Sea, several Groyns were some Years since erected, which have prevented the same; that the said Groyns are now become greatly out of Repairj and the Inhabitants are unable to raile Money sufficient to repair the fame; and that the putting the said Groyns in Repair, and erecting others which should happen to be necessary, may be done by the Aid of a small Tonnage or Duty, to be laid on all Ships importing and unlading Coals on the Beach or Coast, at Brighthelmftoneaforesaid.

King’s Lynn A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Bo-

Pilou. rough and Port of Lenne Regis, commonly called King's Lynn, in the County of Norfolk, whose Common Seal is thereunto affixed, and of the Merchants, Owners, and Matters of Ships and Vessels, and of Gangs of Lighters and Barges, as well residing within, as trading and navigating to and from, the said Borough and Port, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said Borough is a very ancient Borough, and a Port and Harbour for importing and exporting Merchandize; and the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Borough have, by Charter, been a Corporation for zoo Years past and upwards; and by Letters Patent granted them by King James the First, were constituted Admirals within the said Borough, and the Port, Limits, and Bounds thereof; and by virtue of the same Letters Patent, and others since granted tathem by the Crown,

and by long Usage, have erected and put down proper Buoys and Beacons in the Channel of the said Port, and appointed Pilots for conducing Ships and Vessels into, and out of, the said Borough and Port; and that the Channel from Gore End and the Long Sand to the Port or Harbour of King's Lynn, and from thence to Staple Weere, is become very dangerous for Ships, Vessels, and 'Lightens, using the fame, and many Ships have been wrecked, and Lighters and Barges funk, by the large Bodies of Sand, which often shift; and divers un-skilful Persons, without the Licence or Authority of the said Mayor and Burgesses, have often taken upon themselves to act as Pilots and Bridgemen, for the conducting of Ships, Vessels, and Lighters, to and from the said Port; and that the Flood and Ebb Tides in the said Harbour run very rapid and strong, and the Harbour opposite the Town of late Years is become much wider towards the South West; so that, when the Ebb runs strong, and the Wind blows hard at the same Time, several of the Ships and Vessels lying the re are driven from their Moorings, and funk in the said Harbour; and that Fires have happened on board Ships and Vessels lying in the said Harbour, occasioned by the heating Pitch, Tar, Rosin, Oil, or other combustible Matters, on board such Ships and Vessels; and that the Powers and Authorities vested in the said Mayor and Burgesses are found not sufficient or effectual to regulate and go, vern the said Pilots and Bridgemen, and to remedy and prevent the ill Practices and Mischiefs before-men domed; and that Damages to Shipping might in a great Measure be prevented, by placing Harbour Moorings, for the more effectual securing of the Ships and Vessels riding in the said Harbour: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better Regulation, Government, and Payment, of the Pilots conducting Ships and Vessels to and out of the said Port, and of the Bridgemen conducting Gangs of Lighters or Barges to and from the same Port, and for laying down and maintaining proper Moorings in the Harbour of the said Borough and Port; and for demanding, collecting, receiving, and taking, such Tonnage and Duties, for Coals, and other Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, on board Ships and Vessels arriving at, and going out of, the said Borough and Port of King's Lynn, and the Liberties thereof, as shall be judged reasonable and expedient for the Purposes aforesaid; and for preventing Mischiefs by Fire on board the Ships and Vessels in the said Harbour and Port, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Walpole, Sir John See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Paj^rs, and Records.

tee of himself, and of such other Persons resident in Great Britain as may become Co-adventurers with him in certain Mines in New England, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, after great Expence of Time and Money, has discovered, in and hear his own Estate in New England, a peculiar Ore for making Steel, equal in Goodness to the German Steel, which, the Petitioner conceives, will be of great Advantage to this Kingdom, by furnishing the Manufacturers of Steel with a Supply of that useful and necessary Commodity; by Means whereof, large Sums of Money, now annually paid for Steel to Foreigners, will be saved to this Kingdom, and a greater Quantity of the Goods and other Manufactures of Great Britain will be exported to America, in Exchange for such Steel so imported; but the Petitioner finds himself restrained, by an Act; Vol. 34.

of the 2 2d Year of his late Majesty, to encourage the Importation of Pig and Bar Iron from his Majesty’s Colonies in America-, and that the Ores natural to thd making Steel, which he has made a Discovery of in his own and the adjacent Lands, he can make no otherwise than by Hand Labour, as by the said Act he is disabled from using a Tilt Hammer, and is thereby deprived of importing Steel into this Kingdom upon an equal Footing with Foreigners; and that the Petitioner conceives, that, if he had the Liberty of cementing the same in America, where the Materials are very cheap, he might bring the same Steel to the highest Perfection, which must be of great Benefit to this Kingdom, as it would then be suitable for peculiar Uses, wherein the finest Steel is required, and which is so much wanted; and that the Petitioner is desirous that the Benefit of those Discoveries, and the Interest of the Premises, should be fold and conveyed to Persons resident in Great Britain, who may thereby be enabled to make and import Stee. into this Kingdom, in Quantity and Quality, superior to all or any now imported by Foreigners: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Conr sideration, and give Leave to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioner, and all claiming under him, to make Steel in America, either with Tilt Hammers or otherwise, and to import the same into Great Britain, in like Manner as Iron from America now may be imported, or in such other Way as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Manufacturers, and others employed in the Silk Manufacture, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have put in Execution the Act, passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, to prohibit the Importation of Foreign Wrought Silks and Velvets; but, as the said Act does not inflict any Penalty on the Wearer of such Foreign Wrought Silks or Velvets, or the Owner of any Furniture made thereof, and as the'Penalties and For-

1

feitures by the said Act imposed are recoverable only by Action in some of His Majesty’s Courts of Record, and the Power of prosecuting for the same is first solely vested in the Officers of the Customs before any Person can sue for the fame, the said Act is totally ineffectual, and insufficient to answer the Intentions thereof; and that, by Means of the Importation of such Foreign Wrought Silks and Velvets, many Thousands of the said Manufacturers and their Dependents are at this Time out of Employment, and are deprived of the Means of supporting themselves and their Families; and, if the same be not speedily prevented, the said Manufactures will be utterly ruined and destroyed; and that the good Purposes intended by the said Act might be better effected, if a pecuniary Penalty was inflicted on the Wearers of any such Foreign.Wrought Silk or Velvet, or the Owner . of any Furniture made thereof, to be recovered in a summary Way, upon Conviction, before a Justice of the Peace, in Manner directed by the Act of the Seventh Year of his late Majesty King George the First, with respect to the Wearer or Wearers of any Printed, Painted, Stained, or Dyed, Callico: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the above Purposes, or to grant the Petitioners such other Aid as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Edward Aftley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Executioiran Act of Parliament, made in the 22d Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for draining and improving " certain Fen Lands, within the Manor and Parishes of " Upwdi and Out well, and the Parishes of Denver and Welney, in the Isle of Ely, and Counties of Cambridge and Norfolk," and of several other Owners and Occupiers of the said Fen Lands, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. Edward Godfrey, being examined, said. That the Commissioners appointed by the said Act have, in purl'uance thereof, assessed and rated the Lands therein mentioned, and have borrowed considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the said Taxes, which have been applied according to the Directions of thd Ad; that the Engines and Works necessary for draining and improving the said Lands are, by Length of Time and other Accidents, become insufficient for that Purpose; and that the present Tax has been found too little for keeping the Works ir. Repair, and defraying other necessary Expences attending the fame.

That larger Engines and Works are absolutely necessary for the well draining and preserving the said Lands, which cannot be eroded, nor the present Works maintained, without the further Aid of Parliament; and that several of the Clauses and Provisions in the said Act are not sufficient for the Purposes for which they were intended.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend, and render more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for " draining and improving certain Fen Lands, within " the Manor and Parishes of and Outwell, and

" in the Parishes of Denver and Welney, in the Isle of Ely, and Counties of Cambridge and Norfolk." so far as the same relates to the Lands lying on the South Side of Popkam's Eau:And that Sir Edward AJlley

and Mr. De Grey, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. John Walter reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council, and also of the Merchants, Shopkeepers, and other Inhabitants, of the City and County of the City of Exeter, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Heath, Esquire, being examined, said. That in the said City and County there is a large Manufactory carried on, which employs a great Number of People, many of whom contract small Debts, which amount yearly to a large Sum of Money, and who refuse to pay, presuming on the Discouragements their Creditors lie under in suing for the same: That if an easy and speedy Method was established for Recovery of small Debts, it would greatly contribute to promote-Industry, and encourage Trade and Credit, within the said City and County.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the City and County of the City of.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the City and County of the City of Exeter: And that Mr. John Walter, Mr. John and Mr. Recorder of London, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Reverend James Waller, Clerk, was presented to the House; and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner is Vicar of the Parish and Parish Church of Kenfngton, in the County of , and,

in Right of the said Vicarage is seised of certain Glebe Lands, containing in the whole Thirteen Acres, or thereabouts; and that a Close, or Field, called Gravel Pit Field, Part of the said Glebe, containing Four Acres and an Half, or thereabouts, hath been dug up, and the Gravel and other Soil hath been carried away, whereby the Surface of the said Field hath been funk Twenty Feet, or thereabouts, below the Level of the Surface of the adjoining Part of the said Glebe; and that the Petitioner hath been applied to, for Leave to dig up a Piece of the said Glebe next adjoining to the said Gravel Pit Field on the South, and containing in Length from East to West, on the North and South Sides thereof, 120 Yards, and in Breadth from North to South, on the East and West Sides thereof, 42 Yards, for the Purpose of searching for Gravel to amend the Highways, and for Clay to convert into Bricks, Tiles, and Earthen Ware; and the Person who hath made such Application, hath offered to take a Lease of the said Close, called Gravel Pit Field, and of the said adjoining Piece or Parcel of Land, for a Term of Ten Years, at the present improved Rent of Fourteen Guineas a Year; and also to pay the Sum of 1,701, over and above the said Rent; and that great Part of the House belonging to the said Vicarage is very ancient, and it would be for the Benefit of the Petitioner, and his Successors, Vicars of the said Parish and Parish Church, to have the Whole, or the greatest Part of the said House, taken down and rebuilt; and the Petitioner is

willing and desirous that the said Sum of 1,701, or a competent Part thereof, should be applied for that Purpose; and that the said Field, called Gravel Pit Field, and the said adjoining Piece of Land, are in a commodious Situation for being built upon; and it will be beneficial to the Petitioner and his Successors, Vicars of the said Parish and Parish Church, if the Petitioner was enabled to grant a Lease of the said Gravel Pit Field, and adjoining Piece of Ground, for the said Term of Ten Years, in order to raise a sufficient Fund for rebuilding lo much of the said Vicarage House as is necessary to be pulled down, and for repairing such Part thereof as is fit to stand; and if the Petitioner and his Successors were also enabled to grant a Lease or Leases of the said Field, called Gravel Pit Field, and of the said Piece or Parcel of Lind thereto adjoining, for a Term of Years sufficient to encourage Persons to build thereon, and improve the fame: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioner, and the Vicar of the Parish and Parish Church of, Kensington for the Time being, to grant such Leases of the said Pieces or Parcels of Ground, for the several Purposes aforesaid, with such other Clauses, Powers, Restrictions, and Provisions, in the said Bill to be contained, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. John Walter and Mr. Ryder do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Fitzmaurice’s A Petition of David Roberts and Roberts, Esquires,

Estate*. being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been . informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives His Consent, as far as His Majesty’s Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fir.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners were Agents to Ulysses Fitzmaurice, Esquire, lately deceased, who was Lieutenant Governor of His Majesty’s Island of St. Vincent, and, in consequence thereof, they advanced for him, at different Times, Sums of Money to a considerable Amount; and there was, at the Time of his Death, due from him to the Petitioners the Sum of £.500 and upwards; and that the said Governor, at the Time of his Decease, had given Directions for making his Will, the Heads of which were taken down in Writing, containing Bequests to his Relations (some of whom, on his Mother’s Side, are in very indigent Circumstances) but the same were never reduced into Form, nor signed by the Deceased as his last Will; and that the said Governor dying without having appointed any Executor, and being an illegitimate Son of the late Earl of Kerry, his, Effects at Dominica have been seized by Sir William Young, the Lieutenant Governor thereof; and that the principal Persons to whom the said UlyfJ'es Fitzmaurice and bequeathed Legacies (particularly the Earl of Shelburne, to whom he intended to devise the principal Part of his Estates) have given up their respective Claims (if Vol. 34.

any they should be found to have) in Favour of the poor Relations of the said Deceased; and that the Petitioners are endeavouring to procure Administration to the Effects of the said late Governor, in Right of being his principal Creditors; but are informed, the several Devises and Bequests intended by the Deceased cannot take Effect, as his Will was never reduced into any regular Form, nor legally executed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable His Majesty to grant the Estates and Effects of the said Lieutenant Governor Fitzmaurice, now escheated to the Crown, unto the Petitioners, their Heirs and Assigns, in Trust, to be sold for the Payment of his Debts, and for the Purposes intended by the said Lieutenant Governor, in the'Directions given by him for making his last Will, as aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

A Petition of George Hodgson, Edward Gordon, and Hodgson&C* John Debonnair, Brewers, at Boiv, in ,being E^feDuties

offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed’of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; reciting an Act of the Twelfth Year of King Charles the Second, relating to the Duties on Beer and Ale; and Setting forth. That by an Act, passed in the First Year of King William and Queen Mary, for an additional Duty of Excise on Beer, Ale, and other Liquors, it is declared, that in all Places, other than within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality, Thirty-four Gallons should be deemed a Barrel, both of Beer and Ale, and the Allowance for Waste and Leakage Two Barrels and an Half in every Twenty three Barrels; and that, the Petitioners Brewhouse having for some Years been considered by the Collector of Excise, as being without the City of London, or Bills of Mortality, the Petitioners were charged to the Duties of Excise accordingly; but being advised that their said Brewhouse was actually situated within the Bills of Mortality, and thereupon apprehending that they had, through Mistake, paid a very considerable Sum of Money for the Duty of Excise, the Petitioners applied to the Commissioners of Excise for Restitution; who declared, that they thought themselves not justified in altering the Duty, without a legal Determination; whereupon the Petitioners commenced an Action at Law, against the Collector of Excise, for so much Money only as they had so paid since the First Day of March 1769; and in Trinity Term 1769 obtained a Verdict in the Court of King’s Bench, for the Money so overpaid; and that, it being thereby determined, that their Brewhouse is within the Bills of Mortality, they are now, by Order of the Commissioners of Excise, charged the same Duty as other London Brewers; and the Petitioners, apprehending the y were entitled to receive back all the Money they had so paid, from the Month of October 1752, being the Time the Petitioners entered upon their Brewhouse, to the First Day of March 1769, amounting to £.4,363, applied to the Commissioners of Excise for Relief: but were answered, that they had paid over all such Money into His Majesty’s Treasury; and that the Petitioners did thereupon present their Memorials to the Commissioners of the Treasury; but have received no Satisfaction therein: And therefore praying. That the said Sum of £.4,363, so received of them by Mistake, maybe repaid, upon their producing the proper Vouchers, to support their Claim, and justify their Application.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. Thomas Knowles, being examined, said* That, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act, Taxes have been laid, and the Money thereby raised, together with a considerable Sum, which the Commissioners borrowed, have been applied in making and maintaining Works necessary to be erected for draining the Lands in the First District described in -the said Act, by which the Lands in the said District have been much improved; but that, as the Money produced by the present Tax is not more than sufficient to answer the common Expences of keeping the Works in Repair, it is necessary to make some additional Rate, in order to raise Money to discharge the Debt incurred by the Commissioners, and to complete the Drainage of the said Lands — That the Banks of the Ouse, and Bran*

don Rivers, are very' much damaged by Horses haling Boats therein — that the Repairs of the said Banks are constantly attended-with a great Expence, towards defraying which, neither -the Owners of the Horses, nor the Persons employing them, contribute any Thing; And he added. That the Works necessary for completely draining the said First District, cannot be finished, unless the Powers of the said Act, as far as the same relate to the said First District, are explained and enlarged.

Mr. Thomas Hood confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Knowles.

L^pds and A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are S*lby thereunto lubi'cribed, being Owners of, or Persons em-Navijaron. ployed in navigating Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, upon the Rivers of Aire and Colder, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act passed in the 10th anti nth Years of his late Majesty King William the Third, certain Persons therein named were empowered, at their own Colts anti Charges, to make the said Rivers navigable, from a Place called upon the River Aire,

up to the Towns of Leeds and Wakefield, in the West Riding of the said County; and divers Rates and Tolls are thereby granted to the said Undertakers, their Heirs, and Assigns, as a Recompence for the same; and that, by Virtue of the Powers contained in the said Act, the said Undertakers have made a very imperfect and deleft ive Navigation, subject to many Impediments from Sand Banks, Shoals, and other Obstructions; and that the Petitioners conceive, the Legislature intended the Navigation upon the said Rivers should be free and cperi to ad Ills Majesty’s Subjects, upon Payment of 1 ho Toils thereby granted, or such other Sum or Sums 1 pi Money as should be demanded in Ljcu thereof; -lA.it.

the contrary has been the same for many Years past; and that the present Lessee or Farmer of the Rates and Tolls of the said Rivers is the foie Owner of a great Number of Vessels, and concerned, as Partner, in many other Vessels navigated upon the said Rivers, who has monopolized the Freight in such Articles as he chooses to carry, whereby the Employment of the Petitioners and their Vessels, in navigating upon the said Rivers, depends solely upon the Pleasure of the said Lessee; and that the Lock-keepers upon the said Rivers,- and others employed in the Management there* of, shew great Partiality to the Vessels belonging to the said Lessee, or those wherein he is interested as a Partner* and frequently refuse to permit the Petitioners Vessels to pass through the Locks in Rotation as they come there, and oblige them to flop, and give Way to the said Lessee’s Vessels; and also stop the Water at the said Lock Gates, to prevent the Petitioners Vessels getting over the Shoals and Sand Banks within the said Rivers; by which Means the Petitioners Vessels, and the Goods on board, are frequently detained for a long Time, whereby the said Lessee gets his own Goods to Market before any other Persons can come there, to the great Oppression of the Petitioners, and to the Damage of those whose Goods are on board; and when the Petitioners and others have remonstrated with the Lock-keepers concerning the Unfairnels and Injustice of these Proceedings, they have been intuited, and threatened, that if they were difl'atisfied, or made any Complaints, they should pay greater or more Lock Dues the next Time their Vessels should pass upon the said Rivers; and that the: Petitioners are informed. Application is intended to be made, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Navigation, in the Township of Holbeck, near Leeds, to the River Ouze, at or near Selby, in the said County of York, and that the natural Navigation, by the flowing and re-flowing of the Tide of the Sea to and from Selby, is much better than to and from Weeland; and that, if the said intended Cut, or Canal, is made and perfected in a proper Manner, the Carriage and Conveyance of Goods, to and from Leeds and the Sea, will bfc greatly facilitated, and rendered much lei's expensive than by Means of the Navigation of the said Rivers Aire and Colder, and the Public will be relieved from the Oppression and unfair Practices now used upon the said Rivers: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in the said Bill, and that the same may pass into a Law, under such Terms and Conditions, and subject to such llestrictions, as to the House shall l'eem meet.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Thomas Longlands, being examined, said. That the Entrance to the Harbour of Aberdeen is greatly obstructed by a Bar or large Bank of Sand, which runs across the fame, and the Piers, Quays, and other Works, are insufficient for the Accommodation of the Trade of the said City, which of late Years has greatly increas'd.

That the Navigation and Harbour may be greatly improved by running out a Pier into the Sea on the North Side of the Harbour, and by cleaning, deepening, and widening, the fame, and the Entrance thereto, by erecting proper Piers, Quays, and other Works, for the Accommodation of Trade and Shipping, and by veiling the Provost, Magistrates, and Town Council, of Aberdeen, with proper Powers for regulating all Vessels trading into, and going out of, the said Harbour.

Kins’* Bench Mr. Morton reported from the Committee, to whom Bnion. the Petition of Benjamin Thomas, Marshal of the Marshalsea of His Majesty’s Court of King’s Bench, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fa<fl contained in the said Petition, and bad directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition is as follows:

Mr. Thomas Marfden, Clerk of the Day Rules in the King’s Bench, being examined, said. That in Trinity Term 1768, there were 338 Persons, and in the same Term 1769, 443, confined in the said Prison; and that though an Act for Release of Insolvent Debtors was patted between the Years. 1769 and 1770, there were 233 Prisoners in Trinity Term 1770, and 225 in 1771, confined in the said Gaol; and that the Number of Persons confined at present therein, is 214 — ‘that before the said Prison was re-built, in 1754, the same was thought very full, if more than 80 Prisoners were under Confinement therein — that there are only 84 Rooms on the Matter’s Side of the said Prison, which Rooms are 9 Feet wide by 9 Feet 6 Inches deep — that there are 24 Rooms on the Common Side, which are occupied by Prisoners in the most indigent Circumstances, who are supported by Charity, and 12 Rooms 9 Feet 8 Inches wide by 9 Feet 5 Inches deep, on the Crown Side, for Prisoners committed for Offences; and that there are 12 Rooms in the State House, for better Sort of Crown Prisoners, amounting in the Whole to 132 Rooms only — that frequently many Prisoners are obliged to lodge in one Room, which renders it very inconvenient and unwholsome to the Persons confined in the said Prison — that, on Account of the Number of Prisoners always greatly exceeding the Number of Rooms in the said Prison, the Marshal has permitted many to lay in the Chapel, and other improper Places, and that at this Time many are obliged to lay in the Tap Room, on the Staircases and Benches, by which Means they contract Disorders, which often prove fatal, not only to themselves, but the Prisoners in general — that there are no separate Apartments for the Reception of Prisoners who are lick, nor any Place for the Confinement of those who are riotous, nor any strong Hold for Prisoners who are committed for capital Offences — that the Walls of the said Prison are so very insufficient, both with respect to Height and Thickness, that Prisoners frequently escape over and through the fame; and so thin are they in some Places, that Prisoners have been known to break through in less than Half an Hour.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Lowndes reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants, Manufacturers, and others, Dealers in Thread and Silk Bone Lace, manufactured in the Counties of Buckingham, Bedford, Northampton, Hertford, and several other Counties within this Kingdom; and all'o, the Petition of several Persons employed in the Manufacture of Bone Lace, were referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petitions; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in Vol. 34.

at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the First-mentioned Petition is as follows:

It appeared to your Committee, by the Examination of Mr. Daniel Giberne, That many thousand Families are employed in the Manufacture of Lace, in the Counties of Buckingham, Bedford, Northampton, Hertford, and the adjacent Counties, but that of late the said Manufacture has greatly decayed.

That the Persons chiefly employed in the said Manufacture are Women and Children, and some very old and infirm Persons; that some Persons of Eighty Years of Age earn from 4 d.to 6 d.per Day; and that some Persons earn from 8 d.to 1 s. per Day in the said Manufacture; and that Children of Four Years old are employed.

That, notwithstanding the re may be more Persons employed in the said Manufacture now, than were Three Years ago, yet the Trade in general is gone to Decay, and many of the Workers have been lately paid off.

That the Witness imputes this Decline to the clandestine Importation of low-priced Lace; and thinks, that if Foreign Lace, under Ten Shillings a Yard, was prohibited, it would be a Means of restoring the Manufacture to this Country', as a Preference is given to French Lace, and Retailers refuse to buy English.

That, notwithstanding the Number of Workers may be as great now as formerly, yet the Manufacture is much decayed, as the Persons employing them have great Quantities of Goods upon their Hands, for which they want a Vent; and that they are not able to employ the Number of Workers that call for Work; that this Evil has been increasing these Three Years; and that, if some immediate Remedy is not granted, great Numbers of Workmen must be discharged.

That the chief Markets for these Goods, are the Home Markets, Ireland, and America.

That the Demand from America has decreased, but that the Stagnation of the Trade is not entirely owing to that, as the Home Consumption and Exportation to Ireland are also much diminished.

That it is impossible to say exactly what Number of Workers are out of Employment, but supposes about

30,000; and that their Employers are discharging them every Day.

It appeared to Your Committee, from the Evidence of Mr. James Pilgrim, a Wholesale Manufacturer, who keeps a Warehouse in Budge Row, London, That the Number of Workers in Lace, in the Counties before mentioned, are increased within the last Three Years, but that the Sale is much lessened within that Time, especially within the last Two Years, which he imputes in a great Measure to the clandestine Importation of low-priced Foreign Lace.

That there is a greater Quantity of Foreign Lace now fold in London than was Two or Three Years ago; and that it is evident such Lace is clandestinely imported, as a great Part of it is fold for much less than the Duty.

That many Workers in Lace are at present unemployed; that the Witness himself employed near 2,000 Workers Two or Three Years ago, and at present about Fourteen or Fifteen hundred; that he must discharge many more, unless some Redress be given; and that there is hardly one Manufacturer who has not discharged many of his Workers.

That he has a greater Quantity of Lace now on his Hands than he used to have; and that he must either-discharge the greatest Number of his Workers, or have a still greater Quantity on his Hands.

That, upon the whole, he apprehends the Manufacture is decreased One Third, notwithstanding the Manufacture may have extended to more Places than formerly, and the Number of Workers may have increased.

That the Witness thinks he can distinguish English

from

ia8 150 Febrmrii. 1773.

from Foreign Lace j that there are great Quantities of Foreign Lace in the Shops of London, which is fold for much less than the Duty; and that he can now purchase many thousand Yards of such Lace.

That Persons refuse buying Lace, and say,

they can buy Foreign cheaper, which could not be the same if the Duties were paid; and that, for supporting himself and Family, he has been obliged to buy low-priced Foreign Lace to accommodate his Customers; but never did this unless when driven thereto from Necessity.

That he thinks, in Laces of equal Goodness, the Foreign is about One Third cheaper, and that is the Reason why it is preferred to the English.

The Witness being asked, If a Duty, ad might not be laid on Foreign Lace, or taking off the Duty upon the Thread of which Lace is made; or some other Means (besides prohibiting the Importation of Foreign Lace) might not be thought of, to give the English Lace a Preference at Market ? He said, he could not suggest any other Remedy, but a total Prohibition of all Foreign low-priced Laces, under a certain Price, which would be more effectual than the present high Duty, which seems to amount to a Prohibition, be-eause they would then be seizable, which at present they are not.

That Foreign Goods are easily distinguishable from English, and he apprehends the general run of his Customers are capable of making the Distinction.

That he is of Opinion, a Prohibition will not increase the Price of the English Goods, as there is such an Encrease of Workers; and a greater Quantity of Lace being brought to Market, would lower the Price.

That a much less Quantity of Lace was exported to Ireland within the Two last Years than formerly, which he imputes to their being supplied with Foreign Lace; for though there is a Manufacture of that Kind set up in that Kingdom, it is too trifling to be looked upon as the Cause; and he thinks taking off the Duty on English Lace, imported into Ireland, would have little Effect, unless the Foreign was prohibited.

That he apprehends, if an effectual Stop could be put to the Importation of Foreign Lace, there would be a Consumption sufficient to support our Home Manufacture in its full Extent, provided the Trade to Ireland and America was secured; and that considerable Quantities have been sent to , but not so much

now as formerly.

Mr. ... Gurdon informed your Committee, That he

has exported all Sorts of Lace to Ireland, but does not now export One Third of what he formerly has done: — That the Manufacture established there, and the Duty paid there, may have had some Effect; but he imputes this Decay of his Trade chiefly to their being supplied cheaper from Abroad, though he thinks taking off that Duty would certainly be a considerable Encouragement to the EngliOi Manufacture.

The Wit nets then gave an Instance of a considerable Customer of his own for the Irish Market, who is now gone to Flanders to purchase Lace, because he can be supplied there cheaper than the Witness can afford it.

Mr. Daniel Giberne, being again examined, was asked. If he thought he could lately distinguish, upon Oath, Foreign Lace from English ? He said, He thought the London Dealers might, but that the Country Dealers in general could not.

And all the Witnesses agreed. That the only effectual Method of giving Relief to the Trade, would be by a total Prohibition of the Wear of Foreign low-priced Lace, and laying the Proof where the Goods were manufactured, upon the Retailer or Vender thereof.

Mr. William Curry (a Laceman) being asked. What Effect such a Prohibition would have ? answered, That he apprehended it would be of great Use, provided the Proof was laid upon the Vender, and some 9

proper Penalties inflicted on Mailers of Ships who receive Lace on Board for Exportation, and afterwards re-land it.

Mr. 'Thompson Pater (a Laceman at Newport Pagnell)

being examined as to the Decline of the Manufacture, said, That his chief Dealing is to London, and that he used to trade for £.3,000 per Annum, more than he has done for the last Three Years: That he had just settled an Account with a Customer, who used to deal with him for £. 500 a Year, and the last Year’s Account amounted to no more than Twelve Guineas.

That more Foreign Lace than English has beeh fold in England within Two Years last past; which he imputes to its being fold cheaper,

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the Second-mentioned Petition is as follows:

Mr. Daniel Giberne, informed Your Committee, That the Manufacture of Bone Lace labours under many Difficulties, for want of proper Regulations: That the Working Lacemakers now receive Patterns and a Parchment from their Employers gratis, and the Thread intrusted to them becomes a Book Debt; that the Workers, on bringing Lace home, are frequently deficient in Measure, and will not lubniit to allow for the fame, but will carry the Lace to another Lace Buyer, who will purchase it, notwithstanding the Deficiency of the Measure, by which he obtains the Benefit of a good Pattern, at the trifling Expence of such Deficiency. '

That Lace Workers seldom or ever return to pay for the Thread intrusted to them; and it has become a frequent Practice for them to suffer a Copy to be taken from Patterns in their Custody, to the great Prejudice of the Inventor: — That the Value of a Pattern may be estimated from One Shilling to a Guinea; and the Witness apprehends, if this Practice was prevented, it would be a great Encouragement both to the Employer and Worker.

That Lace Workers are often imposed on by having Goods forced on them in Payment, by their Employers, instead of Money, which, if prevented, would be an Encouragement to Industry.

That it is customary for Pattern-makers and Prickers of Parchment to sell the same Pattern to different Persons, to the great Detriment of the Trade in general; and it is also customary for People to frequent the Dwellings of Lace Workers, and offer Money for Goods not manufacturing for them; and the Witness said, if those Practices were prevented, the Manufacture would be greatly benefitted.

Mr. . Gurdon and Mr. . Jennings confirmed the Evidence.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. Adam Pierce, Clerk to the Trustees, being examined, said,.That the Trustees have, in pursuance of the said Act, proceeded to widen and repair the several . Roads therein mentioned.

Mr. William Langford, being examined, said. That a considerable.Sum of Money had been expended in repairing the said Roads; but by lleafon of the great Extent, being near 130 Miles, and the Difficulty and great Expence in procuring Materials in several Parts thereof, and by an accurate Survey lately taken, the same cannot be completed without the further Sum of

£-3*000-

That the Trustees have proceeded to ered a new Bridge over the River Exe, and have expended thereon £. 7,000, and are under Contract to the Amount of £. 3,000 more, which will amount to the Sum origi- nally granted > And,

Mr. Robert Stribbling, Surveyor of the Bridge, being examined, said. That the Trustees have begun to build new Bridge, and have laid out and contijaded for Works relating thereto, to the Amount of £. 10,000: - — That the new Works are excessively bad, the Water having worked Four Feet under the Foundation of -one of the Abutments, which must be taken down; and the Stone made use of is improper for such Works; — That by many unforeseen Obstructions, met with in the Execution of the above Work, they find it will be impossible to finish the same for the Sum allowed to be expended thereon; and that it will be necessary to take down tome Houses, for making the Avenues commodious thereto; which, together with the Sum wanted to

A Petition of the Wardens and Assistants of the Company or Mystery of Goldsmiths of the City of London, in Court assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented, for Leave to bring in a Bill for the establishing an Assay-Office in the Town of Sheffield, in the County of York, for trying, touching, assaying, and marking, of Gold and Silver Plate; and that another Petition has been 41fo presented to the House, for extending the like Provisions to the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick -, and alledging, that the Power of trying, touching, assaying, and marking, of Gdld and Silver Plate, is a very great and important Trust, and ought to be committed to such Persons, and in such Places, only, where the same is likely to be executed and discharged with the greatest Care and Fidelity; and that the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Goldsmiths of the City of London, whose Affairs are governed by the Petitioners, are, and have been, a Guild, or Corporation, Time put of Mind, for the searching, assaying, supervising, marking, and regulating. Wrought Plate, in order to ascertain the Standard thereof; and that the Standard Pieces, appointed for Trial of the Gold and Silver Monies and Wrought Plate of this Realm, have from Time to Time been made, and the Gold and Silver Monies of this Realm, have from Time to Time been tried and compared therewith, by a Jury of the said Company, returned for those Purposes; and that the Petitioners and their Predecessors have hitherto executed and discharged the said Trails with the utmost Care and Fidelity; and that neither of the said Towns of Sheffield and Birmingham are Towns Corporate, nor have any Company of Goldsmiths; and that there are very few real Gold-smiths, Silversmiths, or Plateworkers, in either of those Town -; and therefore the Petitioners apprehend, that, if an Assay-Office was established in the said Towns, pr either of them, for trying, touching, assaying, and marking, of Gold and Silver Plate, the Standards appointed for the Wrought Plate of this Kingdom will not be carefully observed, and various Frauds and Deceits, in the manufacturing of Gold and Silver Wares, will be commit id in the said Towns: And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may be heard, by them-lelves, or their Counsel, against the said Petitions, and also against any Bill or Bills for establishing an Assay-Office in the said Towns, or either of them; and that the same may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Goldsmiths, Silversmiths, and Plate-workers, of the City of London, and Places adjacent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Application; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend, that such an Establishment in those Places might open a Door to Deceit and Uncertainty, in respect to the Standards of Gold and Silver Plate, and tend to destroy that Credit and Reputation which the Goldsmiths Manufactory in these Kingdoms has justly acquired, and consequently impair the Trade of this Metropolis, diminish His Majesty’s Revenue, and sensibly affect the Honour and Riches of the Kingdom in general; and that the Manufactory of such Plate is now carried on in the City of London, in all its Variety of useful -and curious Branches, in much greater Perfection than in any other Place in these Kingdoms, and te an Extent sufficient to supply the greatest Demands; and that the Office of assaying and marking such Plate being performed by Persons appointed by the Company of Goldsmiths of the City of London for that Purpose only, and totally unconcerned in the Manufactory thereof, renders it impossible for any Fraud or Debasement of the Standard of Gold and Silver Plate to be committed; and that, in the Towns and Neighbourhood of

Shefcld,

Sec.

Assay-Office.

Sheffield and Birmingham, there are few Peribhs at all con-veriant with, or /killed in, the Gold or Silver Plate Manufactory; and that the whole Lift of Names subscribed to the said Petitions affords only a few of that Number, the rest being of very different Trades or Occupations; and the Business of those few is confined to some of the least important Branches of the said Manufactory; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the granting such an Establishment will ruin the Goldsmiths Trade in this Kingdom; and that the necessary Expence of an Assay-Office and Officers, at Sheffield and , would render the Charge of assaying Plate at such Office equivalent to the present Charge of assaying the same at London, added to the Expences of Carriage and Agency; and that the regular, daily, and safe. Conveyances, established between London and the Towns of Sheffield and Birmingham, sufficiently remove every Ground of Complaint; and that, if the Goldsmiths Manufactory in the Towns of Sheffield and Birmingham should be encreased, that of London must suffer a proportionable Decrease: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, agaii.ft the said Petitions, and that no such Bill as prayed for may pass.

An Act, passed in the 29th Year of his said late Majesty, for changing and altering Two several Roads, directed to be amended and widened by the said former Act; were read: And

Mr. William Starmer, being examined, said, That the Trustees have, in pursuance of the said Acts, proceeded in the Repair of the said Roads, and have borrowed considerable Sums of Money for that Purpose, and completed a Road of near 40 Miles; and paid off Part of the Money borrowed, and the Interest due thereon; but find, that the Roaids cannot be effectually repaired, and the Debt discharged, unless the Term and Powers of the said Acts are further continued and enlarged.

That the Road leading from the Croft Road, which leads from Truste Church to Truro Quay, over a' River, ata Place called fie Steppings, and from thence to Mo-par, within the Parish or Clement'I, is in a ruinous

Condition, and frequently impassable, on Account of the Overflowing of the Tide; and that the! Road from the End of the present Turnpike Road, at Short Lane's End, to The Four Burrows, in the Parishes of Kenwyn, Perranzabuloe; arid Kea, being about a Mile and Haff in Length, is in many Places in a ruinous Condition; and that the said respective Roads cannot be sufficiently widened, altered, amended, and kept in Repair, by the ordinary Course of Law.

That it would be greatly for the'Safety and Advantage of all Persons travelling that Way, if a Bridge was built across the said River at The Steppings, which is the principal Entrance into the Eastern Part of the Borough of . Truro.

To prove the Allegations of the said'Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. Thomas Steward, being examined, said. That the Commissioners have proceeded to put the said Act into Execution; but, from the small Number of Commissioners thereby appointed, it has been sometimes difficult to procure a sufficient Number to attend the Meetings for doing the Business necessary for the Execution of the Ad; and' that the same has been found in several Particulars insufficient for the Purposes intended.

That the Openings, allowed by the said Act to be made in several of the Streets and Places in the said Town, will be very advantageous, but, on Account of a great Increase in the Number of Carts used there, by Reason of the Navigation now brought to the said Town, it is proper some other of the Streets and Places should be widened: And he Hated,

That it will be necessary to take in Land, and to pull down some small Buildings, to widen the End of New Street, next Paradise Row, the Road by the Side of Saint Phil lip'% Church Yard, Bull Street, Smallbrooke Street, and Moor Street; which Buildings are of very small Value, except those in Moor Street.

And the Witness further said, That he hath known many Dillurbances happen, through the Want of a Nightly Watch in the said Town; which, if established, would be of great Benefit: That, since a Navigation hath been brought to the said Townj the Number of Carts within the same hath greatly increased, and the Carmen frequently impole on the Inhabitants; and it would be of great Advantage if Provision was made, for regulating them, both as to the Price of Carriage of Goods, and their Behaviour; and that the Rates granted by the said Act are insufficient for the Purposes aforesaid; and apprehends it would be proper that Collectors should be appointed, and paid put of the said Rates, instead of the Method prescribed by the Ad, of compelling Inhabitants to take the Office.

And he added, in general, that some /further Amendments may be necessary to be made to the &id Ad.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England trading into the Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protest His Majesty’s Subjects in the Domi-

nions, it has been found necessary that there should be an Ambassador sent from England, to reside at Constan-tinople; and that there should be Consuls, Vice Confute, and other Officers and Servants, in the other Parts of Turkey, where any British Subjects reside, and where the English carry on Trade; the whole Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company; which, together with other Expences incident to the carrying on the said Trade, has, of late Years, amounted to upwards of f. 10,000 per Annum-, and that the said Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishing, is now, from many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance which has been granted to the Petitioners by Parliament, has enabled them to pay off the greatest Part of the Debt which they had incurred, and to lower their Duties, which were so high as to be such a Burthen that the Trade was not able to support; and that, during the last Year, the Exports to, and Imports irom, Turkey, have been much more considerable than they were the preceding Year; which has not only been beneficial to His Majesty’s Revenue, but has likewise been of great Advantage to the Manufacturers of this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners have Reason to apprehend, that, during the Course of the present Year, a new Ambassador will be appointed at Constantinople, which will be a considerable Expence to the Petitioners; and, if a Peace between the Turkish and the Russian Government should take place, this Circumstance will likewise occasion an unavoidable Expence; and that, if the Petitioners should raise their Duties again, they are apprehensive that such an Alteration would tend to diminish the Trade, and consequently would not be a Means of enabling them to support the Expences of it; and that the Petitioners hope they shall not soon be under a Necessity of applying again to the House for Assistance; but they are sensible that they should not discharge the Duty incumbent upon them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public, if they did not declare their present Inability to support their necessary Expences, unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the

Glass Mr. Mach-worth reported from the Committee, to Manufactory, whom the Petition of the honourable Charles Fitzroy, the honourable Robert Digby, Peregrine Cust, Thomas Duttdat, John Mackay, Philip Affleck, Henry Dagge, James

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition is as follows;

It appeared to your Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. Philip Befnard, that he had been engaged in the Manufacture of making Plate Glass 15 Years; and he said. He had studied the Art 25 Years, and had made Plates of Glass in Picardy and Burgundy, Ten Feet high and Six Feet wide, or 130 by 90 Inches, French Measure; and that these Glasses were made by carting them upon a Table; that since his coming to England, which is about 18 Months, he had made Enquiry after lijhPlate Glass, and the largest he has seen, w-as 40 by 36 Inches; has heard of larger being made but could never get the Sight of any: That the English Glass is blown in general, and that it is impossible to blow Plates of Glass to the first Magnitude; that there are all Neceftaries in England for making of Glass, except Barilla, and that it is practicable to make Glass Plates of

in there for

Three Reasons; the Cast Glass may be made larger, clearer, and cheaper, and that the Risque is greater in blowing than calling; the Works and Apparatus for calling Glass, both with Respect to the Buildings, Furnaces, Cooling Ovens, Copper Tables for calling, and other Matters, are formed upon a very different Con-llruction from the Glass Houses in The whole

Apparatus upon an extensive Plan, with every Necessary that is requisite, may be estimated at 50,000, but the necessary Buildings for the First Establishment will coll about £. 12,000; and with the Materials, and Expences attending the Work, may amount tOj£. 25,000, before any Return of Money can be made from the Manufactory: That he is engaged to carry this Plan into Execution with a Set of Gentlemen. — And being asked, Why none of the largest Size Plate Gials was made in England ? he said, Because they don’t understand the Art; that all the Buildings, and every Necessary to carry on the Trade to its utmost Extent, is included in the Estimate of £.50,000. — In France they pay no Duty on Glass or Barilla, because they would encourage the Trade, but when imported into England, it pays a Duty of 80 or 90 per Cent, and he knows Glass has been imported into England to a large Amount, ,£.3,000 being paid for Commission in a Year. And he further said. That the Glass Manufactory in Venice, is now very trifling; but the French cannot cast it fall enough for their Consumption, it being exported over all the World. In England he has heard that a Duty is paid, of about 9 Shillings per Cent, on the gross Materials used, but he thinks Plate Glass may be made cheaper in England than in France, because Fuel is much cheaper here, and the French Manufactory is established in a bad Situation for Fuel — that the French cast Plates, from Ten Guineas to 100 Guineas Value per Plate; the Price of Glass runs from $s. to £. 4 per Foot: And being

asked. Whether the bell Glass that he has seen in France, was better than the bell he has seen in England ? heanswered. That he had seen a great Number of

lish Glasses, but that the French Glass was the bell, because they are more clear, more white; and transparcnt.

It appeared by the Evidence of Mr. James ChriJHe, Auctioneer, that a great Quantity of French Plate Glass goes through his Hands every Year; that the largest English Plate Gials he has ever seen docs not exceed, in Length, the Width of the French Glasses, they measuring from 65 to 68 inches in Width, and from 114 to 118 Q q Inches

Inches in Length; he fold Three Pair of large French Plates for £. 2,500. He further said. That he had seen a large Glass, at a House belonging to the Proprietor of die Glass Manufactory at which was shewn

him as a Prodigy, and he could not help smiling, when he considered its Size in a comparative View with the Glass he had seen of Foreign make; it appeared also to him very faulty: And he lamented much that such large Sums of Money should go Abroad (amounting, as he believed, from 60 to £, 100,000 per for Foreign Glass,

which might be saved at Home, could a similar Manufactory to that in France be established in \ The

Duty on French Glass is 75 per Cent, with 8 d. per Pound or thereabouts on Importation, but he believes not One Third of the Quantity that is imported pays Duty, being in general smuggled; and a Kind of trading Company has been formed here for that Purpose: He thinks, if this Manufactory is brought to Perfection, it will be from 500 to^. 1,000 per Ann. out of his Pocket, which he now gains by Commission on the Sale of Foreign Glass; and the Witness supposed that Foreign Glass, to the Value of 10,000 went through his Hands last Year, and 20,000 through many of the Warehouses; and he imagines, from the Number of Glasses that he has seen of Foreign make, that they must amount to nearly the Sum before-mentioned; he has known One Pair of Glasses fell for £. 1,000. The Witness said. He never saw any Glass manufactured in England, but always understood that it was made by blowing only, which he thinks may be as good in that Mode as if it was Cast, hut that it is not possible to go to so large a Size. In France he thinks he saw 1,000 People employed in a Manufactory in the various Branches, as grinding, pol’tshing, &c. and they seemed to be happy in their Employment. He said. The Proprietor of the Manufactory of Glass at Vauxhall had been applied to for large Plate Glass, but he refused to engage in that Branch, he having a sufficient Trade in the less Sizes; and laid. He did not chuse to run so great a Risque, for the Duty was very^igh. He further said, That he did not know, by Inspection, the Difference between cast and blown Glals; that he has seen French Glass as perfect as possible, and in Proportion to the Number, more perfect than the English; that the large English Glass is apt to wave: And the Witness said. He had often mentioned the Utility that a Manufactory of large Plate Glass would be of to this Country, to the Right honourable Charles , from the great

Quantities of Foreign Glass being imported; and he was given to understand, if such an Undertaking was set on Foot, that every possible Encouragement would be given by Parliament and Administration, as a great National Object. He did not remember to have fold English Glass exceeding 30 Inches wide and 60 long — the Tariff for Glals of the largest Dimension is only 48 I by 60; and he thinks, if Plate Glass could be made upon more moderate Terms, a large Quantity of such Plates would be exported to the East Indies and elsewhere, though at present he knows of no Exportation from England, while a very considerable one is carried on from France.

It appeared by the Evidence of Mr. John Mayo, a Cabinet Maker and Worker of Plate Glals, that he apprehends it to be all blown, as he never heard of its being cast in England; has known French Glass bought by Commission for Exportation; and he does not doubt but great Quantities would be exported from England, if made as cheap and perfect as in and should

suppole it may be made cheaper: And the Witness said. He has been informed, the King of France is concerned in the Glass Manufactory, and is at a great Expence therein; and also, that the Trade is there carried on by a large Company; that he has imported a great deal of French Glass, upon Account of the Size; and, notwithstanding the heavy Duty thereupon, it comes less expensive than the English; that he applied at Vauxkall for 3

Plate Glass, but could get none made there, on Account of the Size he wanted, as there were none so large, and they did not chuse to make them; the largest English Plates of Glass he ever saw, were about 36 Inches by 72.

It appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Bowles, that he made a great Quantity of Plate Glass, the largest Size, 82 by 48; and that he could make larger Plates, but there is no Sale for them; he has a Glass in his Pofiession of 99 or 100 Inches long, and 40 Inches wide, which was formerly cast; but has now no Apparatus for calling Glass, it having been long since destroyed: He does not recoiled the Price of those he made of the larger Sort, except one Glass, 60 by 40, fold for 37. ion in the rough; he believes French Glass is cheaper.

It appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Dickson, that at Mr. Cookson's Manufactory for Plate Glass, the largest

Size made, is 84 by 52 Inches, which he believes were cast. This Manufactory has been carried on for 30 Years; and said. He could be supplied with Plates of that Size from thence; but as there is no call for them (the French underselling us) very few had been made, and he could not tell the Price: That he could not export them, because there was no Demand: And being asked. What he would fell a glass of 84 Inches by 52 ? he said, For any Price, but they are rough. i

Mr. Quinton informed your Committee, that he had made very few Plate Glasses as yet, the largest Size was 84 by 38 Inches, but that he had never fold One; that he could cast large Glass Plates, but not in the Manner they do in France.

A Member present informed your Committee, that he had received a Letter lately, wherein he was informed, that at a Manufactory he was concerned in, they had just begun to blow Plate Glass; and had made One Plate 65 by 38 Inches.

A Petition of the Goldsmiths, Silversmiths, and Plate Sheffield, *cc. Workers of the City of London, and Places adjacent, Assay Office*, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That Application is making, for establishing of Assay Offices in the Towns of Sheffield and Birmingham, for the trying, touching, assaying, and marking of Gold and Silver Plate; and alledging, that the Power of trying, touching, assaying, and marking, of Gold and Silver Plate, is a very great and important Trust, and ought to be committed to such Persons, and in such Places only, where the same is likely to be executed and discharged with the greatest Care and Fidelity; and that the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Goldsmiths of the City of London (whose Affairs are governed and ordered by the Wardens and Assistants of the said Company)

are.

13 Geo. III. 25° Februarii. 155

are, and have been, a Corporation by Prescription, with divers Privileges, confirmed and enlarged, from Time to Time, by several Charters (amongst other Things) for the searching, assaying, and marking. Wrought Plate, in order to ascertain the Standard thereof; and that the Wardens and Assistants of the said Company have hitherto executed and discharged those Trusts with the utmost Care and Fidelity; and that an Establishment of an Assay Office at Sheffield and Birmingham will open a Door to Deceit and Uncertainty, with respect to the Standards of Gold and Silver Plate, and tend to destroy that Credit and Reputation which the Goldsmiths Manufactory in these Kingdoms has justly acquired, and consequently impair the Trade of this Metropolis, diminish His Majesty’s Revenue, and sensibly affect the Honour and Riches of the Kingdom in general \ and that the Manufactory of such Plate is now carried on in the City of London, and Places adjacent, in all its Variety of useful and curious Branches, in much greater Perfection than in any other Place in these Kingdoms; and that the Work wrought here carries with it a deserved and established Credit, for every Quality which can contribute to Elegance, Utility, and true intrinsic Value j and that the Office of assaying and marking such Plate is performed by Persons appointed by the Company of Goldsmiths of the City of London for that Purpose only, and totally unconcerned in the Manufactory thereof; the Power therefore, of assaying Gold and Silver Plate is free from Abuse in such Hands, as much as possible; and that, in the Towns and Neighbourhood of Sheffield and Birmingham, there are few Persons at all conversant with, or {killed in, the Gold and Silver Plate Manufactory; and that in the whole Lift of Names subscribed to the said Petitions, there are but Three or Four Persons concerned in the Manufacture of Wrought Plate only j and that the said Manufactory, in the said Towns and Neighbourhood, being confined to so small a Number of real Manufacturers, and those so immediately concerned together in the same Branches of Bu-liness, will enable them (whenever they please) to abuse that Power which such an Establishment will put into their Hands, and, by so doing, most effectually to ruin the whole Goldsmiths Trade in this Kingdom; and that several or Tome Person or Persons, in or near the said Towns, or one of them, have plated with Silver, Wares and Manufactures made of base Metal, and marked the same with Marks, in order to deceive, and that the same might appear as real Silver Plate; and that other Frauds and Deceits, in the manufacturing of Silver Wares, have been committed, in or near the said Towns, or one of them; and that the necessary Expence of an Assay Office and Officers, at Sheffield and Birmingham, would render the Charges of assaying Plate at such Office equivalent to the present Charge of assaying the same at London, added to the Expences of Carriage and Agency; and that the Goldsmith’s Manufactory in the City of London, and Places adjacent, is already overstocked with Hands, inso much that many experienced Foreign Artificers, who heretofore resided in this City, from whose Skill and Ingenuity the said Manufactory received considerable Improvement, are now obliged to seek Work and Employ in other Countries, to the great Detriment of the Trade of this Kingdom; and that Multitudes of our own poor industrious Countrymen, in this Metropolis, who have been brought up to the Goldsmith’s Business, are now in the utmost Distress, for Want of Work, to support themselves and Families: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Petitions; and that no such Bill or Bills, as prayed for by the said Petitions, may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several of the acting Trustees for the public Roads near the City of Exeter, commonly called the Exeter Turnpike, and other Gentlemen, Clergy, and

Freeholders, of the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Road between a Place called Barnfiaple Cross, in the Parish of

Crediton, in the said County, to a Place called stone Stone, is very narrow, founderous, and inconvenient; and that Persons travelling by the said Road to the Town of Crediton are subject to the Tolls levied at a Gate erected at Barnfiaple Cross, without reaping the lead Benefit of the Turnpike Roads, as they only cross the same; and that the Parishioners of Crediton are willing effectually to repair the said Road, if they were permitted to receive from the Trustees for the said Turnpike a certain Sum of Money, and the same to be afterwards included and deemed Part of the said Turnpike; and that the Road from a Gate near

Broadway,\n the Parish of Sand ford, in the said County, and leading through the said Parish of Sand ford, the Pari fhes of Hennerleigh, Washford Pyne, Woo/fardisworth, Wilieridge, Thelbridge, and East Worlington, to a Place called Drayford Bridge, all in the said County, where

the Southmoiton Turnpike ends, and which is rendered in a great Measure uleless by the Want of such Communication, is also very narrow, founderous, and inconvenient; and that the said several Parishes, having a large Extent of Road to maintain, are incapable ot effectually repairing the fame, without Aid of Parliament; and that it would be of considerable Advantage to the Public, if the said Road was added to, and made Part of, the said Exeter Turnpike; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the Addition of the said Road would not be injurious to the said Trust, if the Trustees were impowered to erect a Gate on some Part of the fame, and to receive the several Tolls heretofore received at the several Gates erected on the said Turnpike Roads, separate from, and independent of, the Tolls and x

Duties at the other Gates: And therefore praying the House to permit the said Roads to be added to, and made Part of, the said Turnpike, and to give them such farther Relief in the Premises as the House shall think proper.

Richmond Sir Francis Vincent reported from the Committee, to Bridge. whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Landholders, and other the Inhabitants, of Richmond, and Places adjacent, in the County of Surrey, whole Names are thereunto lubscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth, viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Stailard, being examined, said. That the Communication between Richmond and the County of Middle f ex is by a Ferry, the Approach to which is very bad and inconvenient by Reason of the Steep nets of the Hill, the Rife whereof from the River to the lload is about 41 Feet; that a loaded Waggon or Cart cannot come from the Ferry to the Street up the Hill, neither can Carriages defeend without a Chain; that People generally get out of their Carriages when they go to the Ferry, which is an inconvenient PaflTage over the River Thames.

That the Witness has frequently seen Carriages come to the Top of the Hill, and the Descent has appeared to them so very bad, that they have gone round by Kingston to get to the other Side of the Water; and that the Communication by the Ferry is cut off several

Months in the Year by Floods and Frosts — That a Bridge-would certainly obviate the above Inconveniencies* be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the adjacent Country, and the Public in general:

That Richmond is not a Market Town, neither is there any great Matter of Trade carried on there; but there is a Communication by the Ferry, between Richmond and Twickenham, from the Counties of;

Sussex, and Kent — That Kew Bridge is about Two Miles below Richmond, arid Kingston Bridge about Four Mile? above it; that there are a Number of People reside at Richmond, whom Richmond, with its own Produce, is not able to supply; and it would be a Matter of great Convenience, if Corn and Hay could be brought from Middlesex to Richmond.

That a Cart or Waggon, loaded with Hay or (jorn* can come over the Ferry at particular Times, but cannot get up the Hill; and the Supply to Richmond, except at those particular Times, is cut off. — And being asked*

Whether there is any other Road from the Ferry, besides coming up the Hill ? he said, When the Water is very low, People can go that Way, but not in Times of Frost.

That there are several new Buildings carrying on at Richmond, and it would be advantageous to the Town

to be supplied with Bricks, Mortar, and other Con-veniencies for Building, and likewise to the Farmers and other Traders in Middlesex, if they had a Vent for the above Articles by Means of a Bridge.

Being asked, In going over Richmond Ferry, how far it is before you join the Great Western Road ? he said.

About 2 or 3 Miles; and by Kew Bridge to the same Place, 6 or 7 Miles; and by Kingston Bridge, 8 or 9.

That the Inhabitants of Richmond could with to have the Bridge at the End of Water Lane, from which there is a Carriage Way already, but not sufficiently wide, and cannot be widened without taking down a Building, which the Witness thinks will not be any Inconvenience to the Inhabitants, as almost all the Proprietors of Houses intended to be taken down have consented; and that if the Bridge is built, it will take off considerably from the Declivity of the Hill.

That Twickenham Park is the opposite Shore to Richmond; and if the Bridge is built any Way below the Ferry, the Communication into the County of Middlesex mutt pass through the Dutchess of Property.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Bridge across the River of Thames, from Richmond, in the County of Surrey, to the opposite Shore, in the County of Middlesex: And that Sir Francis'

Vincent, Mr. Poivnall, and Lord Frederick do

prepare, and bring in, the lame.

A Petition of the Artificers and Labourers in His DockYard*-. Majesty’s several Dock Yards, being offered to be pre- r"nj*rs l'ented to the House.' Labourers.

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners, unwilling to shew any Discontent, have; for a long Time, struggled with Difficulties, to support themselves and Families, upon their present Wages, Which, having been settled near a Century past, and not altered ft nee, are foftind inefficient to give that Support, which, they hope; an industrious and useful Body of People may well deserve; that the great Advance of Price on all the Necessaries of Life, has rendered that Allowance inadequate to the Petitioners necessary Wants, which, at the Time of its first Institution, must have been an ample and generous Provision; and that the great Difference ill the Value of Money has made an ell'ential Alteration, to the Petitioners Loss; and that, though some Perquisites are allowed ill Addition to their Wages, as well as extra Work in the Summer Time, yet they find themselves under great Difficulties to support themselves and Families, with every Attention to the most plain and rigid (Economy; and though the Petitioners would hope, that a small Addition might be made to their Pay, yes, being willing to relinquish all Perqtiifites from the taking of Chips, they apprehend, that the Expence of the Dock Yards would not be thereby irt-creased, but, with proper Regulations, might afford a comfortable Maintenance to the Artificers, at little or no additional Expence to Government: The increased Wages of the private Dock Yards, the lowest of which are One Third more than the Petitioners, sufficiently evince the Reafohableness of this their Request; and they apprehend, that the great Improvement made of late Years in the Method of executing their Work, would in some Measure compensate for an additional Pay: The waiting a considerable Time for Payment of their Wages, makes a Reduction in their Value; being obliged to take up Money at Interest, to defray their necessary Expences till the Pay comes in; and this, under the improved Regulation, is only once every Four Months: And, that the Petitioners have already applied to His Majesty, the Admiralty and Navy Boards, who are all sensible of their Hardships, but unable to grant them a proper Relief, without the Interpofilion of Parliament; and they hope that their great Distress, together with the Importance of the Service in which they are engaged, may be considered an Object worthy its Attention: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration.. and to grant them such Relief as may, upon the fullest Enquiry, be thought fit, leasonable, and convenient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morn- Ways and ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole Mean$-House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morn- supply, ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow

Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Mr. Whitworth presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for defraying the Charge of the Pay and Cloathing of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the 25th Day of March 1773: And the same was received; and read the First Time.
