Ordered That Mr. Morton do make the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the present high Price of Corn and Provisions.

Mr. Morton accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: YVhere the same were read; and areas followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Duties payable upon Beer or Bigg imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of middling British Beer or Bigg, shall be at or above the Price of Twenty-

four Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, 1 That a Duty of Two Pence per Quarter be laid upon Beer or Bigg imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of middling British Beer or Bigg shall be at or above the Price of Twenty-four Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duties now payable upon Pease and Beans respectively, imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of middling British Pease and Beans shall be respectively at or above the Price of Thirty-two Shillings per Quarter, shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That a Duty of Two Pence per Quarter be laid upon Pease and Beans respectively, imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of middling British Pease and Beans shall be respectively at or above the Price of Thirty-two Shillings per Quarter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That, when the Price of middling British Beer or Bigg shall be under Twenty-two Shillings per Quarter, a Bounty, not exceeding Two Shillings per Quarter, be allowed upon the Exportation of all Beer or Bigg of the Growth of this Kingdom.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Navy The Lord Nome reported frottt the Committee, to Captain*, whom the Petition of the Captains of His Majesty’s Navy, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Your Committee find, That by the Deficiency of the Appointmens and Provision made in that Re-spedl, many of the junior Captains, who have no Means of Subsistence except their Half Pay, are under the greatest Difficulties to provide for their Support when out of Employment.

That the Twenty senior Captains of the Navy, intitled to Half Pay, now receive Ten Shillings each; the next Thirty, Eight Shillings; the next Forty, Six Shillings; the next Fifty, Five Shillings; and all the junior Captains, without Distinction, only Four Shillings each, a Day. On which Allowance of Four Shillings, the said junior Captains may probably remain Fifteen, or a greater Number of Years, before they obtain a Place on the Five Shillings Lift; whilst their greatly inferior Officers the Captains of Marines, enjoy a Half Pay of Five Shillings a Day, from the Time they are advanced to that Rank in the same Profession.

That the Half Pay to the Captains of the Navy, being regulated by that Part only of their Sea Pay, called their Personal Pay, is not a Moiety of the Whole Pay provided for them when in actual Service.

That his Majesty King Charles the Second did, in the Year 1674, direct a Provision of Half Pay, the First Time granted to the Captains of the Navy, to be made for those who had commanded Ships of the First and Second Rate in Time of Peace, " equal to the " Value of Half the Pay usually allowed by his Majesty, " in Time of Service, to Commanders and Captains " of like Quality."

That King ’’James the Second, making farther Alterations in the Establishment of the Navy, did, in the Year 1686, order an Allowance of Table Money to be made, in Addition, and nearly equal, to the then Pay of the Captains in the different Classes, according to the Rate of the Ships they respectively commanded. And though he promised them other Encouragement, it does not appear to your Committee that he made any Provision for their Support on Shore; but that, in conference of such Allowance of Table Money, he cancelled several Perquisites they before enjoyed.

That the Allowance of Table Money ending with the Reign of that Prince, his Successor, King William the Third, was pleased, in the Year 1693, to establish, in Place thereof, an Allowance of Double Pay to Captains of Ships of the First, Second, Third, Fourth,* Fifth, and Sixth, Rates, whilst on Service; and Half the Amount of such Pay to Captains of First, Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Rates, in Order (as the Establishment expresses) " for their more comfortable " Support and Maintenance whilst on Shore."

That the Fund provided for the Establishment of such enCreased Sea and Half Pay ending with the War, his said Majesty King William was pleased to order another Scheme of Pay for the Officers of the Fleet to be prepared; and the same being adopted by this House, in the subsequent Year 1700, in Part of the Plan for the Reduction of the Naval Expences, then under Consideration, the said Double Pay, and encreased Half Pay, were reduced One Third in Amount to those Officers respectively: Whereby it appears to your Committee, that, notwithstanding the Assurances given for the Encouragement of those Officers during the Wa$» on the supposed certain Enjoyment of an adequate Provision for their Support in Time of Peace, they were not only disappointed thereof, to save an inconsiderable Expence in the Estimate of the Half Pay, as stated in, your Journals; but likewise, that in Place of the Allowance of Half Pay, provided for One hundred and Fifty-two Captains in the several Classes as before-mentioned, comprehending nearly the whole Number of Captains then on the Lifts, the Establishment of Half Pay last instituted was confined to the Fifty senior Captains only, in total Disregard of the Royal Declaration and Engagements.

That in the Year 1715 a farther Regulation of the Half Pay was made, on the Plan of the Sea Pay ella-blished in 1700, and the Benefit of Half Pay thereby extended to all the Captains of the Navy, without Distinction, who should be, from Time to Time, out of Employment. I11 which State the JHalf Pay of the Captains of the Navy hath continued, with little or no Variation, unto this-Time.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to take into His Consideration the Deficiency ox the Allowance to several of the Junior Captains and Commanders in His Majesty’s Navy, for their Support when out of Employment; and that He will direct such Addition to be made thereto, proportioned to the present Establishment for the Senior Captains, over and above the Provision made for the Year 1773, as His Majesty in His great Wisdom shall think fit; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good such Expence as shall be incurred on that Account.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

A Petition of the Commissioners for building West- Westminster minster Bridge, being offered to be presented to the Bridge. House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth'. That the Petitioners are, by virtue of several Acts of Parliament, passed in the Reign of his late Majesty King Gernge the Second, constituted, appointed, and -continued, Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the Wcolstaple, or thereabouts, in the City of Westminster, to the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey, and for maintaining, preserving, and supporting, the same when built, and for other Purposes therein mentioned; and that the Petitioners, in pursuance of the Powers vested in them . by the said Acts, have, with the utmost Care, caused the said Bridge to be built. Which has been passable many Years; and that the Petitioners have likewise, from Time to Time, proceeded with the greatest Caution and Frugality, in carrying into Execution the other Trulls reposed in them by the said Acts; and that the Petitioners find that they cannot make an effectual and constant Provision for the maintaining, supporting, cleaning, watching, lighting, paving, and gravelling, the said Bridge, and for preserving the same from Annoyances and other Damages, unless the House will grant them Monies for those Purposes: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Sums of Money as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Petitioners perceive, by the Votes, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill for enlarging and altering the Terms and Powers of Two Acts, of the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of King George the First, and the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for repairing the Reads leading from the Town of Bromsgrove to the Town of Dudley, in the County of and from the Town of Bromsgrove to the Town of in the County of Warwick, so far as the same Acts relate to the repairing of the said Road leading from the Town of Bromsgrove to the Town of Dudley; and that the Petitioners are informed, it is intended by the said Bill to repeal so much of the said Acts as retrains the Trustees from setting up any Toll Gate or Gates between the Town of Dudley and a Common, or Heath, called Pet fuel Common, or , otherwise called Dudley.

Wood, being a very finall Part of the Road, which leads not only from the Town of Dudley, towards the

Town of Bromsgrove, but also to the Town of Cradley, and to a populous manufacturing Country, and to the Parishes of Rowley, Northfield,

and many other Parishes and Places near thereto, the inhabitants whereof pass over no other Parts of the said Road leading from Bromsgrove to Dudley than the small Part above-mentioned; which Restraint, if taken off, and any new Toll Gate was to be set up between these Places, it would be a grievous and unnecessary Burthen, not only to the Inhabitants of the said Town of Dudley, and the Neighbourhood thereof, but to all the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Country for many Miles together, who have Occasion to relort to the Town of Dudley or the Markets there, or for the getting Coal and Lime for the Manure of their Lands: And therefore praying. That the Restriction inserted in the said former Acts, for the preventing the setting up any Toll Gate or Gates, between the said Town of Dudley, and the said Chace, or Common, called Penfnet Common or Chace, may be continued, and may not be repealed or altered by the new intended Ad,: and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel or Agents, against the inl'erting any Clause in the said intended Ad, for repealing or altering the Restrictions contained in the said former Acts, restraining the setting up any new Toll Gate, or Gates, within the said District.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are A flay Offices, thereunto subscribed, being Goldsmiths, Silversmith, or Plate Workers, of the City of London, and Places adjacent, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That Frauds and Abuses have been committed in the manufacturing of Gold or Silver Plate, in or near the Towns of Sheffield and,

or one of them; and that divers Artificers there have plated with Silver, Wares made of Iron, Steel, or other Metals, and impressed Marks thereon, in such Manner, that the Wares are made to appear like real Plate marked at an Assay Office; and, as a Committee is appointed to enquire into the Manner of conducting the several Assay Offices in London, York,

Chester, Norwich, and Newcastle upon Tyne, and the Manner in which Wrought Plate is allayed and marked; and also into the Frauds and Abuses that have been committed, and attempted to be committed, by the Manufacturers or Venders of Gold and Silver Plate, and Plated Work: Therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, in order to prove the Allegations of their Petition.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Forth Forth and Clyde Navigation, was presented to the House, and clydc and read: Setting forth. That the Petitioners, after Navigation, having expended almost their whole Subscription Money in the Works already made* have found that a farther Aid of Money will be necessary for completing this great and useful Navigation; and that the Acts of Parliament now in being, relative thereto, require Hill to be further explained, amended, altered, and rendered more effectual, and the Powers of the Petitioners enlarged; and that the Petitioners could not be pofl'efled of the necessary Materials, for preparing and supporting a Petition to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for the above Purposes, till the Accounts and State of their Affairs had been laid before their annual General Meeting, which, in Terms of the Act: of Parliament incorporating the Petitioners, could not be held till the Day limited by the House for presenting Petitions for Private Bills was elapsed; and that a Delay to another Session would be a Loss to the Public and the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House, to permit a Petition to be presented-, for Leave to bring in a Bill, for the Purposes hereinbefore mentioned.

And several Members, in their Places, informing the House, that the said General Meeting could not be held till after the Day limited for receiving Petitions for Private Bills; and that it could not be known, till such General Meeting, that a large Sum of Money was ltill wanting, for completing the said Navigation; and that, for Want of such Sum, the Works now carrying on upon the said Navigation must be flopped till the next Session of Parliament, which would be attended with great Injury to the said Company of Proprietors;

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, and of the Information now given to the House by such Members*

Mr. Skipworth reported from the Committee, to whom

the Petition of several of the Artificers in Silver Plate, in the Town and Neighbourhood of Sheffield, in the County of York, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also, the Petition of Matthew Boulton, on Behalf of himself, and the rest of the Manufacturers of Silver Wares, in the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick; and also, the Petition of the Wardens and Assistants of the Company or Mystery of Goldsmiths

of the City of London, in Court assembled; and also, the Petition of the Goldsmiths, Silversmiths, and Plate Workers of the City of London, and Places adjacent, whole Names are thereunto subscribed; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the Two first-mentioned Petitions; and had heard the Petitioners on the lait-mentioned Petitions; and that the Committee had directed him to report a State of the Two first-mentioned Petitions to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Matter of Fact contained in the first-mentioned Petition, your Committee examined

Mr. Gilbert Dixon, Clerk to the Cutlers Company; who informed your Committee, that he has known the Town of Sheffield 'upwards of Forty Years; that he knows the Persons who have signed the Sheffield Petition, that they were all either Workers in Silver, their Partners, or Refiners, both in the plated and solid Silver Way; and that in both Businesses there were 468 Persons employed in that Town, including those who have signed the Petition, which he thinks are Mailers.

And being asked. If he knew when the Workers in Silver at Sheffield were fewer than at present ? He said. That Thirty Years ago there was not a Twentieth Part of what there are now, and those employed only in making Knife Handles; and that the Increase has been both in the plated and solid Silver Manufactures.

And being further examined, he said. That there are People who have been brought up to other Trades, who now follow the Business of Plate-workers and Silversmiths.

Mr. Joseph Hancock, Senior, informed your Committee, that he has lived' at Sheffield upwards of Fifty Years, in which Time great Improvements have been made there in the manufacturing Silver Wares, particularly in the making of Candlesticks, Salts, Bottle Stands, Castor Frames, Snuffer Trays, and many other Articles, all of solid Silver; which Species of Manufactures have been introduced since he has known

And being asked. How many Houses in Sheffield manufactured those Species of Goods ? he said. Four to his own Knowledge.

And being asked. Whether any one Man, that has signed the Petition, served his Time to the Business ? he said. Several of them served their Time to Silver Cutlers.

Mr. John Parsons, being desired to give an Account to what Extent the solid Silver Manufactory is carried on in Sheffield, said. That it was impossible for him to tell the Quantity of Silver manufactured, but that the House he was concerned in have worked up near 1,000 Ounces per Month, for many Months palt, in the

Manufacture of solid Silver Candlesticks only, Two Thirds of which is fold in London finished, laving burnishing and polishing; that great Part of it is exported, and the rest returned; but if an Assay Office was elta-blished at Sheffield, the Whole, or the major Part of it, would be finished there; but the great Delay of fending it from London to be finished at Sheffield, and returned again to London, would be the Means of losing the Sale of it. — That the Witness has frequently known of Plate being damaged in the Carriage, which very often arises from packing, for which the Carriers are not relpon-fible. — That they are obliged to employ an Agent in London to get the Plate allayed, who llrikes his Mark upon it, and then fends it to the Allay Office.

And being asked. Whether he did not apprehend the employing such Agent is not an Inconvenience and Detriment to the Trade ? he said. Not absolutely so much from the linking his own Mark, as from the Delay and Misfortunes it is liable to on the Road; but if it was equally convenient, he should always be defirou* to set his own Mark, instead of employing an Agent.

Being then asked. Why he employed an Agent to

fit

i3 Geo. III. ia° Martii. I91

fct his Mark ? he said, That he had sent Candlesticks to London with his own Mark on them, and that the Agent had (truck his Mark upon it.

Being asked, If he thought that Act of the Agent’s w’as not to give it the Credit of London Work ? he said. He believed the People of Sheffield would be glad to have the Credit of their own Manufactures.

That the Candlesticks which the Witness makes for the Silversmiths in London, are made according to the Instructions he receives; and that sometimes they fend their own Models and Drawings, but the Silver is his own. — That those Candlesticks are sometimes fold for London Work, upon which Account, the Witness believes, they fetch a greater Price than they would at Sheffield.

Being asked, Whether, if an Assay Office was established at Sheffield, that increased Profit would not be transferred to the Sheffield Plate-workers ? he said. Not altogether, for the London Silversmiths would get some Profit; but in that same he could fell the Plate cheaper.

And being asked as to the Difference of Expence in polishingin London and Sheffield, he said, He apprehended it could be done at Sheffield fox Half the Money.

Mr. Bernard Holbrook informed your Committee, That he is Agent to Hyland and Company at Sheffield; that he is allowed £. 100 a Year, andyf. iofora Ware-house to put their Goods in; — that his Business, as Agent, is to receive Orders from Shops in London for Hyland and Company; — that the Goods he takes Orders for to be delivered unpolished are generally sent to the Shops, and they get them marked and polished; such Goods that are to be delivered polished, he delivers to the Polisher, who gets them Hailed, afterwaros polishes them, and then returns them to the Witness, in order to be delivered to the Shops; — that the Price of polishing Candlesticks is 3 s. a Pair, the Polisher taking the Waste, which the Witness supposes is about 2 s. 10 d.more; but that the Sheffield People have told him that they could polish them for about 20 a Pair, saving the Waste.

And being a(ked. Whether it was a Matter of Choice «r Necessity that, he was employed as Agent to Hyland and Company ? he said, Necdfity.

Mr. Cox, being examined, was asked, What was the Expence of the Carriage of too lb. Weight of Silver from Sheffield to London and back again ? he said, 3, with the Insurance; and that he has seen Goods returned damaged.

Mr. Hancock being again examined, as to the Injury arising from the Delay of the Carriage, said. That he has refused Orders for Goods, knowing that he should not be able to get them from London to finish in the Time; and that there is likewise an Uncertainty as to Time, which the Witness experienced when he was in Trade.

And to prove the Matter of Fact contained in the Petition of Blatthew Boulton, on Behalf of himself, and the rest of the Manufacturers of Silver Wares, in the Town of Birmingham, in the County of your Committee examined

Mr. Samuel Garbit, who said. That he is well acquainted with the Silver Manufactures carried on by Mr. Boulton, at Birmingham; that they are of different Species, such as Tureens, Epergnes, Candlesticks, Vases, Coffee-pots, and many ornamental Utensils, as well solid Silver as plated, both for the London and Country Market; — that Mr. Boulton began the manufacturing of Silv er Plato about Seven Years since; — that it has increased lately, and the Witness has no Doubt but it might be considerably extended: — that there are above 40 other Manufacturers of Plate in Birmingham who have Licences; — and that he knows Mr. Boulton fends Plate to to be assayed and

marked, which is attended with many Inconveniencies, as it occasions Delay, Uncertainty, and very frequently

the Goods are damaged 5 — that one very staple Article of the Birmingham Manufacture is Fire Arms, the Ornaments of which the Workmen find more convenient to have from London ready manufactured, though they could make them for One Half the Expence in the Country; — that another great Article of the Manufacture of Birmingham and its Neighbourhood is Buckles* which employs above 5,000 Workmen; and, for Want of an Assay Office, they do not make any considerable Quantity, as they would be obliged to fend their Patterns to London, whereby they are liable to have their Patterns discovered; but if freed from that Inconvenience, the Witness said, the Manufacture of Silver Plate would be greatly increased, and particularly in the Article of Buckles; — that Mr. Boulton has many thousand Dies, which he could make use of in different Parts of the Silver Manufactory, but does not, on Account of the Inconvenience of assaying; and that there are many other Manufacturers who would avail themselves of the present Tools in manufacturing Plate, if it was not for the same Inconvenience.

( Your Committee then proceeded to receive Evidence in Support of the Allegations of the Petition of the Wardens and Assistants, of the Company or Mystery of* Goldsmiths of the City of London, in Court assembled; and the Agent for the Petitioners having proposed to produce the Charter, to shew the Incorporation of the said Company, the same was admitted, as also that the Standard Pieces appointed for Trial of the Gold and Silver Money, and Wrought Plate, being made, and the Monies tried and compared therewith by a Jury, returned by the said Company to the Privy Council, who have intruded the said Company with -Part of such Standard Pieces, in order to regulate and ascertain the Fineness of the Gold and Silver Plate assayed at Goldsmiths Hall.

And in order to prove that there were but few real Goldsmiths, Silversmiths, or Plate Workers, in Sheffield or Birmingham, notwithstanding what is alledged in their Petitions, he called

Mr. William Abdy (a Silvcrsmith, Plater, and Plate Worker of the City of London) who being examined said, That he knows the Town of Sheffield, and served his Time there, but that it is now 24 Years since he left it, but was there Four Years ago; that at that Time there were Four Houses that carried on Business in the solid Silver Way, but that was only flight Silver Knife Handles; and they were called Cutlers j and that the Witness thinks there is not one real Goldsmith Silversmith, cr Plate-worker, in Sheffield.

And being asked. If there was any one Man in Sheffield, that would be called in London a Goldsmith, Silversmith, or Plate-worker? he said, Yes, by Reason of their making Silver Candlesticks; that he knows of but Four Houses in Sheffield that makes Silver Candlesticks, but there are several Partners in each House.

Being asked, If he knew the Persons who had signed the Sheffield Petition ? he said. Not personally, but thinks they are all concerned in the solid Silver, or plated Way, but not one in the solid Way only* Then

Mr. Richard Hughes, Junior Assay Master to the Goldsmiths Company, being examined, was asked. How many of the Persons, who have subscribed their Names to the Sheffield Petition, have entered their Names at Goldsmiths Hall? he said, No more than Five, that he could recoiled!, and One who has not signed the Petition; — that no Manufactureer of Gold and Silver Wares can have their Goods assayed and marked till he has entered his Mark at the Assay Office, which Mark may be entered either in Person, or by Attorney, without Fee or Reward; that the Goods manufactured at Sheffield, are flight Silver Candlesticks, Knife Handles, Bottle Stands, and Salts, which are struck with

Fly Presses, and Tent to the Allay Office to be marked; but that no other Work, but such as is struck in that Manner, is sent to the Assay Office.

And being further examined, he said, That the Silver Wares manufactured at Sheffield are not confined to those Four Species, for sometimes there may be a Bread Basket, or an Ink Stand, but very seldom, the general Trade being those Four Articles.

The Witness was then asked, How many Persons, in the Town and Neighbourhood of have en-

tered their Marks at Goldsmiths Hall ? he named Five, who he said were all.

Your Committee then proceeded to hear Evidence in Support of the Allegations of the Petition of the Goldsmiths, Silversmiths, and Plate-workers, of the City of London, and Places adjacent, whose Names are there-nto subscribed: And

Mr. John Wakelin, who has been engaged in the Bu-finess of a Silversmith in Londo Seven Years, informed your Committee, That there are great Numbers of People in and about London employed in the Silver Plate Manufactory, who are very skilful Artists, and that the said Manufactory is carried on in a very extensive Manner, and in different Branches, and to greater Perfection than at Sheffield or Birmingham.

Being asked, Whether the Manufacture of Plate is carried on, in and about London, sufficient to supply the Demands for it ? he said. That it certainly might be, but that vast Quantities of Plate is fold in London that is manufactured at Sheffield and that might

be made in London, if the Manufacturers who are now out of Employ were employed; that the Plate wrought in and about London carries with it an established Credit for Elegance, Utility, and Value, and that what is wrought at Sheffield and Birmingham is generally of a more specious and flight Manufucture, and must be less useful.

Being asked, If Plate, after having been marked at any other Assay Office than Goldsmiths Hall, was to come to be sold to the Silversmith in , would

he consider it as Standard or uncertain Value ? he said. Generally they would chuse to assay it again; — that, with respect to the Article of Silver Candlesticks, the Wit-nets said, that the lighted Pair made in London is from 25 to 30Ounces; and in general the heaviest of those made at Sheffield and Birmingham 20 Ounces, but some of the Birmingham Candlesticks may weigh 30 Ounces or more.

Being afited, Whether a Pair of Birmingham Candle-flicks of 30 Ounces, of the same Fashion and Weight as the London Candlesticks, sold at a less Price ? he said. He never law any London Candlesticksof the same Fashion and Weight as the Birminghamthat they are made upon a different Construction; but they might be made upon the same Construction, and for the same Price, if damped.

Being asked. If he could tell whether a Piece of Plate, with the London Mark on it, was* of Sheffield or London Manufacture ? he said, Not for a Certainty; that it would fetch the same Price, if manufactured in

the same Manner ;--and the Witness further said, That the Knife Handle Trade has fallen into Disrepute by the flight Manufacture of Sheffield and Birmingham; but being asked. Whether he was perfectly acquainted with that Manufacture, as carried on at Sheffield and Birmingham ? he said. He was not.

Mr. Drew Drettry, a Goldsmith, being examined, said. That he has been engaged in the Business of a Working Goldsmith and Silversmith 30 Years; and he confirmed the Evidence of the last Witness, with respect to the Extension of the Plate Manufactory in the Skilfulness of the Artists, and the Sufficiency of the Workmen.

And being asked. Whether he was acquainted with the manufacturing Plate at Sheffield and Birmingham ? he said, That he has bought considerable Quantities of Candlesticks that have been made at Sheffield of solid Silver, and the lighted of them weighed 24 Ounces; but he has seen some of 30 Ounces; that they were stamped, therefore not equal in Strength to those that are Cast, but that there are strong Candlesticks stamped; that the particular Manufactures of Sheffield and Birmingham are Candlesticks, Knife Hafts, Buckles, and lately at Sheffield they have made Salts, Bottle Trays, and Castor Frames; — that the Witness is acquainted with a great many Persons employed in the manufacturing Plate at Sheffield, but only One at Birmingham, and that is Mr. Boulton; that the Plate made at She/-fields principally flight, and likewise the Knife Handles . till lately, and even at this Time they cannot be made so substantial and strong as to be equal to those made in London; that the Witness has been a great Sufferer by that Article only, which obliged him to quit that Branch of Business; and that the Slightness of that Manufactory has brought the Trade into Disrepute.

Being asked. What were the Species of Silver Goods manufactured in London, that are not at Sheffield and Birmingham t he said. Every Thing but those he has mentioned to be manufactured at Sheffield and Birmingham.

And being asked, Whether those Goods are fold cheaper, since the Establishment of the Sheffield Manufactory ? he said, Some of them have fell in Price; that Candlesticks and Knife Handles have been made as cheap in London as at Sheffield, but don’t know they have fold cheaper.

And the Witness said, that there are now 1000 People out of Employ, owing, as he believes, to the general Distress of the Times, and not \o the Increase of the Sheffield Manufactory, or to the Decreale of other Markets, a great many of whom are gone Abroad.

And being asked. Whether any of those People offered to work for less Wages than usual ? he said, They had not; and that the Introduction of the plated Business in London has hurt the solid.

Mr. John Carter, a Silver Plate Manufacturer, being examined, said, That he. is well acquainted with that Manufactory in and about London, and that the same was carried on with great Perfection and Utility; that he is likewise acquainted with the Manufactory carried on at Sheffield and Birmingham, and is engaged to a considerable Extent at Sheffield.

Being asked. Whether the Plate manufactured at Sheffield was of equal Goodness with that manufactured in London ? he said, It is worked in a flight superficial Manner, therefore can’t be equal to the London Manufacture in point of Wear; that the slighted Silver Candlesticks, made at Sheffield, weigh about 14 Ounces a Pair.

And being asked, Whether those Candlesticks were not made by his Orders? he said. They were; that he has never seen any of the Silver Manufactures of Shes-field or Birmingham, but Candlesticks and Knife Handles; the first of which he is convinced can be made as cheap in London, and the latter he could not speak to, as not coming within his Branch of Business.

i3 Geo. III. 120 Ma. 193

Being aiked. Whether the Business at Sheffield is increased in the solid Way as much as in the plated ? he said, Not a hundredth Part.

Being examined as to the Injury or Delay in the Carriage of Goods backwards and forwards, he said, He never remembered an Instance of Injury or Delay, excepting. Once, in the Course of Seven Years, and that was occasioned by a heavy Fall of Snow that retarded the Carriage; that the Expence of Carriage is under a Halfpenny an Ounce, supposing to pay Insurance, which is very seldom done, and in that same it is but Two Pence per Pound Weight Averdupoise.

Mr. Abdy, being examined, gave the same Evidence

as the last Witness, with respect to the Increase of the plated Goods, to those of solid Silver, and to the Lon-' don Manufacturer working at the same Price, and making his Goods as cheap, as the Sheffield Manufacturer.

Mr. Fair, Clerk to the Goldsmiths Company, being examined as to the Manner of conducting the Assay Office in London, informed your Committee, That the Company pays to the Officers £.706. 4 a Year; and to the Book-keeper, Accomptant, and other Officers and Servants, Advertisements, and other Incidents, several Sums, amounting, together with the above Sum, to upwards of jC. 1,100 per Annum: That the Prices of aflayingWrought Plate w London, sent from the Country, are the same as those in London; that, though the Prices are established by Act of Parliament, the Company have for several Years past taken only Two Fifths.

Mr. William Bingley, being examined, said. That he served his Time to Mr. Boulton, at Birmingham, in the solid Silver and plated Business, who he left about Nine or Ten Months ago, but lives now in London with Mr. Abdy: That while he lived with Mr. Boulton, he made solid Silver Tureens, Coffee-pots, Candlesticks, and various other Articles; and that the Witness remembers One very large Tureen with a Dilh: That some of the Candlesticks he made were strong, and some were flight, but the Proportion of the flight to the strong were as 24 to 1: That some of them were damped, others cast: That Mr. Boulton likewise made some Buckles, but he never remembers to have known above Three or Four Dozen Pair of solid Silver made during the Time the Witness was with him, which was 13 Years: That he has also known some plated Buckles to have been made by him, but not a great many.

And being aiked. Whether the Silver Manufactory at Birmingham was in an increasing State ? he said. It was when he came from thence, and that the Manufactory of stamped Silver Candlesticks has also increased in London, ftnce he has been here: That there are but Three of those Manufacturers in London, Three at Birmingham, and a great Number at Sheffield.

Being aiked, Whether he meant a great Number of plated Manufacturers, or solid; or both ? he said. Both.

That One of the Three Manufacturers in London came from Birmingham, and One from Sheffield, but he had lived in London before the stamped Silver Manufactory was established any where: That the slighted Pair of Silver Candlesticks the Witness has ever ieen made, since he has been with Mr. Abdy, weighed about 13 Ounces, and the heaviest he ever law made by Mr. Boulton, at Birmingham, were Two Pair that weighed 120 Ounces, and those were the heaviest, the bell made, and the handsomest Pattern, he ever law: That they were made in consequence of an Order from London, and that the Pattern was made in his own Manufactory: That thqfe Candlesticks were allayed at Chester (where Mr. Boulton has all his Goods assayed) and got considerable Damage in the Carriage; but that those were not the only Goods he has known to have been damaged in the Carriage: And he further said, that Plate in its imperfect State in which it is assayed, is not so liable to Damage, as after it is completed. Then,

Mr. Carter, being examined as to the Conveyances for Plate between Sheffield and London ? said. That there are Variety of Conveyances, which set out very regular, and he never remembers but one Instance to the contrary in Seven Years; and that he always considered the Owner of the Carriage responsible for any Damage that might happen.

Being aiked. Whether the Goldsmiths Manufactory in Lotidon is overstocked with Hands ? he said. It was; That a great many Foreign Artificers (many of whom were skilful in their Trade) are and have been employed in it, but several of them have been obliged to return Home for Want of Employ} and that a great Number of Manufacturers of Plate are in great Distress for Want of Employ.

Then the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Corporation of the Borough of mirjler, in Common Council assembled, and of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manufacturers, and Farmers, residing in the said Borough, and in the Parish of Kidder mi njer, and divers other Parishes and Places in the County of Worcester', and also, the Petition of the Bailiff and Burgesses of the Borough of in the County of Worcester;and the Inhabitants of the said Townj and also, the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen* principal Merchants, and Traders, of the City of Worcester; and also, the Petition of the Proprietors of thd1 Furnaces and Collieries, and Barge-owners, of BroJJeyt Coalbrookdale, Madefy, &c. in the County of Salop; were severally referred, was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first*mentioned Petition, Mr. Thomas Jacob White, being examined, laid, That he is well acquainted with the Road from Kidderminster to Redstone Ferry and Dunley, and from thence to the Hundred House, Brontyard, and Hereford; that Redstone Ferry is for the Conveyance of Foot* Passengers, Horses, and Carriages, across the River Severn, but that the Ferry is very inconvenient for such Conveyance, on Account of the Rapidity of the River, at all Times, and at High Water is difficult and dangerous to cross over, and frequently impassable by Reason of the Waters overflowing the Ground adjoining to it; that Bromyard is about Eighteen Miles dillint from the Well Side of Redstone Ferry, and is the nearest Town on the Hereford Road; and that the Road leading to the Ferry is from Kidderminster through Dunley, which Road is completed as far as Stanford Bridge, and now in tolerable good Order, and from thence to Bromyard is in good Order (except about Three Miles); that at present the Road from Bromyard to Kidderminster is not much frequented, and that no Manufactory is carried on at Bromyard; that he never heard of any particular Accident happening on the Ferry, but that he had at Times been delayed, and obliged to wait there Half an Hour before he could go over

That there is a Boat large enough to carry over Horses, Carriages, Hops, Grain, and other Commodities; and that the Road by the Ferry is more frequented by Persons on Horleback than the Road through Bewdley: —

That the Stafjordjlnre and Worcestershire Canal falls into the Severn near Redstone Ferry, at which Place a very extensive Trade is carried on: —;

That the Communication from the Well Side of the Severn to the Canal is not sufficiently open, on Account of the River: —

That the Ferry is about Three Quarters of a Mile dillant from the Canal Bason; and that it would be difficult to effect a Communication between them, on Account of the Fords, unless a Bridge is erected: —

That Goods brought to the Ferry cannot, without Difficulty, be conveyed to the Canal, because the Vessels cannot conveniently flop at the Ferry: And he said. He apprehended that the Produce of the Well Side of the Severn, particularly Hops and Cyder, would be brought to the Canal, if a Bridge was built there: — That in October, Annually, there is a great Fair at Bridgnorth for those Commodities, from whence largo Quantities are sent to Wolverhampton and,

and from these Places into Cheshire, Lancashire, and

other

Redflotlt

Bridge.

£oo i6° Mar Hi. 73*

other Cdlintries, by Land Carriage, which, he apprehended, would go by Water Carriage, if the Communication between the West Side of the Severn and the Canal was effected by a Bridge; and that the Fair of Bridgnorth might, in such Case, be in some respect injured > —

That if a Bridge was ere died, Hops and Cyder would be immediately conveyed to the Canal, and there find a ready Conveyance by Water into Lancashire, and other Places; and that Returns down the Canal, in Coals, Maufadtories, and other Articles, out of Staffordshire, JVarwickJhi and other Places, by which Means the West Side of the Severn might be supplied with such Commodities: —

That the Price of Coals is already abated by Means of the Canal; and the Quality of the Coals brought by such Conveyance is Two Shillings a Ton better than those the Country were formerly supplied with. — Being asked, If the Produce of the West Side of the River Severn could not be conveyed into Lancashire, and other Places, without a Bridge at Redflone Ferry ? he. said, That it might; but that if those Commodities were originally consigned to Bewdley, and for the Canal, they would be first placed in a Warehouse at Bewdley, and shipped there for the Canal, and afterwards re-loaded into Canal Vessels, which would be attended with a much greater Expence: —

That there is a Colliery on the West Side of the Severn, but that the Coals (which are principally used for burning Lime) are much inferior to those brought down the Canal, out of Staffo; and that in most of the neighbouring Places it would be advantageous ta Families to buy the last mentioned Coals: —

That at present the Inhabitants on the West Side of the Severn may be supplied with Staffordshire Coal from the Canal, by conveying the same over the River in Boats, though it would be attended with Inconvenience and great Expence: —

That it would be advantageous to the Farmers, and others, who might carry Hops and Cyder from the West Side of the Severn to the Canal, if a Bridge was erected, as they could then return over it with Coal: —

That the Price of Coals at Stourport is about Eleven Shillings a Ton; and that such Price has decreased every Year since the Canal was opened: —

That Hops and Cyder might be at this Time consigned to Stourport, and conveyed there either by crossing the River at Redflone (which is rather more than a Mile from Stourport) or through Bewdley, about Seven Miles round; but the same would be attended with Inconvenience and Expence

That great Quantities of Hops and Cyder are produced in the Neighbourhood of Bromyard, which is about Twenty Miles from Bewdley, and which, (if a Bridge was erected) he apprehends would be conveyed to Stourport, with a constant Back Carriage of Coals: —

That John Glover, who is Proprietor of the Ferry at Redflone, consents to a Bridge being built there,.and has agreed to accept Five hundred and Ten Pounds for his Interest therein: —

That the Proprietors of the Land on the East Side of the Severn, who can be affected by building the intended Bridge, have given their Consent, except one Person, Sixty-eight Yards of whose Land will be necessary to be used for making an Avenue to the Bridge. And he concluded his Evidence by saying, That the building a Bridge near Redflone Ferry will be of great Public Utility. — Then

Mr. Thomas Dadford,a Surveyor, being examined,

said. That he had surveyed the Road from Redflone Ferry, to Duuley; a Plan of which he produced to your Committee: And said. He is well acquainted with the Staffordshire Canal, having had the chief Management of it for Two Year? past; that great Trade is carried of there, the Tonnage now being Two hundred Pounds per Week; atfo that, as he. apprehended, it will.increase.

to Three or Four hundred Pounds per Week, should the Bridge be built: And he confirmed Mr. White's Evidence, relating to the present Inconveniencies of the Ferry, and the Advantages which the Public would derive from the proposed Communication; and like wife as to the Consent of the Proprietors of the East Side of the River: And added, That he had examined the Bed of the River, at the Place where the Bridge is intended to be built, and found the Situation proper for that Purpose

That the River* at Low Water, is One hundred and Thirty Feet wide; and that, if a. Bridge is built agreeable to a Plan he produced to your Committee, there would be the same Space for the Water to flow or pass down the River as at present, it being intended to widen the River on each Side as many Feet as the Piers will take up in the River, and to make the Bridge as convenient as possible for the Navigation: —

That the only Impediment which the Bridge will occasion to the Navigation, is that of obliging the Vessels to lower their Mails in passing under it: —

That as much of the Road leading to the Bridge as would be overflowed by Floods, is intended to be arched over, in order to prevent any Obstructions at such Times, and that the Water may pass there as ul'ual: And he concluded by saying. It will cost about Five thousand Pounds to build the Bridge agreeable to the Plan he had produced to your Committee.

Then, to prove the Allegations of the Second, Third, and last mentioned. Petitions, Mr. George Edwards, an Owner of Vessels, being examined, said. That there is a Bridge at Bewdley, about Three Miles higher up than Redflone, which has been repaired by the Corporation of Bewdley, from Time to Time: —

That it is the common Market Road from Kidder-minster to Bewdley, and to other Parts of the Counties of Salop and Worcester: —

That the Tolls taken at Bewdley, for unloaded Horles and Carriages, are insufficient to keep the Bridge in Repair; and that, if the intended Bridge is built, the said Tolls will be greatly lessened, and the Navigation of the River hurt, because Vessels coming from cester with the Wind cannot go through in the Night: —

That a Vessel is haled from to Bewdley

(being Sixteen Miles) in about Ten Hours, and if the intended Bridge should be built, Vessels will be detained there a Night, by which they may lose the Wind, in which same the Expence would be Three Pounds or Four Pounds for a Vessel of Sixty Tons Weight, and so in proportion for larger or smaller Vessels; if the Wind blows hard, it will drive the Vessels against the Bridge in coming down; and that, at all Times, there is a Current which would carry Vessels at the Rate of Four Miles an Hour without Oars: —

That the Men who hale the Vessels say, they will not come further from Worcester than the New Bridge in a Day, unless they are paid extraordinary: —

That if the Vessels flop at Stourport, the Men will go back to IVircester, and the Owners, in such Case, myft get Men from Bewdley next Day

That be apprehended all Bridges on Rivers are prejudicial, and subject Vessels to Accidents

That at Bridgnorth Four Vessels were funk by Means

of the Bridge there; and that it is Two Hours Work to lower the Mails and raise them up again: —

That where the Bridge is intended to be built, the Current is not rapid, unless there is a Fresh in the River, which frequently happens, and without which, Vessels of Forty Tons cannot go down; that there is a Fresh of Water almost all the Winter; that, at the Place where the Bridge is intended to be built, the River, at Low Water, is generally Six Feet deep. — Then

That the Petitioners, always ready to unite in every Degree of Support necessary for the Security, Interest, and Honour, of the Nation, cannot help lamenting, with serious Concern, the frequent Toleration of Lotteries, in Time of Peace; and the Petitioners eonceive, that such a Parliamentary Right of Gaming; especially in this Trading City, is highly injurious to the Commerce of this Kingdom, and to the Welfare and Prosperity of the People, tftany of whom; from an.ideal and flattering Pfofpeft of rapidly accumulating Wealth Without the Means of honed Industry, resort to Methods of railing Money by dangerous and unwarrantable Practices, in order to become Adventurers, thereby involving themselves in a Labyrinth of Difficulties, oftentimes terminating in very distressful Consequentes; and to the Ruin of many Families: And therefore praying the House to give so important a Subject that full Consideration which the Nature of it necessarily requires, and to grant such Relief as shall be judged expedient.

A Petition of the linen Manufacturers of the North Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed, that a Committee is appointed, to enquire into the present State of the Linen Manufacture of this Kingdom; and representing to the House, that the Linen Manufacture in that Part of the Kingdom has, within these few last Years, greatly declined; and th^t the Manufacturers are at present in a most distressed Situation, and the Manufacture in Danger of being loft; which, the Petitioners apprehend, is owing to the increased Importation of Foreign Linen: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises under their Consideration, and to pass such Laws as may seem best adapted for the Encouragement of the Home Manufacture of Linen, and to give such other Relief as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to enquire into the present State of the Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland.

Ordered, That Mr. Mackworth do make the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of James Cox, Jeweller, and Citizen of London, was referred.

Mr. Mackworth accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition, and had directed a State thereof to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition is as follows;

'* 9

It appeared by the Evidence of Jasper Jay, Book-keeper to the Petitioner, that Mr. is a Jeweller in Shoe Lane, and has finished many curious and expensive Pieces of Mechanifin, ornamented with Jewels, to the Value of near £. 110,000, which are now in his MufeOm in Spring Garden.

That for about Seven Years past the Petitioner has employed from Eight hundred to One thousand Workmen, in finishing several like Pieces of Mechanism, in the Course of his Trade as a Jeweller; and during that Time has exported to the East Indies, Goods of that,

Kind, to the Amount of £.741,317, and has sold as many there as amounted to £.557,448; the Remainder having been, or being likely to be, returned upon his Hands.

That the said Museum is composed, as well of such Pieces, which have been returned from the East dies, as of others,'which were designed to be lent thither; and, being adapted to the Taste of that Part of the World, cannot be easily disposed of in the common Course of Trade; which Circumstance, together with the present Scarcity of Money, has unavoidably reduced the Petitioner and his Creditors to very great Difficulties.

Charles Grant, Esquire, who was the Petitioner’s Agent in Bengal, produced to your Committee an Account of several Consignments of Mechanical Pieces of the Sort of those composing the Museum, made to him. there from the Petitioner, to the Amount of 80,bop and upwards; and that, upon his Return, he found that the Petitioner had sent over other Goods of the same Kind, to the Amount of£. 17,000 more.

That though Goods of this Sort are much admired in ftfia, and those of the Petitioner in particular, of

greater Estimation than any other that have been sent from Europe, yet, on Account of the present Scarcity of Money in that Part of the World, several of them have not yet nor can at present be disposed of.

Alexander Jameson, Esquire, Captain of the Horsen-

den Indiaman, informed your Committee, That he has disposed of Goods in China, to the Amount of^. 36,000, on Account of the Petitioner.

That the Petitioner’s Mechanical Pieces are highly esteemed by the Chinese; and had not the Manilha Ship loft its Passage for Two Years successively, which occasioned a great Scarcity of Money in China, other Goods belonging to the Petitioner, to the Amount of £. 40,000, might have been disposed of there.

And that the Demand for such Kind of Goods has decreased in China, in consequence of the Diminution of the Trade of the East India Company with the Chinese.

And it appeared to your Committee, That the said Goods are of too great a Value to be disposed of by the common way of Sale.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enabling James Cox, Jeweller, to dispose of his Museum, commonly called Cox's Museum, by way of Chance, in such Manner as may be most for the Benefit of himself and his Creditors: And that Mr. Mackworth, Mr. Alderman Harley, and Mr. Burke, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Supply. Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Wayi »n< Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the Means. whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tuesday Morning next. Ten of the Clock.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition, is as follows;

Mr. Thomas Marfden, Clerk of the Day Rules in the King’s Bench, being examined, said, That in Trinity Term 1768 there were 338 Persons, and in the same Term 1769,413, confined in the said Prison; and But, though an Act for Release of Insolvent Debtors was passed between the Years 1769 and 1770, there were 233 Prisoners in Trinity Term 1770, and 225 in 1771, confined in the said Gaol; and that the Number of Persons confined at present therein, is 214 — That before the said Prison was re-built in 1754, the same was thought very full if more than 80 Prisoners were under Confinement therein — that there are only 84 Rooms on the Master’s Side of the said Prison, which Rooms are 9 Feet wide, by 9 Feet 6 Inches deep — that there are 24 Rooms on the Common Side, which are occupied by Prisoners in the most indigent Circumstances, who are supported by Charity; and 12 Rooms 9 Feet 8 Inches wide, by 9 Feet 5 Inches deep, on the Crown Side, for Prisoners committed for Offences; and that there are 12 Rooms in the State House for better fort of Crown Prisoners, amounting in the whole to 132 Rooms only. — That frequently many Prisoners are obliged to’lodge in One Room, which renders it very inconvenient and unwholesome to the Persons confined in the said Prison. — That on account of the Number of Prisoners always greatly exceeding the Number of Rooms in the said Prison, the Marshal has permitted many to lay in die Chapel and other improper Places; and that at this Time many are obliged to lay in the Tap Room, on the Stair-cases and Benches, by which Means they contract Disorders which often prove fatal, not only to themselves but the Prisoners in general. — That there are no separate Apartments for the Reception of Prisoners who are side, nor any Place for the Confinement of those who are riotous, nor any strong Hold for Prisoners who are committed for Capital Offences. — That the Walls of the said Prison are so very insufficient, both with respect to Height and Thickness, that Prisoners frequently escape over and through the fame; and so thin are they in some Places, that Prisoners have been known to break through in less than Half an Hour.

William Robiufin, Efauire, Secretary to the Board of Works, being examined, said, That the Walls of the present Gaol are too thin and low; — that the Rooms are too small, and so much out of Repair that the Floors of some of them are already fallen in; — that they are oonftrufted in a very inconvenient Manner, the Chimneys being so placed as not to leave proper Spaces for the Beds; — that the Area between one Part of the old Building and the other is only Thirty Feet wide; — that the present Gaol cannot Hand many Years, being built of bad Materials, and by reason of its low Situation is extremely damp, and incapable of being drained: And he produced to your Committee, a Plan of a Building which he said would be proper for the Purpose of a Gaol; as also an Estimate of the Expence, both which are annexed to the Report, N° 1 and 2; and the said Estimate is as followeth; viz.

Estimate of an additional Building, containing 70 Rooms for Prisoners, and 2 Rooms for the Sick, according to the Plan, and build a Lodge and Office £. at the Entrance of the Prison - - 5,206

A new Fence Wall round the Prison, making use of the old Bricks that are fit for the Purpose - - - 1,956

To convert the present Kitchen (being much too small for that Purpose) into a Place for the Custody of Persons committed for Capital Offences ----- 55

To convert a Room intended for the Lodge on the common Side into a Kitchen, and strengthen the Walls to D* - - - 90 -

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, William Lloyd, Esquire, being examined, said, that the Bridge over the River Towey near the Town of Llandovery, is a County Bridge; that the said Bridge lately fell down, and a new Bridge was built in the Year 1772, upon the Foundation of the old one, which is since likewise fallen down; that the County has been at the Expence of near £. 4,000 in repairing the said Bridge, and endeavouring to confine the River within a certain Channel, but to no Purpose; and he further laid, that a Bridge cannot be securely built upon the old Spot.

A Member present confirmed the aforegoing Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a new Bridge over the River Towey, near

A Petition of Sir Simeon Stuart, Baronet, Edward Pratt, Esquire, John Heaton, Esquire, and Thomas Goddard, on Behalf of themselves, and of son and Benjamin Adamson, Esquires, and also on Behalf of the other Owners and Proprietors of Fen Lands and Low Grounds, situate on the North Side of thl River, called Stoke and Hilgay River, in the County of Norfolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Year 1771, An Act passed for draining and improving the greater Part of the said Fen Lands and Low Grounds; and that the Petitioners and others have, at a very great Expence, raised Banks on the North Side of the said River, and caused several Drains and other Works to be made, by which Means the Petitioners Lands have been drained, and thereby greatly encreased in Value; and that the Petitioners ob-serve, a Bill is depending, for draining and preserving certain Fen Lands and Low Grounds, lying South of the said Hilgay and Stoke River; and that the several Works proposed to be done will, if carried into Execution, destruy the Banks before mentioned; and that the Petitioners having, by the Assistance, and under the Faith, of Parliament, drained and improved their said Estates, hope the House will not suffer the present Bill to pass into a Law, without making effectual Provision for the Preservation of the Petitioners Lands, and the Works which have been made for their Protection: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as affect their Property; and that the Owners of the Lands now proposed to be drained may not be suffered to carry into Execution any Works that may tend to the Detriment of the Petitioners; and that such further and other Provisions may be made, for the Petitioners Security, as to the House shall appear equitable and just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for draining and preserving certain Fen Lands and Low Grounds, lying in the South Level, Part of the great Level of the Fens, commonly called Bedford Level, between certain old Rivers, or Drains, called Stoke River, and Brandon River, and a certain Level or District called Feltwell New Distribi, and the Hard Lands of in Helgay, and Helgay, in the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be ah Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And

Mr. John Jones being examined, said. That the Commissioners had made a very considerable Progress in the Execution of the said Act; but find it defective, and other Powers necessary: Then,

An Act, made in the Eighth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for regulating the Nightly Watch of the said Parish, was read; whereby it appeared. That the Nightly Watch is under the Direction of the Vestry-men of the said Parish, which is found inconvenient'; that if the Nightly Watch were placed under the Management of the Commissioners appointed by the said Act of the 10th Year, with sufficient Powers, it would be of more public Utility, as the Commissioners meet regularly once a Week. — That the Water Companies ruin the Pavement, by neglecting to relay it properly, and making Use of Dirt and Dull instead of Gravel, and also omitting to relay many of the Stones they take up; and the Witness further added, That Duftmen, who do rtot contract with the Parish, take away the Dull from the real Scavenger, whereby the Price of cleansing the said Parish is enhanced; and that further Provisions and Regulations are necessary to complete the good Purposes of the said Act of the Tenth Year of His present Majesty.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending and rendering more effectual Two Acts, made. One in the Eighth, and the other in the Tenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles, and for paving, repairing, cleans-. . ing, and lighting, the Parish of Saint Mary le Bone, in

A Petition of the Trustees whose Names are there- Turnpike unto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution Three 0dUi* Acts of Parliament, One passed in the Eighth Year of the Reigrt of his Majesty King George the First, One other passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and One other passed in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, for:'repairing the Highways from the Stones End at Whitechapel Church, in ,the County of Middlesex, to Shenfidd, in the County of Essex, and the Bind of the Parish of Woodford leading to Epping, and through the Parishes of and Lam-

bourn, in the same County of Essex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the General Laws now in being, for regulating the Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, a discretionary Power is lodged in the Trustees of all Turnpike Roads, to erect any Engine for weighing of Carriages for the conveying of Goods, or Merchandize, and to take an Extra Toll of 20 s.for every Hundred Weight, which such Carriages shall, together with the Loading thereof, weigh over and above the Weights therein-mentioned; and that, although the Tolls for such Carriages, passing on the Roads under the Care of the Petitioners, are very moderate, yet they have made Use of the said Power with great Caution, and never directed any but Carriages with Four Wheels of Ids Breadth than Nine Inches so be weighed, being at first of Opinion, and now convinced from Observation, of the then continued, and still good State, of the said Roads; that the Number of Horses limited, by the said Act, to such Carnages, according to the Breadth of the Tire of their Wheels, cannot draw any Weight hurtful to the said Roads; and that the Petitioners are informed, it is proposed, by a Bill now depending, to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the General Laws now in being, for regulating the Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom; and for other Purposes; to take away the said discretionary Power, and to compel Trustees of Turnpike Roads, at all Gates, which shall have produced in the last Year the clear Income of £. 100, over and above the Collectors Salary and Wages, to cause to be erected and built such Engines, and to weigh the several Carriages therein mentioned, together with the Loading thereof, and to take the said Extra Toll for all that shall weigh more than certain Weights therein specified, but in most Cafes less than the Weights now allowed by Law; and that the Petitioners are fully convinced, from Observation and Experience, that such Engines, although the erecting, maintaining, and uling, them, is very expen-five, do not answer the good Intentions of the Legifla-ture, can have, if on any, an Effect on but a very small Part of the Turnpike ltoad; are the Cause of private Rbads being much worn, by Carriages turning out of the Turnpike Road to avoid the fame; are a great and unnecessary Check on Trade, whilst the present Regulations as to Horses and Wheels subsist; tend to make Merchandize and Provisions dearer, by an Increase of the Price of Carriage; and to put many industrious. well-meaning, and innocent Persons, to heavy Penalties, for accidentally and undclignedly carrying au Over-weight of such Goods as vary in their Weights, cannot be weighed, and will not bear the Expence of weighing: And therefore praying, That so much of the said Bill, as relates to the said Compullion and Difference of Weights, may not pals into a Law: and that either the said discretionary Power may remain in all Trustees, as under the present Law, or that an Exception may be inserted in the said Bill, as far as regards the Petitioners, and the Roads under their Care, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. .; >.

Mr. Thomas Heathfield, being examined, said. That the State of the Manufacturers in this Country is deplorable; Three-fourths of the Throwing Mills are Handing entirely still — and in some Parts of the Country they have not Employ for One-fifth of their Hands. — At Stockport (where there are large Mills which have employed 1,000 Hands) they do not at this Time employ 200; — that there are other smaller Mills at Stockport which have employed about 600 Hands, but Three-fourths of them are Handing still.- — At Macclesfield the Distress is almost as great — they used to employ from 2,500 to 3,000 Hands, but Half of those are now out of Employ. — That within a few Years past, a large Manufactory For Throwing of Silk hath been established at Blockley in Worcestershire, but almost all the Mills are now (landing still j — they used to employ there about 1,500 Hands, and there are not 300 employed at this Time in the whole Place. — At Overton in Hampshire, where another large Manufactory is eroded, they are in the same Situation, and also at Derby, Congleton, and Bruton, and in Somer-

fetshire, and Ludlow in Shropshire. — At Congleton, only One Mill is going out of or 5. — At Bruton and Wells, and at Overton.» they are almost entirely Hopped. —

In some Parts of the Country they have not Employ for One-fifth of their Hands, and even those Mills which are going, are not half worked. — And the Witness produced several Letters from Correspondents in the Country, which confirmed the1 Account above given? viz.

One from Mr. George\ tVardated Bruton, October

19th 1772, wherein' he states. That he had received the Witness’s Favour of the 13th fnstant; in Consequence of which, he had shortened his Hands o at least; but what the poor Creatures would o for Work he knew not, be pitied them with all his Heart, and would willingly work for nothing himself to serve them; but as Matters flood, did not fee any Possibility of doing it. — He hoped he should receive in due Courie the Italian the Witness mentioned, and as soon as the Witness could confidently spare him some long Silk, he should be thankful for it, as much on his People’s Account, as his own.

One other Letter from J. Franklin, Junior, dated Blockley, OQober21st 1771, letting'forth, That it would (hock him to hear the Cries of the poor Creatures, was he to attend the Scale as he did; many Women with 8 or 10 Children come crying and begging for Work ? Provisions and every Thing excessive dear, and not a. Penny to buy them a Morsel of Bread. — As to the Perjhore Hands they mull do without, till such Time as Trade gets a little better; he would not willingly quite drop them if he could help it; hoped some Time or another they will make a little Amends for his Expence and Trouble; he knew he had been at more than £. 100 Loss by them.

One other Letter from the said George Ward, dated Bruton, January 2d 1773, setting forth. That if the Witness could with any tolerable Conveniency fend him some thing by next Waggon, he would do him great Service, as he was much in Want of Work; if not, should be much obliged with an Answer by Return of Pod, when the Witness thought he might expert some from him, as the poor Creatures that did work for him were greatly distressed.

One other-Letter from Mr. J. Franklin, Junior, dated Blockley, January 6th 1773, setting forth. That life was sorry to hear Trade still continue so bad; but as it could not well be worie, he hoped it was then at. the word, and would soon mendThat he would for the present do no more than he could possibly help: — That he had taken none to the Out Towns above 2 Months, and had given none to any but them he thought the bed Hands, and even some of them was out of Work near a Fortnight before he received the last Brutia; and when the Brutia did come, it did not last above 2 Days, for as soon as the People heard Silk was come, they came in such Crouds that he was hardly from the Scale from Morning till Night for 2 Days; he gave moll of the bed Hands some, but as he gave it out in so little Quantities, luppoled he should have it all in again that Week; and he wished the Witness would (end some more Silk the next Saturday, but as the Winders had all got a little in Hand, and Trade so very dull, and the Witness such a large Stock on Hand, desired it might (lay till Saturday Sevennight before he sent it, and that the People mud make what they had serve them; prayed God to fend better Times, or there wa§ no knowing where Things would end.

One other Letter from the said J. , dated

Blockley, January 20th 1773, setting forth. That he was extremely lorry that Trade dill continued so bad; what the poor People would do he knew not, but he still lived in Hope that by the Time he had got that that he had in Hand done, he should find a Turn of Trade.

The Witness said. That Smuggling was got to such a Pitch, that foreign Goods might now be bought to any Amount, and delivered under Insurance to Gentlemen’s Houses; — being asked, How that could be prevented ? — he said, by laying a Penalty upon the Wearer, unlel’s such Wearer will give up the Vender, which might be done by Information and Summons of the Party before a Justice of the Peace, and the Wearer to be discharged upon discovering the Vender. — But to

{►revent any Insult or Attack upon the Wearer of a upposed foreign Wrought Silk, every Person should be liable to Punishment that presumed to (lop or moled any one upon that Account; — Being asked, Whether, If the Act was amended so as to authorize Cloaths to be seized upon Information in private Houses, it would not remedy the Grievance complained of? — he said. He thought it would be but small Relief, because the Informations would be few in proportion to the Goods smuggled in: — And being asked. If Silks could be sold at the usual Prices which they have been upon an Average for some Years pad, should the Importation of foreign Wrought Silks be effectually dopped ? he said. They might and cheaper, for that the East India Company within these few Years have brought (particularly from Bengal) much larger Quantities of Raw Silk than usual, and they have given Orders to increase the Quantity, which they will be able to do to the Amount of some hundred Bales in a Year; but supposing the Trade to continue in its present State, they will be obliged to dop that Importation for want of Consumption, and they have within this Year or two brought a Quantity of Raw Siik from Gillan in Perfta, by the Way of Bombay; but for want of Consumption the Prices have fell, and they have ordered no more to be brought. — -That there is now in the Warehpufes a larger Quantity of Bengal Raw Silk than has been known for many Years, which though fold and paid for, cannot be taken out. — That 1,000 Bales of Italian Raw Silk were imported lad Year, and this Year not 150 between the Months of November and April, the usual Time of Importation.

Mr. Samuel Lavprance, a Silk Manufacturer, informed your Committee, That he attended the Distribution of the Money given for the Relief of the poor Weavers out of Employ. — That or 5,000 who had no Employ had been relieved, many of which had Wives, and some two Apprentices each; — that there are full 10,000 Persons now unemployed in Spita/fields.

Being asked. If there is no other Business which they might be employed in ? — he said. They were not able to get Employ any where; that he hath been in Trade 20 Years and never knew it so bad. — That the Didress bath been coming on for some Time, owing to the bringing in of foreign Wrought SilksBeing asked,

0 V01.34,

Whether the Trade had been extended in his Time,

— he said. In Weaving of Silk it had to a small Degree, but not more than in proportion to the Consumption; — and that the Consumption in the Kingdom had been more than equal to the Increase of the Manufactory: — That he employed 100 Looms a Year ago, and does not flow employ 50. — That 6 or 7 Years ago; he employed rather more than at present, but not so many as formerly.

Upon the "whole your Committee observe, that frotii the above State of Facts, it appears to your Committee, that the Act passed in the 6th Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, prohibiting the Importation of foreign Wrought Silks and Velvets, has by no Means answered the Purposes for which it was intended, there being a very considerable Quantity of Silks and Velvets smuggled into this Country contrary to the true Intent and Meaning of the said Act. And that, in consequence of such Evasion of the La w the Silk Manufactory of England hath been greatly prejudiced, and is now reduced to a very low and declining State;

— that notwithstanding many Branches of the said Manufactory are carried on in Places didant from,

yet the Decline of Trade is equally felt in those Parts, and the Didress amongd the Workmen for want of Employ is very alarming. — That your Committee having received the Return from the Cudom House, hereunto annexed, setting forth the annual Account, of Raw and Thrown Silk imported into this Country, from the 5th January 1760 to the 5th January 1773, do find, that the Average Amount for the fird 6 Years was about 128,680, and for the lad 7 Years about 131,562; so that, upon the whole, there does not api pear to have been any considerable Extension of the Manufactory from the Quantities of Raw and Thrown Silk so imported for the Term of 13 Years before-mentioned. — And although your Committee do not apprehend that the Wear of Silks in this Country is by any Means diminished, but on the contrary (from the bed Information they could obtain) it seems to have been much increased of late Years, yet the Demand of Wrought Silk from the Manufacturer hath been lessened within these 2 or 3 Years to a Degree much beyond what has ever been known before, and the* Trade is now upon an universal Decline. — Your Committee do not find that the Prices of Silks and Velvets have of late Years been raised, but have on the contrary funk in Value, and in case the Demand could be increased for British-m3.de Silks and Velvets, some of the Manufacturers informed your Committee, that the Prices might (and probably would) be further lowered; and that, in their Opinion, the most effectual Remedy to increase the Demand would be to enforce the Act before-mentioned, by making the Wearer liable to be called upon, under proper Regulations, to discover the Vender of any foreign Wrought Silk or Velvet, and in case of llefufal, to be subject to a Penalty. — Your Committee beg Leave to observe, that from a comparative View of several Patterns of foreign Wrought Silks and Velvets with those made in this Country, the former could by no Means claim a Preference in Quality, but were less in Price, about One-fourth upon an Average. — This Difference seems to arise partly from the Duties laid upon the raw Materials, partly from the higher Price of Labour in this Country, and partly from the Smallness of the Demand, which makes a very essential Difference in the Profit to the Manufacturer; because the setting a Loom for a small Quantity only of the Produce, incurs a very considerable Loss, and much increases his Expence of Work. — Your Committee upon the whole find, that the present State of the Silk Manufactory in this Kingdom is in great Want of some parliamentary Aflidance; — that the Laws now in being, intended to support and encourage the fame, are very ineffectual; and that, being an Object of great Concern to this Country, it merits theonod serious Attention of the British Legislature.
