A Petition of John Harrison, Of Red Lion Square, Harrison* London, was presented to the House, and read; Set- Time-Piece ting forth, That, in the Year 1714, an Act passed, offering a Reward of £.10,000, for the Discovery of any Method of ascertaining the Longitude at Sea, to be paid to the Author of such Discovery, when a Ship should thereby actually fail from Great Britain to the Indies, without losing her Longitude more than Thirty Geographical Miles; and that the Petitioner, confiding in an Authority so sacred, did, in the Year 1726, abandon every other Pursuit, and has now, for near Fifty Years (for the moll Part under the immediate Inspection and Orders of the Board of Longitude) devoted his whole Time to the Accomplishment of the Purpose of the said Act; and that his Son has, in the same Confidence, spent upwards ol Twenty Years in assisting the Petitioner therein; and that in the Year 1764, it was certified by the Commissioners of Longitude, that, by Means of a Watch made by the Petitioner, a Ship had actually failed from Great Britain to the West Indies, without losing'her Longitude more than Ten Geographical Miles, whereby the Petitioner is advised, and apprehends, that his Right to the Reward promised by the said Act became absolute; and that, in the Year 1765, an Act passed, reciting the Success of the Petitioner’s Invention, to the Effect above Hated, and also that this Method of finding the Longitude may be made generally practicable, and of general Utility, if mote Watches of the same Kind can be made; and that a Moiety of the said Reward should be paid to the Petitioner upon disclosing the Principle and Construction of his Watcn, and the Remainder when more such Watches should be made, and tried, to the Satisfaction of the Board of Longitude; and that the Petitioner received the First Moiety of his Reward, and has disclosed the Principles of his Invention in so effectual a Mariner, that another Workman employed by the Board of Longitude, has thereby, without any Communication whatsoever with the Petitioner, made a Copy thereof, which, upon a Trial under the Orders of the Board of Longitude, has been proved to be a correct one j and that the Petitioner has also made another Watch, with some Improvement, which, upon a Trial of Ten Weeks, has never erred quite Miles, instead of 30 allowed by the said Act, of which the Petitioner has laid undoubted Evidence before the Board of Longitude, and is ready to produce the same to the House: And therefore the Petitioner apprehends, that it can be no longer a Matter of Doubt, that more Watches may be made, of the same Kind with that which Hands recognized, by the said Act of the 5th Year of His Majesty’s Reign, to have fulfilled the Terms of the said Act of the 12th of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and to be an effectual Method of accomplishing the Purpose thereof; and that the Petitioner has repeatedly attended the Board of Longitude for his Certificate, as other Watches have now been made and tried, and the Petitioner having done all in his Power to explain his Invention, and give Satisfaction to the Commissioners of Longitude; but, by their ltefufal to grant the Certificate, the Petitioner finds himself not only deprived of the promised Recompence of a long Life spent in the public Service, but also of the Means of establishing such a Plan for the Instruction of Workmen, by the Help of proper Engines to make the different Parts of the Watch, as alone can bring the same into general Ule: And therefore praying the House will take his same into Consideration, and restore to him his legal Right, under the Act of the 12th of Queen Anne, or give him such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Trustees impowered by an Act for repairing the several Roads mentioned in an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of his late Majesty, intituled, "An Act for enlarging the Terms " and Powers granted by several Acts of Parliament " for repairing the Highways between Sheppards Shord " and The Devizes, and from Stert Stone, in the Parish of Urchfont, to Rowd Ford, in the County of Wilts; and for changing and altering Part of the said Highways j and for repairing the Road from the " Top of Red Hone to Stert aforesaid," was pre-» fented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, after Waggons and Carriages, the Wheels whereof roll a Surface of Sixteen Inches, were permitted to pass for small Tolls, and carry unlimited Weight, the greatest Part of the Carriages travelling on those Roads have been converted to that Construction, and carry such heavy Loads, that the Petitioners find, by Experience, that to pay the Interest of 4.400 advanced on Mortgage of the Tolls granted by the said Acts, and keep the said Roads in Repair, will be impracticable; and that, if certain Clauses in a Bill, which, the Petitioners are informed, is brought into the House, whereby Carriages, whereof the W heels roll a Surface of Sixteen Inches, shall not be liable to be weighed at an Engine, which they lately caused to be erected on the said Road, but that such Carriages shall be permitted to carry unlimited Weights, and whereby Carriages drawn with Wheels of the Breadth of Sixteen Inches shall be permitted to be drawn with any Number of Horses, carry unlimited Weights, and pass Toll-free for Three Years, shall pass into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend, it will be impossible for them to pay the Interest of the Money advanced on the Credit of the said Tolls, and also to repair the Roads mentioned in the said Act; but apprehend that the said Roads will soon become*ruinous, and impafiable for any Carriages whatsoever, and that there will be no Means afterwards left of repairing the same: And therefore praying to be heard, by Counsel, against the said , Clauses, respecting the said Roads, passing into a. Law.

A Petition of the Trustees appointed in and by an Act of Parliament, made in thje Eighth Year of the Reign of Hispresent Majesty, intituled, "An Act for com " tinuing the Terms of several Acts, made in the " Thirteenth Year of King George the First, and in the " Seventeenth and Thirty-second Years of his late Mar " jesty, for repairing several Roads leading from and " through Chippenham, and from Chippenham Bridge, in

" the County of Wilts; and for amending the said Acts, " and reducing them into One Act," was also presented to the House and read Setting forth. That the Petiti-Voi: 34. *

oners have borrowed the Sum of £. 4,000 and upwards, on the Credit of the Tolls granted by the said Act, and expended the same in the Reparation of the said Roads; and the Petitioners observe, that, by a Clause in a Bill depending in the House* to explain* amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the Laws now in being, for regulating the Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, and for other Purposes, it is proposed, that Carriages having the Rollers or Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Sixteen Inches, shall be permitted to pass and be drawn upon any Highway or Turnpike Road, by any Number of Horses, Toll-free, for the Term of Three Years* to be computed from Michaelmas next; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if the said Bill, with the Clause, should pal's into a Law, that they shall not be able to keep the said Roads in Repair, and to pay the Interest of the Monies now due on the Credit of the Tolls granted thereon: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Clause passing into a Law, with respect to the said Road described by the said Act.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of John Grant, appointed by the East India Company a Major in the East Indies, and Secretary to General Coote on his last Expedition to India, On Behalf of David Mackenzie, in Bengal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, having perused the Report made by the Committee of Sefcrecy, (in Wednesday the 24th Day of March last) finds that the Conduct of a British Subject (not named in the Report, but who, from the Circurnstances of the same as there reported, appears to be Captain David Mackenzie, Brother-in-law to the Petitioner) is there refledled on in the moll affecting Manner; and the Petitioner therefore begs Leave to acquaint the House of the following Fads, for their Consideration: That the Petitioner was in Bengal, when the Charges of Op. predion exhibited against Captain Mackenzie were first framed; and that they were made in consequence of a Representation, which the Petitioner exhibited against Messieurs Laurel and Purling in particular, and which, from the Defence of the latter, extended to the whole Board of Revenue, for collusive Practices in letting the Lands at Rungpore; and that those Informations the Petitioner had obtained through the Means of Captain Mackenzie-, and that in consequence, Captain Mackenzie was brought to a General Court Martial, the President whereof. Major Morgan, is now in England and that, after long Deliberation, the Charges exhibited at the Court Martial were confined to some frivolous. Points of Duty; and that Captain Mackenzie frequently and repeatedly, by Word, by Letter, and at the Court Martial, called on the Gentlemen who had threatened him with those Charges of Oppression (in order to flop the Petitioner’s Complaint) to bring those Ac-cufations publicly in the Face of his Country, that he might be acquitted or condemned by an open and legal Trial; and that Mr. Alexander, who was the Chief of the Board of Revenue, and signed the Charges against Captain Mackenzie, -refused to attend the Court Mar-

tial; nor was it till after various Negociations of Ten Days that he would appear, although on the Spot; v and that no AccuCition of Opprefiion was stated to the Court Martial, npr did any appear on Evidence; and with respect to all the other Charges, Captain Mackenzie was fully acquitted by the Court Martial; and that the Cause assigned, for not exhibiting the Charges of Opprefiion against Captain Mackenzie at the Court Martial, was, that those A^dls were not cognizable before such a Court; whereas, in Truth, a General Court Martial was the only proper Court before which they could be tried, beyond the Limits of the Charter; and they were fully within the Words and Construe-tion of the Articles of War; and that instead of a fair and legal Trial, the Board of Revenue (who flood accused) proceeded to examine into those Complaints against Captain Mackenzie, the Petitioner against Messieurs Laurel and Purling being first imprisoned, and afterwards Myrza HuJJ'ein, the former Aumil or Civil Governor of Rungpore, during the Time that those Op-pressions were said to have been committed, was confined to his House, by Order of Mahomed Reza this Man was Captain Mackenzie's principal Evidence; and must, from the Nature of his Station, have been best acquainted with the Fads; and it was the Duty of the Board to have compelled his Attendance; and that, notwithstanding the severe Indisposition of Captain Mackenzie, rendering him unable to Hand, as con-

sessed by Mr. Middleton himself, in a Representation he^tnade to the Governor,- the Board of Revenue still proceeded to take ex parte Examinations; and that, when Captain Mackenzie was able to stir, and desired to produce his Witnesses in Exculpation, he was denied that Right; and that Major Morgan was ready then, and is ready to testify now, that from the Nature of the Military Subordination at the Out Settle-

ments to the Chief of the District, it was impossible those Severities could have flowed from Captain r-enzie,e\en supposing the y had existed; and that the chief Complaints against Captain Mackenzie were from Men indebted to him,; who, so far from - paying exorbitant Interest, have always refused to pay the Principal; and that_ in general it is a notorious Fact, that; when the Terrors of Government, by Imprisonment and other Severities, are held out on the one Hand, and Favours on the-other, in the arbitrary Government of any Depositions that are wished for may be obtained; and where the Parties, accused preside as Governors,'and fit as the Judges, we may expect a Decision correspondent to such incongruous Proceedings; and that the Petitioner, having wrote the Purport of the foregoing Petition, by Way of Letter, dated the 15th of February last, to the Chairrtiah of the Committee of Secrecy, the Petitioner expected that himself and -Major Morgan would have been examined by the said Committee, respeaing the said Charges, in case the said Committee thought proper to report upon them > but hitherto neither of them have been summoned to appear before the said Committee: And therefore praying, That he may be permitted, by his own and other Evidence, to dojustice to the Character of Captain;

and to set forth to the House, the Source and Spring of the Prosecution which has been carried on against him.

The House was moved. That so much of the Report, which, upon Wednesday the 24th Day of March last, was made from the Committee of Secrecy (appointed to enquire into the State of the East India Company; and, for that Purpose, to inspect the Books and Accounts of the said Company; and to report to the House what they find material therein, in respect to the Debts, Credits, and Effects, of the Company* as also to the Management and present Situation of the Company’s Affairs; together with their Observations thereupon) as relates to the Conduct of one of His Majesty’s British Subjects employed in the East India Company’s Service, in Bengal, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That so much of the said Report as (in order to shew to the House in what Manner many of the Abuses stated in the said Report still exist in Bengal) contains Charges made in India against a British Subject there (the Enquiry into which was not finished when the last Ships were dispatched from Bengal) be re-committed;

A Member returned upon a new Writ, having taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration; and having delivered in to the Clerk of the House an Account of his Qualification, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Qualification; according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The Question was put, That so much of the said Report as (in order to shew to the House in what Manner many of the Abuses stated in the said Report still exist in Bengal) contains Charges made in India against a British Subject there (the Enquiry into which was not finished when the last Ships were dispatched from Bengal) be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table* until the said Report be taken into Consideration.

Turnpike A Petition of the Trustees appointed to repair the Roads. District of Road leading from the West End of

Street, in the County of Wilts, to the Herse and Jockey', in the Parish of Box, in the said County, by virtue of an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said District of Road is- the high arid most frequented Road from the City of London to the Cities of Both and Bristol, lies in an inclosed Country, the Soil whereof is of a deep Clay, and Materials are lb scarce, that the Petitioners are obliged to fend many Miles for the lame; and that, after Waggons and Carriages, the Wheels whereof roll a Surface of Sixteen Inches, were by Law permitted to pass for small Tolls, and carry unlimited Weights, most of the Carriages travelling on that District: were, and are, converted to that Construction, and carried, and still carry, such enormous Loads, that the Petitioners found it was impossible for them, after paying the Interest of £. 4,400 on the Mortgage of the 'l olls, to-keep the said District in Repair; and that the utmost Frugality and (Economy has been used, in procuring Materials, and employing Workmen, in Repair of the said Turnpike Road; and that, if a certain Ckufe, in a Bill, which the Petitioners are informed is brought into the House, whereby Carriages, the Wheels whereof roll a Surface of Sixteen Inches, shall not be liable to be weighed at an Engine which the Petitioners may ered on the faic} District of Road, but that such Carriages shall be at Liberty to carry unlimited Weights, and whereby the Tolb of such Carriages will be greatly reduced, or whereby Carriages drawn with Wheels, the Fellies whereof are of the Breadth of Sixteen Inches, shall be permitted to be drawn with any Number of Horses, carry unlimited Weight, and pass Toll-free, for Three Years, the Petitioners apprehend, it will be impossible for them to pay the Interest of the Money advanced on Mortgage of the said Tolls, and -also repair the said District of Road; but, the Petitioners apprehend, the said District of Road will inevitably become impafiable for Carriages of any Kind whatsoever: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by Counsel, against the said Clause, respecting the aforesaid District, passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Bast India. Mr. Bacon, according to Order, reported from the Affairs. Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to take into Consideration the Affairs of the East India Company, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, for effectually relieving the East India Company under their present Difficulties, the Supply of a considerable Sum of Money will be necessary.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Method bed calculated for giving the requisite Relief to the Company, without impairing the Security of their Creditors, and without Detriment to the State of Credit in general, would be, that such Sum of Money should be advanced by the Public to the Company.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Sum of One million Four hundred thousand Pounds will be sufficient for the present Relief of the Company.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That it may be expedient for the Public, to advance to the Company the said Sum of One million Four hundred thousand Pounds; provided, at the same Time, due Care be taken to secure, by proper Regulations, the future good Government of the Company’s Affairs.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in case a Sum of Money shall be advanced by the Public, for the Relief of the East India Company, the Company ought to be restrained from increasing their Dividend beyond Six Pounds per Centum per,

until such Money shall have been repaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in case a Sum of Money shall be advanced by the Public, for the Relief of the East India Company, the Company ought to be restrained from increasing their Dividend beyond Seven Pounds per Centum per until their Bond Debt shall be reduced to One million Five hundred thousand Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it may be for the mutual Benefit of the Public and the East India Company, that the Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues lately obtained in India, should, under proper Restrictions and Regulation?, remain in the Possession of the Company, during aTerm not exceeding Six Years, to commence from the Expiration of the present Agreement between the Public

paid upon the Importation of such Teas.

Resolved,' That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Provi’fion be made, for impowering the Commissioners of the Treasury to grant Licences to the East India Company, to export Teas to the Plantations in America, or to Foreign Parts; provided that, at the Time of taking out such Teas for Exportation,-there be left remaining in the Company’s Warehouses a Quantity of Tea not less than Ten millions of Pounds Weight; and that, upon all Teas which shall be so exported, a Drawback be allowed, of all the Duties of Customs paid upon the Importation of such Teas, and an Exemption from the Inland Duties charged thereupon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, upon all Bohea Teas, which shall be purchased at any of the East India Company’s Public Sales after the loth Day of May 17.73, in Lieu of the Deposit of Forty Shillings, payable by the Act of the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of King George the Second, a Deposit be made of Four Pounds, for every Chest of such Bohea Tea.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the Three last of the said Resolutions: And that Mr.

A Petition of the Grand Jury, and other Gentlemen Wa]K. and Clergy, of the County of Anglesey, was presented to Vexatious the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to Guitj. discourage the Practice of commencing frivolous and vexatious Suits in His Majesty’s Courts at in Causes of Action arising within the Dominion of Wales; and for further regulating the Proceedings in the Courts of Great Sessions in Wales; and Setting forth.

That, by the perpetual Statute of Incorporation of England and Wales, of the Twenty-seventh Year of King Henry the Eighth, the Dominion of Wales was for ever to continue to be united, incorporated, and annexed to the Kingdom of England-, and the Inhabitants of Wales to enjoy all the Freedoms, Liberties, Rights, Privileges* and Laws, which the People of England enjoyed; whereby the Liberty and Privilege of commencing Actions in the Courts at Westminster, for Causes arising within the said Dominion, was confirmed to th&n; and that, the Courts at Westminster having Four Terms in the Year for the transading of Business, and the Courts of Great Sessions in Wales only Two, of Five Days each, the Inhabitants of Wales prefer the Courts at Westminster to those of the Great Sessions, for the better and speedier Recovery of their Demands, more especially in Cafes of Special Pleading; and as the Costs of prosecuting Actions.in the Courts at Westminster do not exceed those of the Great Sessions, the Inhabitants of Wales ought not to be restrained from commencing Actions in the Courts at Westminster, but that the English Circuits ought rather to be extended to Wales, so that the Inhabitants thereof may fully enjoy the Liberties and Privileges intended by the said Act -, and that, the Welsh being the only Language ljpoken in common within the Dominion of Wales, great Inconveniencies will arise, in providing proper Juries for trying Causes in the Enrlish j Language;

A Petition of the Clothiers and Manufacturers of Line* Trade, Devonshire Kersey, and Plain Cloth, was presented to &c* the House, and read; Setting forth. That their Manufactory is greatly reduced; and that consequently the Consumption of Wool, the Growth of this Kingdom, is proportionably lessened, to the great Injury of the Farmer and Landholder; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the great Decay of this Branch of the Staple of England, is materially injured by the great Consumption of Russia Drabs, and other Low Foreign Linens, which is well known to be substituted by Numbers of the lower Class of People, in lieu of the Woollen and Linen Manufactures of this Kingdom: And therefore praying; That such an additional Duty may be laid on Low Foreign Linens, as will prevent the ill Corifequences of farther lessening and reducing both the Woollen and Linen Manufactory of England, or in such other Way as the House shall see fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to enquire into the present State of the Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the United Company of Merchants East India of England, trading to the East Indies, was presented Company — to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Pe- *-oan-titioners observe, with the greatest Concern, That some of themost material Articles of the Propositions, which they presented to the House on the Second Day of March last, are substantially rejeited, by the Resolutions of this House on the 27th of last Month; and the Petitioners conceive, that, after the Loan which they presumed to request from Parliament (not less for the Credit of the Public than their own) shall shall be fully discharged, it seems unreasonable to require any further Terms on Account of the said Loan; and that the Limitation of the Company’s Dividend to Seven per Cent, after the Discharge of the said Loan, until their Bond Debt shall be reduced to One million Five hundred thousand Pounds, appears to the'

Petitioners to be a Limitation not founded upon any just Calculation of the Company’s Commercial Profits;

nor

Call of the House.

096 30 Mail. A. 1773.

nor can it with Reason be alledged, that it is necessary, either to their Credit, or that of the Public, that they should be so restrained, as the additional Dividend of One per Cent, contained in the Company’s Propositions, though an ObjeCV of considerable Con* sequence to the Proprietors, could be no material Delay to the Reduction of their Bond Debt; and the Petitioners submit to the House, that the Hardship of this Limitation is exceedingly aggravated by a Consideration of the great Losses which they, as Proprietors, have sustained, and the Expences they have incurred* in acquiring and securing the Territorial Revenues in India, at the Rilk of their whole Capital, while the Public have reaped such great Advantages; more especially as they received repeated Assurances from their late Chairman, that the Intentions of the Chancellor of the Exchequer were totally different in this Respect; upon the Faith of these Assurances, the Proposals which have been made th^ Ground of the said restrictive Resolutions were offered by the Company to Parliament; Restrictions which they cannot but consider as peculiarly hard upon Men who have already suffered so much; and representing to the House, that the Resolution, limiting the Company to a Term not exceeding Six Years, for the Possession of their Territories in India, appears to be altogether arbitrary, as it may be construed into a conclusive Decision against the Company, respecting those Territorial Pof-sessions to which they infill they have an undoubted Right; a Right against which no Decision exists, nor any formal Claim has ever been made; and that the Petitioners cannot acquiesce in the Resolution, whereby Three Fourth Parts of the Surplus Nett Profits of the Company at Home above the Sum of Eight per Cent, per Annum upon their Capital Stock, should be paid into the Exchequer, for the Use of the Public, and the remaining Fourth Part be applied, either in further reducing the Company’s Bond Debt, or for composing a Fund, to be set apart for the Use of the Company in case of extraordinary Emergencies; because such Disposal of their Property, otherwise than by their own Consent, by a general Description, comprehending their Trade as well as Revenues, does not appear warranted, even by the largest Pretensions that have ever been formed against them; and that when the Petitioners offered a Participation in a different Proportion of the said Surplus, it was in a full Assurance that they might freely enjoy the Remainder; and that the Limitation prescribed by the said Resolution, respecting the Application of the One Fourth Part allotted them in such Participation, after Payment of all their simple Contract Debts, and after reducing their Bond Debt to the Point of Credit which the House has fixed, appears to the Petitioners to be so subversive of all their Rights and Privileges, by denying them the Disposal of their own Property, after all their Creditors shall be fully secured according to Law, that, rather than submit to such Conditions (as proceeding from their own Consent expressed or implied) they declare to the House their Desire, that any Claims against the Possessions of the Company, that can be supposed to give Rife to such Restrictions, may receive a legal Decision; from which whatever may be the Event, they will at least have tire Satisfaction of knowing what they may call their own-: And therefore praying the House will not annex such Terms to- the Loan proposed by the East India Company, as will tend to weaken the good Faith and Confidence which the Subjects of this Country ought ever to have in the Justice of the Legislature.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That tire Order of the Day, for the Call of the House, be now read.

Mystery of Goldsmiths of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for appointing Wardens and Assay Mailers, for alfaying Wrought Plate in the Towns of Sheffield and Birmingham; and Setting forth, That moll of the Plate that is made in those Towns, is made or stamped with Dies; and that their chief Employment is in plating or covering bale Metal with Silver; and that the Power of allaying and marking Wrought Plate is too great and important a Trull to be committed to Persons in Places where the same is likely to be abused, or to be prejudicial to the Public; and that the Petitioners are appre-lienfive, that, if the said Bill should pals into a Law, it will greatly iacrease, the Number of Frauds in Wrought Plate, and render the Detection of such Frauds more difficult: A.nd therefore praying. That they may be Heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ditto. A Petition of John Harrison being offered to be presented to the House:

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been* informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, from a natural Inclination to the Study and Improvement of Mechanic Art, and from a Conviction that Machines may be so constructed as to ascertain the Longitude at Sea (for doing which great Encouragement was held out by the Public) hath neglected every lucrative Pursuit, and devoted with the closell Attention his whole Life from the Year 1727, and that of his Son for near 30 Years pad, to the Invention of such a Machine as might be lead; affected by any Difference of Climate or Weather, and, by keeping equal Time, attain the desirable Purpose of ascertaining the Longitude at Sea, and give additional Security, as well to the Marine as to the Commerce of thele Kingdoms; and that the Petitioner conceives he hath succeeded in this Pursuit, having constructed several Machines, the lad of which (a Watch) on a Trial to the tVefi Indies, did not vary its Time in the Passage

more than Forty Seconds, or Ten Miles; and that the Petitioner hath received, from the Public Bounty, several Sums of Money for his Support, under the very great Expence incurred in thele repeated Researches; and that he is now upwards of Fourscore Years old; and that both himself and his Son, wholly intent on this Object, have precluded themselves from the ordinary Means of providing for their Families; and that the Petitioner, disabled by his great Age from constructing other Machines in Conformity to the Act of the Fifth of His present Majesty, has communicated his Invention to other able Mechanics, and reds his Pretensions on the Bounty of Parliament, praying such Affidarice«as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the several Accounts presented to this House, in this Session of Parliament, relating to the Linen Manufacture, which have not been already referred to the Committee appointed to enquire into the present State of the Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for better regulating the Assize and Making of Bread, was re-committed, be taken into further Consideration upon Wednesday Morning next.

Mr. Speaker,

Exeter The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act Roads, &c. for more efledtually amending several Roads leading from the City of Exeter; and for re-building or repairing Exe Bridge, and making the Avenues leading thereto more commodious; and for building a Bridge over the River Exe, at or near Countess;

and for amending several other Roads therein mentioned; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Road from the North Turnpike Road near Scot Gate, otherwise Sco Gale, in the Town of Stamford, in the County of Lincoln, to Oakham, in the County of Rutland, and from Oakham, through Burley, to a Gate on the North Side of a certain Close, in the said Lordship of Burley, called Booth's Close, adjoining to the open Fields of Coltefmore, in the said County of Rutland; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging and altering the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for repairing the Roads leading from the Market House in Stourbridge, and other Roads therein mentioned, in the Counties of Worcester, Stafford, Salop, and Warwick, respectively; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for draining and preserving certain Fen Lands and Low Grounds, lying in the South Level, Part of the Great Level of the Fens, commonly called Bedford Level, between certain old Rivers or Drains, called Stoke River and Brandon River, and a certain Level or District, called Feltwell New DiflriB, and the Hard Lands of Woodhall, in Helgay, and Helgay, in the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk; without any Amendment r And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the several Open Fields, within the Township and rarish of Dr ad, in the West Riding of the County of York; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to allow a Drawback of the Duties of Customs, on the Exportation of Tea to any of His Majesty’s Colonies or Plantations in America; to encrease the Deposit on Bohea Tea, to be sold at the India Company’s Sales; and to impower the Commissioners of the Treasury to grant Licences to the East India Company to export Tea Duty free} without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for Sale of certain Charity Estates therein mentioned; and for applying the Money to arise therefrom, in the building of a Town Hall and Shambles, in the Town of Newark upon Trent; and in the purchasing of Lands and Hereditaments, for enlarging the Church Yard of the said Town, and for opening the Avenues thereto; and for laying out the Residue of the Money in purchasing other Lands, to be settled to the charitable Uses therein mentioned; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

Resolved, That all Acquisitions, made under the In* fluence of a Military Force, or by Treaty with Foreign Princes, do of Right belong to the State.

Resolved, That to appropriate Acquisitions so made, to the private Emolument of Persons entrusted with any Civil or Military Power of the State, is illegal.

A Motion was made, and the Question being pfo* posed, That very great Sums of Money, and other valuable Property, have been acquired in Bengal, from Princes, and others of that Country, by Persons eti-trusted with the Military and Civil Powers of the State; which Sums of Money and other valuable Pro* perty have been appropriated to the private Use of such Persons;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by inserting, after the Word " State" and before the Word " which," the Words " by means of " such Powers."

Resolved, That very great Sums of Money, and other valuable Property, have been acquired in Bengal, from Princes, and others of that Country, by Persons eri-trusted with the Military and Civil Powers of the State, by Means of such Powers; which Sums of Money and valuable Property have been appropriated to the private Use of such Persons.

4

the Petitioner, and Several other Gentlemen having Lands in that Neighbourhood; and that the said Trustees have of late caused a Turnpike Gate, which for many Years flood at a considerable Distance from Leeds, to be set up so near the said Town, that all Persons residing at Holbeck and HunJIet, and l'cveral other Towns and Places, are compelled to pay a full Toll for going only about 250 Yards upon the said Road: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confederation, and that Provision may be made in the said Bill, for restraining the said Trustees from diverting the Course of the present Road near the said Town of Leeds, and for compelling them to take down the present Turnpike, and that the same may be removed to the Place where it formerly flood at; and that

A Petition of the Right honourable John Earl of Sandwich, and the humble Petition of Sir Charles Hardy, Knight, Governor of the Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Greenwich, in the County of Kent, and several others Commissioners and Governors of the said Hospital, in General Court assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by several Acts of Parliament, the forfeited and unclaimed Shares of Prizes taken from the Enemy were given and appropriated to, and for the Support and Maintenance of, the said Hospital; and that, during the late Wars with and Spain, many Ships, Vessels, Goods, and other Merchandize, belonging to and Spanish Subjects,

and of very considerable Value, were taken, and made Prizes, by His Majesty’s Ships, and carried into different Ports, in the Plantations and Colonies in America, the West Indies, and the Leeivard Islands, and were con-ligned to Agents there, for Condemnation and Sale; and that such Agents did procure such Ships, Vessels, Goods, and other Merchandize, to be condemned, and caused Sale thereof to be made, and did obtain Bills for Bounty Money given to the Captors of Ships of War, and received the Money mentioned in such Bounty Bills; and that such Agents did pay to many of the Captors their Shares of the Produce of such Captures, but have detained in their Hands the forfeited and unclaimed Shares of such Prizes, to a very considerable Amount; and that several Bills have been exhibited,-in the Court of Chancery of the Island of Jamaica, against several of the said Agents, for a Discovery of the Captures which have been sold by such Agents, and to compel Payment of the forfeited and unclaimed Shares thereof, to the Treasurer of the said Hospital, for the Benefit thereof; and the several Defendants to such Bills having demurred thereto, such Demurrers have been over-ruled; and thereupon the Defendants have appealed to His Majesty in Council; and some of those Appeals, for want ol Prosecution, have been dismissed; and the Defendants having thereupon put in insufficient Answer to such Bills, Exceptions have been taken thereto; and, on allowing such Exceptions, the Defendants have again

Richmond ',in the County of Surrey, to the opposite Shore, in the County of Middlesex and to enable His Majesty to grant the Inheritance of the Ferry at Richmond to certain Persons to be therein mentioned; and Setting forth, That the Petitioner, as Assignee of William Windham, Esquire, is Lessee of the said Ferry, by virtue of Letters Patent from the Crown, for Two Terms, of which about Twenty-five Years are yet to come; for the Purchase of which, the Petitioner ptiid a veiy large Sum of Money; and that the Grant of the said Ferry was originally made by the Crown, and has been constantly renewed in Consideration of a small Fine; and that the Application to the House for the said Bill has been carried on without any Communication with the Petitioner; and that, should the said Bill pass into a Law, the same cannot be carried into Execution, as the Tolls will not be sufficient to defray the Expence thereof; and representing to the House, that the Property of the Petitioner in the said Ferry will be greatly depreciated thereby; and that the proposed Bridge, from its Situation, can never be used by Travellers in general, but by the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Villages only: And therefore praying, That the Petitioner may be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the same may not pals into a Law, until such Time as the Petitioner has a Compensation for the Loss he will thereby sustain.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Upon the whole Matter, Your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws now in force are insufficient to compel the Agents for Prizes taken in the late War, by His Majesty’s Ships of War, and carried into the Plantations and Colonies in America, to account for and pay the forfeited and unclaimed Shares of such Prizes, which, by leVeral Acts of Parliament, are appropriated to the Use of the Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Greenwich.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, That Leave be giveri to bring in a Bill.for the better fecufing to the Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Greenwich, all forfeited and unclaimed Shares of Prize Money remaining in the Hands of Agents, in any of His Majesty’s Colonies and Plantations in America, the West Indies, and Leeward Islands; and to compel the more speedy Payment thereof.

Appendix, Ns 1.

SIR,

In our Letter of the 7th of November, we took the Liberty to inform you, and the honourable Commissioners and Directors of the Royal Hospital at,

that the Demurrers put in to Two of thd Bills filed in the Court of Chandery, on Behalf of the Hospital, against the Executors of George Papley, and the Demurrer filed in like Manner by Mr. Patrick Lynch, were over-ruled, and the several Defendants ordered to put in then: Answers without Delay; but that they had appealed from the Chancellor’s Decree to the King in Council; the Appeal Papers, on Behalf of the Hospital, were soon after forwarded.

We acknowledged, at the same Time, the Receipt of His Majesty’s Order in Council, for dismissing the Appeal of Jasper Hall. — We have now. Sir, to acquaint you, and the honourable Directors, that, in consequence of such Dismission, this Gentleman has since been compelled to give in his Answer; which, however, being altogether evalive and insufficient, we prepared Exceptions thereto, and our Exceptions having been lately argued before a Master of the Court, were every one of them allowed, and a Report was returned by the Master accordingly — But Mr. to give all the Obstruction, and to create all the Delay which Chicanery can invent, has lodged Exceptions ro the Matter’s Report, intending, without Doubt, in case he is defeated in this Particular, and ordered to give in a further Answer (as he certainly will, when the Matter comes to be argued before the Chancellor) to appeal once more to the King In Council; in which same he will most undoubtedly be followed by the other Defendants, who regularly tread in this Gentleman’s Steps. By this Means a further Delay will be obtained of at least Sixteen Months, and even then,.Qthci Appeals may be made from every subsequent Order of the Court; lo that we venture to pronounce it scarct possible, by the present Mode of Proceeding, to obtain a final Depree against any of the Parties within the Space of Ten or Twelve Years, not to mention the additional Delay which the Death of any of the Parties, rpay create; and yet. Sir, we can lafely affirm, that no. Attention is wanting on our Parts; that every Proceeding has beetl pushed forward with the utmost Vigour, and proper, and even liberal. Encouragement given to the Lawyers concerned on Behalf of the Hospital. But, though- it is a Grievance to the Hospital of a very serious and alarming Nature, that a 'Set of Men should have the Power to detain such large Sums

i3 Ge6. III.

2i Maii.

327

in their Hands for such a Length of Tithe (not lets, we presume, than Thirty or Forty thousand Pounds Sterling) and probably, in the End, from the Fluctuation of Property in this Island, to defraud the Hospital of the Whole, yet we doubt, if any Thing less than the Interpolation of Parliament can remedy so great an Evil.

We presume not to prescribe to the Hospital; but we would beg Leave humbly to give it as our Opinion, that the Penalties inflicted by the Laws now in Force, on the Prize Agents neglecting to make out, and render the Accounts, of the Produce and Payments of Prizes, within the Times limited (especially those Prizes on which there are Monies remaining after the Space of Three Years) are neither sufficiently severe nor coercive, to answer the good Purposes for which they were intended. In FaCl, the Legislature did net leem aware what very large Sums might remain in the Hands of the Colony Agents, nor foresee, that in all Cases of Appeal from the Plantations, it mull necessarily happen, that a very considerable Number of private Shares mull remain unclaimed beyond the Time limited. — We should conceive therefore, were the Supreme Court, or feme other Jurisdiction in each Colony, upon Complaint, on Oath of the Treasurer of the Hospital, or his Deputy (in which Oath might be enumerated, from the Records of the Court of Vice Admiralty, the Names of the Vessels condemned, Three Years previous to such Application) empowered to order the several Agents complained of to deliver over, within a certain Time, the Accounts of the Disposal of such Vessels, on Oath, to the Clerk, or other proper Officer of the Court, for the Inspection of the Treasurer or his Deputy, on Pain (in case of Refusal) of Commitment without Bail; that this, or some other such summary Method of Proceeding, would be much more effectual than the Penalties now in Force. The Hospital would, at least, in this Cafe, have an immediate and certain Foundation for future Proceedings; the great Difficulty we at present labour under being to ascertain the Money really due for want of the Accounts j for, having once established the Sum, a Judgment or Decree may be obtained thereon without any great Difficulty, and with little Delay. We think it all'p of high Importance to the Hospital, and a Kind of Penalty in itself, that the several Agents should be compelled to pay the legal Interest of the Colony, on all Monies detained in their Hands from and after the Expiration of the Three Years.

But all this, Sir, we mention with great Submission to superior'Judgments; observing only, that it appears to us, some Steps are absolutely necessary to be taken, beyond the common Mode of Proceeding, as well for the Benefit of the Hospital, in recovering the Monies now due, as for its Security against the like Conduct in future Agents.

We have the Honour to be, with great Respect, Sir,

Your most faithful,

and obedient Servants, Jamaica, £.

'Appendix, N* 2.

SIR,

Having done myself the Honour, some Time ago, to lay before you a Sketch of tire Proceedings carrying on in Chancery, for the Recovery of the unclaimed Shares of Prize Money forfeited to the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, and Hill remaining in the Hands of the

Agents in this Island, I now beg Permission to submit to your Perusal and Consideration fotne Fads, which the Gentleman concerned with me, and myself,"have thought it necessary tp slate to the honourable Commissionerp and Dicedprs, jn a Letter to the Treasurer, of which ' Van. 34* '

the inclosed is'a Copy; prfifutning, Sir, to hope (if the Circurftstancest which we relate, and our Reasoning thereon, shall appear deserving the Attention of the Hospital) that you will be pleased to honour us so far with your Countenance and Support, as to give our Representa-tionr that Weight, which they cannot fail to have, when strengthened and enforced by the concurrent Sentiments of a Gentleman of Sir George Rodney's Distinction and Character.

To restrain the irregular Afledions of Men, in Proportion to the Impulse of Temptation, is perhaps a Talk too hard for human Wisdom; but, if the great End of Legislation be to guard against the Imperfections of human Nature, by wholesome Regulations, and to apply new Remedies for growing Evils, I prelume to say, that the Interpolation of Parliament is as loudly called for, on the present, as on any Occasion whatever. That the Penalties inflicted on the Agents for a direct Violation of the Laws, are inadequate effect any salutary Purpose, mull readily be admitted, when it is considered, that an Agent refujtng to deliver his Accounts (without which we are obliged to have Recourse to the flow Proeefs of Chancery, obstruded by almost endless Appeals) forfeits only One hundred Pounds; while, by this very Refusal, he has the Means of detaining in his Hands (perhaps for Twenty Years) half as many Thousands. What has happened in Times past, it is easy to suppose, Sir, may happen in Times to come. When the Temptation is powerful, and the Penalties are disproportioned, some new Expedient is obviously necessary. I need not observe to you, Sir, that most of the Prizes taken in this Part of the World are of greiat Value, nor that the Unbealthiness of this Climate, its Distance from the Mother Country, and the Delay in all Cases of Appeal, from a Combination of Circumstances, whence jt will unavoidably happen, that very considerable Sums of Money must remain in the Hands of the Agents, till the same becomes forfeited to tire Hospital; but I would beg Leave to remark, that, independent of the Temptation which too often arises in the Minds of Men of loose Principles, on the Possession of large Sums (which perhaps they consider as something less sacred than private Property) to convert a Part thereof to their own Emolument, there are local Motives that influence the Conduct of the Colony Agents in a particular Manner. Ip a Country where a Notion prevails almost generally, that a Sugar Estate, under good Management, makes greater Returns for the Capital than any other Kind of Property, every Man is tempted to become an Adventurer in the Saif: Hence it is, that the Prize Agents, alipost to a Man, instead of paying the Hospital, apply the Money to th,e Purchase of Lands, expecting perhaps (though they should admit, which I believe tew of them do, that in the long Run they may be obliged to refund with Interest) to make in the mean while Twenty per Cent, per Annum of that Money, for the Use of which they pay only Six. But, in Fact, they cannot be compelled to pay Six per Cent, (the legal Intcrell of the Colony) even if Interest be ultimately recovered j for, from the Failure of paying such Interest annually, according to the Intention, and Custom of Loans, they must necessarily profit a Third in every Seven Years, by paying k in the Aggregate, at the Determination of such Periods. So that what should operate as a Penalty, becomes an additional Encouragement; what should effect a Remedy, aggravates the Injury !

But what, Sk, shall we think of the Honour and Honesty of the Agents, who, in the Answers which they have severally exhibited in Chancery, absolutely deny that they are subject to any Interest whatever ?

That Agents have been influenced by the Motjves above suggested, I can aflfett, from the Authority of One of themselves. This Gentleman offered to give Bond?, payable at distant Periods, for the Balance due from him, which he candidly admitted was several thousand

Pounds;

3^8 2i°Mail 1773-

pounds; but on being told ’twas not in the Power of the Persons acting for the Hospital, to give the Indulgence he proposed, he positively refused coming to a Settlement) or to produce his Accounts; intimating, that he could obtain more Time in the Courts of Law, before the Debt could be ascertained, than he required for its Discharge, in case his Proposals were accepted.

And yet, Sir, the Delay, incidental to the present Mode of Proceeding, bears no Proportion to the Hazard which the Hospital is expoled to from the Priority Laws of this Bland; according to which, the Creditor, who first lues and obtains Judgment, has a Preference and Superiority over all the other Creditors, and must first be paid, whether are sufficient for the junior Creditors or not, and so on with the other Creditors, according to the Order of Time in which their Judgments were severally obtained.; Hence it is no uncommon Thing for a Debtor to admit Judgment, on the Prornife that the Writ of Execution shall not be issued, but lodged only, from Time to Time, for the Purpose of maintaining its Priority; and should a Writ of Execution be issued in the mean while on a junior Judgment, and a Levy made in Consequence thereof, the Provost Marshal is bound to apply the Proceeds of such Levy to the Discharge of the prior Judgment in the first Place, and the Surplus, if any, is applicable to the next in Priority, except where there are several Judgments on the same Footing. The Court of Chancery (which indeed cannot, as I conceive, contravene the positive Acts of the Legislature) regulates its Adjudications in the same Manner, and its Decrees for the Sale of Property, for the Discharge of Debts, always direct the Payments to be made in due Course of Priority} so that, perhaps, while one Creditor gets fully paid, another loses every Shilling. Wither this Law operates to the general Benefit or Disadvantage of the Colony, is nothing to the present Purpose; but, I believe, Sir, you will readily agree with me, that its Regulations, with respect I to the Hospital, are very alarming; and that it is pofll-ble, and even probable, that after Ten or Twenty Years Contest at Law with an Agent, who may now possess a very responsible Estate, the whole Money' in dispute may be swallowed up by Judgments obtained in the-mean while by other Persons.

If to this be added the enormous Expences attending a Process in Chancery, I believe I need say little more to point out the absolute Necessity for the speedy Interposition of Parliament, on Behalf of the Hospital.

I ought now. Sir, to apologize, in a particular Manner, for this great Trouble, which nothing would have justified, but the Certainty, that the Gentleman I address has the Interest of the noble Institution concerned, much at Heart; and the pleasing Hopes which I entertain of promoting that Interest, through his Means, and acquitting myself with Credit in the Trust reposed in me.

I have the Honour to be, with great Respect and

Esteem,

Sir George,

Greenwich Park, Your most obedient,

1 ft July 1772. and very humble Servant,

B. Edwards.

To Sir George Rodney, Bart.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That it appears to this House, that Robert Lord Clive, Baron of Pla()ey, in the Kingdom of Ireland, about the Time of the deposing of Surajah , Nabob of

Bengal, and the establishing of Meer Jaffier on the Muf-nud, did, through the Influence of the Powers with which he was intruded as a Member of the Select Committee, and Commander in Chief of the British Forces, obtain and possess himself of 2 Lacks and 80,000 Rupees as Member of the Select Committee; a further Sum of 2 Lacks of Rupees as Commander in Chief* and a further Sum of 16 Lacks of Rupees, or more, under the Denomination of private Donation; which Sums, amounting together to Twenty Lacks and 80,000 Rupees, were of the Value, in Money, of

Mr. Thomas Walpoie reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of John, Robert, James, and -Ham, Adam-, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition, is as follows:

It appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Archibald Campbell, Clerk to John, Robert, James, and Adam,

that the said Messieurs Adam have built Three large and expensive Houses, one in Queen Ann Street, and Two in Mansfield Street, in the Parish of Saint le-botte, and also all that Building upon a Parcel of Ground formerly called Durham now called The Adelpki, between the River Thames and the Strand, in the Liberty of the City of Westminster, and several Houses adjoining thereto, in the Strand.

That all those Houses and Buildings, except a very few in the Adelphi, that have been fold, are the Property of the said Messieurs Adam.

That great Part of the filbterraneous Works in the Adelphi, and many of the Houses, are already finished, and they are proceeding to complete the Remainder.

The Witness then produced to your Committee, an Account, by which it appeared, that the Sum of £.147,271 has been expended in the Buildings already erected in the Adelphi; that the said Messieurs Adam have received £. 29,271 from the Sale of Houses and Rents there: That consequently they have disbursed £. 118,000 more than they have received. — And he produced an Estimate, by which it appeared, thar the Sum of £. 57,000 is still wanting to complete the said Buildings.

That the Sum already expended in the Parish of Saint Mary-le-bone, is £.25,876, and that there is still necessary, to complete one of the Houses in Mansfield Street, the further Sum of £. 1,500.

The Witness being examined as to the Estimate of the future Expence, said, That he had no Doubt of the Estimate being exact; that it was made by very skilful Surveyors, a few Months after the Buildings at the Adelphi were begun; that he has compared it with the Expence of the Buildings as far as they are gone, and finds, that the Expence has always corresponded with the Estimate very nearly.

Mr. Cosmo Wallace, a Surveyor, being examined as to the Truth of the Estimates, informed your Committee, That he giade the principal Estimate himselfi and has seen all the others, and that he has not the least Doubt but they are all very exact.

Mr. Campbell being again examined, said. That if these Works had not been delayed for want of Money, it would have been a very beneficial Undertaking, but that, by reason of the Scarcity of Money, and the general Stagnation of Credit, the said Messieurs Adam have been obliged to proceed very slowly for the last Ten or Eleven Months.

That from the same Cause, the said Messieurs Adam have not been able to dispose of such Houses as are already built, notwithstanding their having exposed them to Sale by Auction and otherwise.

Bankers in the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making the Estates of Bankers liable to the Payment of their Partnership Debts; and for further punching Bankers Clerks for Breach of Trust; and setting forth, That the Petitioners are convinced of the Expediency of several of the Regulations therein contained; but, by a Clause in the said . Bill,:which subjects every Person dealing as Bankers to a Penalty, who shall deal or trade, or permit or suffer any Person or Persons whatsoever, either in Trust or otherwise, to deal or trade with, any of the Stock* Monies, or Effects, of, or any way belonging to, such Banker or Bankers, in the buying or selling of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandizes whatsoever, the Petitioners apprehend, is depriving them of carrying on those Commercial Concerns, which may greatly tend to the Benefit of Trade, and may be the Means of laying great Restraint thereon, and also take from them that Right which every Member of the Community has of employing his Fortune in such Manner as he shall judge most conducive to his Interest, as well as the Welfare and Benefit of the Public; and that the Petitioners are very desirous that any Clause may be inserted in the said Bill which may restrain them, under the severest Penalties, from employing any Part of the Monies lodged in their Hands as Bankers, in any Trade, Goods, Wares, or Merchandize whatsoever: And therefore praying, That the said Clause, so restrain-

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Petition was read: Taking Notice East India of the Bill for establishing certain Regulations, for Afiairi. the better Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, as well in India as in Europe; and setting forth, That the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the said Bill is a direct and dangerous Attack on the Liberties of the People, and will, if passed into a Law, prove of the most fatal Consequences to the Security of Property in general, and particularly the Franchises of every Corporate Body in this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners are the more alarmed by these Proceedings, as the Privileges the City of London enjoy stand on the same Security as those of the East India Company; and that the Bill has been brought into the House with a Degree of Secrecy incompatible with the Principles of the Constitution in Matters of such public Concern: And therefore praying the House, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

EastTndi*. A Petition of the United Company of Merchants of Abuts. England, trading to the East Indies, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for - establishing certain Regulations, for the better Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, as well in India as in Europe; and Setting forth, That the said

Bill, if paSed into a Law, will destroy every Privilege which the Petitioners hold under the most l'acred Securities that Subjects can depend upon in this Country; and that the appointing of Officers by Parliament, or the Crown, to be veiled with the whole Civil and Military Authority of the Presidency of Bengal, and also tSibrdeittg, Management, and Government, of all the Tdrntotfal Acquisitions and Revenues of the Company, in the Kiftgdoms'of Bengal, and Orijfa, together

With the-other superintending Powers over the Settle ments of Bombay and Madras, independent of any Choice in the Company, or any real Power of Controul in she Directors or General Courts of the said Company, or Power in the said Company of removing the said

‘‘Jo*

Officers for Misbehvaiour, or filling up of Vacancies in case of Death or Avoidance, is a Measur so extraordinary (while the Poflessions are alledged to remain in the Company) that the Petitioners beg Leave to call the Attention of Parliament to this most alarming Circumstance, before the House shall give a Sanction to an Act, which, under the Colour of Regulation, will annihilate at once the Powers of the East India Company, and- virtually transfer them to the Crown; and that the said Bill is destrudive of the essential Rights and Interests of the Petitioners in many other Respects; and is further defective as to many of the Purposes for which it is declared to be framed; and that the Petitioners look upon this Bill as tending to destroy the Liberties of the Subject, from an immense Addition of Power it must give to the Influence of the Crown , and that the Petitioners have never been made acquainted with any Charge of Delinquency having been made against them in Parliament, and if any such Charge has been made, they have never been called upon to be heard against it; and that they cannot therefore suppole that any such Delinquency on the Part of the Company has been voted; which Delinquency, however, is made the Ground of this Bill: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the same may not pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the other Order of the Day, for the Dittfr. House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for establishing certain Regulations, for the better Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, as well in as in , be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

" Resolved, That the Sum of One million Four hundred thousand Pounds will be l'ufficient for the pre-,

" sent Relief of the Company.

" Resolved, That it may be expedient for the Public,

" to advance to the Company the said Sum of One " million Four hundred thousand Pounds; provided,

" at the same Time, due Care be taken to secure, by " proper Regulations, the future good Government of " the Company’s Affairs.

Resolved, That, in case a Sum of Money shall be " advanced by the Public, for the Relief of the East India " Company, the Company ought to be restrained from " encreasing their Dividend beyond Six Pounds per " Cent, per Amt. until such Money shall have been repaid.

" Resolved, That, in case a Sum of Money shall be " advanced by the Public, for the Relief or the East India Company, the Company ought to be restrained

" from encreasing their Dividend beyond Seven Pounds " per Cent, per Ann. until their Bond Debt shall be re-

" duced to One million Five hundred thousand Pounds.

" Resolved, That it may be for the mutual Benefit " of the Public and the East India Company, that the " Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues, lately obtained " in India, should, under proper llestrictions and Regulations, remain in the Pofiession of the Company " during a Term not exceeding Six Years, to commence " from the Expiration of the present Agreement between the Public and the Company; that during the " said Term, the Public should forego all Participation in the Produce thereof, until the Company shall " have repaid such Sum of Money as shall be advanced " by the Public for the Relief of the Company, and " until the Bond Debt of the Company shall be reduced to One million Five hundred thousand Pounds;

The Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 1. 1. last. To leave out " Six," and insert "Seven" instead thereof.

Pr. 2. 1. 4; To leave out " Eight," and insert " Nine" instead thereof.

Pr. 3. 1. 15. To leave out " the Space of," and insert " any Term, not less " than" instead thereof; and after " Six," to insert " nor more than " Twelve."

1. 16. To leave out "or until the fame," and insert " unless such Penalty" instead thereof.

1. 17. After " be" to insert " sooner;" and after " paid" to insert " and such " Offender shall, if the Justices " shall think proper, be Once " publicly whipped, for such Offence, at the Expiration of such " Commitment, in the Town or " Place where such Gaol or House " of Correction Ihatl be, between " the Hours of Twelve and One " of the Clock in the Day."

Pr. 4. 1. 34. After " Moiety" to insert " of the " Forfeiture." 1

Pr. 5. 1. 39. To leave out " Justice or Justices, " whose Acts are cqmplained of," and insert " Informer" instead thereof.

Pr. 6. 1. 33. To leave out " not being hereby altered, amended, or explained."

Pr. 7. 1.. 2. After " Time" to insert " knowingly " and wilfully."

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act to repeal an Act, made in the Tenth Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the " better Preservation of the Game, within that Part " of Great Britain called England," and for making other Provisions in lieu thereof.

Ordered, That Mr. Whitworth do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Edward Stanley, Esquire, Secretary to the Commissioners of the Customs, informed your Committee, That though the Quantity of Furniture, lately imported under Privilege, had been very considerable, the Practice was confined to v&ry few Persons — That many of the Foreign Ministers difcpuntenanced it; and particularly mentioned Two Instances of Count Belgiojojo, who had given Notice to the Board of Customs, to seize Foreign Manufactures, attempted to be imported in his Name, had dismissed Servants for being concerned so the Practice, and had taken Measures with the Officers of the Revenue, to prevent it for the future.

Upon the whole Matter your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That great Quantities of Foreign Furniture have been of late imported into the Port of London, by some of the Ministers of Foreign Powers, at the Court of Great Britain; and that a considerable Part of the said Furniture appears to have been so imported for Sale.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it may be expedient to make some Regulations in resptfdt to the Importation of Furniture by Foreign Mi-; miters, as-well for the Accommodation of such Mini-5

fters, as for the Security of His Majesty’s Revenue, and the Encouragement of the Manufactures of Great Britain.

Presentment, 27th June 1707, relative to examining the Baggage of Ambassadors, with a Warrant /or the fame. Dated the 2d July 1707.

For the more regular Dispatch of all Foreign Ministers, in the Visiting and Passing their Goods and Baggage, either on their Arrival or Departure, and as well with regard to the Civilities and ltefpects paid to her Majesty’s Ministers, as to prevent such Complaints as they find Occasion to make, ondifeourfing with one another, of unequal Usage in this Particular by Partialities in Practice;

It is humbly proposed, That every Foreign Minister . on his Arrival, giving a particular Schedule, subscribed by himself, of the Package of his Goods, and what is contained in them, and being Household Goods, Wearing Apparel, or relating to his Equipagfc, for his own Use, and not for Merchandize, as also the Remainder of his Stores, not exceeding a Ton of Wine for every Minister having the Character of Ambassador, and Two Hogsheads for any other Public Minister of an inferior Character, and at their first coming only, may have their Goods, in pursuance of a general Order, sent immediately to their own Houses, on the Officers visiting, by the Commissioners Directions, Two or Three Parcels-only, to fee they agree with the Schedule: — The same Respect to be shewn to all Foreign Ministers in Shipping their Goods, by a Schedule, on their Departure, without fending an Officer to their Houses, or examining all at the Quays: That her Majesty’s Ministers may have the like Favour on their Dispatch Outward and Inward; saving, that as they know the Laws of England, their Schedules are to contain no prohibited Goods, nor customable, beyond their Wearing Apparel, Household Goods, or for their Equipage, without their being fub-jeCl to Duty.

C. Godolphin, T. Werden,

Sam1 Clarke, Hall,

W. Culliford, M. Dudley.

After our hearty Commendations, upon considering of what is by you proposed, in your Memorial aforegoing, 1 approve thereof; and do accordingly hereby authorize and direct you, from Time to Time, to observe and follow such Rules and Methods, with respect to all Goods -and Stores that shall belong to any Foreign Mi-nifter, as you have therein proposed, taking Care not to pass any prohibited Goods; and that all customable Goods, beyond their Wearing Apparel, Household Goods, or for their Equipage, be subject to the Duties payable for the fame.

And for so doing this shall be your Warrant.

Whitehall Treat ury Chambers, 2d July 1707.

Minute, 27th March 1764.

Regulations to be observed in the Examination and Delivery of the Baggage of Foreign Ministers on their Arrival, and of His Majesty’s Ministers on their Return to this Kingdom.

1 ft. That upon the first Arrival here of any Foreign Minister, and upon the Return of any Minister of His Majesty to this Kingdom, upon his giving a particular

Schedule

13 Geo. III. a Junii. 351

Schedule of the several Packages belonging to him, and of the Contents of each Package, such Schedule being signed by the Minister himself, a Copy thereof be delivered to the Inspectors of the River; who are, with the Utmost Care and Dispatch, to bring the Goods therein expressed, either to the Quays, or to the King’s Ware-house, as may be most convenient for the Examination . thereof.

ad. That another Copy of the said Schedule be delivered to the Land Surveyor, in Turn, who, with the Land Waiters to the Ship, are, with due Civility and the utmost Dispatch, to examine, in the Presence of some Person belonging to the Ambassador or Ministers, a reasonable Number of the Packages, to see that they agree with the Schedule; and in case they do, and that it appears from the said Schedule, that the Remainder of the Packages contain nothing beyond their Wearing Apparel, Household Goods, or for their Equipage; and if the Quantity of Wine docs not exceed the Amount of One Ton for every Minister having the Character of Ambassador, and Two Hogsheads for every other Pub* lie Minister of an inferior Character, they are then to suffer the Whole to be carried to their Houses, without further Examination or Delay; but if the Packages, so examined, do not agree with the Schedule, or there are any prohibited or Customable Goods, beyond their Wear-ing Apparel, Household Goods, or for their Equipage; or in case there be any Surplus in the Wines, beyond the Quantity mentioned above to be allowed to Ministers, according to their several Characters; the Officers are then immediately to inform the Board thereof, for their special Directions; and Notice thereof is to be given to the Land Surveyors and Inspectors of the River, for their Government.

Signed, Sl Mead.

Memorial, 5th December 1765, shewing the Necessity of abiding by the established Rules for examining the Baggage of Foreign Ministers, &c. on the Quays at the Custom House.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

May it please your Lordships,

The Applications which we observe are made by the Ministers of Foreign Princes and States, for procuring their Baggage, and other Trunks and Packages, arrived from Abroad, and declared to belong to them, to be sent to their own Houses, without being examined at the Custom House, renders it incumbent on us to represent to your Lordships,

That the Treasury Regulation in the Year 1707, in regard to the Admission of the Baggage of Foreign Ministers. which appears to have been made with a View to accommodate these Ministers, directs. That, upon the Arrival of such Baggage, a Schedule of the Packages, and of their Contents, be produced at the Custom House, and that some of the Packages being the re examined, and found to agree with the Schedule, the whole may be delivered. This Regulation, which is renewed at the Beginning of every Reign, in Favour of Foreign Minifteis, not only requires in this Manner an Examination of their Baggage to be made at the Custom House, but exprel'sly excludes the free Admission of Goods customable and prohibited, and extends only to the Delivery of Household Goods, Wearing Apparel, or such as relate to the Equipage of these Ministers, being for their own Use, and not for Merchandize, and this only upon their first Arrival.

That the Indulgence to these Ministers having increased by Degrees, in consequence of their repeated Applications, at length prevailed so far, that it became Vol. 34.

the general Practice, in pursuance of Directions from the Treasury, to permit their Baggage to be sent, without any Examination at the Custom House, to their own Houses, in order to be examined there in the Presence of Officers of this Revenue, appointed to attend such Baggage; but that this Practicd was found by Experi ence to be liable to continual Abuses, such Officers not being allowed, at Houses of these Ministers, to make an effectual Examination, except of such Packages which were known to contain no Goods liable to Objection; and thereby the richest Foreign Manufactures, either subject to nigh Duties or prohibited to be imported, could be introduced without any Check into this Kingdom.

That the Officers of the Customs, whole Department it is to examine Baggage, are not empowered by Law to receive any Duties j which Branch is confined to the Collector, with the Concurrence of the Comptroller and other Officers in the Port of London; so that the Removal of any Goods from the Custom House, before they have paid the Duties, withdraws them from the Cognizance of these Officers, by whom such Duties are to be charged and received.

That this Board, observing the Mischiefs resulting from this general Indulgence, found it necessary, in March 1764, to come to a Resolution, That the Baggage and Effects of Foreign Ministers, and of other Persons of Distinction, should, upon their Arrival here, be examined at the Custom House, under certain Rules conformable to the Treasury Regulation of 1707, which Rules were settled with the Approbation of the Treasury, and a Copy thereof we beg Leave to annex. *

That this Regulation being communicated to the Foreign Ministers, they acquielced in the Examination of their Baggage and Effects at the Custom House, agreeably to the Rules established; which Examination, at the same Time that it was highly expedient for the Security of this Revenue, was directed to be made with the greatest Care and Respect, in the Presence of the Secretaries or Agents of these Ministers, and was conducted in such Manner, that no Cause of Complaint was given thereby to these respectable Persons.

That these Rules, thus established and acquiesced in, as a Security against the Inundation of Foreign Commodities, through the Channel of Foreign Ministers, having been superseded of late in some Instances, we are apprehensive, that, if they are further departed from, and a general Indulgence again granted in regard to the Baggage of these Ministers, whole Number is very considerable at His Majesty’s Court, it will open a Door for the free Importation at this Port of large Quantities of high-priced Foreign Manufactures of this Kingdom.

Custom House, London, S. Mead,

cth Dec. 176c. E. Hooper,

H. Pelham,

Frederick,

H. Bankes,

Pennington,

C. Morris.
