21st July 1772.

Report of Messieurs Brooke, Brice, Strachan, and Oakley, Officers of the Customs, relative to the Seizure of Cabinet Ware, at the Houses of Messieurs Wall and Riley, Mr. Cullen, and Mr. Cobb.

May it please your Honours,

In obedience to your Honours Minute of the 14th Instant, we humbly report; That, in consequence of receiving Information from a Committee of Cabinet Makers, that a very large Quantity of Foreign Cabinet Work was for Sale in the Houses of Messieurs and Riley, in Sherrard Street, Mr. Cullen, in Greek Street, and Mr. Cobbs, in Saint Martins Lane, we found and seized, at each Place, the particular Quantities as are hereunto annexed.

That, soon after the said Goods at Messieurs Wall and Riley's, were found, and about being taken away, one Richard Shepley (who, we believe, is well known to your Honours to be a Smuggler, he having been convicted as such in the Court of Exchequer) came and infilled, the Cabinet Work should not be taken away; saying. That he was the Landlord of Messieurs Wall and Riley, who were Bankrupts; that these Goods were a Part of the Estate, and would ffiortly be sold for the Benefit of their Creditors; and that the Goods were at that Time particularized in a printed Catalogue for that Purpose. Here we beg Leave to observe, that the Assignees to the Estate of the said Wall and Riley did, a few Days ago, pray, by Petition to your Honours, the Delivery of the said Cabinet Work, aflTerting it to be a Part of the Bankrupts Estate; which Application we humbly refer your Honours to, wherein we have alledged, that we have credible and positive Proof, that the Cabinet Work was, very lately before the Seizure, brought to the Bankrupts House, and we have not the lead Doubt of the Goods being intended to be sold at the Bankrupts intended Sale; but not for the Benefit of the Creditors, as they could not be a Part of the Estate, they being brought there so long after the Estate being in the Possession of the Assignees; and further humbly observe to your Honours, that we believe the Intention of their being brought there was, from the Advantage of having them seemingly sold as a Bankrupt’s Effects, by the Contrivance of Shepley, who might then think they would hereafter be free from Seizure.

On the 4th Instant we went into the House of Mr. Cullen, in Greek Street, Soho, who, on being acquainted with our Business, very readily shewed us the Goods, and acquainted us, that all he had to do in the Matter was to be paid for Warehouse Room, during the Time the Goods were on his Premises; and said. That when he was first applied to for Warehouse Room, he understood it was for a small Quantity, but to his great Astonishment there was brought there Thirteen loaded Carts, or upwards, full packed of Foreign Cabinet Work; declaring the Cabinet Work which we had found, and which was all that he then had in his Possession, was not a Thirtieth Part of what was first brought to him; and said. That, had he known the Quantity to have been so large, he'Would not have suffered them to have come there, for that he was not employed in the lead as a Cabinet Maker, either to finish, or in any respect work on, the said Goods; and told us, that very large Quantities of the said Thirteen Loads had been delivered at different Times by him, in consequence of receiving written Orders for that Purpose (one of which he produced) but always in the same State as they came to him, without any Alteration whatever; but where they went, or to whom, he said, he did not know: That we understood by Mr. Cullen, that he never had been once employed #as a Tradesman by Baron Berlindy,-he often repeating, that he thought it a grea

The Goods; viz. Seven circular Slab Frames gilt and bumished, with Marble Slabs for the same; One variegated Commode with a Marble Slab for its Top; were found and seized in the Public Sale Room at Mr. Cullen's, and was, as we were informed by Mr.

Dominica. A Petition of John Esquire, Agent for the

(Expiring I (land of Dominica, was presented to the House, and ^*w‘l read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner has received a Memorial from the Commander in Chief, and the Council and Assembly, of the said Island, addressed to the House, taking Notice, That an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for opening and establishing certain Ports in ^he Islands of Jamaica and Dominica, for the more free Importation and Exportation of certain Goods and Merchandizes; foi granting certain Duties, to defray the Expences of opening, maintaining, securing, and improving, such Ports; for ascertaining the Duties to be paid upon the Importation of Goods from the said Island of Dominica into this Kingdom; and for securing the Duties upon Goods imported from the said Island into any other British Colony, will expire on the First Day of November 1773, or at the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and setting forth. That the said Act is, in many Respects, highly beneficial to the Kingdom of Great Britain, and to the said Island, by increasing the Navigation, the Consumption of Manufactures, and occasioning a general Improvement and Advantage to Trade and Plantations, by which His Majesty’s Revenue is considerably augmented; and x

that the Conveniencies or Inconveniencies arising from new Acts of Parliament are seldom discovered till they are put in Force; and that, although it is evidently clear, from the general Tenor of the said Act, that it was calculated and meant by the Legislature to benefit the said Island, as well as the Mother Country, yet there are several Clauses therein, that clalh very much with the Landed Interest of the said Colony, and lay particular Hardships upon its Inhabitants; and that the Duty of Thirty Shillings on every Slave imported, and of Sixpence on every Barrel of Beef, Pork, and Firkin of Butter, is considered to be very detrimental to the Interest of the said Island; and that the Memorialists conceive, the Parliament never intended those Duties should fall on the Inhabitants, but on Foreigners, who, for being readily supplied with SlaVes and Provisions, would chearfully pay a Duty for such Convenience; and that, by the said Act, the Duty on Slaves is not confined to those imported from Africa only; consequently it has been demanded of, ‘and paid by. Inhabitants who have had Occasion to bring seasoned Slaves from their Ellatcs in the other Islands, to make new Settlements in the said Island of Dominica, and even on all Negro Tradesmen, hired for certain Times, and brought by their Renters, being Mailer Workmen engaged to come from the neighbouring Islands to erect Works and other Buildings, who are frequently returned, and, on new Engagements being made by their Renters or Mailers, pay the Duty on every Return, which is found a Grievance, greatly detrimental to the Settlement of the said Colony; and therefore the Memorialists wish, and hope, that, in case the said Act is continued, the Duties on Slaves and Provisions may be laid on the Exportation to Foreign Islands, which would ease the said Colony much, without lessening His Majesty’s Revenue, and put them on a Footing with the Island of Jamaica, and in Time be the Means of increasing Shipping, Cultivation, and Trade; and the Memorialists represent, that they cannot account for the Difference that was made between the Two Islands of Jamaica and Dominica, unless Dominica was then considered only as a convenient Place for Trade with Foreigners; and if that was the Cafe, the great Quantity of Land sold by His Majesty’s Commissioners, the large Exports of the Produce of the said Island of Dominica, and the Number of Sugar and Coffee Estates now under Culture, fully Ibew its now interior Consequence to the Mother Country, and proves to a Demonstration, that it gives place in no respect to any of the British Windward Islands, and that the Landed Interest is equal to the Trade of it; and that the respective Clause, which prevents the Exportation of European Commodities from the said Island of Dominica to any British Island, tends equally to the Prejudice of the Trade of all the said Islands; for, in case of a Redundancy of Provisions, it must be totally loft to the Merchant, or sold to Foreigners at an under Value, who, well knowing of the Hardships thrown upon them in this respect, are too apt to take an Advantage of an Over Supply; and that a melancholy Instance of the Effect of that Part of the Act has lately happened; for, although they had, at the Time of the late Hurricane in the Leeward Islands, Abundance of European Salt Provisions, yet they could only pity the Misfortunes and Distresses of the Inhabitants, without the Power of assisting them; and that another Inconvenience arising from the Clause is, that it prohibits the Exportation of that valuable and ule-ful Commodity Mill Timber, from the said Island of Dominica, to any British Islands, whereby immense Sums are carried to Foreigners; and that Article, which might be profitable to them, is rendered quite useless, and becomes a total Loss; and that the Clause in the Act, whereby Coffee and Cocoa, the Produce of the said Island of Dominica, are esteemed Foreign Commodities, liable to the same Duties, Regulations, and

Entries,

13 GeO. IlL

Entries, which amount to a Prohibition of their Consumption in Great Britain, is a particular Hardship on the Planters, and makes such an unnatural Distinction, that they are Upon no Kind of Footing with those of the other Islands; and that thence arises, notwithstanding the Vigilance of the Custom House OfEcers, the infamous Practice of Smuggling, and felling those Articles of Produce to Foreigners rather than export them to the Mother Country; to remedy which, Coffee and Cocoa should (they apprehend) be allowed to be exported in the same Manner as certificated Rum and Sugar; and that it is evident, from daily Experience* that a Coffee or Cocoa Plantation is settled at One-third of the Expence necessary for the Settlement of a Sugar Estate; and that a small Quantity of Lands in either of the first Commodities* will afford a comfortable Support to a Planter and his Family; and therefore they conceive, that, instead of making those Commodities Foreign, as they now are* some Encouragement from the Mother Country for the Cultivation of Coffee and Cocoa would be highly advantageous to its Manufactures and Commerce, and greatly, tend to the Increase of the White Inhabitants of the said Island of Dominica, an Object which appears to have been very early attended to by Government; and representing to the House* that Labour in that Country )s procured at a most exorbitant Rate, and much more so, perhaps, than in any other Part of the World; that, in curing and preparing the Article of Coffee, a great Number of Slaves are required, which Slaves would be more advantageously employed in increasing the Cultivation of this Commodity, was it made lawful to import it into Great Britain in the Berry or Shell, paying Duty for the Nett Coffee only, in which State it would receive no Damage in the Carriage, and the Quality would be preferred so as to make it equal to any East India or Turkey Coffee, and be the Means of giving Bread to many poor People in Great iaiu, who would consequently be employed in cleaning it for Market* besides adding to the Demand of the coarse Linen Manufacture (Coffee in the Shell being generally sent Home in Bags) as well as a great Convenience to Freight in the Stowage of Ships, and an Increase to the Number of Vessels employed in carrying it to Great Britain; and that, at the Time the Petitioner received the said Memorial, he also received Directions to cause the same to be laid before the House; but the Petitioner is advised the said Memorial cannot be presented to the House, on account of the Informality thereof: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; And that the said Act may be continued, with Amendments, agree* able to the Purport of the said Memorial.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of Lieutenant General Robert Monckton was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for establishing certain Regulations for the better Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, as well in India as in Europe-, and that the' Petitioner is informed, that it is proposed to fill One of the Blanks of the said Bill with the Name of some Person in a Military Character, as One of the Supreme Council for the Government of the Company’s Territories in that Part of the World; and setting forth. That the Petitioner has been employed in some of the . most memorable Services in the late Wars, and Twice received the Thanks of this House; and that he has been duly elected to the Office of Supervisor, chiefly . with a View to Military Arrangement, by the Directors of the East India Company, which Choice was approved by the Body of Proprietors; but the Effect of that Choice has been suspended by an Act of Parliament; and that His Majesty had given the Petitioner His Royal Permission to accept the said Office; and that the Petitioner hopes, that, if it should seem expedient to the House to alter the Mode of the Supervision lately suspended, they will not fix so disgraceful a Mark upon the Character and Conduct of the Petitioner, as to take away the Trull now legally re-posed in him, for the Purpose of naming another Military Person to execute an Office of a similar Nature under another Name; and that the Petitioner does not presume to remind the House of his Service, his Sufferings, or his Successes, in the Line of his Duty, nor would he oppose himself to the Pretensions of any other Gentleman; but, as he Hands already appointed by the East India Company, with His Majesty’s Leave and Approbation, he apprehends he cannot be let alide without a strong implied Censure, which, he trulls, he has not merited from the Representatives of his Country: And therefore requests to be nominated by Parliament to the Military Department of the said Council.

A Petition of several Proprietors of the East India Company, possessed of £. 500, or more, but less than £. 1,000, of the Capital Stock Of the said Company, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and others, was prefettted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, by the Charter granted to the East India Company by his late Majesty King William, arid since that Time repeatedly recognized and confirmed by several Acts of Parliament, in Consideration of many large Sums of Money lent, or otherwise advanced, by the said Company, to the Public, ate legally possessed of a Right of voting at any General Court of the said Company, for the Election of Directors, the making of Bye Laws, or in any other Matter relating to the Affairs or Government of the said Company; and that the Petitioners find, that, by an Alteration made in a Clause in the Bill for establishing certain Regulations for the better Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, as well in India as ih Europe, they are to toe deprived of that Right, and of every Degree of Influence in the Management of To considerable a Property; and that, notwithstanding the false and groundlels Aspersions which have been thrown out against so great a Number of the Petitioners, which they trust the House will not makea Ground of Proceeding to affect their Rights, while unsupported by Evidence, the Petitioners, who are, bona , Proprietors in their own Right, represent to the House, that ho Persons can be more interested to prevent such illegal Practices, whereby their best Endeavours for the Good of the Company are liable so be defeated by the undue Influence of a few wealthy Proprietors-, and that an Act passed in the Year 1767, obliging the Proprietors to hold their Qualifications Six Months at least before they should have a Right to vote; and that the Company, being still further desirous to effectuate the Purposes of that Act, havedireftfed an Application to be made to Parliament, for extending the Time prescribed by the said Act of the Seventh of His present Majesty, from Six to Twelve Months; and that the Petitioners, willing that every real Remedy may be applied to this Evil, are desirous that all the other Provisions of the said Bill now depending, for preventing collusive Transfers (except the Increase of the Qualification of the Voters, which cannot answer that Purpose) should pass into a Law; which Provisions, together with the Extension of the Time to Twelve Months, must effectually put a Stop to that Practice, which has already been in a great Degree prevented by the Operation of the said Act made in 1

1767; and that the proposed Increase of the Qualify cation of the Votets cannot in any Degree contribute to the End desired, but will rather facilitate than discourage so pernicious a Practice; and that it is evident that the real Effect of the said Clause will be, the throwing the Power of the Company into the Hands of a few opulent Men; while the only effectual Balance to such an Oligarchy, by the Exertions of independent Proprietors of moderate Fortunes* will be totally destroyed; and that the Petitioners conceive* the Alteration now proposed cannot be supported upon any Principles of Expediency, or ahy just Arguments respecting the purposse. for which it is professed to be intended: And therefore hope the House will give them Leave to be heard* by themselves* in Support of their own legal Rights, against the said Bill, which, without Consent, Compensation made, or Charge of Delinquency proved, deprives so great a Number of Proprietors of the Fran-chises which they have purchased under the Faith of Parliament, and has not the Excuse of Public Necessity, or even Utility, to palliate so violent an Act.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill was committed, be taken into further Consideration; and that the Petitioners be then heard, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of Alexander Dalrymple, Esquirfe, was pre-feftted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner is a Proprietor of £. 500 East India Stock, under Faith of the Charter granted by his late Majesty King William, with the Consent of Parliament, for a

valuable Consideration paid to the Public, and confirm-fed by divers Act of Parliament, particularly by an Act passed in the Third Year of King George the Second; wherein the Rights of the Company are fully established and clearly explained, in Consideration of a specific Sum then paid by the said Company to the Public; and that the Rights to which, as a Proprietor of India Stock, he is entitled, under the Sandiion of a Bargain with the Public, cannot be taken from him without his Consent; and that the Bill now depending in Parliament, for establishing certain Regulations for the better Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, as well in India as in Europe, would, if passed into a Law, deprive the Petitioner of his Rights and Property; and therefore he trusts in the Justice of the House, that the same will not be passed into a Law.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Harrifott, of Red Lion having, under

the Encouragement of an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of her Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act " for granting a Reward for the Discovery of the Longitude at Sea," applied himself with unremitting Industry, for the Space of Forty-eight Years, to the making an Instrument for ascertaining the Longitude at Sea; and having constructed a Time-keeper for that Purpose, and discovered the Principles of constructing the fame, by which other Time-keepers have been already made, and found to answer with great Exaftriefs; from which Discovery, it is apprehended, that great Benefit will arise to the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms; is highly deserving of public Encouragement and Reward.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight thousand Seven hundred and Fifty Pounds, be paid, by the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, out of any Sums of MoDey now in his Hands, to the said John Harrison, as a further Reward and Encouragement, over and above the Sums already received by him, for his said Invention of a Time-keeper, and his Discovery of the Principles upon which the same was constructed.

Mr. Whitworth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Doctor Rich of Saint Margaret's, Westminster, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition is as follows:

It appeared to your Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. George Farmer (formerly a Dyer) That there is not a fast Green or Yellow Dye, on Cotton and Linen Yarn, now in Use, except a Preparation invented by Doctor Richard Williams, which, the Witness said, he had made a very severe Trial of, and found both the Green and Yellow to be permanent and fast, even standing the Force of Soap Suds and long Bleaching, which are the severest Trial they can undergo, and the only necessary ones to prove their Merit; and did not doubt but it would restore the Reputation of our Cotton Fabrics in Spain and other Countries, where they are daily losing Reputation, on Account of the Colours not standing the Test of those Climates; and would venture to give it as his Opinion, that when the Secret is- known among the Dyers, that it would prove a Fixer to many of the flying Colours now in Use, and raise that valuable Branch of Business higher than ever it was.

Mr. John Yandall (Partner in the principal House of Cotton Dyers in London) informed your Committee, That they had tried Doctor Williams's Green and Yellow Dyes on Cotton in the large Way, and also on Handkerchiefs, which puts Colours to the severest Trials, and when worn to Rags, the Colours ftiii remained good; but by their former Method of dying Green or Yellow on Cotton, he had never seen any that would stand the Air, even for a few Days, or refill a Third or Fourth Washing; and that he thought it a great Discovery; and, if properly encouraged, would much increase the Manufactory in the Cotton- Trade, and also, being permanent and fast'on Silk Handkerchiefs, will enable them to make that Article to rival the India, employ a Number of Hands, and totally de-

stroy the contraband Trade in- those Goods, and be ati Increase of the Revenue; this Trade being reduced from 60,000 Dozen per Year, to about 16 or 17,000.

Mr. John Paltrau (Partner with Mr. James Giles, Silk and Cotton Manufacturers) confirmed this Evidence, in regard to Doctor -Dye being fast

on Silk and Cotton; and added, That the Goods he had made up and" fold, were so: much approved of; that his Customers were enquiring for more of the same Colours.

Mr. Richard Clough (a Cotton Manufacturer at Manchester) informed your Committee, That he and many others, in Manchester, had made Experiments on Doctor

Williams's Dye; and fitid it proved-a-fast Dye; and the Use of it would be a very considerable Advantage to the Trade of that Town; And, being aflfed to give his Reasons, he" laid. The Furniture Checks are a large Branch of Trade in Manchester, in which they are obliged to use Worsted instead of Cotton, when green or yellow Colours are wanted; that the Worsted causes the Checks to pucker in Washing, and in Time will Moth-eat, which Cotton will not. /

A Certificate, signed by the principal Manufacturers at Manchester, dated November 1769, to the Board of Trade, certifying Doctor William's Green and Yellow Dyes to be fall and permanent, was laid before Your Committee; a Copy whereof is. hereunto annexed by

way of Appendix, 1: And also,:

Copy of a Representation of the Lords of Trade to the King, dated July 13th 1770, is hereunto annexed in the Appendix, N° 2: 'And also.

Copy of a Memorial of the principal Manufacturers of Manchester, to the Right honourable Lord North, dated May 3d 1772, is hereunto annexed in the Appendix, N" 3.

APPENDIX, N° 1.

We the Cotton Manufacturers of the Town of Manchester, whole Names are hereunto subscribed, having seen Specimens of a new-invented Green and Yellow, dyed on Cotton Goods and Yams, by Doctor Richard Williams, of Downing Street, Westminster, which we have proved to be permanent and fast Colours, Handing the necessary Tests of Washing and Wearing: And whereas the former known Greens and Yellows, dyed on the Cottons fabricated in this Town, have hitherto proved fugitive and defective, and thereby prejudicial to its Trade; we do hereby certify, to all whom it may concern, that if the Method of dying the aforesaid Doctor Richard Williams's above new-invented Colours, is laid open for the Use of the Manufacturers, provided it can be done at or about the Price of the Greens or Yellows now in Use, as he takes on him to prove they can, that the same will then be not only of Angular Advantage to this Town in particular, but, we apprehend, of great national Utility, and give this Kingdom a peculiar Advantage over all other Countries that are now her Rivals in the Cotton Manufacturing Business; as it is a well known Fact, that no other Country has discoveretj any Method of fixing a green or yellow Colour on Linen or Cotton, either in Goods or Yarn, in the Mode of Dying.

Manchester,

November 1769.

A P P E N D I X, N° 2.

To.the King’s most Excellent Majesty.

May it please Your Majesty,

We have had under our Consideration a Petition, presented unto us by Doctor Richard Williams, of Downing Street, Westminster; Setting forth, That, after several

Years Labour and Application, he has discovered a Method of fixing Yellow and Green Dyes on Cotton Yarns, to stand the Test of common Washing and Wearing, and greatly to exceed in Beauty the fugitive Yellows and Greens now in Use; and therefore praying to have such a Reward from the Public, as shall be proportioned to the Merit of this Discovery, and to the great Expence of Time and Money he has been at in the Pursuit of it: Whereupon we humbly beg Leave to represent to Your Majesty,

That it does appear to us, as well by a Certificate from the principal Manufacturers of the Town of Manchester, as by the Information which we have received from a Manufacturer, and from a Dyer of the City of London, who have made Experiment of the Petitioner’s Method of dying Green and Yellow in Cotton Yarn, that the said Dye has been proved to be

permanent

37

14* — 150 Jtitiii.

A. 1773.

permanent and fast, (landing the necessary Test of Washing and Wearing, in a better Manner than any other Greens and Yellows hitherto uled; and therefore, as this is, we conceive, a great Improvement in a very material Branch of the Manufactures of this Kingdom, which mult have the Effect to increase and extend its Commerce, we are humbly of Opinion, that the same does merit the public Attention; and that, if the Method of fixing these Colours, discoveted by the Petitioner, can be brought into Use, without any considerable Advance on the Price of the Greens and Yellows now in Use in the Cotton Manufactory, it would be adviseable to induce the Petitioner to disclose his Secret, by such a Premium or Bounty from the Public, as shall be judged adequate to its Merit*

Which is most humbly submitted,

Eliot,

John Roberts, Whitehall, lVm Fitzherbert,

APPENDIX, N# 3.

To the Right honourable Lord North, First Lord of the Treasury.

We the principal Manufacturers of the Town of chester, do now hereby certify to your Lordship, That Doctor Richard Wiliams's new-invented Green and Yel-

low Dye, for Cotton Goods and Yarns, are fast Colours, perfectly refilling the Air, which no other green or yellow Dye on Cottons will do; that, if the same is laid open for the public Good, it cannot fail to produce additional Labour to the Poor, and increase our Exportations, and hereby become a very considerable' national Advantage: And the Doctor, to avoid all Appearance or Apprehensions of his entertaining Intentions of making a Job of his Secret, and in the thorough Confidence of its peculiar Excellence, and the Integrity of your Lordship, candidly offering to communicate it to us, before he expects any national Reward; and also wholly relying on its Merits, for our further certifying for that Purpose, after the Process is known to us, and that the lame, besides Beauty and Fastness, is attended with the further Requisites of being practicable, easy, and cheap: We humbly pray your Lordship, to take this Affair into your immediate Confederation at the Treasury Board; and, as the further Loss of Time, in this Business, would be a real Loss to the Trade of this Town, we again humbly pray your Lordship, now to give it that Dispatch as to your Lordship shall seem meet, and encourage the Doctor to come, down to Manchester, to lay his Secret open to us, as soon as his private, Affairs will permit him.

Manchester,

A Petition of the United Company of Merchants of England \trading to the East Indies, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for granting to His Majesty a Sum of Money, to be raised by Exchequer Bills, and to be advanced and applied in the Manner, and upon the Terms, therein mentioned, for the Relief of the United Company of Merchants of England, trading to the East Indies; and setting forth. That various Restrictions and Conditions are imposed on the East India Company, respecting the Disposition

of their Property, which the Petitioners conceive to be highly injurious to their Rights, Interest, and Credit, which Restrictions and Conditions are chiefly founded on a Petition, which they presented on the Second Day of March last, with a View to an amicable Agreement between the Public and the East India Company; and that the Petitioners were in Hopes they might have obtained the Assistance of the Public, without annexing Terms to that Assistance, which mull render it more prejudicial than advantageous; and that the Petitioners, sensible of the Sufficiency of their Credit, have determined to depend on the Laws of their Coun-

John Hug,

try, and submit to the temporary Difficulties which may attend the present Situation of their Affairs, rather than receive the Loan offered to them upon the very severe Conditions prescribed; and that the Petitioners are extremely sorry to find that the Territorial Acqui-fitions, which they obtained at so great an Expence and the imminent Risque of their whole Capital, should have created so much Prejudice against them; since it is evident, whether those Acquisitions belong to the India Company or the Crown, they must ever be considered as of the highest Advantage to this Nation; but it is far from the Desire of the Petitioners to possess what doth not of Right belong to them; therefore, finding the undue Interposition and the various Op-pressions which have flowed from this pretended Source, the Petitioners have before called for a legal Decision of those Rights; and therefore it is with the more Surprize, that the Petitioners now find the holding Possession of those Acquisitions should be made the Ground of overturning their most efi'ential Privileges, and of establishing a mingled Jurisdiction, comprehending both their Trade and Revenues, which hath no Foundation in the Principles of the English Constitution/or of any other well governed State; and must prove as prejudicial to the Liberties of the People, by the

East India Company’s Kelief.

Jamaica

and

Dominica.

13 Geo. III. 150 — 1

encreased Influence of the Crown, as it will prove to the Rights and Property of the India Company: And therefore praying the House, to grant the Petitioners Leave to withdraw their said former Petition, presented to the House on the 2d of March last, and all'o their other Petition, presented on the 17th of May last, which accompanied certain Regulations proposed by themselves, for the more advantageous Management of their Affairs, and the due Administration of Justice in India; an Indulgence which they are the more earned to obtain, least Posterity, reviewing the Transactions of this Period, should impute to the Petitioners the having been accessary to Measures, which, by veiling unnecessarily in the Crown the Disposal of so many great and lucrative Employments in India, tend, in the Petitioners Opinion, not only to bring Ruin upon the Company, but to destroy the just Balance of this free Constitution.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put. That the Petitioners have Leave to withdraw their laid Petitions j

It passed in the Negative.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition is as follows;

Mr. Matthew Lothian, Collector of Excise for the Hertford District, informed your Committee, That he had collected the Duties of Excise from the Petitioners, as considering their Brewhouse to be without the Bills of Mortality, and they paid tho same accordingly.

And it appeared from the Evidence of Mr.

thinfon, that, upon an Action brought in the Court of King’s Bench, against the Collector of Excise, for so much Money as the Petitioners had overpaid, a Verdict was given for the Petitioners; and it was thereby determined that their Brewhouse is within the Bills of Mortality.

And, by the several Receipts produced to Your Committee, it appears. That, from the 18th Day of November 1752 to the 24th Day of July 1769, the Petitioners had paid the Sum of £. 4,363 more than if they had been charged as London Brewers.

Longitude. " Resolved, That John of Red Lion

" having, under the Encouragement of an Act, made

" in the Twelfth Year of her Majesty Queen Anne,

" intituled, "An Act for granting a Reward for the Dif-,c covery of the Longitude at Sea," applied himself, with " unremitting Industry for the Space of Forty-eight " Years, to the making an Instrument for ascertaining the Longitude at Sea j and having constructed a " Time-keeper for that Purpose, and discovered the " Principles of conlirufting the fame, by which other " Time-keepers, have been already made, and found to " answer with great Exactness; from which Discovery,

*it is apprehended that great Benefit will arise to the " Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms; is highly " deserving of public Encouragement and Reward."

" Resolved, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight thousand Seven hundred and Fifty Pounds, be paid, by " the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, out of any " Sums of Money now in his Hands, to the said John " Harrison, as a further Reward and Encouragement,

" over and above the Sums already received by him,

" for his said Invention of a Time-keeper, and his Discovery of the Principles upon which the same was " constructed."

AN ingrossed Bill for granting to His Majesty a certain Sum of Money out of the Sinking Fund; and for applying certain Monies therein mentioned for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-three* was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for granting to His Majesty a certain Sum of Money out of the Sinking Fund; and for applying certain Monies therein mentioned, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-three; and for further appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament; and for paying to rifon a further Reward, for his Invention of a Timekeeper for ascertaining the Longitude at Sea, and his Dil'covery of the Principles upon which the tame was constructed.

Ordered, That Mr. Cooper do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

An ingrossed Bill to indemnify Justices of the Peace, Deputy Lieutenants, and Officers of the Militia, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act to indemnify Justices of the Peace, Deputy Lieutenants, and Officers of the Militia, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes.

The Lord North reported to the House, That their Address of Friday the 18th Day of this Instant June (that His Majesty would be gracioutly pleased to confer some Mark of His Royal Favour upon the honourable Lieutenant General Robert Monckton, in Confederation of his meritorious Services to His Majesty and to his Country, either by a Grant of Lands in some of the Hlands in the West Indies, which were ceded to His Majesty by the late Treaty of Peace, or in such other Manner as His Majesty should think proper) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that He will take the same into Consideration.

Ordered, That the Journal of this House, from the End of the last Session of Parliament to the End of this present Session, be printed.

Ordered, That One thousand Five hundred Copies of the said Journal be printed, by the Appointment, and under the Direction of, John Esquire, Clerk of'

this House.

Ordered, That One thousand Five hundred Copies of the several Reports from Committees of this House, which have been printed by Order of the House, and are not inserted in the Journals of this House, be reprinted; together with the several Reports which have been 'made to this House, in this Session of Parliament, from the Committee of Seprecy, appointed to enquire into the State of the East India Company; and also the several Reports which have been made to this House, in this Session of Parliament, from the Select Committee, appointed to enquire into the Nature, State, and Condition, of the East India Company, and of the Vol. 34.

British Affairs in the East indies; and that the same be printed by the Appointment, and under the Direction, of John Hatfell, Esquire, Clerk of this House.

Ordered, That the said Journal and Reports be printed by such Person as shall be licensed by Mr. Speaker; and that no other Person do presume to print the fame.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to order the Sum of Two thousand Pounds to be advanced to John Hatfell, Esquire, Clerk of this House, towards defraying the Expence of printing the Journal of this House, from the End of the last Session of Parliament to the End of this present Session; and also the Expence of re-printing the Reports of this House; and to defray such extraordinary Expences as have been incurred on Account of the printed Journals of this House; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good the fame.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to order a Sum, not exceeding Five hundred Pounds, to be advanced to such Person or Persons as the Speaker of this House shall authorize to receive the same, towards further defraying the Expence of making a General Index to the Journals of this House; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good the fame.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to order the further Sum of Five 'thousand Pounds to be advanced, towards defraying the Expence of printing One thousand Two hundred and Fifty Copies of such Parliamentary and other Records as His Majesty shall think fit; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good the fame.

Ordered, That the said Addresses be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to order the Sum of One thousand Pounds to be issued to the Chairman of the Committee of Secrecy, appointed to enquire into the State of the East India Company, to be by him distributed amongst the several Clerks at the East India House, for their extraordinary Trouble in attending the said Committee; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good the same to His Majesty.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to order the Sum of Two hundred Pounds to be issued to the Chairman of the Committee appointed to enquire into the Nature, State, and Condition, of the East India Company, and of the British Affairs in the East Indies, to be by him paid to Mr. Samuel Johnson, One of the Clerks at the East India House, for his extraordinary Trouble in attending the said Committee; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good the same to His Majesty.

Ordered, That the said Addresses be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are bf His Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

And then the House adjourned till Wednesday Morning next. Ten of the Clock.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I cannot close this Session without alluring you, that I have observed, with much Satisfaction, the Zeal, Alfiduity, and Perseverance, with which you have applied yourselves to the very important Business which, at the Meeting of Parliament, I recommended to your particular Attention: And I hope, and trust, that the L^ws, which have been the Relult of your Deliberations, will be found to answer the Salutary Purposes for which they were intended.

The Continuance of the War between Russia and the Porte, with both of whom I am dofely connected in Friendship, although under no Engagement to either, gives Me great Concern. But, from the pacific Dif-politions of other Powers, I have Reason to hope, that 5 G those

those Troubles will extend no further. I shall persevere in My earned Endeavours to preserve the general Tranquillity of Europe; at the same Time, it shall be the constant Object of My Care, to be sufficiently prepared against any Event which may affect the Honour, Safety, oc Interest, of My Kingdoms.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my hearty Thanks, for the Supplies which you have granted Me with so much Cheerfulness: And I fee with Pleasure, that, notwithstanding the ample Provision which you have made for every Branch of the Public Service, and the effectual Relief and Support which you have afforded to the East India Company, you have been able to make some Progress in reducing th.e National Debt.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Experience I have had of your Attention to the Public Good, and of your Attachment to me, convinces me, that you will, in your several Stations, use your utmost Endeavours to assist Me, in promoting the Happiness of My People. I have no other Object but their Welfare; and no other View, but to employ the Powers, with which I am intruded, in maintaining the Credit, Reputation, and Prosperity, of My Kingdoms.

Mr. Speaker teported, That the House had attended' His Majesty in the House of Peers, where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz. '

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The unusual Length of the last Session of Parliament made Me desirous of giving you as long a Recess as the Public Service \yould admit. I have, therefore, been glad to find Myself under no Necessity of calling you from your respective Counties at an earlier Season; and I doubt not but you are now met together, in the best Disposition, for applying yourselves to the Dispatdi of the Public Business.

You will, lam persuaded, agree with Me in regretting, that the Peace, so long expected, and so very de-firable, is not yet effected between Russia and the Porte; but it is with real Satisfaction I can repeat. That other Foreign Powers continue (till to have the same pacific Dispositions with Myself. I can have no other Wish than to see the general Tran'quillity restored; for the Establishment and subsequent Preservation of which, no Endeavours of Mine, consistent with the Honour of My Crown, and the Interests of My People, shall ever be wanting.

In this State of Foreign Affairs, you will have full Leisure to attend to the Improvement of our internal and domestic Situation, and to the Prosecution of Measures more immediately respecting the Preservation and Advancement of the Revenue and Commerce of the Kingdom. Among the Objects which, in this View, will come under your Consideration, none can better d^t serve your Attention than the State of the Gold Coin; which I must recommend to you in a more particular Manner, as well on Account of its very high Importance, as of the peculiar Advantages which the present Time affords, for executing, with Success, such Measures as you may find it expedient to adopt with respect to this great National Concern.

To allure His Majesty, That we sincerely regret that the Peace so long expected, and so much desired, is not yet efieded between Ruflta and the Porte; but at the same Time, to express the Satisfaction we feel, in learning that other Foreign Powers continue still to hare the same pacific Dispositions with His Majesty.

That we receive, with the utmost Gratitude, the Affu-nance which His Majesty has been pleased to repeat to ris, drat He has no other With than to see the general Tranquillity restored and preserved, confidently with the Honour of His Crown, and the Interests of His People; and that we consider this gracious Declaration of His Majesty as a fresh Instance of His Majesty’s paternal Care for the Welfare of His Subjects, and of His generous Concern for the Happiness of Mankind.

To declare. That we are truly ienfible, that it is our Duty, as it shall be our Care, to employ the Leisure which this State of Foreign Affairs allows us, in attending to our internal.and Domestic Situation; and that we cannot but acknowledge His Majesty’s great Wil-dom, in recommending and pointing out to our serious Consideratkm the State of the Gold Coin of this Kingdom, as well on Account of its very extensive Importance, as of the peculiar Advantages which the present Time affords for conducting, and executing with Success, any Measures touching this great National Object.

That we saw, with the deepest Concern, the Difficulties and Distress in which the Nation was on the Point of being involved, by the very alarming Degree of Diminution which this Coin had actually suffered, before the Evil was checked by the Regulations made in the last Session of Parliament; and that, imprefied with a just Sense of our Duty to our Country and our Fellow Subjects, we will exert our best Endeavours to accom-pfish the great Work of putting the Gold Coin upon such a Footing, as. may not only completely remove the present Grievance, but, as far as the Nature of the same 6

will admit, render the Credit and Commerce of the Kingdom secure from being again exposed to the like Danger.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee -thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the Utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a conve" ment Time to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the.Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person so taken into Custody, bedischarged out of Custody, without the Special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Cham-.berbe locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume

to bring any Strariger of Strangers into the Housej dr Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take Cate, that, from

Eleven of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Af- ’’ ternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through: the Streets> between Temple Bar and shall be kept free iuld open and that no ObftmCtions be made by Cars, DrayS, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Paf- lage of thfc Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take Care, tbafcthere be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in . Wstminster-Hall, or the Passages leading to the House, . duripg the fitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance, by Chairmen, Footmen,.- or otherwise, therein, or' thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Member^ of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the 'Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey. the Orders of the House ;Cand that' no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody but by the Special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Poll Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Post-master General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the lead immediately after the Rising of the House, and also from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take Care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Post-master General.

Ordered, That when any Letter or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame; and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, when the House is going to Prayers, give Notice thereof to all Committees; and that all Proceedings of Committees in a Morning, after such Notice, be declared to be null and void.

Address The Lord Guernsey reported from the Committee, ap-on pointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be pre-iented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn ' up an Address accordingly; which they had directed

him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Recommendation, and excited by Your Example, we will apply ourselves with the utmost Zeal and Diligence to promote the Welfare of our Country'; and that we will not fail to direct our Attention to such Parts, of.^ the Public Service as appear to us most important; having a perfcdl Confidence, that whatever Measures we may propose, that will serve either to secure or advance the Happiness and Prosperity of Your People, will always meet with Your Majesty’s gracious Appro- bation and Concurrence.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to His Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of His Majesty’s Most honourable Privy Councli, do humbly know His Majesty’s Pleasure, when He will be attended by this House.

Ordered, That His Majesty’s most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty our most humble Thanks, for Your Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Permit us. Sir, to alfure Your Majesty, that we fin-cerc-iy regret that the Peace so long expected, and so much desired, is not yet effected, between Russia and the Porte-, but, at the same Time, we beg Leave to express the Satisfaction we feel, in learning that other Foreign Powers continue still to have the same pacific Dispositions with Your Majesty: We acknowledge, with the utmost Gratitude, the Afl’urance which Your Majesty has been pleased to repeat to us, that You have no other Wilh than to see the general Tranquillity restored and preserved, consistently with the Honour of Your Crown, and the Interests of Your People: and we con-lider this gracious Declaration of Your Majesty as a fresh Instance of Your Majesty’s paternal Care for the Welfare of Your Subjects, and of Your generous Concern for the Happiness of Mankind.

We are truly sensible that it is our Duty, as it shall be our Care, to employ the Leisure which the State of Foreign Affairs allows us, in attending to our internal and domestic Situation: And we cannot but acknowledge Your Majesty’s great Wisdom, in recommending and pointing out to our serious Consideration the State of the Gold Coin of this Kingdom, as well on account of its very extensive Importance, as of the peculiar Advantages which the present Time affords, for conducting and executing with Success any Measures touching this great National Object: We law, with the deepest Concern, the Difficulties and Distress in which the Nation was on the Point of being involved, by the very alarming Degree of Diminution which this Coin had actually suffered, before the Evil was checked by the Regulations made in the last Session of Parliament; and we beg Leave to allure Your Majesty, that, imprefied with a just Sense of our Duty to our Country and our Fellow Subjects, we will exert our best Endeavours to accomplish the great Work of putting the Gold Coin upon such a Footing, as may not only completely remove the present Grievance, but, as far as the Nature of the same wiil admit, render the Credit and Commerce of the Kingdom secure from being again exposed to the like Danger.

Your faithful Commons will, with the utmost Chear-fulness, grant to \rour Majesty such Supplies as shall be found necessary in the present Situation of Affairs: And Your Majesty may be assured, that, animated by Your

A Petitiort of the Gentletrien, Merchants, Traders* and other the principal Inhabitants, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by a Rc-survey of the Line Levels and Surveys taken in the Year 1772, it appears that a Ctit, or Canal, for the Navigation of Boats and other Vessels with heavy Burthens, may be conveniently made, from the Leeds and Liverpool Navigation, in the Township of tiolbeck, near Leeds, over the River in the Township of Methley, to the River at or near Selby, in the said County; and that the same will open a ftiort, easy, and commodious. Communication between the said Town of Leeds and the several Townships or Places through or near which the said Cut, or Canal, is intended to be made, as well as to the Port of Hull, the City of York, and the interior Part of the County, and will be of great Advantage to the Trade and Manufactories carried on at, between, or near, the above Places, will tend to the Improvement of the adjacent Lands, the Relief of the Poor, the Preservation of the public Roads, and will be of great public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Navigation, in the said Township of Holbeck, near Leeds, to the River Ouze, at or near Selby aforesaid, and also to make a Navigable Cut, from the said Canal, into a Field belonging to Bradley

(now a Minor) in the Township of Hunjlett, near Leeds aforesaid, wherein to make a Bason and Wharfs, for the Purposes of mooring, loading, and unloading, Vessels employed in the Conveyance of Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, upon the said Canal, in such Manner, with such Powers and Provisions, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of Sir John Goodricke and Sir William ner, Baronets, Richard WilfonThomas Wilson, and John Burton, Esquires, on Behalf of themselves, and of the rest of the Undertakers of the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Calder, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act passed in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for making and keeping navigable the Rivers Air and Calder, in the County of York; and that the several Works executed under the Authority of the said Act have proved very beneficial; and that, since the passing of the said Act, the Trade and Commerce in the Neighbourhood of the said Rivers have been much advanced and increased, and a greater Number of Vessels than heretofore have been employed on the said Rivers; and that Complaints having been made to the Petitioners, that Goods carried up and down the same had of late not only been longer on their Passage than heretofore, but Embezzlements more frequent, the Petitioners, upon Enquiry, found the principal Inconveniences complained of to be occasioned by certain Mills belonging to private Persons upon the said Rivers; one of which, the most capable of distressing the *said Navigation, has been purchased; but find that there are still some Obstructions arising from Shoals in the said Rivers, lying as well out of, as within, the Limits

7

prescribed by the said Act , and thdt, by the Removal of such Impediments, and by some additional Works, the Petitioners apprehend the said Navigation may be greatly improved, and left liable to the Defects and In- conveniences complained of, the Freight of Goods considerably lowered, and Vessels not only enabled to carry larger Burthens, but to perform their Passage with greater Dispatch, Safety, and Certainty; and that, by Levels and Surveys lately taken, it appears, that a Cut, or Canal, ma y be conveniently made, from the River Air, in the Township of Haddlefey, to the River Ouze, at or near Selby, in the said County, which will open a short and commodious Communication for Vessels from Leeds, Wakefield, Halifax, and other Trading Towns situate upon the said Rivers Air and Calder, to the City of 7ork, and all Trading Towns upon the River Ouze, above Selby; and that the Petitioners are desirous, at their own Costs, to extend and improve the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Calder, and also to make, complete, and support, such new Cut, or Canal, from . Haddlefey to Selby i And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Petitioners as well to extend and make all necessary Improvements in the Navigation of the said Rivers, as to make complete, and support, a Cut, or Canal, from the River Air, in or near the Township of Haddlefey, to the River Ouze, in or near the Township of Selby aforesaid, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Daniel Lascelles. Sir Richard Sutton, Scc.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Mom- ing, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

From the House of Commons, 19th January 1774.

Sir,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to acquaint, you, That you are, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, to attend their Service in Parliament on Tuesday the Fifteenth Day of February next; and you are to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereon, upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure of the said House.

I am. Sir,

Your humble Servant,

Flr Norton, Speaker.

From the House of Commons, 19th January 1774.

My Lord,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to desire your Lord fii ip, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Members of Parliament for the Cinque Ports, to attend their Service in Parliament on Tuesday the Fifteenth Day of February next; and your Lordship will also be pleated to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereon.

I am* with the utmost Respect,

My Lord,

Your Lordship’s Most humble and obedient Servant, Flr Norton, Speaker.

The Right honourable the Earl of Holdernesse, Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports.

Swansea A Petition of the Burgesses, and of several of the In-Markets, habitants of the Borough and Town of , in the County of Glamorgan, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the present Mode, within the said Borough and Town, of exposing Butchers Meat to Sale, is by hanging it up in Penthouses in the public Streets, which is attended with many Inconveniences $ and that it will be more advantageous to have fixed and regular Shambles, the most convenient Place for which Purpose will be the Garden within the Castle of the said Town, and the Postern thereunto adjoining; and that it has been a Custom within the said Borough and Town, Time immemorial, to pay to the Portreeve of the said Borough, several small Sums for Pitching, and also the Skin of 'every Calf killed or exposed to Sale by Persons not being Burgesses; which Skin the Portreeve, in order to encourage and improve the Market, hath agreed to give up, on Payment of a reasonable Composition: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, with such Powers, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Mackworth, Mr. , &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber j Voi. 34.

Hand limited, by the Will of the said Sir Richard Atkins, to Sir William Bowyer, Baronet, since deceased, and the Petitioner the said Sir William Stonhouse, for a Term of Ninety-nine Years, in Trust for the Petitioner Pitt, with divers Remainders over; and that the said Church is a very ancient Fabric, and, by Length of Time, is become very ruinous, and the Number of Inhabitants within the said Parish is so greatly increased, that, if the said Church was in a Condition to be repaired, it would not be large enough to; contain them, for the Purpose of Divine Worship; and that the Petitioners . are desirous of having a new Church built within the said Parish, on a more extensive Plan, and on Part of the Waste Ground, Parcel of and within the said Manor, by a Rate and Assessment to be paid by the Parishioners of the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for veiling a convenient Part of the said Waste in proper Trustees, for the Purpose of building the said new Church; and to enable the Petitioners to build a new Church thereon, by such Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

That, by the said Act, the several Fen Lands and Low Grounds within the said District were charged with an Annual Assessment, not exceeding Two Shillings per Acre; and that, by the said Act, the Commissioners acting for the said District were empowered to borrow any Sum not exceeding £.600, for the Purposes of the said District; and that the said Sum has, together with the Assessment of Two Shillings per Acre, been applied towards the draining and preserving the Fen Lands and Low Grounds within the said District; notwithstanding which, they are still very much overflowed; and that the Petitioners are

A Petition of Sir Watkin Lewes, Knight, Was pre- Worteftet fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, at the late Election of a Member to represent the City of Worcester in Parliament, in the room of the late Henry Crabb Boulton, Esquire, deceased, the Petitioner and Thomas Bates Rous, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the said Thomas Bates Rous, by himself and his Agents, after the said Vacancy happened, and previous to and during the Poll, was guilty of bribing and corrupting, and attempting to bribe and corrupt, those who had a Right to vote in the said Election, in order to procure himself to be elected to serve in Parliament for the said City; and that many of the Aldermen of the said City acted as Agents for the said Thomas Bates Rous, and also did bribe, and attempt to bribe, with Money and otherwise, a great many Freemen of the said City, to induce them to give their Votes for the said Thomas Bates Rous at the said Election; and that William Mathers,

Esquire, Sheriffand Returning Officer of the said City, acted partially and unfairly, before and during the Poll, in rejeding good Votes for the Petitioner, and admitting Persons not qualified to vote for the said Thomas Bates Rous, and in many other Respects was guilty of Partiality in the Execution of his Office; and that, by these and other.illegal Means, the said Thomas B procured

a Majority of Votes upon the Poll, and was returned to serve in Parliament for the said City, in Prejudice of the Petitioner, and in open Defiance of the Law, and the Freedom of Elections: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief therein as shall, upon Examination, appear to be just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Wednesday Sevennight, the Second Day of February next, at Two of the Clock in the Afternoon.

That the Poor of the said Parish are of late greatly increased, and are maintained and supported at a great Expence; and the Workhouse of the said Parish is too fma'll for the Reception of the Poor; and that the present Method of raising and applying Money for the Maintenance of the Poor is attended with many Inconveniencies; and that if the Petitioners had a Workhouse suitably regulated, in which they might employ their Poor, with sufficient Power to compel them to work, such Poor would contribute to their own Support, and be of Use to the Community) and that the Burial Ground of the said Parish is quite filled with dead Bodies, and the Parishioners are at a Lots for a Place to bury their Dead; and that, if a proper Piece of Ground was purchased, for a Burial Place and for a Workhouse, and a convenient House and Buildings were erected thereon, the same would be of great Benefit to the said Parish: And therefore praying. A Petition of several Inhabitants of the Parish of

Saint James Clerkenwell, in the County of Middlesex, on

Behalf of themselves and other Inhabitants of the said

Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting

forth, That the several Streets, Lanes, and other public

Passages and Places, within the said Parish, are not

properly paved, cleansed, lighted, or watched, and are

greatly incommoded by Posts, Projections, and other

Annoyances; and that it would be a great Benefit to

the Petitioners, if Commissioners were appointed, with

proper Powers, for paving, cleansing, lighting, and

watching the said Streets, Lanes, and other public

Passages and Places, and for removing Obstructions and

Annoyances thereift, and preventing the same for the

future; and also for keeping the Highways and

Roads within the said Parish in good Repair; and

that the Money necessary for defraying the Expences

attending the same should be raised by one Rate or

Assessment; and that the Passage from Clerkenwell Green

to the Parish Church is narrow and inconvenient, and,

in order to make the same of a proper Width, it will

be necessary to take down Part of a House, known by

the Name of The Three Queens; and that the Laws in *

being are ineffectual for collecting the Monies assessed within the said Parish for the Relief of the Poor* and some Powers are wanting, for the better Management and Employment of Persons in the Workhouse belonging to the said Parish: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid.

A Petition of the Clothiers and Makers of Woolleii Broad Cloth, in the several Counties of and Somerset, on Behalf of themselves and all others

concerned in the said Trade, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Cloathing Trade is the grand Staple Trade of these Kingdoms, constituting a considerable Branch of our Foreign Commerce, and employing and rendering useful many Thou-fartd Hands, who otherwise would be a heavy Burthen on the Public; and that several Laws have from Time to Time been passed, for preventing the Frauds and Embezzlements the Trade is liable to, but that many new Species of Frauds and Embezzlements have been discovered and practised by the Manufacturers of every Denomination employed in the said Trade, against which the present Laws are by no Means an effectual Remedy, but totally inadequate thereto; and that the heavy Loss the Trade sustains by those Frauds are become alarming, and the Work-people are greatly encouraged therein by the Difficulty of Detection; and, when discovered, the Punishment is very trivial: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the more easy Detection and Conviction of, and for a Punishment more adequate to, such Frauds and Embezzlements, than are provided for by the several Laws now in being.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to tire Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Sir William , Mr. well, ice.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Sir George Savile reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir John Ramsden, Baronet, a Minor, by his Trustees Dame Margaret Ramsden and Thomas Ramsden, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of t1'- said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follow-eth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Joseph Atkinson, being examined, said, That the Town of Huddersfield, in the West Riding of the County of York, is the only Market for Narrow Woollen Cloths in that County, and is situated about Four Miles from the Calder, which is a Navigable River.

That it would be of great Advantage to the Town of Huddersfield, and all Persons having Estates in that Part of the County, if the Navigation was continued from the Calder, near Cooper's Bridge, to a Place called the King's Mill, near the Town of Huddersfield-, as it

would be a Means of supplying the Country with Coals, Lime, Corn, and many other Articles, much cheaper than they can be supplied by Land Carriage.

That at present the Carriage of Lime from Cooper's Bridge to Huddersfield is 45. a Ton, and that when this Navigation is made, it is computed that it will be carried for 1 s.a Ton.

The Witness also informed your Committee, that he had assisted in taking a Survey of the Lands through which the Canal is proposed to be made; and that it is practicable to make the same near Cooper's Bridge, and along the North West Side of the River Colne, to the King's Mill, near Huddersfield.

And, by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making the River Calder navigable, it appears, that the Proprietors of that 3

Navigation are restrained from doing any Works to prevent the making a Navigation from the River Calder to the Town of Huddersfield.

Mr. Atkinson, being again examined, said. That Sir John Ramsden is Lord of the Manor of Huddersfield, and Owner of the whole Town (except One House) and of a considerable Part of the Lands through which the Canal is intended to be made. Then,

Mr. Luke Holt, a Surveyor, informed your- Committee, That he had surveyed the Lands \yhere the Canal is proposed to be made, in which he was assisted by Mr. Atkitfon; and he confirmed the Evidence given

by Mr. Atkinson.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enabling Sir John Ramsden, Baronet, to make and maintain a Navigable Canal, from the River Calder, between a Bridge called Cooper's Bridge, and the Mouth of the River Colne, to the King's Mill, near the Town

of Huddersfield, in the West Riding of the County of York: And that Sir George Savile, Mr. Bacon, Mr.

Jenkinson, Mr. Weddell, and Mr. Frederick Montagu, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of George Lewis Newnham, Levett Black-borne, John Coxe, Walter Long, John Parry, and John Madocks, Esquires, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Benchers of the Society of Lincoln's Inn, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Lincoln's Inn is One of the Four Inns of Court, and hath been for Time immemorial, and now is, a Society intrusted with the Education of young Gentlemen studying the Law, and with the Power of admitting them to pra<ftife the fame; and hath accordingly been always governed and regulated by the Benchers of the said Society; and that the Lands and Tenements, and other Estates, of the said Society, have from Time to Time belonged, and now do belong, to the Members of the said Society, or some of them; and that the said Society have always considered themselves as having no Concern with any Parish or Parishes whatsoever, either with respect to bearing any Parochial Burthens, or deriving to themselves any Parochial Benefit; and now do, and always have, paved, lighted, watched, and cleansed, the said Inn, within the Limits and Bounds thereof, at their own Expence; and also relieved all their Members, Officers, and Servants, when they have been unable to provide for themselves; and that the said Society, with the Inns of Chancery (Members thereof) have always been considered by the Legislature, particularly in the Land Tax and Window Tax Acts, as a separate Body, and as such they proportion and raise those Taxes amongst themselves; and that a Claim has been lately made, by the Parish of Saint Clement Hanes, in the County of Middlesex, upon Part of the said Society, to make the same contributory to the Poors Tax of the said Parish, not only by charging it thereto as Part of the said Parish, but also rating every Chamber as a separate Messuage; by which Attempt not only a new and heavy Burthen is laid upon the said Society, but, in consequence thereof, the Members may be called upon and made to serve Parochial and other Offices, inconsistent with, and entirely subversive of, their original Design and Institution; and therefore, that the declaring the Members of the said Society, and the Lands and Tenements within the Limits and Bounds thereof, not to be liable to Parochial Duties or Burthens, would tend to the great Ease and Benefit of the said Society, and is highly necessary to their Establishment as a Society, and cannot be injurious to any Parish, no Parish having heretofore been able to subject the Members, or the Estates, of the said Society, to any Parochial Burthens; nor hath the same been attempted till very lately, and more especially as the Petitioners disclaim all Parochial Benefits, and undertake to maintain their own Poor: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes

aforesaid.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Reverend Mr. William being examined, said,

That the present Method of exposing Meat to Sale, in the said Borough and Town, is by hanging it up on Penthouses in the public Streets; and that this Practice is very inconvenient, and not only a Nuisance to the Inhabitants, but a great Obstru<ftion to Persons resort-;ng to, and passing through, the Streets of the said Town ‘ and Borough:

That regular and fixed Shambles for the Sale of Meat, would be attended with more Advantage to the Inhabitants, and more Convenience to the Public; and that ' the Garden within the Castle of the said Town, and the Postern thereunto adjoining, will be the most convenient Place for that Purpose:

That it Has been a Custom within the said Borough and Town, Time immemorial, to pay to the Portreeve of the said Bofough, the Skin of every Calf killed or exposed to Sale within the said Borough or Town, by any Person-avho is not a'Burgess.

A Member present informed your Committee, That several small'Sutns are paid to the Portreeve of the said Borough for pitching; and that he was present at a Meeting of the Corporation, where the Portreeve consented to relinquish his Right to such CalfSkins for a reasonable Composition, in order to encourage and improve the Market of the said Town.
