A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Farmers, and Turnpike Yeomen, Inhabitants of the County of Wilts, whose Roads: Names are thereunder signed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act passed last Session of Parliament, to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the general Laws now in being, for regulating the Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called England, and for other Purposes,

<no Carriage liable to be weighed by virtue of the said Act is allowed to pass along any Turnpike Road, being above Twenty Miles from London or W.cfiminster, unless the same be made and constructed in the Manner directed by the said Act; and that such Part of the Act is peculiarly oppressive to be carried into Execution without very great Injury and Loss to the Petitioners, and, inks Operation, tending to ruin anddestroy.aJl the middling and small Farms; and the Petitioners conceive, that, besides the very heavy Expence of the necessary Alteration of their Carriages, all the Parish Roads . throughout the County must be entirely altered, to be adapted -to the passing and rc-passing of Carriages‘of; such Gonstruction as by the said Act. is di-redted ;1 and that' to re>Jmake and repair: those Roads will be1 a grievous Burthen upon the Occupiers of ‘Lands and Tenements; and many Evils and Inconveniences will attend the [Execution, of the said Adfc:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to repeal a Clause in the said Act, providing for such Regulations in the Construction of the Wheels of" Carriages travelling on Turnpike Roads above Twenty Miles from London or Wefi-'ininfier.

Plymouth A Petition of the several, Persons Whose Narhei arse Paving, &c. thereunto subscribed, who are-Owners and Occupiers of Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, within the Town and Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read'; Taking Notice of Two Acts, passed in the ioth and 12th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for paving, lighting, and watching, the Town of , in the County of Devon, and for regulating the Carmen and Porters within the said Town; and Setting forth, That Doubts and Disputes have arisen, touching the Limits to which the Assessments for the Purposes of the said Acts do or ought to extend; and that many Parts of the said Borough consist of Fields and uninhabited Trails of Ground, and of Houses which lie at a great Distance from the populous or Town Part of it, lb that no Benefit under the said Acts accrues to the Owners and Occupiers of such Premises by virtue of the said Acts; which Premises have been lately assess'ed to the Purposes of the said Acts, under a Notion that the Generality of the Words thereof is comprehensive enough to take them in; which, the Petitioners conceive, was not intended; and that the Commissioners, not being directed in express Words to exclude them, or to draw a particular Line, cannot be warranted in so doing; and that, by the Law now in being, the Petitioners, as well as other Inhabitants of the Two Parishes that are comprized within the said Borough, are liable to the Statute Labour for repairing the Highways of the Parishes wherein they reside, which, together with the Assessments directed to be levied by the above-mentioned Acts, may be very burthensome to the Petitioners, and extremely grievous to the poorer Sort of Inhabitants; and that such of the Petitioners as are possessed of such Premises as from their Situation can receive no Benefit from the said Acts, and other Persons in the like Situation, are willing to take upon themselves the foie Repair of the Highways in the outlying Parts of the said Borough, provided they are declared to be exempted from Assessment under the said Acts; and that such others of the Petitioners as are subject to Assessment under the said Acts, are willing that the said Exemptions should take Place, provided they are themselves relieved from the Burthen of repairing the Highways in the outlying Parts of the said Borough; and that the Appeal to the Quarter Sessions for the County of Devon, concerning any Matters within the said Acts, greatly obstructs the Execution thereof, and occasions a Wade of the Money raised for the Purposes of the said Acts, as well as much Vexation and Expence to the Land Owners and Inhabitants within the said Borough; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if the said Appeal was confined to the . Quarter Sessions for the said Borough, not only the said Acts would be executed with greater Facility, but would free the Land Owners and Inhabitants of the said Borough from being put to any unnecessary Inconvenience or Charge: And therefore praying for such further Amendment of the said Acts, in thele and all other Re-spedts, as may remove any Inconvenience attending the Execution of the said Acts, and may make the same as little burthensome, and as largely beneficial, to the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and as conducive to the Resort of all Strangers, as possible.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Graves, Mr. Elwes, &c.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power td fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Election and Return, according to the Directions of Two several Acts of Parliament, passed in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members, on the Business of the House:

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 104 Members being found to be present;

The Petitioner, Sir Watkin Lewes, and his Counsel and Agents, who also appeared as Counsel and Agents on Behalf of the said other Petitioners, and the Counsel and Agents for the Sitting Member, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Bar: The Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee attending: also at the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Orders of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Box, containing the Names of all the Members of the House, and sealed with Mr. Speaker’s Seal, was placed upon the Table; and the Seals being inspected by Mr. Speaker, the Attestation annexed to the Out-side of the said Box, signed by Mr. Speaker, purporting, " That the said Box was, on the 1 ft Day of February 1774, made up in his Presence, in the Man-

ner directed by an Act, made in the Tenth Year of " the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, " or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament," vva* read.

And the Seals being broken, and the Box opened, the Attestation incloted therein, and signed by the Clerk, purporting, " That the Names of all the Members were by him, in the Presence of the Speaker, " put into the said Box, on the 1 ft Day of February " 1774," was read.

And the said Name*, written on distinct Pieces of Paper, being all as near as might be of an equal Size, and rolled up in the same Maijner, were, by the Clerk, taken out of the said Box, and put in equal Numbers into Six Glades, placed on the Table for that Purpose, and were there shaken together; and then the Clerk publicly drew out of the said Six Glasses, alternately, the said Pieces of Paper, and delivered them to Mr. Speaker, who read the same to the House.

And the Names of Thirteen Members, then present* were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Lord Clare being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age or upwards; and having, at the Table, verified the Cause of such Requisition, upon Oath, he was ex* cufed accordingly.

And the Names of Thirty-two other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Lord George Germaine being’ drawn, the Counsel for the Petitioners declared, that the said Lord GeorgeGermaine was intended to be no-

minated by the said Petitioners; and the said Lord George Germaine having, in his Place, consented to such Nomination, and no Objection being made to his serving on the said Select Committee, as such Nominee, his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Four other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members ft drawn, and not excused, or set aside, being complete, tha Counsel for the Sitting Member was called upon, by Mr. Speaker, to nominate one from amongst the Members then pielent, whose Names had not been drawn, to be added to those chosen by Lot, to lerve on the said Select Committee.

Gom A Petition of the Merchants of London, Importers &enega. ancj Exporters of Gum Senega, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read I Setting forth. That, by an Act of the Fifth Year of His present Majesty, several Duties were imposed upon Gum Senega and Arabic imported into, and exported from, Great Britain; and that, by the said Act, the Importation from Africa was confined to Great Britain, under the same Restrictions as those prescribed for Goods of the Growth and Produce of the British Colonies in America, by Two Acts of the Twelfth and Twenty-second of Charles the Second; and that the high Duty on the Exportation of Gum Senega has afforded great Temptation to smug-gling it out of this Kingdom, as also to the fending it direct from Senegal to Holland and other Parts, to the great Prejudice of His Majesty’s Revenue, and Injury of the fair Trader: and that a very small Proportion of the Quantity of Gum Senega imported from Africa is consumed in the Manufactories of this Kingdoms he principal Consumption being in Holland,

and other Places, which are continually increased or diminished, in Proportion to the Price it can be afforded at from Great Britain \ and that the Quantity imported for some Years past has exceeded the usual Consumption, which has been greatly diminished by the high Duty on Exportation, and has occasioned a Fall in the Price of that Commodity from /.120 to £.30 Ton; and that the Petitioners apprehend, it will be impossible to prevent the illicit Practice of a fraudulent Exportation of this Article, either from Africa or Great Britain, while the Export Duty is so high, and affords so great a Temptation to Smuggling; and that the principal Consumption of Gum Senega over all Europe commences early in the Spring; and that many of the Petitioners have received very considerable Orders for this Commodity, to be executed in case a Reduction of the Exportation Duty shall take place: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and give them such Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and date to the House, the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Mr. Anthony Bacon, Mr. Prescott, &c.: And they are to meet To morrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the Persons whose Names are thereto Crediton subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and other Inhabi- F*r«-tants of the Town and Parish of Crediton, in the County (Land Tax.) of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; repre-fenting to the House, That, on Monday the First Day of May 1769, afudden and most terrible Fire happened in the West Town and Borough of Crediton, whereby the belt Part of the Town, together with the Market Houses, were consumed to Allies; which unhappy Accident hath occasioned a Deficiency of the Land Tax (from Lady Day 1769 to Lady Day 1772) of the Sum of 115/. 4.1. 7 d. being the Sum charged and afiefled on the said Houses, and Hill in Arrear, as will appear by the Account annexed to the Petition; and that, by Means of the Poverty of the Inhabitants, who were entirely unprovided with Materials for Building, and from the Scarcity and excessive Price of such Materials, none of the new Buildings were completed till Lady Day 1772, and many of the said Houses are at present in Ruins, and cannot be re-built, not only on Account of the

freat Poverty of the Owners, but that the Fee of the ands whereon the Houses flood is veiled in Minors, so that a Title cannot be made to the Persons who would have taken Building Leal’es thereon; and that the Petitioners intended to apply to the House on the id Day of February 1773, the last Day of receiving private Petitions, to pay an Abatement of the Land Tax on the Houses and Buildings so consumed, from Lady Day 1769 to Lady Day 1772; but were informed that they were too late in their Application, the Land Tax Act for the then next Year having passed before that Time: And therefore praying the House, That a Clause may be inserted in the Land Tax Act for the Year 1774, whereby the Sufferers may be eased from paying the Arrears and Deficiencies of the Land Tax on the said Houses so burnt down and consumed as aforesaid, from Lady Day 1769 to Lady Day 1772; and that all Proceedings may be Hayed in the Exchequer on Account of such Deficicencies; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Charles Fanjliaw, Esquire, being examined, said. That Doubts and Dil'putes have arisen with respect to the Extension of the Powers of the said Acts; that the major Part of the said Borough consists of uninhabited Tracts of Ground, and scattered Houses, which lie at a great Distance from the Town Part of the Borough; which Premises have been assessed to the Purposes of the said Acts, as not being expressly excluded, and the Owners and Occupiers thereof are still liable to the Repair of the Highways.

And the Witness further said. That such of the Owners and Occupiers, as from their Situation can receive no Benefit from the said Acts, are willing to take upon themselves the foie Repair of the Highways in the out-lying Parts of the Borough, provided they are exempted from Assessment under the said Acts; and such others as are subject to the Assessment, are willing that such Exemption should take Place, provided they are relieved from the Repair of the Highways in the out-lying Parts of the Borough.

That the Appeal to the Quarter Sessions for the County of Devon, concerning Matters within the said Acts, greatly obstructs the Execution thereof, being attended with a great Expence, the Quarter Sessions being held between 40 and 50 Miles from the Borough; but if such Appeal was confined to the Quarter Sessions for the said Borough, the Acts would be executed with greater Facility. And he further said, That the said Acts are in other Respects defective.

Merchants, Traders, and other the principal Inhabitants, in the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s 7 Table:

Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr, Thomas Yeomans [An Engineer) being examined, informed your Committee, That he had surveyed the Line of the proposed Canal; a Plan of which he produced: and said, That it is practicable to make the said Canal through the several Lands therein laid down; that i;t is proposed to supply the same with the Water, from

several Brooks and Streams which may be brought into the Summit of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, which Streams now flow into the Kibble, and Western Ocean; the taking of which Waters will not diminith the Waters now flowing into, the Rivers and Colder.

And he produced to your Committee an Estimate of the Expence of making the said Canal, amounting to ^f.65,35 i. ys. $d.y which, he said, would be sufficient, in his Opinion, for completing the fame; that the Canal, when finished, will be capable of navigating Vessels from 50 to 60 Tons Burthen, which may go from Leeds to Selby in Eleven or Twelve Hours.

Being desired to give an Account of the Particulars of the Observations and Calculations upon which he formed his Opinion, that the Canal might be made without taking any Water from the Rivers Air and Colder;

He said. That in the Month of March last he examined several Brooks and Streams that may be brought into the Summit of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal; which, according to his Estimate of them, after a Frost of Six or Seven Days in the Month of March, pro- -duced upwards of 30,000 Tons of Water a Day; One Half of which, he- imagined, will be used for the Liverpool Side of the Canal, and the other Half for the Leeds.

Being asked, If there had been any Quantity of Snow fell at that Time, or soon before it ?

He said. There had not.

And being asked, Whether he had ever seen any of those Brooks in the Month of ?

He said. He had not: But the Reason for his supposing the re would be a sufficient Quantity of Water in the Month of August was, he being the re in September, and that there was then more than double the Quantity of Water than in the Month oi March before; but as it is usual for great Rains to fall in September, it might have been occasioned by that: That he had made all the Enquiry he could, if the Brooks had been fully kept up with Water during the Summer; and was informed, that it had been the driest Seal'on for Six Weeks that had been for Thirty Years before.

Being asked. Whether, when he viewed those Spring after Seven or Eight Days Frost, they appeared to him to be continual Springs, or only Land Waters coming down; and if they would be hifficient to supply the proposed Canal with Water ?

He said, They appeared to him to be all Springs; that he measured them, and believes that in the . shorteft Water Time Half of that Water would be fuf-heient; that there are Four other Springs he did not measure, as not having Occasion for them, that run to the Western Ooean, called Marfden, Water Meetings, and Two Small Brooks, which may be brought into the Summit; that there is a Place-called White moor, where the Waters may be collected for more than a Mile Square, which now run to the Western Ocean whenever it rains, and will join the Pendle Water in its Course to the Summit, the Source of which Water arises from a small Spring upon the Moor; but the Water the Witness depends on from that Place, comes from the Heavens.

Being hiked. In what Quantities he supposed that would fumish the Canal ?

He said, That, supposing no more than Twenty Inches fall in a Year, that, upon a Mile Square, would produce a Sufficiency to supply the proposed Canal for Five Locks in a Day throughout the Year.

Being asked. If, by the Course of Trade, it should prove convenient that more Water should go down Westward, the.Engineers of the proposed Canal will be authorized to divide it, as the Witness has said, without interfering with the Rights of the Liverpool Canal ?

He said, He'apprehended that, under the present Act of Parliament for making the Liverpool Canal, they have a Right to take more Water on the Lancashire Side than on the other; but that will not be the Cafe, as the Trade upon the East End of that Canal is expected to be more than on the Lancashire Side; that if the Liverpool Canal should want a certain Share of their Water Westward, the proposed Canal will not have that Half of the Springs before mentioned, which the Witness thinks necessary for the Supply thereof, without the Permission of the Proprietors of the Liverpool Canal, which he has heard they are consenting to; and that, in his Opinion, those Proprietors will not want more Water than is allotted to them for the Purpose of that Navigation.

Mr. John Reed (a Merchant and Trader at Leeds') being examined, said. That he thinks the proposed Canal will be of great Advantage to the Trade of Leeds, and the West Riding of Yorkshire; as the raoft material Advantages to Trade in general arises from the cheap Mode of Conveyance, the Dispatch, and of Consequence the leis Risk there is of Loss and Embezzlements; all which Advantages in exporting and importing Goods, will of Consequence proceed from this- Canal.

Being asked. In what Proportion the Price of the Carriage of Goods will be reduced from Leeds to Hull, by Means of the proposed Canal ?

He said, he apprehended many Articles would be carried One Third, some One Half, and in various Proportions, cheaper than they are at present. And the Witness laid. That there is ,£.70,000 subscribed for carrying the proposed Undertaking into Execution.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making a navigable Cut, or Canal, from the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Navigation, in the Township of Hol-beck, near Leeds, to the River Ou at or near Selby, in the County of York: And that Mr. Lascelles and Mr.

Cholmley do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Petition of George Lewis Newnham, Levett

John Coxe, Walter Long, John Parry, and John Ma-docks, Esquires, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Benchers of the Society of Lincoln's , in the County of Middlesex; Were severally referred That the Committed had examined the Matters of Fast contained in the said Petitions, and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in ,his:^Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fadl, contained in the First-mentioned Petition, is as follows:

It appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Thomas Adams, that Gray's Inn is one of the Four Inns of Court, and is a Society intrulled with the Education of young Gentlemen lludying the Law; that the Benchers of the said Society have a Power of calling Gentlemen to the Bar; and that the Society is regulated and governed by the Benchers:

That several Persons reside within Gray's Im, who are not.Members of the Society, and rent fepacate Houses to themselves:

That Chambers in Gray's Iun are granted to Students and Members of the Inn for Twenty-one Years absolute, by an Order of Pension, subject to future Orders of the House; but that Chambers are granted to no Persons, except Students and Members; and the Society have given Orders to Persons to quit their Chambers, as not being Members.:

Being asked, Why so many reside there who are not Members ? he said. Sometimes an Executor of a Member lets Chambers contrary to the Orders of the House. And being asked, In what Manner the Society have removed Persons not being Members ? he said. By fending Orders to the Owners of the Chambers to remove them; and apprehends the Society have a Power to remove Persons in case of Refofal:

That the Witness has read, in the Books of the Society, of Officers having been ordered to remove Per-. fons out of Chambers; that lie has been Steward to the Society Twenty-two Years, and was under the former Steward Fourteen or Fifteen Years, but never recollected . Vol. 34.

an Instance, in his Time, of forcing Persons out of Chambers:

That Terms in Chambers belonging to Members are renewed (if let to Persons who are not Members) on paying an extraordinary Fine, but Chambers devolving upon Executors are not renewed; that Executors have had Notice to remove Strangers out of Chambers, and to let them to Members of the Inn; and the Witness himself has given Executors Notice, that if the Chambers were not parted with to Members, their Terms would not be renewed; that there are no Parts of Gray's Inn, except what he has mentioned, but what are in the Hands of Members or Executors; and believes the Society have it in their Power to put an End to Terms before the Expiration, upon Breach of Orders of the House, but never knew an Instance of it.

That Two of the Houses in Warwick Court, belonging to the Society, are let on repairing Leases for Thirty-. nine or Forty Years, and the other Four are let by the House at Rack Rents; but that the Chambers of the Society are not let in that Manner:

That Gray's Inn is in the Parish of Saint Andrew, Holborn, and the Witness has been present at a Perambulation of the said Parish; that they go into the Cha* pel and Hall belonging to the Society, and the Society entertain them; but he never knew the Reader resign over the Delk to the Parochial Clergyman; and that they go the Perambulation once in Three Years, which he looks upon to be the customary Mode of perambulating:

That the Lands and Tenements belonging to the Society of Gray's Inn are vested in the Benchers, who are Trustees for the rest of the Society:

That the Society have a Scavenger of their own, who cleanses the Courts and Places within the Limits of the Inn, and carries the Dirt to a Place appointed for its Reception; and Once a Week, or Fortnight, a Parish Scavenger, after the Society’s Scavenger has put the Dirt in the Place appointed for its Reception, takes it away; for which, and for the cleansing that Part of the Lane which has been paved by the Society, they pay the Parish; that he knows of no other Parochial Rate which the Society pay, and that they never paid any Poor’s Rate, nor derived to themselves any Parochial Benefits, except that of the Scavengers:

That there is no Register kept of Births or Burials, arid he never knew, of a Child being baptized by the Reader or Lecturer; that Children dropped in the Inn have been font to Saint Andrew’s Parish, but not by any Order of the Society:

That Marriages have been performed in the Chapel before the late Act of Parliament for preventing Clandestine Marriages, but never since:

That he knows of no Overseer of the Poor belonging to the Society, nor any public Officer to whom the Poor can be lent for Relief; and that the Society have no Fund for Relief of the Poor:

That there are no Constables or other Parochial Officers within the Society, neither is there any Officer to whom a Justice might direct his Warrant:

That he knows of no Servants or other Persons (haring derived Settlements from their Service to the Gentlemen of the Society) being relieved at the Expence of the Parish. of Saint Andrew's, Holborn:

That the Servants of the Society have been relieved by the Society; and he never knew an Instance of a poor Person of Gray’s Inn, upon Application, being refilled Relief; and that the Society have always relieved the Poor belonging to the Inn, but thinks they have it in their Power to refuse Relief; and that the Poor are relieved out of the General Stock of the Society:

That he never knew the Servants of any Gentleman or Tradesman, refilling within Gray's Inn, claim Relief from the Society or Parish; but that he is not in a Situation of knowing what Efertwnds are made upon the Pari fti:

That the Society have a Preacher, Lecturef, and Reader, who are elected by the Benchers, and paid by the Society; and that they perform Divine Service in the Chapel according to the Rights and Ceremonies of the Church of England, but never christen, or perform Burial Service in the Chapel:

That the Society pave, light, watch, and cleanse, the Inn at their own Expence, and contribute to the Paving Rate made by the Pari Hi of Saint,

Ho/born j but the said Parish does not pay any thing for paving done within the Limits of the Society.

Then an Act made in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of Ring George the Second, for granting certain Rates and Duties upon Houses, Windows, or Lights; and also, an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax; were read; whereby it appeared, that the said Society have been considered by the Legislature as a separate Body, and are taxed accordingly.

Mr. Adams also informed your Committee, That a Claim has been lately made by that Part of the Parish of Saint Andrew's, Holborn, which lies above the Bars, and the Parish of Saint George the , in the County of Middlesex, upon the said Society, to make them contributory to the Poor’s Rates of the said Parishes; that the Society refused Payment, and a Distress was made j the Consequence of which was, that an Action of Replevin was brought against the said Parishes by the Benchers of the Inn; that the Records of the Proceedings were withdrawn, but the Witness knows not at whose Request.

A State of the Matter of Fast, contained in the Second-mentioned Petition, is as follows: r

Mr. Thomas Grint informed your Committee, That Lincoln's Inn is a Society entrusted with the Education of young Gentlemen studying the Law, and is regulated and governed by the Benchers thereof.

That every Member of the Society inhabiting Chambers in Serle’s Court, is admitted during Lite, paying a certain Fine and Fees to the Society, which are called Freeholds, subject to the Orders and Regulations of the Bench; and that they all belong to Members of the Society who never paid any Parochial Rate.

That the Witness has known a Perambulation of the Parish of Saint Andrew, Holborn, and the Perambulators have come into the District of Lincolns Inn, claimed by the Society; that the last Time the Parish went this Perambulation was in the Year 1771, and the Witness believes they went in the customary Mode of perambulating Parishes.

That the Society have no particular Fund for the Support of the Poor, except the General Fund of the House; that no Poor’s Rates are collected,. and that there are no Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, or Constables, nor any Officer to whom a Justice of the Peace might direct his Warrant:

That there is a Chapel belonging to the Society, but the Witness never knew any Children christened there; that Marriages have been performed in the Chapel before the late Act of Parliament for preventing Clandestine Marriages, but none since; that there is a Burial Place for those who die within the Limits of the Society, but no Burial Fees are paid to the Parish, and he never beard that the Minister of the Parish claimed any Fees.

Being asked. How many Inns are claimed by the Society of Lincoln's Inn ? he said, Only one now, Thaive's Inn being fold, which is become separate Property from the Society; and he apprehends they have the same Power of alienating Furnivaf s Inn, and the District of Lincoln's Inn.

That the Witness knows of no- Children being born in Lincoln's Inn, no Families living the re, and never knew of any Children being dropped there.

That the Preacher and Reader belonging to the Society, are paid by the Benchers, and the Sacrament is administered every Month; that there is a Register of

A. 1774.

Burials kept there , and the Witness never heard that any Pew or Gallery in the Churches of Saint Clement Dams, or Saint Andrew's, Holborn, was appropriated for the Use of the Society of Lincolns Inn.

That the Limits and Bounds of the Inn are lighted, watched, and clean fed, by the Direction, and at the Expence, of the Benchers.

That Persons belonging to the Society have many Times been relieved by the Benchers out of the General Fund of the Society j and that one Isaac a lu-

peranuated Porter, at this Time receives Two Shillings ‘ a Week, but he is the only Person at present who receives a Weekly Allowance, and that it was a voluntary Act of the Benchers; that other Persons have sometimes received Five or Ten Guineas at a Time; and the Witness never knew any of the Officers or Servants of the Inn applying for Relief, and being refused.

That no Perfop has ever been returned upon the Society from any Parish as a Pauper having gained a Settlement, and the Witness knows no Instance of any Person gaining Relief from a Settlement there.

That no Persons are permitted to reside within the District of Lincoln's Inn, but what are of the Society; that the Stamp Office is within the District, but the Servants employed there do not live in the Inn, except the Housekeeper, who is not a Member.

That the Commissioners of the Stamp Office pay Dues to the Society for the House, and many of the Chambers are purchased by the Crown, for the Use of the Stamp Office, in the Names of some of the Members of the Inn, and whenever they drop, they apply for a fresh Nominee, that being the Terms they are held upon j that they are obliged to bold them in the Name of a Member of Lincoln's Inn, and the Commissioners have been charged with Part of the Fund'. And being asked, Whether there is any legal Process of enforcing Payment of their Share towards this Fund ? he fai<L All Persons who are admitted, give. Bond for securing the Payment of it; and that no Rate is paid by them to the Parish of Saint Andrew's, Holborn', that this. Fund is afieffed upon the Members who are admitted to the Chambers, and made out in their Names, and paid Aanually by the Commissioners, in the.Names of those Gentlemen who are admitted to the Chambers,

Being asked, Whether he ever knew of any Charge or Demand being made, by the Parish of Saint Clement Danes, or Saint Andrew's, Holborn, relative to the Paving Rate ? he laid. There was, in the Year 1771 or 1772 j :that he could not recollect the Sum exactly, but believed it was about £. 25. is. 6 and apprehended it was laid for Serle Street and Carey Street; that the Answer of the Benchers to this Demand was, That it should be collected and paid by the Occupiers of those -Chambers on the West and South Sides of Serle’s Court, exclusive of the annual Dues paid to the House.

That the Gates of the Inn are shut at Eleven o’Clock every Night, and he never knew the Constable of the Night, or Watchman, demand an Entrance for Search of Vagrants, or exercise any J urtfdiction in the Inn after the Gates were once shut; neither did he eVer know the Parochial Beadles come into the Inn in the Day Time to take up Vagrants or Beggars, to remove them into other Parts of the Parish.

That he was appointed one of the Assessors of the Land and Window Tax by the Benchers, and collects the same in Serle's Court, as Part of the Inn; and he produced, to your Committee the Books of Assessment on Lincoln's Inn, in the Years 1740 and 1748, for the - Land and Window Taxes. Then,

Sir William Guise reported from the Committee, to Woollen whom the Petition of the Clothiers and Makers of Manufacture.’ Woollen Broad Cloth, in the several Counties of -cefier, Wilts, and Somerset, on Behalf of themselves and ail others concerned in the said Trade, was referred;

That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition is as follows:

Thomas Pettat, Esquire, a Clothier in Gloucestershire, informed your Committee, That many Frauds and Embezzlements are practised by Persons employed in the Clothing Trade, of which he gave the following Instances: That when the Wool is delivered to the Pickers, they can embezzle One Pound or more in Twenty, without any Possibility of being detested; their Method being of throwing the Wool upon wet Stones, whereby it impregnates the Water, and they bring it home full Weight:

That with respect to the Scribblers, they can, by adding 1 lb. £ of Oil, keep out the same Quantity of Wdol, whereby they will get 35. $d. and the Clothier loses 45. being the Worth of a Pound of Spanifo Wool in the Picking State:

That with respect to the Spinners, their Method of Fraud is by holding the Yarn over a boiling Pot, whereby the Steam impregnates with the Yarn, and the Clothier loses Haifa Pound in Six Pounds; which Fraud cannot be discovered:

That with respect to the Weavers they can keep

back 5 or 6 Pound of Yarn; which, if Spanish, is worth 4-r. 6d.or 5 s. a Pound, out of every Piece of Cloth containing 30 Ells, and weighing 6olb.; and which

Fraud cannot be discovered, as the Cloths are always

brought home wet.

And the Witness gave your Committee the following Instance of a Fraud committed by one of his own Weavers: That the Weaver had wove 8 or 10 Pieces of Cloth before either of them came to the Scale to be weighed, when it appeared they were 7 or 81b. a Piece too light; upon which Discovery the Witness examined his Books, to fee wfiat the Weaver was then at work upon, and found he had two Blues; which, when he brought home, he certified he had put the Whole of the Yarn intrusted to him into the Two Cloths; but, upon searching his Houft, the Witness found 131b. of blue Yarn, which he should not have suspected, if the former Cloths had not come home lighter than they ought to have been; whereupon the Weaver was committed to Prison for 14 Days, as the Law directs.

Being asked, Whether there are no Methods by which he might discover the Frauds he had complained of, by weighing the Manufacture some Time after he had received it, and comparing the Weight at that Time with the Weight at the Time of Delivery ?

452 t i° Februarii. A. 1774.

He. said, That in respect to the Wool and Yarn, it may ;be done, by putting it in a Room where there is a Fire or other warm Place; but would be very inconvenient, upon Account of the Room and Time it would take ;up. And the Witness said. That the Embezzlement of the Chain and Abb by the Weaver tenders the Cloth of less Value than was intended by the Clothier.

Thomas Tippets, Esquire, likewise a Clothier in Glou-

cefterjhtre, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Pet tat, with respect to the Frauds committed by the Pickers, Scribblers, and Spinners; and added. That he has had Cloths come from the Weavers 3 or 41b. lighter than they ought to have been; and that tome Pieces of Cloth have fold above£. 4 cheaper than they would have done, on that Account: That although, upon Search, large Quantities of Ends and Yam have been found in Possession of divers Persons; yet, for want of being able to prove the Identity of the Goods, the Persons in whole Custody they were found could not be punished, the Laws at pfefent not compelling the Persons in whose Possession they are found to discover how they came by them.

Mr. Nicholas Pearfe, a Factor for Mr. Tippets and other Clothiers, said, That from the bad Quality of the Cloths, occasioned by such Embezzlement, they are often sold at an inferior Price.

Mr. Thomas Cooper, a Clothier, at Hampton, in cejlerjkire, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Pettat, with respect to the Frauds committed by the Scribblers, Pickers, and Spinners; and that, with respect to the Weavers, the Witness apprehends they can easily embezzle or 51b. in a Piece of 30 Ells, or 60 lb Weight.

And the Witness gave your Committee the following Instance of a Fraud committed by a Weaver employed by hi me That the Weaver having Two Chains, and between 40 and 501b. of Abb, delivered to him, the Value whereof was £. 13; he fold the whole Quantity for about jf. 6, and set off for London, but was taken up at Oxford, and brought back, tried, and coqvicted j and that his Punishment was only Imprisonment for 14 Days, and Whipping.

And the Witness further said. That he had, in search-tng of lulpedted.Persons Houses, found a large Quantity of Wool and Yarn of various Sorts, different Colours, different Wools, and in many small Quantities, and not being able to swear to the Identity of any of it, the Persons could not be prosecuted.

Mr. William Peach, a Clothier, near Hampton, being examined, informed your Committee, That he put out Two Pieces of Cloth to a Burler, to pick out the Knots, or any thing else that did not properly belong to it;

that the Burler fold one of the Pieces, and kept the

other till it was rotten; and all the Witness could do to her, was to imprison her for 14 Days, and hav'e her whipped, there being no other Punishment by the Laws in being; and that the Piece which was rotten was fold for Half the Value, and the other loft entirely.

Europe, Africa, and North America, furnish the great Importation; their Vessels, especially such as are not well acquainted with those Seas, will chuTe to stop at the First Port to which they can go before the Wind, and without being entangled amongst a Number of HJands: It is rarely visited by Hurricanes, and affords Conveniences and Refreshments to the Trader; and that the Utility of Barbadoes, as a Place of Rendezvous for Fleets and Armies, by reason of its Situation, has been shewn from the repeated Experience of the last War; and that the Crops of Sugar Canes in the said Island have failed for a long Series of Years, and this Misfortune having been aggravated by repeated Calamities of Fire, the Aid of a more extended Commerce is become necessary for the Support of the said Colony: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Assistance and Relief to the Inhabitants of the said Island as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Privilege The Order of the Day being read, for the Attendance Contempt! ^e Reverend John Horne;

And the said Reverend John Horne not attending, according to Order, the Messenger to w!*om the Order of Monday last, for the Attendance of the Reverend John Homet was delivered, being called upon, to give an Account of the Service thereof, acquainted the House, that he served the said Order on the said Mr. Horne, on Monday Evening last, at the House of Mr. Tooke, in Serjeant's Inn, Fleet Street; and had delivered -to, and left the said Order with, the said Mr. Horne:

And Mr. Speaker having informed the House, that the Clerk of this House had received a. Letter from the said Mr. Horne, relative to the Service of the said Order j.

The said Letter was read; - and is as followeth;

' Sir,'

Late last Night I received a Notice, ligried with your Name, of an Order, which the House of Commons made Yesterday, for the Attendance of a particular Person on Wednesdaynext.

I apprehend, that Notice mult have been intended for some other Person, and delivered to me by Mistake: of which I informed the Bearer the very Moment after I had read it: At the same Time adding, that whenever the House of Commons shall desire Attendance, I will pay to them all proper and prudent Respect.

I have the Honour to be,

Sir,

Tuesday, Feb. 15. 1774. Your most obedient,

humble Servant,

John Horne.

A Petition of Sir John Goodricke, and Sir William

Milner, Baronets, Richard W, Thomas Sawer, John

Smyth, Thomas Wilson, and John Burton, Esquires, as well on the Behalf of themselves as of others the Undertakers and Proprietors of the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Colder, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making a Navigable Cut or Canal, from the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Navigation, in the Township of heck, near Leeds, to the River Ouze, at or near Selby, in the County of York; and Setting forth, That, in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of King William the Third, an Act passed for making and keeping navigable the Riven Air and Colder, in the County of York; and divers Tolls for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, passing and repaying the said Rivers, were thereby vested in the several Undertakers therein named; and that, upon the Credit of the said Act, the said Undertakers, and their Successors, laid out large Sums of Money, in making and keeping the said Rivers navigable; and their rdpe&ivd Shares and Properties have been, from Time to Time, fold and conveyed in the Nature of Estates of Inheritance, and are become a considerable, if not a principal, Support and Dependence of several Feme Coverts, Widows, and Infants; and that, under the Powers of the said Act, the said Rivers were made and have been kept navigable, from the said Towns of Leeds and Wakefield, to the Tide Water; and, in order to render the Navigation of the said Rivers more convenient and useful to the Community, the Petitioners are now applying to Parliament, for Powers to extend and make all neoeflary Improvements in the said Navigation; and to make a Navigable Cut from the River Air, in or near the Township oiHaddlefey, to the River Ouze, at or near Selby, at their own Charge; and that the several Improvements, so proposed to be made, will render the said Navigation commodious, and fully sufficient to answer all the Purposes of the Country, and render any Canal from Holbeck to Selby unnecessary; and which intended Cut will not exceed Five Miles and a Quarter in Length, and will open a short, easy, and commodious. Communication between the Town of Leeds and the City of York, and the interior Parts of the County, and between the Towns of Halifax, Wakefield, Huddersfield, and other Places, on the Upper and Lower Colder, Rochdale, and other trading Parts of and the said

City, and other Parts lying on the said River Ouze, above Selby, and which Advantage cannot result from the proposed Canal from Holbeck to Selby, and that the making such proposed Canal will not have the beneficial Effect which the Persons who appty for it pretend, and will deprive the Petitioners said Navigation of so considerable a Part of the Water whiclj now supplies the

feme, as will greatly incommode the Passage of Vessels; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Evidence, by which the said projected Canal from Holbeck to Selby has teen hitherto attempted to be supported, will appear insufficieitt to prove its Utility or Practicability; and besides, the Plan of its Execution requires Powers and Authorities of a very extraordinary Natwe and alarming Extent; and that the said Canal fjom Holbeck to Selby is intended to be carried over the said River, within the Limits of the Petitioners said Navigation, by the Means of an Aqueduct Bridge, which will greatly impede the Passage of Vessels on the said River, and may, in Times of Floods and High Water, occasion the Passage under the said Aqueduct difficult and dangerous; and that the making such Canal will bein many other Respects highly injurious to the Petitioners:

And therefefre praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, before the House, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Right honourable Six John Good- Diuo. ricke. Baronet, and Sir William Lowtker, Baronet, Owners of Collieries and Lands in Swillington, Kippax, and Allerton Bywater, and of Thomas Smith, Gentleman, William Fenton and Thomas Fenton, Esquires, Tenants of the said Collieries, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed the said intended Canal is proposed to be carried over the said Collieries, and through the said Lands of the Petitioners, by which the said Collieries will be much injured, if not utterly ruined, and the said Lands very greatly damaged: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against such Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of the Council and Assembly of the Island port# of Antigua, was presented to the House, and read; (Antigua.) Setting forth, That, from a Series of bad Crops, from a dreadful Fire which happened in the Town of Saint John in the Year 1769, from a Hurricane in 1772, and from the Emigration of the Inhabitants therepf, the said Island is reduced to a State truly alarming, and such as the Petitioners fear mull, if not speedily succoured, occasion its entire Destruction; and that the Distresses of the few who yet remain on the Island are continued by the unremitting Severity of the Drought, which has occasioned such a Scarcity of the Staple Commodities, and consequently such a general Decay of Trade, that many of the Inhabitants are without the.

Means of procuring the Necefiaries of Life, while the total Ruin of others is almost daily brought about; and that the Petitioners cannot think of any Means so likely to alleviate their Distresses, and the Distresses of their Fellow Subjects, and to restore that Country to its former flourishing State, by a Return of its Inhabitants and Trade, as an Act for making Saint John's and Parham, in the said Island, free Ports, similar to those of the Island of Dominica; and that the Act for making free Ports in the Islands of Dominica and Jamaica being to expire in the next Session of Parliament, and as the Petitioners are informed that Applications have been, or will be, made for a new Act to continue them, they therefore make Use of this Opportunity to endeavour to get the Ports of Saint John and Parham included therein; and that the said Island, being to the Windward of all the Leeward Charibbee Islands, and happy in its many excellent Harbours, is well situated to become

the

14 Geo. III. i8° Febr 471

the principal Mart and Storehouse of the Whole; and the Petitioners are well satisfied that, by clierishing the Spirits of the present Inhabitants, bringing back the Emigrants, and restoring Trade to the Island, the most l'anguine Wilhes of the Petitioners will be fulfilled, and the Revenues of the Crown will be considerably en-crealed; and that the said Island, although more fe-verely alllided with Drought and other Calamities than the other Leeward Charibbee Islands, has, at a considera-bie Charge, accommodated His Majesty’s Regiment quartered there, for a great Number of Years, a Circumstance from which the other Islands derive almost equal Advantage and Security, although they do not at all contribute their Assistance towards the Expence: And therefore praying the House, to take their unhappy Condition into Consideration, and to pass a Bill for making Saint John and , in tfcis Island, free

Ports, or to give the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Thomas Frankland reported from the Committee,' Air to whom the Petition of Sir John Goodricke, and Sir and CalJer

Ham Milner, Baronets, Richard fVilfon, Thomas Navigation,

and John Burton, Esquires, on Behalf of themselves, and of the rest of the fJndertakers of the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Colder, in the County of was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and her rfad the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered if in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as folio wet h; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act, passed in the 10th and nth Years of King William the Third, intituled, "An Act for making and " keeping navigable the Rivers of Air and Colder, in the County of York," was read. And,

Mr. John Gott, being examined, said, He is Surveyor of the Works upon the Rivers Air and Colder, and has been in that Station ever since August 1760; — that the Works consist of Locks, Cuts, Dams, and Weirs, whereby the said Rivers are made navigable; — that the Trade in Coal, Stones, Lime, Manure, and other Articles of Trade in general, in that Neighbourhood, is encreased, by means of the Works upon the Navigation, without which those heavy Commodities could not be carried to such a Distance so conveniently, or so as to answer the Purpose of Trade; — that he has known the Navigation above 30 Years. — And being asked. If the Navigation was in as good a State 30 Years ago as it is now ? he said. It was the same as to the passing of Vessels, but not a» to the loading of them , that since that Time Deals have been set upon the Dams, and Flalhes are commonly made upon the Rivers, which the Trade of the Country did not so much require then as it does now; and that by means of the above-mentioned Deals and Flalhes, Vessels are enabled to draw

Six Inches more Water than formerly. — And being asked, When such Deals were first put up ? he said, In 1760; that they have been hung at all the Danis belonging to the Proprietors, and at most of those belonging to the Mills. — And being asked, When the Vessels began to draw Six Inches more Water ? he said, About 10 Years ago. — And being asked. What Number of Boats were employed upon the Rivers Ten Years ago? he laid, He could not be particular as to the Number, but he knows there are more now than there were then j that he believed, from his own Observation, they are encreased as 3 to 2.

Then several Petitions, which had been addressed to the Proprietors of the Navigation, from Merchants,

Traders, and Owners of Vessels, complaining of Stoppages on the said Rivers, and of Embezzlements and other bad Consequences resulting therefrom, were produced and read to your Committee. Then,

Mr. John Smeaton, an Engineer, was examined:

And being asked. What has been done in consequence of those Complaints ? laid. He was applied to in June 17 7 x, first by Mr. Birt, and afterwards by the Proprietors, to view the Rivers, and give them his Opiniop in what Manner the Navigation might be improved to the great eft Advantage j that he thereupon took a

View _

478

View of the Rivers, and gave them his Opinion, that the same might be considerably amended, but that a complete Navigation could not be made without fresh Powers from Parliament; that the principal Obstructions he found to the Navigation,'were Mills, from the Manner of the Millers using the Water, from Shoals, and from almost the Whole of the Works being laid too high — -And being asked, If those Mills and Shoals are the principal Causes of the Embezzlements complained of ? he said. He believes they are; for, by flopping the Vessels the Men have Opportunities of embezzling; and he apprehends the Mills to be one of the principal Causes of the Stoppages before-mentioned. — And being asked, If he knew any other Causes besides the Mills and Shoals? he said. He believes there are mt>re, but that he could not enumerate them immediately, as he apprehended he was only to specify the principal ones; — And being asked. Which Mills he conceived to have been the greatest Obstruction to the Navigation ? lie said Nottingleyand Brothertm Mills.

It was then made appear to your Committee, that the Undertakers of the Navigation have lately purchased the l|id Mills. And,

Mr. Smeaton being asked, If there are any Obstruc-tionsin the River below Weylaf he said. Yes. — And being asked, If the River below Weyland stood in need of Improvements ? he said, Yes.

Then Mr. Gott was again examined. — And being asked. If he was acquainted with the Construction of Mills ? said. He had been employed in re-building and repairing Mills and Dams on the River for 15. or 16 Years. — AncI being aiked, If there are any Mills upon the River Air,.which, by their Construction, are capable of annoying the Navigation ? he said. There are, particularly Nether- Mill, at Legds, Hunjleet Mills, New Mill, Thwayte Mill, and Fleet Mill, some of which are Corn Mills, and the others Filling Mills. — And being asked. If the Millers at those Mills had done any thing to prejudice the Navigation ?-he laid. They had frequently. drawn down the Water from the Dams, above the Mills, lb as to lay Vessels a-ground, and stop them in their Passage. — And being asked. If this had been in corilequence of the natural Working of the Mills ? he said. It sometimes may have so happened, but very leldom; that they frequently do it to distress Vessels in their Passage, when there is no Nec^fiity for. doing it in the Working of the Mills, in order to collect Money from the Owners and Matters of the Vessels before they will permit them to pass.

Mr. Smeaton was then asked, Whether, as and Brotherton Mills, which had been proved to be one of the principal Obstructions to the Navigation, are now in the Hands of the Undertakers of the Navigation, they might not turn the Water to which Use they pleased, and by that means give a Preference to one Boat before another ? he laid. The several Boats on the River are so intermixed; and that it will require so great a Time to draw dowm the Water, that the Undertakers are as likely to hurt their own Boats (if they have any) as those of other People. What they described ? said, That N° x is a general Plan of the Rivers Air and Calder, from Leeds and Wakefield to Armine, and of the River Ouze, from Armine to Selby, describing the Cuts intended to

be made as an Improvement to the Navigation; and that the smaller ones are Five of those Cuts on a larger Scale; that he assisted in taking the Survey of those Cuts; and that the Admeasurements upon the large Plan are the respective Lengths of those Cuts. And

it less liable to the Inconvenience complained of And being asked, What Effects will be produced to the Navigation of the River Air, by the Execution of those Cuts, and other Improvements, in the Bed of the River below Weyland bhe said, One principal Effect will be,

that the Vessels will go in much less Time, and without Impediment in the dry Seasons; and the Freight will be consequently lowered, and Vessels may pass with greater Burthens than they do now, taking-the Average of the Year; and they may pals with greater Certainty and Safety. — And being asked,1 If the making of thele Cuts will prejudice the Mills in respect'to their Water? he said. What will be the Distance between Leeds and Selby, in case the above Plan be executed ? he laid, 29 Miles and Chains. — -And being asked, Whether, in case the Plan is executed, and the River improved below Weyland, the Navigation will be sufficient to answer all the Purposes of the Country ? he said. He had reason to believe it will be more than sufficient; because, as there will be no Stoppages but the Time taken up in passing Locks, there will be Time enough for 100 or J2o Vessels to pass in a Day, which he believed to be twice or three Times as many as ever have Occasion to pass. — And being asked, If the Lands through which the Canal is to pass, require Lime for Manure ? he said. They will be greatly improved by it, and a Communication will be opened between them and the Lime Kilns at Knolting/ — And being asked. Hop A Petition of several Hop Merchants, Exporters, Dealers, Factors, Brewers, and others. Dealers in, and Consumers *c* of Hops, within the Cities of London and

and Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act of the Ninth of Queen Anne, an Allowance of One Tenth, or 10 Pounds in every 100 Pounds Weight, is directed to be paid to the Hop Planter, as a Tare for the Package or Bag; notwithstanding which, the Planter never makes any Allowance to the Buyer or Consumer of Hops for Tare; and that, since Hops have encreased in their Value, it has become a common Practice amongst the Planters, to pack their Hops in very heavy coarse Bagging, weighing from 20 to above 40 Pounds each Bag, for which Bagging the Buyer pays the same Price as he does for the Hops contained therein; and that the Petitioners have, for many Years past, endeavoured to remedy this Evil, in which they have had the Countenance of several Hop Planter’s, but their Endeavours have proved ineffectual; and, as the Price of Hops en-creases, the Grievance becomes the greater: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief as shall be thought just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie lipoh the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Land Owners, Carnarvon, and Occupiers of the several Messuages, Tenements. Lands, and Premises, near and adjoining to the stone*.* Sea Shore, between the Orms Head, in the County of Carnarvon, and the River at Voryd, which bounds the several Counties of Flint and Denbigh, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That from the Orms Head to Voryd is about Twelve measured Miles along the Sea Coast, and the Freehold Lands in most Parts thereof are situate near High Water Mark, where the Tide flow? very rapidly, and for upwards of Three Miles the Banks are from 14 to 20 Yards perpendicular above High Water Mark, and the Soil at the Foot of the greatest Part thereof is of a Clay or Marly Nature, and in the rest of a soft Lome intermixed with Stones; and that, at the Foot of these Banks, along the Sea Shore, there were, not many Years ago, several hundred thousand Tons of Stones, some of which were Pebbles made use of in Paving, biit chiefly Lime., Stones, and several so large that no Power could remove them in

Bulk,

14 Geo. III. 250 Februarii 493

Bulk, which Stones prevented the Tides from waffling down the Banks; and that of late Years the lower Clals of People in the Neighourhood, with all the Labourers they could meet, after breaking the large Stones, they gathered them and the smaller Stones along the Sea Shore into different Heaps, and invited the Mailers of Flats and Vessels to carry them off, which those People fell to the Owners or Mailers of such Flats or Vessels, by which Means the Shore becomes very even, and the Tide flows higher, and with more Violence, and undermines and washes down the Banks of the Freehold, whereby the Land Owners have loll several Acres of Ground, worth from 155. to ^c)s. an Acre; and that Part of the Road near Penman Rhofe has been entirely washed away, and the same is changed to the other Side of the Hill, detached from the Sea, whereby all the Passengers going from Chester to Holyhead are obliged to climb up a lleep

Hill near Half a Mile about, before they get into the ancient Road; and that, in order to put a Stop to such Practices, several Actions have been brought in His Majesty’s Court of Exchequer at , and some

of the Defendants appeared, whereby several Causes were at Issue, and the Records brought down to the last Salop Assizes, when the Judge and Counsel were in Doubt as to the Legality of such Action, although the Proof of the Damage done to the Lands by carrying off the Stones was clear; and they recommended that the Plaintiffs in those Actions should wave the Colls, and accept of a Verdict, which they agreed to do, as the Defendants were very Poor, as well, as all the other People who gather Stones there; and that some of the - Stone Gatherers, against whom Actions were brought, did not appear to those Actions, and Attachments being sued out, they were arrested, and imprisoned, for want of entering an Appearance, and their Families became a Burthen to the Parishes; and that, at the last Great Sessions for the County of Denbigh, Six several Actions were brought against the Persons who gathered Stones since the Assizes at Salop, and none of them have appeared; yet they Hill continue doing the fame, to the great Detriment of the Land Owners, Clergy, and Inhabitants; and, unless some Method is taken to prevent this growing Evil, many hundred Acres of the bell Corn Land in North will be carried

away by the Sea; and it is much feared the greated Part of the High Road from Holyhead to Saint AJaph, bordering upon the Shore, will be all'o carried away; and that, by further prosecuting Actions at Law, the lower Oafs of People will be undoubtedly ruined, and large Sums of Money expended, without any certain Remedy to prevent the carrying away the Stones, and Loss of Land: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the effectual preventing the carry ing away any more of the Stones which lie along the Sea Shore from the Orms Head to For yd aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Williams, Sir Watkin Williams Wynne, kc.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the most Noble Henry Duke of Buc- Ayr cleugh, and the most Noble Charles Duke of Queensberry and Dover, in Behalf of themselves and the other Copartners of the Banking Company, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, known under the Firm of Douglas, Heron, and Company, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners

and

494 a5° Februarii. 1774.

and others did, 101769, enter into a Partnership, and subscribed a Capital or Stock of £.160,000 for carrying on the Business of Banking, in that Part of Great Britain cajled Scotland, chiefly with a View of promoting Manufactures and Agriculture in that Part of the Kingdom, by accommodating Farmers and Manufacturers with Money, and extending their Credit; and that, by too great an Enlargement of the Credit given to Farmers, Manufacturers, and others, the Partnership, in 1772, came to be in great Want of Money to satisfy the Demands made upon them, owing to the Check given to Credit by the many Bankruptcies which happened at that Time in different Parts of the Kingdom; and that the Partnership, in order to raise Money to satisfy the Demands upon them, and thereby prevent the Bankruptcy of many, which their flopping Payment would necessarily have produced, did raile, upon Annuities of One and Two Lives, the Sum of £. 450,000, and upwards, with a Power, by a verbal Agreement, to the Partnership, of redeeming the Annuities, by repaying the Price, and One Half Year’s Annuity more, in the Way of Premium; and that the Partnership, in order to extricate their Affairs, and to enable them to redeem the Annuities, did, in the Month of 1773, in a

general Meeting of the Partners, resolve to discontinue for the future the Banking Business, and, at that and a subsequent Meeting, did nominate and appoint a Committee of the Partners of the Partnership, to be a Committee for managing and transaCling all Business necessary for winding up the Affairs of the Partnership; and that the said Committee, after much Consideration of the most proper and effectual Method of redeeming the Annuities, and finding it was impossible to raise immediately any considerable Sum for that Purpose out of the Funds of the Partnership, without bringing great Distress upon their Debtors, and hurting the Credit of that Part of the Kingdom, where their Debtors chiefly reside, did, upon the 9th of February current, call a Meeting of the Annuitants, by Advertisement in the Public Newspapers, and delivered them the following Proposals in Writing: That his Grace the Duke of Buccleugh, the Duke of Queensberry, Archibald Douglas, Esquire, and others, being the present Committee chosen and appointed by a general Meeting of the Proprietors at Edinburgh, to manage the Affairs of the said Messrs. Douglas, Heron, and Co. do execute Bonds of £. 50 each, some few broken Sums excepted, to the Amount of the original Sums paid for the said Annuities, with the Addition of Half a Year’s Purchase, or £. 50 more, on every Annuity of £. 100. and pro rata for every greater or leller Annuities; the said Committee binding themselves, and their Heirs and Executors, and having a Power to bind all the Partners of the Company, and their Heirs and Executors, to the due Performance of the Obligations in the said Bonds; and that the said Bonds of£. 50 each, carrying an Interest of£. 5 per Hundred, be made payable to a Person named, his Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, by Indorsement, and rendered to all Intents and Purposes negotiable and vendable, like East India Bonds, Navy and Exchequer Bills, or any Effects of a similar Nature; and that, as the Principal of the said Bonds, the Premium of Redemption included, is estimated nearly at £. 480,000 and the Interest at £.5 per Cent, thereon at £. 24,000 Annum, it is further proposed. That specific Estates, in Land unentailed, in Scotland, to the clear Amount in Rent of £. 32,000 per Annum, or upwards, be fub-jected, by Mortgage, as a corroborative Security for the Discharge of the Principal and Interest of the said Bonds; that is to say; of the Interest every Half Year m don, and of the Principal by Four Instalments; videlicet; One fourth Part, as nearly as the whole may be conveniently divided, at Midsummer 1778, One fourth Part; at Midsummer 1779, One fourth Part at mea 1780, and the lait, whether foipdhing more or lel$ than a Fourth Part, at Midfum,1782 ;.and that the ,. 9

A Petition of Richard Arkwright and Company, of M Co^ton Nottingham, Spinners of Cotton, and Manufacturers of (Arkwrijht’*; British Cotton Stuffs, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in the Year 1769, the Petitioner Richard Arkwright obtained Letters Patent, for spinning Wool, Flax, and Cotton, in a.better and more expeditious Method than theretofore, by Means of a Machine, which Machine is peculiarly adapted for spinning Cotton Yarn for Warps, and is principally used for that Purpose; and that, with such Warps, there are wholly made in Great Britain, from raw Materials, Velverets, and a Variety of other Goods, particularly a new Manufacture of White Cotton Stuffs, adapted for Printing; and that a few Pieces of the said White Cotton Stuffs, lb made with Cotton only, were some Time since vended in London and Lancashire, and in the latter Place printed, and thereupon charged in Lancashire with Two Duties of Three Half Pence each per Yard, amounting together to Three Pence a Yard, the first of which laid Duties is the Duty charged by an Act of the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for laying a Duty on certain Silks, Callicoes, Linens, and Stuffs, printed, painted, or stained; and the other Duty is the additional Duty charged by an Act of tl^ twelfth Year of her said late Majesty’s Reign, for laying an additional Duty upon certain Linens, Silks,

Callicoes, and Stuffs; and that tnofe Goods so made with Cotton only beipg.approved of; a considerable Quantity thereof were mjade and sold to several Linen Drapers and . Callico Printers in and about London, where the Officers for collecting His Majesty’s Duties of Excise infilling such Goods were liable by the same Acts as Callicoes to Two Duties of Tfyiee Pence per Yard each, making together Six Pence a Yard, many Orders for the same were countermanded, to the great Prejudice of a new and promising Manufacture,

and to the Poor of this Kingdom, as well as of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners are adviled, that the said new manufactured Goods, if printed, stained, or painted, ought at most to be only considered/as Stuffs printed, stained, or painted, and, as such, chargeable with such Two Duties of Three Half Pence each per Yard only; and that so high a Duty as Six Pence per Yard will operate as a Prohibition on the Manufacture in Question; and that a Doubt has arisen, whether such White Cotton Stuffs are not, when printed, painted, stained, or dyed, prohibited to be used and worn in Great Britain; and that the Two Duties of Three Pence per Yaid on Callicoes is conceived to be a Duty on Foreign Callicoes imported, and afterwards printed, painted, or stained, in this Kingdom, and not on British Goods made from raw Materials; the Petitioners allure themselves, the said Manufacture, if not crushed by so heavy a Duty as Six Pence a Yard, will rapidly increase, and find, new and effectual Employment for many Thousand British Poor, and increase the Revenue of this Kingdom; and that it is probable such Warp, made of Cotton which is manufactured in this Kingdom, will be introduced in the Room of the Warps before used, made of Linen Yarn (great Part of which Linen Yarn is imported ready-spun from Foreign Parts) in making Lancashire Cottons, in regard Cotton Goods so made wholly of Cotton will be greatly superior in Quality to the present Species of Cotton Goods made with Linen Yarn

Waips,

4.

14 Geo. III. 25 0 Febmariu497

Warps, and will bleach, print, walh, dnd wear better, and, by Means thereof, find further Employment for the Poor: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for ascertaining the Kate or Duty on the said White Cotton Stuffs wholly made of Cotton Wool, and manufactured within the Kingdom of Great Britain, when printed, painted, Rained, or dyed, at Three Pence per Yard only, and for the free Vending, wearing, or using, by all Persons, in Apparel, Househokl Stuff, Furniture, or otherwil'e, any Sort of the said Cotton Stuffs, when so manufactured, and printed, painted, Rained, or dyed, with any Colour or Colours, without incurring, or being liable to be deemed or adjudged, or taken to incur, any Penalty or Forfeiture whatsoever, for vending, wearing, or using, such Manufactures, so printed, painted, Rained, or dyed, as aforesaid; and that there may be allowed, upon the Exportation of the said White Cotton Stuffs, when exported without being printed, painted. Rained, or dyed, the like Bounties as are allowed on the Exportati >n of British and Irish Coarl'e Linens, to be paid under the Regulations of the Acts of the Fifteenth, Sixteenth, and Eighteenth Years of his late Majesty King George the Second; and that there may be allowed, upon the Exportation of the said Cotton Stuffs, when printed, painted. The Lord North presented to the House, pursuant to their Address to His Majesty, of the 7th Day of in the last Session of Parliament,

A Paper, intituled, " Extracts of Letters, and other Informations, received by His Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, concerning Duties, or Prohi- bitions, laid since the Year 1720, on the Importation " of British Manufactures into the Dominions of any of " the Princes or States of , of Rtiffia, or of

" Holland."

And the Title of the said Paper was read;

Ordered, That the said Paper do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the.Member* of the House.

The said Paper is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

The House being informed that the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door; they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth. That, by a Level and Survey lately taken, it appears, that a Cut, or Canal, for the Navigation of Boats, and other Vessels, with heavy Burthens, may be made, from a Place called Moorfields, in the Neighbourhood of the said City, to a Place in the River Lee, near Waltham Abby, in the County of Essex; and all'o to communicate with the said River, near Lee Bridge, by a Branch from the said Canal; whereby the Conveyance of Corn, Flour, Malt, and sundry other Kinds of Provisions, Coals, Timber, Lime, Manure, Goods, and other Things, will be greatly facilitated, and rendered less expensive; and the Petitioners conceive, that the said Undertaking, if carried into Execution, will be of great Advantage and Encouragement to Trade, tend to the Improvement of the adjacent Lands, and be of public Utility: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable them to make and maintain the said intended Navigation, and the several Works thereunto belonging, with such Powers and Provisions, and under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof j and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Oliver, Mr. Alderman Sawbridge, &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records; and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriff, and Common Council, of the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, in the County of the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Reciting Letters Patent of Incorporation to the said Town of Newcastle Tyne-, and setting forth, That the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Town are seised, to them and their Successors, in Fee, of a Tract or Parcel of Uninclosed Ground, called The Tou-n Moor, within the Liberties of the said Town and

County; and that, for the Purpose of improving a Part of the said Town Moor, a Lease was granted to Hopper, of Turfdale, in the County of Durham, Farmer, for the Term of Twelve Years, from the 12th Day of May 1772, under certain Rents and Covenants; and reciting Articles of Agreement, to establish for ever, to resident Freemen, and the resident Widows of the deceased Freemen of the Town of Newcastle, the full Right and Benefit to the Herbage of the Town Moor, for Two Milch Cows, in the Manner therein mentioned;" and further setting forth. That the said Mayor and Burgesses are all'o seised of a Tract of Uninclosed Ground, called The Nun's Moor, adjoining upon, and lying open to, the said TowA Moor\ upon which said Nun’s Moor the Milch Cows of resident free Burgesses, and resident Widows of deceased free Burge lips, have grazed in like Manner as upon the said Town Moor; and that the said Mayor and Burgesses are also deiled of a Parcel of Inclosed Ground, called contiguous to the said Town Moor, upon, which laid Parcel of

Ground called The Leazes the Milch Cows of resident free Burgesses, and resident Widows of deceased free Burgesses, have, during a Part of the Year, been ac-' customed to graze; and that the said Nun's Moor and the said Leazes do respectively stand in Need of Improvement; and that, although the said Agreement is manifestly calculated and intended for the Benefit of the resident free Burgesses and resident Widows of deceased free Burgesses in particular, and the Inhabitants of the said Town in general, and the Improvement of the said Nun’s Moor and Leazes respectively would tend to the like Benefit, yet the same cannot be effectually carried into Execution without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for carrying the said Agreement effectually into Execution, and for other the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for amending the said Act, and for continuing the Term and enlarging the Powers thereof in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.
