To prove the Allegations of the said Petifiofy An Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for improving and completing the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and from the City of London to the Town of , in the County of Wilts, was read; by which Act the said Navigation

is directed to be divided into Six Parts or Districts, the first of which is between the City of London and the City Stone, above Staines Bridge; and in the said Act there is a Proviso, that the same should not^ctend to take away the Rights of the City of London, or any Body Politic or Corporate, or other Person or Persons whatsoever; or to enable the Commissioners of the said Navigation to erect Weirs, Locks, Turnpikes, or Toll Gates, within the Liberties or Jurisdiction of the City of London, Then,

Doctor William Batty, being examined, said, That the Sum of £. 23,000 has been laid out in the Second and Third Districts; the Navigation of which Districts, before the passing of the said Act, was frequently difficult, unsafe, tedious, and expensive, and is now become l'afe, cheap, and expeditious.

Being asked the Nature of the Improvements made in those Districts ?

He said, That Pound Locks have been substituted in the room, and by the Side, of Flafti Locks, in the Third District: — That there has been a Horse Towing Path made, from Windsor Bridge up to Boulter’s Lock, in the Second District, and from Boulter's Lock to the Kennett’s Mouth, in the Third District, which conveys the Barges up to Reading: — That by making the Flafti Locks, there is a considerable Improvement, besides the Pounds themselves: — That there has been a considerable Advantage gained by getting rid of the expensive Mode of towing with Men, which could not be done while the Flafti Locks were only the Passage, because it required Men to get the Barges up through the Flafti Locks, and, from the Necessity of it, they made their own Terms with the Bargemasters, and the Bargemasters with their Customers, which raised the Price of Freight (in about 8 or 10 Years) from 7 to 1 or. a Ton; therefore there was Reason to apprehend, if the above Improvement had not been made, it would have been much higher by this Time; but, on the contrary, the Price of Freight has been reduced a Ton, between Windsor and the Kennett’s Mouth, notwithstanding the additional Toll paid by Bargemasters in passing through the several Pound Locks in the Third District. And the Witness said. That Mr. Barnard, of Newbury, declared to the Commissioners, that he laved £.12 out of £.18 in navigating a Barge from Marlow to Reading.

Being asked. If, from his Knowledge, those Locks have not occasioned some Shoals being thrown up in some Parts of the River?

He said. He did not know they had; that he knew nothing of the State of the Navigation of the First Distfift, to Staines Bridge, but, by Report, and Complaints of the Bargemasters.

Being asked, If he knew what additional Tolls were paid upon the River, in the Third District, since the passing of the Act ?

He laid, That at Boulter's Lock, there is 4 a Ton; at Marlow, id.-, sx Temple Lock, id.-, at New Lock, 1 d.; at Hamilton Lock, id.-, at Marsh Lock, id.-, at Cotter ell's Lock, 1 d. -, and 1 d. at Sunning.

Being asked. If those Tolls were equal to the highest Power given by the Act ?

He laid, They were less, all but at One Lock; — That they were as high as could be laid at Boulter’s Lock, which is 4 d.and One Penny a Ton only at every one of the others; — and, that he hoped those Tolls were fuffacient to keep, perpetually, that Part of the River in Vo L. 34.

good Order, which he believed is dow peffectly havi-> gable.

And the Witness said; That he had attended several Meetings of the Commissioners in the First District, where several of the Inhabitants of that District* attended, and Enqtairy was talked of to be made into the State of the Navigation between London and Staines-, but it was unanimously concluded, that nothing could be done in it,- on Account of the Restrictions laid by the before-rheritioned Proviso, otherwise the Witness thinks the Commissioners Would have tnended the Navigation in that Place.

Being asked, If he knew whether ahy Intimation Was given, at any of those Meetings, to the Corporation of London, of the State of the Navigation' below Staines, and of the Commissioners Desire to improve it ?

He laid, That, at a general Meeting of the Com-rhissioners, a Memorial was ordered to be delivered, in the moll respectful Manner, to the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, expressing the Difficulties the commissioners lay under, with respect to amending the River in the First District, and their Apprehensions that, for Want of a proper Amendment; the Navigation would be rendered difficult, if not impracticable; and likewise acquainted them with their Intention of applying to Parliament for Relief; and as . they looked upon the Interest of the City, of,

and of the Western Counties through which the River runs, inseparable, they desired and hoped the City of London would concur, and give them what Assistance they could in that intended Application; — That the said Memorial was signed by the General Clerk, by Order of the Commissioners, and presented in October 1772, but no Notice taken of it by the City of London to the Commissioners from that Time to this.

Being asked. Whether the Commissioners had amended the River from Boulter’s Lock to the London Stone?

He said. As far as Windsor Bridge only; and it Will require Time before they can proceed, for Want of Money, to amend it in the Manner it could be wished.

Being asked. If he knew whether the Gentlemen who have signed the Petition, or the Commissioners, or any other Set of Men, were willing to improve the Navigation of the River, without taking Tolls, in the First District ?

He said, He believed not, because he apprehended that the Thames, in that District, could not be amended without Money; that there is no Fund out of which Money can be borrowed, that either the Petitioners or the Commissioners know of, that can be a Security for the Payment thereof.

Being asked. If he imagined it would be more for the Advantage of the Public to contribute to any prafti-cable Amendment of the Thames by the Corporation of London, who desire noTolls, than by charging the Public with a Toll by any other Means ?

He said. He did not think it would; in the First Place, he did not think that the Corporation of London -had any Thing to do with amending the River, it being veiled in Commissioners alone, by Two Acts of the Twenty-fourth of King George the Second and the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty, from London to Cricklade; and in the next Place lie thinks, that Two different Sets of Trustees, separate and independent of each other, for one and the same Puvpose, are incompatible.

Mr. Joseph Nickalls, Surveyor to the Commissioners, informed your Committee, That nothing has been done towards improving the Navigation of the First District, since the passing the Act of the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty; that the same is very bad at present, owing to the great Number of Shoals; but that the same is full as capable of Improvement as either of the Districts which have been improved; — that many of the Towing Paths are so bad as to render the River not navigable long in the Time of a Rife of Water, or

B^ing asked. Whether the effectual Improvement of the River would not remove many of the Arguments that were urged in Favour of an Application from the City of London, for making a Canal from Monkey to Ifieworth f

He said, If by those Arguments it was meant the Reduction of the Price of Freight, it would.

Being asked, If the Works that have been carried on within the Third District, have done any Injury to any Parts where they have been erected ?

He said, None whatever: And the Witness said. That he had never been instructed to make any Estimate of the Expence of the Works of the First District since the Application was made, but he had made a Model for the Second District, which he apprehended is most eligible for the First.

That the Commerce of the Petitioners, in the Cutlery Manufacture, into Germany, Russia, Poland, Ko~ ningjlurg, Dantzick, Hamburgh, and Riga, now is, and for a long Time has been, a very extensive Branch of their Foreign Trade, and One of the greatest Supports of the poor and laborious Manufacturers of the said Place and Neighbourhood, and which has been chiefly owing to the Encouragement given to the Importation of German and Russian Linens, by which those Countries have been enabled to make their Payments for the Manufactures of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, the State of the Linen Trade of Great Britain and Ireland is now under Consideration; and that they have Reason to apprehend, that the Persons applying in Favour of the said Linen Manufactures may endeavour to obtain an Act to lay further Duties upon the Importation of Foreign Linens, or otherwise to discontinue the present Drawback upon such Part of those Linens as shall be exported to America and the West Indies, which may tend to prejudice " and endanger the valuable Branch of Commerce which the Petitioners now have with Germany and other ISTorthern Countries: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and permit the Petitioners to be heard by themselves or Agents, against any Propositions which may appear to them likely to prejudice and endanger the Interest of their Manufacture and Trade.

A Petition of the Merchants, Exporters and Manu-(fadurers of Cloth and other Woollen Goods, in the Parish of Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of

‘.York, whole Names are thereto subscribed, was pre-lented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend it is proposed to lay ariadditional Duty on Foreign Linens, with a Retention of the Duty on their Exportation to our Colonies; and that the Petitioners believe that the Value of Wool-

len Goods, exported to Places froip whence Linens are imported, exceed the Value of the Linens brought from thence , and the Duties on our Manufactures in those Parts being at present very moderate, the Petitioners fear the Effects of a Foreign Retaliation, which would be highly detrimental to the Petitioners, as well as to all other the Woollen Manufacturers in this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House will’take the Premises into Consideration, and'permit the Merchants, Exporters and Manufacturers of Cloth and other Woollen Goods, in this Kingdom, to be heard against any Innovation by additional Duty on Foreign Linens, or will grant them such other Relief as to the House may seem meet.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of Ditto. Kirkaldie, and Manufacturers and Dealers in Linen in (Kiikaldi?.) that Town: and Neighbourhood, was also presented to the House, and read j Complaining of the Decline of the Linen Manufacture, which for many Years has been the Staple Manufacture of North Britain, and particularly of the said Town: And therefore praying the House to take th6 same into Consideration, which is of the greatest Importance to this Kingdom, as well as to the Petitioners, and to grant such Relief as shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of Dyfart, and the Dealers and Manufacturers in Linen in ' y ' that Parish, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise complaining of the Decline of the Linen Manufacture; and praying for such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants of London trading to Ditto. North America, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are Exporters 0;

of Goods to His Majesty’s Colonies of North America in all Branches of the British Manufactures, and of tish and Foreign Linens to a very considerable Amount, necessary for the Use and Trade of the Inhabitants of those Colonies; and that the Petitioners have been informed of an Application for Leave to bring in a Bill to alter the present Duties and Drawbacks on Foreign Linens; and the Pet itioners are of Opinion, that in case an Act shall pass to increase the Duties on Foreign Littens, without allowing the Drawback of such Duties, it will greatly encourage the clandestine Importation of Foreign Linens into the said Colonies, and with them many other Foreign Manufactures, and lessen the Demand for American Produce: And therefore praying the above Measure may not be adopted by the House.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of Dittos

the Burgh of Firth, in Common Council assembled (Perth.)

And also,

A Petition of the Manufacturers and Dealers in Lmep in the Burgh of Perth ;:

Were also severally presented to the House, and read; Complaining of the Decline of the Linen Manufacture; and Setting forth, That the fam'e mud soon be reduced to the last Extremity, un-Icfs some speedy and effectual Encouragement be granted for the Revival of it: And therefore praying the House to consider the Premises, and to give such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, Council, and Ditto. Merchants, in the Town of Dundee, North Britain, was (Dundee.) also presented to the House, and read; Complaining of the Decline of the Linen Manufacture; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe; that the Quantity of Foreign Linens imported into England is annually increasing, which they consider as;the great Cause of the Decrease in the Home Manufacture; and are afraid that, if not properly reltrained, will always bear hard upon the Manufacture . of Great , and may bit

last confirte it within very narrow Limits: And therefore, praying the House fully to consider the present State of the said Trade, and grant it such Relief as may be thought effectual to save this Country* from Ruin, and preserve to Britain and Ireland this valuable Manil-Fadure, and that inestimable Treasure of useful and in-dullrious People, who, if the Trade is not supported, must be thrown out of Employment, become destitute and forlorn, and will probably be obliged in Delpair to desert their native Country.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to enquire further into. the present State of the ' Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland.

and that the said Estates of the Petitioners are in Settlement under an Act of Parliament; and that, upon the Determination of such Leases, the Petitioners will become entitled to the improved Value of such Houses or Tenements, but are restrained by the said Act from faking Pines upon granting future Leases; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Place where the Market is now scept is by much the most convenient Place for the Inhabitants in the whole Town, for a Shambles or 'Market for the Sale of Butchers Meat; and that the Place where the said Market is intended to be held is the moll inconvenient Situation for a Market in the whole Town; and representing to the House, that if it should be thought proper to remove the present Shambles or Market, the Petitioners are Owners of Lands and Grounds where a Shambles or Market might be made much better and more convenient than the Place proposed by the said Bill, though not so convenient and ufefill to the Inhabitants as the present Shambles; and that the Petitioners understand, that the Portreeve of the said Borough claims a Right, by Custom, tefthe Skin of every Call killed or exposed to Sale within the lame, by Persons not being Burgefl’es, and is willing to give up his Claim to such Right upon a reasonable Compensation being made to him for the same; but these Petitioners deny that the Portreeve has such Right: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill as it now Hands, and have such Relief as the House shall think equitable and just.

Ditto. A Petition of several Freeholders, Lessees, and Occupiers of Houses and Tenements, within the Borough and Town of Swansea, in the County of , was

Air Sir Thomas Frankland reported from the Committee,

an^P^er to whom the Petition of Sir John Goodricke and Sir Wil-and l‘,am Milner, Baronets, Richard WilJ'on, Esquire, Thomas Navigation. Wi/fon, Esquire, and John Burton, Esquire, on Behalf

of themselves and the rest of the Undertakers of the Navigation of the Rivers .4/rand CalJer, in the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had di-

rected him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William JeJj'of, an Engineer, produced a general Plan of the Rivers Air and Calder, from Leeds and Wakefield to Armine-, and of the River Otize from Armine to Selby-, describing Five several Cuts, intended as an Improvement to the Navigation. And he produced Plans of those Cuts on a larger Scale. And being asked, If he assisted in making those Plans ? he laid, He made the Survey, and drew the Plans, under Mr. Smeaton’sDirections. Then,

John Smeaton, Esquire, an Engineer, being examined, said, He was employed, in the Year 1771, by the Undertakers of the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Calder, to take a Survey of those Rivers, for the Purpose of improving the Navigation, and for making it as complete as the Nature of it would admit of And being asked. If the several Cuts, described by the Maps produced, were recommended by him to the Undertakers, as Part of his Plan for the Improvement of the Navigation of the River Air, between Leeds and Hadd/efey ? he said. They were all recommended by him in 1771, except the Cut by Brotherton Marsh which he recommended since, according to the present Plan. And being asked, What Obstructions are to be avoided by those Cuts ? he said. The Obstructions, meant to be avoided, arose from Shoals in the Rivers from the Bottoms of the Locks lying too high, and from the Millers introducing an artificial Impediment, by drawing down the Water of their Dams; and that he apprehends those Obstructions may be effectually avoided by Means of those Cuts, but not without; that the principal Object of the Undertakers Application to Parliament, at this Time, was, for Power to make those Cuts; and that he advised them to apply for those Powers. And being asked. If the Shoal, near Woodlesford Lock, can be avoided without theproposed Cut there? he said. He apprehended it could not, in a proper Manner; — that he was influenced by other Motives, besides the Shoals, to recommend the making of that Cut; which were, to avoid that ‘Mill Dam, and Sivillington Bridge, which is a local Impediment in that River. And being asked, What Impediment there is in navigating Fleet Mill Dam he said, That the Dam, when full, only makes a dead Level in Times of Low Water, not quite Two Feet and an Half above the Shoals; and when drawn clown a Foot and an Half, which he supposes the Millers might occasionally do, there will be only One Foot Water upon the Shoals; whereas his Proportion is for making Three Feet and an Half Water at those Times, without flashing. And being asked. If there are any Shoals between Swillington Bridge and Fleet Mill? he said, There are none qearcr than the navigable Cut. And being asked. What are the Lengths of the Shoals between Sivillington Bridge and Woodlesford Lock ? he said. About 38 Chains of such as would become Impediments when the Dam is drawn down 18 Inches, and still leaving 3 Feet 6 Inches Water over those Shoals. And being asked, What will be the Expence of removing those Shoals ? he said. He could not tell; that it being a Work of so great Uncertainty, was one of the Reasons for avoiding the entering into it at all. And being asked. Copy‘Right Mr. Feilde reported from the Committee, to whom of 8 the Petition of the Booksellers of London and Westmin-

Booksellers, jler, on Behalf of themselves and others. Holders of Copy Right; and also the Petition of John

Bach and Charles Frederick Abel, on Behalf of themselves and several other Composers and Proprietors of Books, Works, and Compositions in Mulic, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fad contained in the First-mentioned Petition; and had also examined the Matter of the Second-mentioned Petition; and that the Committee had directed him to report a State of the Fadts contained in the First-mentioned Petition, and also the Matter of the Second-mentioned Petition, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read.

A State of the Matter of Fadl contained in the First-mentioned Petition, is as follows; viz.

It appeared, that by an Act of Parliament, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for the Encouragement of Learning, by veiling the Copies of printed " Books in the Authors and Purchasers of such Copies, during the Times therein mentioned," it was, amongst other Things, Enacted, That, from and after the 10th

Day of April 1710, the Authors or Proprietors of such Books as had been already printed, should have the lole Liberty of re-printing and publishing the same foe Twenty-one Years, and no longer: Then your Committee proceeded to examine,

Mr. William Johnston, who had formerly been a Bookseller, but had left off Business; who said. He entered into Business in the Year 1748, and left it off in June last; during which Time, he attended all the Capital Sales of Copy Rights: That, on his first entering into Trade, he purchased the whole Stock of Books and Copy Right of Mr. John Clarke, for which he paid near j^. 3,000; above One Half of which. Sum was for Copy Right: That the Sales are open to the whole Trade; but he never knew any but Booksellers apply to be admitted; that, from that Time, he continued to purchase Copy Right to the Amount of near f. 10,000 more; and believed Three-fourths of the Books in Trade had his Name, as Part Proprietor, especially the Old Copies; the Rights to which are expired, according to the Act of Queen A me: That many of them had been printed above Twenty-eight Years j and that he never imagined the Act of Queen Anne interfered with the Common Law Right; and it was most undoubtedly the general Idea of the Trade, before the late Judgment in the House of Peers, that the Booksellers had a perpetual Right in the Copies they had purchased of Authors, and their Assigns, by the Common Law; and, if any Doubts had been entertained before the late Determination of the Court of King’s Bench, that Judgment would certainly have removed them.

Being asked, Whether he did not Claim a Copy Right in feme of the Editions of the Classics in ufum Delphini? he said. No such Right was ever claimed,- lb as to exclude any other Person who chose to print them: That he had purchased the Right of printing in Part feme of those Classics; but never supposed that Right protected by any Law, nor considered it in any other Manner than as the Purchase of an honorary Right; which he explained to be a Maxim held by the Trade, not to re-print upon the First Proprietor: That, in the Sum of £. 12,000 mentioned to be paid by him for Copy Rights, feme Shares in the Classics in ufum Delphini are included; but to the best of his Recol-ledion such Shares do not amount in the Whole to £. 100.

Being examined as to the Book called Tatler, he produced Sir Richard Steele's Assignment of the Copy Right; and laid. He had heard that the Toilers were originally pubjished in Numbers as Newspapers.

Being examined as to his Title to a Share in Britannia, he said, He never heard of, or saw, any Assignment from Cambdetr, that it was Bishop Gibson's Edition of Cambden, of which he purchased the Share; that he knows not what Bookseller first printed Gibson's Cambden; and has bought many Shares in Books without looking into the Title.

That the Purchase Deed does not specify any Assignment from Cambden, nor was it requisite; that Cambden's original Work was in Latin, and translated by Doctor Gibson, afterwards Bishop of London; that he believes there were two or three Editions printed of that Translation, and one particularly within these Four Years, from a corrected Copy of the late Bishop, which Edition cost the Booksellers £. 800, and the Edition before that, was eighteen Years in felling off; that the Consideration given to Mr. Scott, for the Copy with the said Corrections, was only a few Copies of the Book, for Presents to his Friends; that.he never heard there was any Assignment from Cambden, but has always understood that the Translator of any Work, is protected in the Right to his Translation by the Common Law.

That had he imagined a Common Law Right not to exist, he should not have laid out so large a Sum on a precarious Title; nor did he recoiled ever to have heard the Common Law Right talked of, till agitated in the

ouct

14 Geo. III. 240

Court of King’s Bench; that they always took Assign-tnents from those of whom they purchased, which they supposed to be Assignments of the Common Law Right; and he produced an Assignment of the Guardians, from Sir Richard Steele.

That he never heard of either Common Law or Statute Right being infer ted in an Assignment, but supposes and always understood, that when a Man fells all his Right and Title for ever, it means a Common Law Right, independant of any Statute; and that is the Idea on which the Trade have always acted in purchasing Shares of Copy Hights; and that be never law a Term of Years mentioned in an Assignment: That he purchased his Share in the Guardians, at s Sale, the 18th of

August 1767, and Sir Richard Steele’s Assignment is in 1713, and that he had never met with any Interruption in that Right, since he purchased it.

That he never saw or heard of any Assignment, where the Second Term of Fourteen Years, mentioned in the Act of Queen Anne, was reserved to the Author; but that undoubtedly he gets more Money for his Copy for Twenty-eight Years, than he would for Fourteen, and fells the Chance of the Reversion, when he assigns it for ever: That all the Assignments he has ever seen, ancient and modern, run in general to the Bookseller and his Assigns, for ever; and some of them go so far as to bind themselves, their Heirs and Executors, to protect the Purchaser, his Heirs, and Executors, in the full and free Enjoyment of such Copy Right for ever: And he produced to your Committee, the Assignment of Doctor Robertson to Andrew Millar, of the History of Scotland', which appeared to be of that Form.

Having mentioned several other Books of which he had purchased Shares, and, among others, and

Lord’s Works, he said, He had no Assignment of Mr. Dryden, but bought it at Mr. Tonfon s Sale (and one of the Assignments at Mr. Tonfon's Sale was produced) — That he had never seen an Assignment of Mr. Locke's Works, and never heard any Question about it before; but he really believes there was an Assignment, which Belief he founds upon the Practice of the Trade; for that the Person felling was never required to shew or deliver up the Original Assignment; for in the Purchase of this Property, they never inquire into the Title, if they have an Opinion of th£ Seller.

That it is always prelumed, in the Course of Trade, that a long Possession of Copy is a Proof of Title from the Original Author; that Sums to a very large Amount have been laid out upon this Presumption; and that he, in particular, should never have laid out so large a Sum *s he had done, if he had entertained any other Idea of it; and that he never inquired into the Length of Time that the Seller had been in Possession of the Copy, in case he thought the Vender to be an honest Man.

Being asked, Where a Copy Right is divided into many Shares, where a Person might learn the several Proprietors of those Shares ? he answered, That when a Book is reprinted, the general Rule of the Trade is, that the Man who has the largest Share makes up the Account, and every Person claiming a Share in that Work gives in his Claim, and has his Proportion according to his Share; so that any Person wanting to know who are concerned in such a Work, by applying to the Person who makes up this Account, may get the Information; and the Person who makes up these Accounts fends written Summonses to all whom he knows to be concerned.

That he knows of no Prosecution at Common Law, against any Person either in Town or Country, for printing any Book unprotected by the Statute of Queen Anne-, that l\ich Books have been printed, but there was a much easier Remedy that an Action at Law, for by filing a Bill in Chancery, the Booksellers always obtained an Injunction, and by the Answer given the Bookseller could ascertain the Damage he had sustainecl, as the Defendants were obliged to declare the Number they had printed: That he never made Use of this Re-Vol. 34.

Martii. 589

medy but once, which was in the same of printing the Pilgrim's Progress, written by Runyon, which was printed by one Luckman of Coventry; who delivered up

all the Books, paid the Expences, and promised never to offend again: That this Affair was made up by private Agreement, Luckman made the Proposal, and the Witness accepted of it: That the Title he set up to the Pilgrim's Progress, was by Purchase of the Stock of Clarke

aforesaid, among which was assigned to the Witness, by Clarke's Executor, the Whole of the Copy of the Pilgrim's Progress, but he did not look into the Title which Clarke had to it; and that he can suggest no other Real'on for Luckman's delivering up the Copies and paying the Expences, than that he thought he was doing an unlawful Act: That it is the Custom of the Trade, as he always understood, to prosecute Offenders, in Cafes of Piracy of Copies, at their own private Expence; and that the Witness himself prosecuted at his own Expence in Two Instances, the first about Eighteen Years ago, and the other about Three or Four.

That he never consulted any Counsel in making the Purchases of Copy Right, but laid out his Money, upon the general Opinion of the Common Law Right.

Being asked. Whether, in the course of Trade, the undisturbed Possession of a Copy Right, by any Bookseller, has not been deemed such a Presumption of an Assignment from the Original Author, as to warrant Persons to lay out their Money in the Purchase of it ? he laid. He always was of that Opinion, and never would have laid out the Sum he did, if lie bad had any other Idea of it.

That when an Author chuses originally that his Name should be concealed, no other Proof than Possession can be had of his Assignment; or if the Author chuses to make a voluntary Present of his Work to a Bookseller, it would appear very inconsistent to alk such a Thing; and upon the Prevalence of such Presumptions, original Assignments are not always carefully kept, and transmitted from Hand to Hand, as Titles, when the Transaction has been a long Time past, the Nature of the Trade not admitting of it.

That, had a Doubt existed in the Mind of the Witness of the Principle of the Common Law Right, it would have been entirely removed by the frequent Injunctions granted, unappealed from, and submitted to; and he certainly should have been the more inclined to lay out his Money in Copy Right, and to have given larger Sums for l'uch Purchases, upon the Authority of such Injunctions.

Being asked. If he knew any One Injunction which turns upon the Claim of Common Law Right, independant of the Statute? he said, He recollected but One, and that was Tonfon and Walker, in regard to Milton's Paradise Lojl: That he never took a Lawyer’s Opinion of the Common Law Right, because he thought it unnecessary; and never heard the Question agitated till it came into the Court of King’s Bench, and then Three, if not Four, of the Judges were clear as to the Common Law Right; there were Two Causes agitated in that Court, One, Tonfon against Collins, when Three Judges fat there. Two of whom are dead, and One retired (Mr. Justice Sir Michael,

and Sir Eardly WilmotJ and the Opinion of the Court then was in Favour of the Common Law Right; and in the same of Millar and Taylor, in the Year 1769, a Judgement was obtained in Favour of such Right: That, in the said same of Tonfon and Collins, the Court of King’s Bench did not proceed tojudgment, because (as he hath been informed within these Two or Three Days, and collects from Sir James Burroughs Reports) Ixxrd Mansfield declared, in giving Judgment in the same of Millar and Taylor, that the Reason of the Court’s not proceeds ing to judgment, in the same of Tonfon and ,v did not arile from any Difference of Opinion in the Judges of that Court, but because they understood that it was a collusive Action.

That

24° Martii. A. 1774-

That, upon his quitting Business, lie assigned his Property in Copy Rights to his Son, on Condition he should be jointly bound with himself to pay all his Creditors; who, not doubting of the Validity of the Security, readily consented to it. Upon which the Copy Rights^ were valued by Meffis. Longman and Two

Booksellers of the first Reputation, at between 8 and £.9,000; and the Witness believes they would have fold for that Sum in June last, when he quitted Business; but that since the Determination in the House of Lords they would not fell for a Fourth Part of that Sum; and had there remained a Doubt in the Mind of the Witness of a legal Property in those Copies, exclusive of the Statute of Queen Anne, he should never have involved a Son, who had a genteel Fortune left him by his Grandfather, to take them as a Security for any Debts the Witness owed.

That if Relief is not granted in the present Session of Parliament, so many Books will be printed, both in London and the Country, as will make it impossible to grant the Sufferers Redrels, without Injury to the other Publ illiers.

Being asked, What had reduced the Value of the Copy Rights, between the Time of his purchasing them and transferring them to his Son ? he laid. That many Circumstances contributed to reduce the Value of Copies: Moll Books are capable of Improvement, in all Arts and Sciences; that a Copy this Day may be worth /.500, which, in a Twelvemonth, may not be worth £.5; because other Works of a like Nature come out with Improvements which render the old Books on the same Subject of no Value; and a new Edition of a Work, with Improvements, after the Purchase made,*lessens the Value of the Copy for a Time.

Being asked. Whether, when Booksellers buy a Copy Right, they don’t, at the same Time, buy all the Copies then printed off ? he said, They frequently do, and frequently not; but they never re-print any Copy under that Predicament, until the Books remaining are fold off.

Being asked the Question, he said, That when he fold his Property in Copy R'ght to his Son, it was known among the Trade, that there was an Appeal depending before the House of Lords, upon the Point, Whether there was any Literary Property at Common Law ? but that the Witness, and the Trade in general, was so well confirmed by the Determination of the Court of King’s Bench, that he thought there was little or no Risque at all; for, that had such a Doubt existed in his Mind, he could have fold that Property iome Years ago, for nearly as much, if not the Whole, it cost him. And that he knows not of any Sale of Copy Rights derived under Authors at Common Law, since the Determination in the House of Lords; nor of any within Six Months previous to that Decision, except his own.

Being asked. Whether, in his Opinion, if Relief is not granted in consequence of this Application, there is not a Danger of valuable Books being out of Print, from a dread of Competition by the Multitude of Copies that may be printed by different Booksellers, in different Parts of the Kingdom ? he said. That would certainly be the Consequence as to elegant Editions.

That he thinks, a Month before the late Decision in the House of Lords, he could have disposed of his Property in Copy Rights for a very inconsiderable Loss.

Being asked, Why it was not the Custom of those who are possessed of Copy Right, to enter them in the Books of the Stationers Company? he said. He could only answer for himself, that he never thought the Penalties prescribed by the Act of the Eighth of Queen Anne were worth contending for, as a much shorter and more complete Relief might be had, by filing a Bill in Chancery; that the Trade of a Bookseller is circum-, feribed by no Law, nor any Bye-Law of the Stationers Company; and every Man that pleases may let up in the Business, without an Hour’s Servitude to the Trade;

and the Wholesale Booksellers in London, solicit the Country Booksellers, to supply them with Books.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition, is as follows:

Robert Pardoe, Esquire, informed your Committee, That the late Earl of Powis, some Time before his Death, purchased certain Estates, in the Counties of Montgomery and Salop, heretofore belonging to Charles Mason, Esquire, deceased, formerly Treasurer of the Transport Service.

And it appeared to your Committee, from the Certificate from the Deputy Auditor of the Imprefts, which was annexed to the Petition, That the said Charles Mason, on the Foot of his final Account, was indebted to the Crown the Sum of £.3,170. 12s. 3 to the Payment of which Debt your Committee find his Estates were liable.

Mr. Pardoe then produced to your Committee, the Memorial presented by the late Earl of Powis to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, Hating, That by Reason of the numerous Incumbrances, prior to the Claim of the Crown, on the said Mr. s Estate, the same will not be sufficient to answer any Part of the Debt due to the Crown, and expressing his Willingness to pay to the Crown such Composition as to their Lordships should appear reasonable, in order to dilincumber the fame; which Memorial their Lordships referred to the Solicitor for the Treasury, for his Opinion; by whose Report thereon, which was produced to your Committee, it appears, that he gave it as his Opinion, that the Claim the Crown has on the said Estates can never be satisfied, and that therefore, if their Lordships thought fit, they might properly consent to the said Estates being discharged from the Debt due to the Crown; and he at the same Time submitted to their Lordships, whether it would not be proper to direct the Matter to be laid before the Solicitor of the Tax Office; which was accordingly done.. And,

Mr. Pardoe produced to your Committee, the Report of the Solicitor of the Tax Office on the said Matter; by which it appeared to your Committee, that he gave it as his Opinion, that as the Incumbrances on the said Estates appeared to him greatly to exceed the real Value of the Estates, and as those Incumbrances will always be prior to the Debt of the Crown, and may be set up by the present Owners against the Crown Debt, and as the Rents of the said Estates will not near pay the Interest of those Incumbrances, which consequently will annually increase, and as it would not, in his Opinion, be at all adviseable for the Crown to redeem the Mortgages on the said Estates, he thought it might be proper lor their Lordships to permit the Petitioner to apply to Parliament to enable their Lordships to compound the Debt due to the Crown, and that, after such Act should be obtained, their Lordships might compound the said Debt, at such Sum of Money as, under all the Circumstances of the Cafe, their Lordships should think reasonable; but that he was of Opinion, their Lordships could not compound the same without the Aid of Parliament. And it appeared to your Committee, from the Evidence of Mr. Pardoe, that the said George Edward Henry Arthur, Earl of Powis, on the Death of his late Father, became, and is now, entitled to the greatest Part of the said Estates of the said Charley Mason, whereof his said Father was seised as aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideratiop of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning

next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Sleaford Lord Brownlow Bertie reported from the Committee, Navigation, to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Merchants, Farmers, Tradesmen, and others. Inhabitants in the County of Lincoln, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Your Committee called Mr. James Creajfy, an Engineer; who produced a Plan of a River intended to be made navigable from the Castle Causeway, through Sleaford, in the County of Lincoln, to join the River Wit ham, at or near Chapel Hill, the Length of which is rather more than 12 Miles, 2 Miles and an Half of which are already made navigable. And being asked, What will be the Expence of making the River capable of carrying Vessels of 20 Tons Burthen ? he said, It will cost about

£.6,000. And being asked. Whether the River is capable of being made navigable? he said, It is. And being asked, Whether the adjoining Lands will be injured by its being made navigable ? he said, By the necessary scouring and deepening the River, and forming the * Earth arising therefrom into Banks, it will

Vol. 34.

render the adjoining Lands much more secure from Floods, which now frequently happen there and do great Damage. And being asked. Whether the Mills will receive any Damage ? he said, He presumed not; that they are not to be meddled with, and only the waste Water taken for the Purposes of the Navigation; that the Course of the Mill Streams is to be deserted, and the Old River followed. And being asked,

Whether the Course of the Old River is to be deserted any where ? he said. Yes, in Two Places; one near Sleaford, in order to avoid several little Turns in the River; the other a little above Flax Dike, for the Purpose of avoiding the Mill Stream. And being asked.

What Advantages will accrue to the Public from the carrying of the above Scheme into Execution ? he said, „

It will furnish an easy and cheap Conveyance for the Produce of the Country, and the Returns of Coal and other heavy Commodities, and will also open a Communication with Boston and Lincoln, and from thence into the River Trent. And being asked. Whether he had made any Calculation of the Sum likely to arile by the Tonnage on the River ? he said. He had; and that, if laid at One Shilling per Ton, he is of Opinion the Amount will be about £. 500 a Year.

Mr. Robert Bankes, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence, with respect to the Utility and Practicability of the Scheme, and the Sum likely to arise by the Tonnage; and added, that the Money necessary for executing the Plan will be easily raised at legal Interest.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making navigable a certain Stream or River, and the Branches thereof, from Sleaford Castle Causeway, through the Town of New Sleaford, in the county of ,

to the River Witham, near Chapel Hill, in the said County: And that Lord Brownlow Bertie, Mr. cotts, and Sir Cecil Wray, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Savage Lloyd, Esquires, and the several other Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors of, or otherwise interested in, the several Low Grounds and Carrs, lying contiguous to, and on each Side of, the River Hull, in the East Riding of the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by virtue of Two Acts, made for the draining and improving the said Low Grounds and Carrs on the East Side of the said River,

£. 20,000 or upwards have been already laid out, for effecting the Purposes of the said respective Acts; but that it hath been found, by Experience, the same cannot be completed, or effectually carried into Execution, without further Powers be given for widening and deepening the said River, and removing the several Incroachments and Obstructions therein; for which Purposes, the Petitioners have lately applied to, and obtained Leave from, the House, to bring in a Bill, by which Bill all the Low Grounds and Carrs on the West Side of the said River, as well as on the East, containing together, by Computation, more than 40,000 Acres, are intended also to be drained and improved; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Application has been made, for Leave to bring in a Bill, for making and establishing legal Quays or Wharfs, in the Port of King/lon upon Hull, and for other Purposes therein mentioned; and that, as the Petitioners have been informed, besides the said public or legal Quays proposed to be made on the North Side of the said Town, some of the Merchants of the said Town are to be thereby authorized, and do intend, to erect Sufferance Quays in Hull Haven, on the West Side of the said River, contiguous to their respective Staiths or Warehouses, to project Fifteen Feet further into the said River; and that the Petitioners apprehend, such additional Projection from the said Staiths or Warehouses, all or most of which have t>een built, and are now Incroachmfents, upon the said River, will create such an Obstruction near the Mouth or Utterance of the said River (through which all the Waters from the said Low Grounds and Carrs are to pass into the River Humber) that it will, as the Petitioners ate advised, defeat and render ineffectual the Purposes of rite said intended Drainage, and consequently will be highly prejudicial to the Estates and Interests of all the Petitioners in the said Low Grounds and Carrs j and that, as the same intended Sufferance Quays cannot, as the Petitioners apprehend, any ways improve, or tend to the Benefit of, the public Revenue, but are calculated only for the Convenience and private Emolument of some few of the Merchants in the said Town: Therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law: but that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, before the House, against such Parts thereof as will so affect the Estates and Interests of the said Petitioners, by making or erecting any such Sufferance or private Quays in the Haven or Mouth of the said River Hull; and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as the Nature of their same may require, and to the House may seem just and reasonable.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered Jo be referred to the Confederation of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for making and establishing public Quays, or Wharfs, in the Port of Hull; for the better securing His Majesty's Revenues of Customs, and for the Benefit of Commerce in the said Port; for making a Bason, or Dock, with Re-forvoirs, Sluices, Roads, and other Works, for the Accommodation of Vessels uling the said.

Mr. Frederick Montagu reported from the Committee, Private who were appointed to consider of proper Rules and Bill*. Regulations, to be observed by Persons applying to (Raleaand this House for Private Bills, and to report their Kegulttiom) Opinion thereupon to the House; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had come to several Resolutions thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in hi's Place: and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That after this Session of Parliament, before any Petition is presented to this House, for inclosing, draining, or ins-proving, any Lands, Fens, or Commons, a printed or written Notice of such intended Application to Parliament be affixed on the Ch,urch Door of the Parish or Parishes in which such Lands, Fens, and Commons, dd lie, for Three Sundays, in the Month of Septemlei-, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented; and that Proclamation be made in open Court, at thp then next ensuing General Quarter Sessions of the Peace to be held for the County or District in which such Parish or Parishes lie, that such Notice hath been affixed, and that such Application is intended to be made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, 1 That after this Session. of Parliament, in all Bills for inclosing Lands or Commons, the Names of the Cons* missioners proposed to be appointed, and the Compensations intended for the Lord of the Manor, and the Owners o# Tithes, in lieu of their respective Rights, where any Bargains or Agreements have been made for such Compensations, be inserted in the Copy of the Bill presented to the House; and that all Copies of fufh Bills, whether, printed or written, which shall be 9 font

v-j£* -

14 Geo. III. 30° Martii. 609

sent to any of the Persons interested in the said Manor, Tithes, Lands, or Commons, for their Confept, do contain the Names of such proposed Comniiuioners, and also such intended Compensations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That before any Petition is presented to this House, for making a Turnpike Road, or for the Renewal or Alteration of any Act of Parliament passed for that Purpose, Notice of such intended Application to Parliament be given at the General Quarter Session of the Peace which shall be held for every and each County or District, through which such Road pafles, or is intended to pat's, at the Michaelmas immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That this Notice be given, by affixing to the Door of the Sessions House, where such General Quarter Sessions are held, a printed or written Paper, describing the Parishes through which the said Road pafles, or is intended to pass, and by making Proclamation thereof in Open Court at the said Sessions; and that such Notice be also printed in some One Newspaper of the County, or, if there is no such Paper printed for that County, then in the Newspaper of the nearest adjoining County, Three Times, at least, in the Month of September immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That after this Session of Parliament, when any Petition is presented to this House for making a Navigable Canal, or for making or improving the Navigation of a River, or for altering any Act of Parliament passed for either of those Purposes, there be presented, with such Petition, a Plan describing the Line of such intended Canal or Navigation, and the Lands through which the same is to be carried; and that previous Application be made to the Owners and Occupiers of such Lands, for their Assent to the proposed Canal or Navigation j and that separate Lists of the Names of such Owners and Occupiers be presented also with the said Petition; dif-. tinguishing which of them, on such Application, have' affcnted to, or difiented from, the said proposed Canal or Navigation, or are neuter in respect thereto.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That after this Session of Parliament, when any Petition is presented to this House, for making a Navigable Canal, or for making or improving the Navigation of a River, or for making a New Turnpike Road, or for railing any further Sum of Money for any of those Purposes, there be annexed to the said Petition, an Estimate . of the proposed Expence of such Undertaking, ligned. by the Person or Persons making the same; together with an Account of the Money subscribed for carrying the said Work into Execution, and the Names of the Subscribers, with the Sums respectively subscribed by them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That after this Session of Parliament, in all Bills for making a Navigable Canal, or for making or improving the Navigation of a River, or for making a New Turnpike Road, there be inserted a Clause, compelling the Subscribers for carrying any such Work into Execution, to make Payment of the Sums severally subscribed by them.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Friday Fortnight, the 15th Day of April next.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed.

A Petition of the Magistrates of the Burgh of [uunicimUuo fermline, in the County of Fife, North Britain, subscribing, for themselves, and in Name and Behalf of the whole Council and Community of the said Burgh, and the numerous Linen Manufacturers thereof.

And the said Petition was read; Complaining of the Decline of the Linen Manufacturee of Great Britain and Ireland, which, the Petitioners alledge, will be entirely lod, if some Remedy be not speedily provided; and letting forth. That some Years ago there were One thousand Linen Looms employed in the said Burgh and . its Environs, which are now greatly reduced, although

the Petitioners are sensible that the Numbers could soon be encreased to double, if proper Encouragement was given, by discharging the Importation of Foreign Linen; and they are well satisfied, that the said Town, in Conjunction with other Manufactures of Table Linen in Great Britain and Irel are fully able to supply the whole Demand of Damalk, Diaper, and all Kinds of Table Linen, both for Home Consumption and Exportation: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give such Aid and Relief therein as they shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to enquire further into the present State of the Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland.

Mr. William Russell, Mr. Joseph Jefior, Churchwardens, and Mr. Edward Davies, Mr. Thomas Porter, Overseers of the Poor, confirmed the foregoing Evidencei and added, that if a Piece of Ground was purchased, and a proper Workhouse built thereon, the Poor would be much better maintained and managed, and at a less Expence to the Parish, than they are at present.

Then Mr. Edward Cleve and Joseph Burley, Overseers of the Poor, and the said Mr. Thomas Porter, were examined; who informed your Committee, that the Parish of Barking consists of Four distinct Wards, and each Ward has a separate Overseer, who collects the Rates within his own Ward, and has a discretionary Power of relieving such poor Persons as he thinks fit; that this Mode of Collection is attended with great Delay; and from the Negligence, as well as Partiality in the Officers, many Losses happen in the Collection. And the Witnesses added, that they attributed the Increase of the Poors Rate of late Years to this Mode of Collection, and to the Overseers in each Ward having a discretionary Power of distributing the Money by them collected towards the Relief of the Poor. — And they produced to your Committee an Account of the Sums collected for the Relief of the Poor for several Years past, by which it appeared, that the Poors Rates had greatly encreased of late. And the Witnesses added, that if the present Mode of collecting and distributing the Money raised for the Relief of the Poor was altered, it would be a great Saving to the Parish.

the Ebb of the said Tides, empty themselves into the Channel in the said Bay, and greatly affill in keeping open the same; and that the Petitioners apprehend that, if the said Bill pals into a Law, and the said Marsh be embanked, the Tidal Waters will be lhut out from the said Marsh and Creeks, and the said Channel, for Want of the Scour made by the Waters running out of the said Creeks into the lame, upon the Ebb of the Tide, will be choaked up with Sand and Silt brought into it by the Influx thereof, the Navigation of the said River, and the Trade of the said Port of Wisbech, in a great Measure, if not entirely, loft, and the Petitioners said Lands left without a Drainage:

Were severally presented to the House, and read; reciting Part of an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to regulate the Importation and Exportation of Corn; and Setting forth, That Oatmeal is the Bread of by far the greatest Part of the Inhabitants of Scotland, the Price of which has been encreasing for Sixteen Years past, and has contributed, with ether Causes, to encrease the Distrefle*, and promote the Emigration, of the Poor; and that the said Act has a maniflft Tendency to encrease those Evils, as, by the former Laws, Oatmeal could be imported, when the Price exceeded 13s. 4 d Boll, and is now raised to i6r.; and that, although Wheat, and all other Grain, is allowed to be imported, when the Duties not repealed by the said Act shall be due, and again re-exported, yet no such Provision is made with respect to Oatmeal, which,

the Petitioners apprehend, was not intended by the Legislature: And therefore praying the House to consider the Premises, and to give such Relief as shall be thought proper.

A Petition of the Traders, Manufacturers, and other Ditto. Inhabitants, of the Burgh of Renfrew, was also presented (RciUscw.) to the House, and read; Setting forth, Thar, by the Laws in Force in Scotland, prior to the First of January 1774, Oatmeal could be imported into when

the Price exceeded 134. 4 d.per Boil; but, by an Act of the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, to regulate the Importation and Exportation of Corn,

Oatmeal can only be imported into Scotland when the Price exceeds 16 s.per Boll; and that the Consequence of this Law must be, to advance the Price of Oatmeal in Scotland, which is the Bread of the greatest Part of the Inhabitants, especially the lower Sort, a Consequence which it can ill bear at this Time, from the declining State of its Manufactures; and the Petitioners hope.

That, to prevent the said Evil, the House will pass a Law, allowing Oatmeal to be imported into Scotland, when the Price shall be at or above 131. 4 per Bo!!, and containing the same Provisions, with respcCl to Oatmeal being warehoused, as is contained in the before-recited Act, with respect to Wheat and all other Grain: And therefore praying the House to consider the Premises, and to grant Relief to the Petitioners accordingly.

A Petition of the Magistrates of the Burgh of Perth, Ditto, for themselves, and in Name of the Community of (Perth.) the said Burgh, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act of the Parliament of Scotland, made in the Year 1703, the Law, prohibiting the Importation of Meal, fell to be suspended when the Price should exceed Eight Pounds Scots (or Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence Sterling) per Boll; and that by an Act of the Fourteenth Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, the prohibiting Laws for the Importation of Meal were subject to be suspended, when the Price of Oatmeal did exceed the like Price of Thirteen, Shillings and Four Pence Sterling per Boll; and that, by the late Act of the Thirteenth of His present Majesty, Oatmeal may be imported where the Price at the Port of Importation does exceed Sixteen Shillings Sterling Boll; but may not be imported until it exceed that Price; and representing to the House, that Oatmeal is the principal Food of the greatest Part of the labouring Poor of Scotland, the Price of which has of late Years greatly encreal’ed, and thereby heightened the Distresses of the Poor, and the operative Manufacturers; and that the said Act has a manifest Tendency to encrease and continue these Evils; for, by the former Laws, Oatmeal might have been imported when the Price exceeded Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence per Boll, but cannot now be imported, unless it exceed Sixteen Shillings Boll: And therefore praying the House to consider the

Premises,

14 Geo. III. t2° J 6ii

Premises, and pass an Act to reduce the Rate, at which Oatmeal may be imported, to Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence per Boll, for alleviating in some Measure the Distrefl'es of the Poor, and encouraging the Trade and Manufactures of this Country; or to give such other Relief as shall be thought proper.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of so much of an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to regulate the " Importation and Exportation of Corn," as relates to the Importation of Oatmeal into that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Ordered, That the said Account do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

The House being informed that Mr. from the Ofijce of the Accountant General of the Court of Chancery, attended at the Poor; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Orders,

An Account of the Calli belonging to the Suitors of the Court of Chancery, in Custody of the Bank, Handing in the Name of the Accountant General of the said Court: And also,

An Account of Securities, purchased with the Surplus Money, placed to the Account of Interest arising from Monies placed out in pursuance of Three Acts of Parliament, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and in the Fourth and Ninth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty: And also.

An Account of Securities, purchased with the Surplus Money, placed to the Account of Interest arising from Monies placed out in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of King George the Third.

And then he withdrew.

And the Titles of the said Acounts were read.

Ordered, That the said Accounts do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

The said Accounts are preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

The House being informed that Mr. from the Commissioners of the Customs, attended at the Door; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Orders,

An Account of the Value of the Imports, from Germany, Holland, Russia, and Ireland, into London and the Out Ports of England, for the last Ten Years that can be made up; distinguishing each Year, the Value of the Linens, and the Quantity, converted into Yards: And also.

An Account of the Quantity of Irijk Linen imported into England, in British Yards, from the 5th January 1770 to the 3 th January 1774.; distinguishing each

Year, which is as far as the same can be made up; and also distinguishing what is imported into the Port of London, from what is imported into the Out Ports.

And then he withdrew.

And the Titles of the said Accounts were read.

Ordered, That the said Accounts be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to enquire further into the present State of the Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland.

The said Accounts are preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

A Bill for dividing and inclosing the Common and Warmingtoa Open Fields, Meadows, and Commonable Lands, in the . ln?lofore- Parish of Warmington, in the County of Northampton, was read a Second Time.

Refolded, That the Bill be committed to Sir William Lolhen, Mr. Skipwith, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

Mr. Howard reported from the Committee, to whom Eggers’* the-ingossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Adtfor M*1-naturalizing Gujlav Nicolaus Eggers, was committed;

That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Bill to the House, without any Amendment: And he delivered the Bill in at the Clerk’s Table.

And the said Bill was read the Third Time.

ReJ'olved, That the Bill do pass.

Ordered, That Mr. Howard do carry the Bill to the Lords; and acquaint them, that this House hath agreed to the fame, without any Amendment.

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Complaining of the Hardships the Petitioners alledge they labour under, by so much of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for regulating the Importation and Exportation of Corn, as relates to the Importation of Oatmeal into that Part of Great Britain called Scotland: And praying the House to take the same into Consideration, and give such Relief as shall be thought proper.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to tie referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of so much of an Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, " An " Ad to regulate the Importation and " Exportation of Corn," as relates to the Importation of Oatmeal into that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

A Petition of the Provost and Baillies, and remanent Members of the Town Council, of the Borough of Sanquhar, and of several others subscribing, Manufacturers of Linen Yarn and Linen Cloth within the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Quantity of Linen manufactured in this Country is greatly dimini (lied within these few Years; and that the Spinning of Yam for supplying the Ma-nufadurers in England is much decreased, and must be entirely given up, unless some Measure is adopted for the Support of that Manufacture: And therefore praying the House to take the same under Consideration, and to adopt such Measures as they shall judge most expedient for the Relief of the Linen Manufacture in this Country.

A Petition of the High Sheriff and Grand Jury of the County of Lincoln, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are apprehensive, that it may be proposed to lay an additional Duty on the Importation of Foreign Linens; and that, if such Duty should take place, its Consequences would be very detrimental to the Woollen Manufacture of this

Kingdom, and to the Interest of the said County in particular: And therefore praying the House, That, in any Steps which may be taken for the Advantage of the Linen Trade, nothing may be done which shall tend to lower the Value of Wool.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to enquire further into the present State of the Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland.

Sir Charles Whitworth reported from the Committee, Westminster to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for carrying into Execution the several Acts for paving, cleans- -c 1 ing, lighting, and regulating, the Squares, Streets,

Lanes, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent; and also, the Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Petition of several Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants of House9 in Piccadilly, as lie between Berkeley Street, and Hyde

Park Corner, within the Liberty of Westminster, were

referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, Mr. Luke Idefon, Clerk to the Paving Committee for the Parish of Saint James, being examined, said, That the Commissioners have observed some Defects in the Provisions of the Acts for paving Westminster, particularly with regard to the WateF Companies taking up Pavements; to the regulating and entering Scavengers Contracts, which ought to be in a more summary Wav than at present; that idle Persons go about and collect Dull and Allies, though not appointed Scavengers by the Commissioners or Committees, to the great Injury of the Contradors; — that it is a common Practice for the Scavengers to sweep Dirt into the Sewers, or so near them, that it is waftied in by the Rains, to the great Detriment of the Public; — that the present Mode of paying off Money borrowed by equal Proportions, is found inconvenient; — that there is no Clause forpunish-ing Persons forging Assignrfients or Certificates, nor any Power to sue for Rates, which is found very inconvenient in Cafes where the Landlords are answerable for the Rates, and live at a great Distance, and also sometimes where the Tenants remove; — that Money is frequently loft in collecting the Rates, by Persons removing a short Time before the Quarter Day; — that Justices are not required to indorse Warrants for collecting Rates; — that there is no reciprocal Appeal allowed; — that the present Mode of removing Nuifences has been found ineffectual in the following Articles; videlicet, driving Wheelbarrows on the Foot Pavement; in Carriages, Calks, and other Obstructions, being allowed to remain Six Hours before Removal; throwing Tiles and Rubbish from the Tops of Houses; carrying long Poles, Planks, Ladders, Boxes, Trunks, and other Things, upon the Foot-7 ways;

Mr. George Box, Clerk to the Commissioners, and Mr. Fowler, Treasurer, confirmed the lame, as iar as relates to the Inconveniences attending the present Mode of paying oft' Money.

To prove the Allegations of the Second-mentioned Petition,

Two Acts of Parliament, one of the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the First, and the other of the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for repairing the Roads from Park Corner, were

read; whereby it appears, that the Trustees for putting the said Acts in Execution, are required to cause the Street from Berkeley Street in Piccadilly, to Hyde Park Gate, to be watered during the dry Weather, and when the Dull is troublesome to Passengers, and the Expence of Catering the same is to be defrayed out of the Tolls collected by virtue of the said Acts.

And it appeared to your Committee, That by ap Ad, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Trustees for the Care of the said Roads are 'll iicharged from the Management of so much of Piccadilly as lies between Clarges Street and Hyde Park Corner; and also from the Management of the Road from the South End of Park Lane, to the North Side of Hertford Street; and the said Hoads are by the said Act put under the Management and Direction of the Commissioners for paving the several Streets, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster; and by the said Act

a clear annual Sum of One thousand Pounds is directed to be paid to the said Commissioners, out of the *' Tolls collected at Hyde Park Corner, to be applied as

therein is directed. Then,

Mr. George Box, Clerk to the said Commissioners, was examined; who informed your Committee, That in pursuance of the Directions of the said Act, the Commissioners have caused the Street from Hyde Park Corner to Clarges Street, to be paved.

Mr. John Garden and Mr. John Wriglit, Inhabitants of Piccadilly, being examined, informed your Committep, That while the Street from Hyde Park Corner to Berkeley Street, remained under the Direction and Management of the Trustees appointed by the said former Acts, the whole Carriage Way of the Street, from Berkeley Street aforesaid, to Hyde Park Gate, used to be watered, at the Expence of the said Trustees, in dry Sea-fons, but that since the Trustees of the Turnpike have been discharged from the Care of the said Street, the same hath not been effectually watered in dry Sealbns, and that the Dull is frequently very troublesome to the Inhabitants, and to Persons passing and repassing along the fame.

' through or near to which the said Cut, or Canal, is to be carried, as well as to the Convenience and Utility of the Public in general: And therefore praying the House, That all proper Encouragement may be given to the said Undertaking) and that a Bill may be brought in, for completing the fame, in such Manner as to the House shall appear reasonable.
