Were also severally presented to the House, and read; likewise Taking Notice of the said Petition) and Setting forth. That the said Cut, or Canal, will greatly contribute to the Convenience and Cheapness of Communication betwixt London and Waltham, and the Country adjoining; will improve the Property of the Owners and Occupiers of Estates contiguous to the said Cut or Canal) and be of great Service to the Public in general: 'And therefore praying, That the said Plan of making the said Cut, or Canal, may he adopted by Parliament, and be carried into Execution, under such Regulations and Provisions as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, is referred.

Mr. Alderman Oliver, according to Order, reported Ditto, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord

Mayor,

14* Aprilis. A. 1774.

Moorfieldi Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of Lott-. t04,. don, in Common Council assembled, was referred; j^nal. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth 3 viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Whitworth, a Surveyor, being examined, produced to your Committee, a Plan of a Navigable Canal intended to be made from Moorfields to Waltham with a Branch to the River j a printed Copy of which

Plan is annexed to the Report. And being asked, If the carrying of that Plan into Execution is practicable ? he said, It is much easier to execute, than most that have been made; and that he had been employed in Things of that Nature many Years. And being asked, If, in the Course of his Survey, he had endeavoured to do as little Damage as might be, by the Canal, to private Property ? he said, He had. And being asked. Whether any Canal could be better or more ealily supplied with Water, than the one proposed ? he said. No one that he had ever seen could; that the Lands on the Banks of Canal Navigations, in moll Countries, arejincreased in their Value by Means of the Canal; that it will require only One Horse to navigate a Vessel of 40 Tons Burthen on the proposed Canal; and that it generally requires about 80 Horses to draw the like Weight by Land. And being asked. Whether Vessels can be navigated up the River Lee in Times of Floods ? he laid, It is impossible; but that, on the intended Canal, they might. And being asked, Whether he had made any Estimate of the Expence of carrying the proposed Scheme into Execution ? he said, He had; that it will be necessary to purchase a considerable Quantity of Land; that he had valued it at £. 90 per Acre, except a small Part, being the Branch to Lee Bridge, which he had valued at £. 50 per Acre 3 and that, admitting his Estimate of that Article to be sufficient, the Expence of making the proposed Canal, including every Thing, will be £.55,810. And being asked, How much Land mud necessarily be purchased for making the Canal ? he said,'i40 Acres for the Line, and for the Branch. And being asked, Whether, from his Knowledge and Experience in those Kinds of Works, he could, with any Degree of Certainty, say, that the Sum of Money above-mentioned will be sufficient to complete the Work, as it appears upon the Plan? he said, He could, except the Estimate of the Value of the Land should fall short. And being asked. How he proposed to supply the Canal with Water? he said, From the River Lee; which, in his Opinion, will not affect the Mills thereon so much as the present Navigation on it does And being asked. If the Canal will be as cheap and expeditious a Conveyance as Land Carriage ? he said. That supposing the Tonnage laid at One Penny Halfpenny per Mile, it will be but One Fifth of the Expence, and equally expeditious; and that he believed the carrying of the proposed Scheme into Execution, will be of Advantage to Trade, and of public Utility. And being asked, If he included the Damage to be done to Land by Fences, or otherwise, in the Value he set upon the Part to be taken at £. 90 per Acre ? he said. The temporary Damage done in the Execution of the Work, is not included in the Sum of £. Acre, but that the Fences necessary on the Towing Paths are made a separate Article, and the Damage done by dividing Fields he luppoled included in the Price of the Land; and that, in all Cases where Fields are divided. Bridges are allowed. And being asked, If the Damage the Mills now suffer by the old Navigation, will be remedied by the Canal ? he said,. It is supposed that in that Length there will not be much passing on the old River. And being asked. Whether the Water being taken out of the River Lee, will be a Prejudice to that

Navigation ? he said, The Water required for the Canal will not be any sensible Detriment. And being asked. To what Extent he was acquainted with the River Lee ? he said, As high as Waltham Abbey. And being, asked. Whether he could say, that as far as that Place, there is not sometimes, in dry Seasons, . a Want of Water ? he said, That upon the Shoals thrown up. at the Tails of the Locks, there is; and that it is the same with all River Navigations; that the Method of getting over those Shoals, is to draw the Upper Clough of the Lock; which occasions great Waste of Water.. And being asked, If that Method will be sufficient when the additional Quantity of Water is taken away by the proposed Canal ? he said, He supposed it will,; that the; Quantity taken will be so small as not to be perceived; and that, as he supposed, the Decreale of Draught Water in the River will not be the Eighth of an Inch. And-being asked, If he had accurately calculated the Quantity, of Water that will be necessary for the Canal ? he said,: That is absolutely impossible. And being asked. If die had surveyed all the Mills which will be affected by taking Water out of the River Lee he said, He had seen.some of them below Waltham; and that the present Navigation pens so close upon their Tails, that if some Water was taken from the lliver, it would in moll Sea-Ions be of Service to them. And being asked. Whether he meant when the Water is high or low ? he said. When it is above a mean. State. And being asked. Whether the Mills, which he^had surveyed, could be prejudiced ? he said. He knew that no Mills could be sensibly affected. And being asked, How wide the Canal is intended to be made ? he said. He supposed it to be, 6a Feet at the Surface of the Water in level Cutting; where there is Banking, extra Cutting, or Buildings int the Way, it is to be contracted; and that it is to be 4: Feet and a Half deep; that in some Places it will be level with the adjacent Lands, in some below,' and in others above them: That at the highest Part, which will be below Hackney, it must be 20 Feet above the Surface of the Country; and that in that and other Places, where the Water is to be raised so high, the Basis of the Work must be 150 Feet; but that he did not know of any Part of the intended Canal where the Water was intended to be above the Level of the Land, except where-it is necessary. And being asked, Whether, in those Lands where he meant to raise the Water above their-Level, he supposed the Canal to be an Improvement, to them ? he said. There will always be Drains to take the superfluous Water away at any Time. And being asked. If he knew that fu’ch Drains often fail lo to do ? he said; It is very easy to make them take it off in any Case. And being asked. Whether adjacent Lands are not often damaged, for want of drawing Locks and Pens of Water ? he said. There will be no Pens on this Canal; except One at the regulating Lock,. One Mile and a Half from Waltham Abbey, the Waste Water being to be thrown off by Wiers. And being asked. Whether, besides the Advantages which he had stated, as likely to arise from making the Canal, he had any View, of serving the City of London with Water ? he laid. It will be too low to supply Houses in general with Water, but that it may furnish some to cleanse Sewers, or in Cafes of Fire. And being asked. How many Locks there are to be on the Canal ? he said. Only One in the Line, as is marked on the Plan. And being asked, If a small Quantity of Water would not therefore be necessary to keep the Canal navigable ? he said, A very small Quantity would; and that the Water which fills the regulating Lock, may be immediately thrown back into the River Lee, and will be above all the Mills. And being

asked, Whether the New Cuts on the River Lee have not removed all the Obstacles on that Navigation ? he said. He had heard they now exist, and was told so last July or August; that he supposed the Navigation of the River Lee, between Waltham and the Thames, will not be so much used if the Canal is made. And being

asked, What is the Space between whefe the Water is to be taken out of the River , and where it is to be returned to it? he said, It is 10 Miles and a Half. And being asked, How many Locks there are on the Old Navigation ? he laid, Nine; and that if a great Part of the Traffick now carried on by the River be removed to the Canal, there will certainly be a great Saving of Water to the River; and that he is very certain by the present Mode of Navigation, more Water is taken from the Mills than will be by the Canal. And being asked, Whether any of the Brooks which cross the North Road might be taken into the proposed Canal ? he said, They all might; but that a Glass Mill might be injured by it, and that it was not proposed to take in any of them; that if the Traffick on the River Lee be diminished, the Mills will be able to keep up a Head of Water for their Supply more constantly. And being asked. Whether all Waste of Water mutt not be supplied from the River Lee ? he laid. If the Works be properly executed, he supposed no Banks would break. And being asked, If he supposed the Water at the Mill Tails will be continued there, by taking the Water away from above them? he said, The Canal will not take the Water from the Heads of the Mills, so much as the present Navigation on the River Lee does; and that though the Mills do y?ant Water in the dry Seasons, the Canal will not add to that Inconvenience; that he meant all the Mills from Waltham Abbey to the End of the Canal in Moorfields. And being asked. Whether, for any Water to be taken from Tottenham Mills, Hackney , and Hackney Water Works, an equal Quantity was to be returned ? he said. No: It is importable. And being asked. Whether a Quantity is brought in, equal to what is afterwards taken from the Mills ? he said, It is impossible for a Vessel to pass a Mill without taking a Lock full of Water, which mutt be a Loss to the Mills. And being asked,' What is the Difference between the Level of the Branch at Hackney and Waltham Abbe he said, 38 Feet and 5 or 6 Inches; that in the scarcest Time of Water, he estimated that the Water would stand 5. Feet and 5 or 6 Inches higher above than below the regulating Lock, and when the Water was highest, he supposed about 3 Feet more; that it will always rife as the Floods rife, but he did not know how high they do rife there exactly; that the Distance from the regulating Lock to the Occupation Bridge in Cheshunt is about Seven

Furlongs and Four Chains, and from thence to the River from Waltham Abbey, 3 Furlongs and a Half. And being asked. Whether the Canal would be passable to Waltham. Abbey in Times of Floods ? hd said, It always will, to the Occupation Bridge, and from thence to the Turnpike Road from Waltham Abbey to Waltham Cross. And being asked, Whether that Road is always passable to Waltham Abbey ? he said, No; but that from the Point where the Canal is to come up to that Road, to Waltham Cross, is always passable; and that the Reason why there is no going at all Times to Waltham from the Occupation Bridge,: is, because the Turnpike Road is not. always passable, by reason of Floods. Your Commit t tee then called Mr. Teamans, a

Surveyor; who being asked. If he knew the Track of the proposed Canal ? he laid. Me did; that in his Opinion it is practicable to make a Canal Navigation over the Ground described in the Plan; and that he did not believe a better Line could be followed, for a Navigation from Moorfields to Waltham Abbey; that he believed Mr. Whitworth, the Surveyor, had been careful in his Survey to do as little Damage to private Property as the Nature of the Undertaking will admit of; that the Plan is as accurate and perfect as any he ever took or saw for the Purpose of a Canal Navigation; that the best he ever saw was that taken for the Leeds and Selby Navigation, and that this Plan is equal to that; and that he had compared the printed Copies with the Original very carefully. And being asked, What Difference there is between the Copy and the Original, with respect to the Diversion of the Road at Hanger's Lane, in the Parish of Tottenham ? he said, He believed no Difference; but that, by Mistake of the Engraver, in one it appears as if there was a Bridge, and in the other it does not; but that it does not make any Difference in Point of Expence, or other Inconvenience. And being asked, If he had examined Mr. Whitworth's Estimate ? he said. He had; and that he believed the Navigation can be completed for the Sum he had estimated it at. And being asked. Whether, in the Course of his Experience and Knowledge in Canal Navigations, the same have been found to be detrimental to the Landed Property through which they pass ? he laid, They did not, where proper Care had been taken to prevent the overflowing of the Water upon the adjacent Lands at improper Times; that he believed Canal Navigations have been advantageous to the Land where they pals, by furnishing a Conveyance for Manure; that the proposed Canal from Moorfields to Waltham Abbey will greatly improve the Landed Interest, and advance the Trade and Commerce of all Places near its Course; will be convenient for the Carriage of Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, and be of public Utility. And being asked. Whether Mr. Smeaton and he had, in the Year 1767, formed a Plan for the Improvement of the River Lee Navigation? he said, They had, and that the Plan wais carried into Execution. And being asked, If he recollected the Estimate ? he said, He did not recoiled; it. And being asked. And being asked, Whether, if the River Lee was as defective now as it was when he gave his Plan for its Improvement, he would vary the present Navigation ? he said, under all the Circumstances of the Question he could not give a direct Answer to it; that the other was carried on with a View to favc Expence, and preserve the old Navigation, and Communication with the Thames. And being asked, If the present Navigation is capable of doing all the Business of the Country ? he said. Yes, but not without great Interruptions from Floods. And being asked, Whether the Lee Navigation could do a Hundred Times more Bufi* ness than it does at present ? he said. It could do Ten Times more. And being asked, How the Canal is to be always ready to extinguish Fires in any Part of the City, if the Water is not conveyed in Pipes? he said, He had no Acquaintance with that Proposition. And being asked. If he was certain that the intended Canal will never be obstructed as a Navigation ? he said, He was not certain of that; that he did not know whether there was any Estimate of the annual Expences of keeping it in Repair, nor did he ever consider it. And being asked. Whether Leakage and Soakage of such a Length of new Works is not very great ? he said. No, if they be well executed; which does not depend upon the Ground a Canal goes through, but upon the Performance of the Work. And being asked, Whether, where the Banks have been broke in the present Cuts to the River , they had not been obliged to carry a great Quantity of Gravel and Clay ? he said, No Breaches happened while he had the Care of it, but since that Time there have, and Gravel and Clay have been carried to make them good again. And being asked, What he meant by the Execution of the Works ? he laid, He meant that where the Canal is to be carried upon new made Ground, and l’ome Part of it is above the Level, there is great Care taken to secure the Banks, by what, in new Navigation, is called Puddling, and that is by letting Water into the Cut, or into Channels on the Banks, into which the Earth is thrown and mixed together, till it becomes a Puddle; the Water, when it is let or driven off, leaves a Perma-' nency in the Bank that is Proof against Water; that this Method is used in all Cases where Clay cannot easily be got. And being asked. What is the Use of Stop Gates? he said. Their Ule is, that in case of a Breach in a Bank by mischievous People, or any Accident whatever, that might happen where the Navigation is carried over Vallies, those Stop Gates will prevent the greatest Part of the Water in the Canal from running out. And being asked. What is the greatest Height of the Banks of the present Navigation ? he said, At Endfield Mill it is about Seven Feet high.

And being asked. Whether all Locks are not liable to great Damage and Leakage ? he said, They are liable to Damage by constant Use, and to Leakage for want of Care. And being asked, whether the River Lee is not the Sewer, for all the Northern Parts of and Part of Hertfordshire, for many Miles? he laid. Yes.

And being asked, Whether he took upon himself to say, that the several Properties through which the Canal is intended to pass, are accurately laid down ? he said, No; for he never measured them. And being asked, Whether the Canal will not, in its intended Couri'e, disunite private Property in many Parts, so as to become very injurious to that Property? he said, It would be so, if ample Satisfaction was not made; that those Damages have been fully estimated, but he could not tell how many small Pieces of Land will be rendered useless to the present Possessors, and mull; be paid for, but apprehended they must be purchased, or full Satisfaction made for cutting through. And being asked. How near the Canal will go to Mrs.

Garden at Edmonton ? he said, So very near that there . must be some Support in the Canal to prevent Damage to the Garden Wall. And being asked, Where he intended to get Earth for the Bank between Stamford Hill, and 'Tottenham High Cross ? he said. There is deep Cutting at each End, and what comes out of the Cut both Ways, will be carted or boated to fill up the Valley, which has been the same in many other Places, and will be more than sufficient. And being asked, Whether the separating of the Arable Lands will not be detrimental to the Cultivation of them? he said. It will, as far as the Canal goes.

Your Committee then called Mr. Thomas;

who being examined, said, He was a Barge Owner, Miller, and Coal Merchant; that he employs Three Barges on the River Lee, and is well acquainted with the Navigation of that River between Lee Bridge and Waltham Abbey, that Barges are frequently Hopped on the River, on Account of Floods, and that the Stream is so very strong as to require an additional Number of Horses; that the new Cuts made for the Improvement of it are often drawn dry by the Wilfulness or CarelelT-nels of the Bargemen, and other People for Fishing, and the Locks, of which there are a great Number, are frequently out of Order; besides which Impediments, in Times of short Water, there are Shoals, but none at present; that in order to get over those Shoals, in Short Water Times, the Bargemen draw the Slackers of the Locks, jnd run out Blocks to make Purchases, in order to force the Barges over, which greatly damages their Bottoms, and occasions a great Waste of Water to the Mills, his own having often been stopt on that Account. And being asked. How many Locks full of Water he believed were necessary to force the Barges over those Shoals? he said, It is uncertain — it may be Seven or Eight, more or less, as the Shoals rife; that he was certain he had more than Seven Locks of Water to get over One of those Shoals: That from the Obstructions he had mentioned, it is very uncertain how long a Barge may be going from Lee Bridge to Waltham Abbey. And being asked, Ilow many Horses it required to navigate a Barge of Forty Tons Burthen, at present? he said. They cannot at this Time carry that Quantity of Goods: That they can carry Twenty-one Chaldron of Coals, or about Twenty-six Tons of Goods; to draw which, in the Stream, when the Waters are strong, from a little beyond Lee Bridge to Mr.

Wyband's Mill, and sometimes further, they have Two Horses; and sometimes the same Number from

nard1 s Mills to Waltham: That he had known it so strong, that Three Horses could scarcely weigh the Barge a-head. And being asked. How many Horses will be required to navigate a Vessel on the intended Canal ? he said. If there be a sufficient Depth of Water, One will be quite enough. And being asked. Whether the Passage upon the Canal would be at expeditious as upon the Road ? he said. He apprehended the Canal to be further about than the Road; but that if they were of equal Lengths, he imagined one would be as expeditious as the other. And being asked, What are the Articles now brought down the River in Barges, from Waltham Abbey to the Thames he said. The Commodities at present are. Timber, Corn, Malt, and Flour; and he believed many other Commodities would come, had they a safe, easy, and expeditious, Passage. And being asked. Whether he would not rather discharge his Loading at Moorfields, and return from thence to Bromley Lock for Coals, or other Back Carriage, than to proceed from Wdltham to Bromley Lock, and there discharge the Loading ? he said. He had rather discharge it in Moorfields, where he should discharge it safe, than run the Rilk of going to Bromley Lock, the Thames, or other Places, the Uncertainty being great on Account of the Tides. And being asked, Whether any of the Commodities he had mentioned were brought from Waltham to London by Land ? he laid, That Flour is, for which Eight Shillings a Ton Carriage is paid. And being asked. If he apprended that great Part of the Goods and Merchandize, now conveyed by Land between Waltham Abbey and London, would, in same the intended Canal takes Place, be conveyed by Water ? he said, It would be the Interestof the Proprietors of those Commodities to fend them by Water, as they would come to Town as lafe and as expeditioully, and at a much cheaper Rate than they are brought at present. And being asked, Whether he believed, that, in same the intended Canal should take Effect, there will be such a Quantity of Trade by Water Carriage as to be almost: immense ? he said, There will be a much greater Quantity than there is at present, owing to the Certainty of the Navigation; and that the Canal will be a great Advantage and Improvement to the adjacent Lands, and of public Utility; because as the Navigation seems intended both for Business and Pleasure, he imagined a Number of Buildings would beerested upon the adjacent Lands; — there would be a great Number of Gardens for lup-plying the City with Herbs; — there would be a cheap and easy Conveyance for Manure to those Lands, and their Produce would be conveyed in a cheap, safe, and expeditious, Manner to Town. And being asked. If he was examined at Guildhall, touching the Utility of this Canal? he said. No. And being asked. From what Places his Barges worked ? he said, from Hertford to London and back again: That, if the Canal was made, he should be able to carry more Goods in his Barges than he does now, because he should avoid Barnard's Mill Stream, where the Stream is lo strong as to prevent their carrying greater Burthens. And being asked. Whether the Obstrucftion to she present Navigation, from Waltham Abbey to Ware and Hertford, was at Barnard's Mill Stream ? he said. That is the greatest they meet with at present, and a little below the Tumbling Bay at Waltham. And being asked. Whether if those Defeats were removed, he could convey as much Tonnage as they proposed to do by the Assistance of the intended Canal Navigation ? he laid. Not between Ware and Waltham-, but they could lighten their Barges at Waltham, and go up with the rest of their Loading to Ware or Hertford: — That they could bring small Quantities, or Cotchels, of Corn or Coals to Waltham, which would be a great Addition to their Freight. And being asked, If the great Advantage he expected from the intended Navigation was by leaving small Parcels, or Cotchels, being about

Thirty

.14 Geo. III. 14° j.

Thirty or Forty Quarters of Corn, at Waltham Abbey ? he said, They could carry more, by Forty Quarters, by the intended Canal, than they can by the present Navigation on the River Lee. And being aiked, Whether it would enable him to bring more from the Thames to Lee Bridge ? he said, No; and that he could now bring Twenty Tons more to the upper Part of the Cut at Lee Bridge, than he could carry up the Country above Waltham. And being asked, What great Consumption there is at Waltham, at present, to take off the Quantity of Goods he proposed to deliver to them ? he said, It is well known, that there is a great Quantity of Coals consumed at Waltham, Chefliunt, and the Places adjacent; and that he was of Opinion, if the Millers at Waltham could get more Grain from London, they would do more Business. And being atked. Whether it was his Opinion, that the carrying Corn up to Waltham to be ground, would biake it come cheaper to Market than if it was ground at the Four Mills at Bromley? he laid, There are already large Quantities of Wheat carried up to Ware and Hertford to be ground, and brought down again, in Flour, to the City of London, and that he imagined was further up the Country than Waltham; and as the Carriage to and from the Mills will be cheaper, it will certainly answer. And being atked. Whether he knew that the Mills between the Thames and Waltham Abbey, have not been fully employed for many Years? he said, he could say little to that; that ,he had Goods brought up to his Mill to be manufactured, and brought down again. And being atked, If he imagined more Coals would be consumed at Waltham Abbey, Ware, and Hertford, if this Canal was completed ? he said. The cheaper they get them to those Places, the further they can afford to carry them into the Country, and the Consumption consequently mutt be the greater: — That he can carry Coals to Ware for Eight Shillings a Chaldron, Pool Measure, or Twenty-One Chaldron to the Score. And being atked, By what Estimate he could assert, that they could be carried cheaper by the Canal ? he said. He did not imagine, that to Hertford or Ware they would be carried much cheaper, if any; that at present Coals are carried for Six Shillings a Chaldron to Waltham. or Chejkunt, but, if the intended Canal is carried into Execution, he should be glad to carry them for Five Shillings a Chaldron, if not less. And being atked. If he, as a Man of Business, before he made a Contract, made an Estimate ? he said. It is the usual Way with all Tradesmen. And being desired to state at what Estimate he now carried Coals at Six Shillings a Chaldron ? he said, It was a Question he desired not to answer, as it opened the Mystery of Trade. And being atked. By what Estimate he undertook to say, when the proposed Canal is made, he could carry Coals for Five Shillings a Chaldron ? he said. He imagined he should be able to put out Five Chaldron of Coals at Waltham, which will be so much more Advantage to him in his Voyage, as he could carry no more up into the Country. And being atked, If it was usual for Coal Merchants to store their Yards by Five Chaldrons at a Time, as it may suit the Convenience of any Person to drop them there ? he said, No; but that many People chuse to take in only Five Chaldron at a Time, as it may suit them best. And being atked, At what Price he would contract to deliver Coals at Waltham Abbey, by Barge Loads, if the intended Canal was completed ? he said, It would not suit his Purpose to deliver Coals by the Barge Load at Waltham Abbey, as he must go the rest of the Navigation to Hertford empty: — That there are only Two Barges now’ em* ployed between Waltham Abbey and London, and whether those are fully employed he could not tell. And being atked, Whether he w'as not Matter enough of the Subject, to inform the Committee, at what Rate of Tonnage, or per Chaldron, a Barge could get her Livng between Waltham Abbey and the Thames, if the Vol. 34.

And being asked, Whether, supposing all the Obstrudions he had complained of in the old Navigation were removed, he would come down the River Lee, rather than go Two Miles about by the intended Canal ? he said, He looked upon it that the Obstructions cannot be removed, as they arise from the Number of Locks; and by which Means, was he to go the Two Miles about, he ftiGuld be sooner at Lee Bridge than by going the present Navigation; but that, if all the Obstructions could be removed, he would come down the present Navigation, but would not go up. And being asked, How many Feet of Lockage there are between Lee Bridge and Waltham Abbey, upon tbd present

Navigation ? he laid, He could not tell: — That there are Nine Locks: — That a Barge is always drawn from the Thames to Lee Bridge, and from thence to Waltham Abbey, sometimes by One Horse, but usually by Two, as it is too great a Strain for One up to Mr. WybancCs Mill: — That from Barnard's Mill he had always Two, which were hardly sufficient to do that Business: —

That some of the other Barges have but One Horse, but it is when they are lighter loaded: — That Persons drawing Slackers in the present Navigation are liable to Penalties, but they have not prevented the Practice,

And being asked, If he expected that Penalties will be more effectual upon the intended Canal than they are upon the present Navigation ? he said. The Locks are at such a Distance from each other, that it would be almost impossible for One Man to look after them; but as the Three Locks upon the intended Navigation are to be but at a small Distance from each other, One Man may look after them, and prevent the Obstructions which are met with on the River Navigation ? And being asked, If he knew how many Sluices there were to be on the intended Navigation, by which the Water might be emptied ? he said. No. And being asked.

If the present Navigation ever wants V^ater ? he said,

In the Cuts they cannot want Water; and that, since the Tumbling Bays hhve been erected, there has been little Want of it any where; and that if the Shoals in the River were removed, he was of Opinion there would always be Water sufficient to prevent Injury to the Bottoms of the Barges. And being asked. Whether he had rather discharge his Loading at than at Mr. Belts Wharfs, or at Lee Bridge ? he said,

As a Bargeman, he thought it almost equal; but as a Proprietor of Goods, he should much rather have them landed at Moorfields: — That he should get a Back Loading sometimes there, sometimes at Mount, and sometimes at the Thames. No. And being a(ked, Whether, if he had a Kitchen Garden, he should think the Value of it improved by having a Bridge at the Corner of it Fourteen Feet and an Half high ? he said, If it was a large Garden, and came so near, be should put up with the Inconvenience of the Bridge, for the Convenience he should receive. And being asked, Whether, if he had Garden Ground at Eight Pounds an Acre, he should think it improved by the Canal going through it ? he said, If he raised Vegetables for the London Markets, he should think it improved by the Cheap nets of the Carriage to the City from that Ground. And being asked. Whether he supposed in general, the Crops would be carried for nothing ? he said, No; but at a cheaper Rate than they can be conveyed at present. And being asked, Whether, supposing those Garden Grounds should happen to be the very Spot where the Grand Port is to be made, it would be any Benefit to the Owner? he said. He did not know where the Grand Port in Moorfields is to be made, as there may, perhaps, be some Alterations made in the Plan for the Sake of Convenience; that, when he spoke to the lad Question, he meant generally, and not particularly.

Your Committee then called James Esquire;

who, being examined, said, That the Price of Land Carriage, from Waltham to London, is from Six Pence to Eight Pence a Hundred: — That the Length of the

intended Canal being Fourteen Miles, if a Toll of One Penny Halfpenny per Ton per Mile, should be taken, the Expence would be reduced to One Penny a Hundred Weight: — That, if the intended Canal should take Effect, he believed it might be the Means of encouraging Trade and Commerce, be an Improvement to the adjacent Lands, and be of public Utility; and that the present Tolls on the Navigation, from Waltham Abbey to the Thames, he believed, are Eleven Pence a Ton on Goods, and One Shilling and Four Pence per Chaldron on Coals carried up. And being asked, If lie knew the Height of the several Bridges, and the Depth of the Cuts to be made, and the Height and Extent of the Banks to be made on the intended Canal ? he said. He did not. And being asked. Whether, if he had a Garden open to the present Navigation, he should expect to get much of its Produce for his own Use ? he said, He had never received any Injury thereby, in Twenty-four Years Residence near the present Navigation. And being asked. If he was not obliged, by the Nature of his Business, to keep Watchmen ? he said, Yes: — That all in his Business had, whether near a Navigation or nor; but that his Business was at a Distance from the Navigation, though his House was near it. A Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the Burgh of Forfar, was presented to the House, and read; Complaining of the Decline of the Linen Manufactory; and setting forth, That if some speedy Assistance is not granted, to put the Trade in a better State; the Inhabitants of that Part of the United Kingdom in general will be under a Necessity to desert their native Country, and betake themselves to Foreign Places, to procure the Necessaries of Life; And therefore praying the House will grant such speedy Relief to the Linen Manufacture, as they shall think proper.

A Petition of several Freeholders, Shopkeepers, Householders, and others, within and near the Parish of Saint George, in the Borough of , and County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting

forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that Application is making, for making, a Carriage Way, from the High Street in the said Borough, at or near the Greyhound Inn, and from thence, through Duke Street and Queen Street, to Gravel Lane, thereby to open a Communication with Black Fryars Bridge Road; and that the Petitioners are satisfied that such Opening will be of great Advantage to the Trade and Commerce carried on between the Eastern Parts of Southwark, and all Places to the Westward of the said High Street, and will be of particular Advantage to the Estates in the Neighbourhood of the said Opening, and be of great public Utility: And therefore praying. That a Bill for that Purpose may pass into a Law.

A Petition of several Inhabitants of the Parishes of Saint Mary at Lambeth, and Christ Church, in the County1 of Surrey, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Petition has been presented, for a Bill to make a Carriage Way from the Black Fryars Bridge Road, to the Eastern Parts of Southwark; and that the Petitioners find, that the Road of Way intended to be made from the Black Fryars Bridge Road, and through Duke Street and Queen Street, and through the Greyhound Inn, into the High Street in the Borough of Southwark, will be near Haifa Mile less than the present Road; and that the only present Carriage Way from the East End of Queen Street, into the said High Street, to the Front of the said Greyhound Im, is upwards of a Quarter of a Mile about, and is in some Parts so narrow as to make the Passage for Carriages very difficult and dangerous; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the intended 5

Opening will be the least injurious of any, that can be suggested, to private Property, and will be of reciprocal Advantage to the Inhabitants of the Eastern Parts of the Parish of Lambeth, near the Thames, of the Parish of Christ Church, and of the Borough of Southwark: And therefore praying, That the Bill applied for, to make such Opening, may pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are H thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and other Dealers in and Consumers of Hops, in the Town of Kingston upon Hull, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That it now is, and hath hitherto been, the constant Usage and Practice for Planters,

Growers, and Owners, of Hops, to pack the same in heavy Canvass Bags or Pockets, and to make the Purchasers and Consumers pay for such Bags and Pockets at the same Price as the Hops, thereby defrauding and greatly injuring such Purchasers and Consumers; and that in order to redress and prevent such Abuses for the future, the Petitioners are informed. Application hath lately been made for the Aid of Parliament; and that a Bill hath been brought in for that Purpose; and that the Petitioners have perused and examined the Contents of the said Bill, and highly approve thereof, as a falu-tary Remedy to answer the Purposes thereby intended:

And therefore praying, That the same may pass into a Law, with such Alterations and Amendments as shall be thought necessary.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prevent Abuses in the Packing or Bagging of Hops, is committed.

Mr. Brickdale reported from the Committee, to whom St. Stephen,

the Petition of the Churchwardens and Vestrymen of Bristol, the Parish of Saint Stephen, in the City of Bristol, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and the Landholders of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Roger Watts, being examined, laid, That the Avenues to the said Church are very narrow and incommodious, and the Burying Place thereto belonging so final 1, that the Surface thereof is raised at least Five Feet higher than the natural Surface of the Earth; and that if proper Avenues were made, and a sufficient Burial Ground purchased, it would be a great Convenience to the Parishioners.

Mr. John Lewis, being examined, said, That the Parishioners have actually purchased some Lands and Buildings, and contracted for others, for the Purposes aforesaid; but‘are unable to effect such Purchases for Want of Money, and by Reason that the Persons who are seised and possessed of such Buildings and Premises are unable to make Conveyances thereof.

That proper Openings to the said Church would be highly beneficial to the said Parish; and that the Application for that Purpose, to Parliament, was approved of at a very numerous Meeting of the Parishioners, which was held in Consequence of an Advertisement publishijd Two successive Weeks in the Bristol Newspaper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill lor making commodious Ways and Passages to and near the Parish Church of Saint Stephen, in the City of Briftoli and for enlarging the Burying Ground belonging to the said Parish: And that Mr. Brickdale, the Lord Clare, and Mr. Laroche, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Provost and Magistrates of the

Borough of Inverkeithing, in the County of Fife, North Linen Trade. Britain, subserihing for themselves, and in Name and llnoetkel«hi««< Behalf of the Town Council and Community of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read;

Complaining of the Decline of the Linen Manufacture, which the Petitioners alledge is chiefly owing to the great Importation of Foreign Linens; and, unless some speedy Remedy be provided, that valuable Branch of Trade mull entirely be given up; and letting forth,

That if proper Encouragement was given to our Manufacture, and the Importation of Foreign Linens discouraged, the Trade would be easily doubled, and the Manufacturers of Damalk and Diaper and Table Linens would, in a little Time, be fully able to supply the whole Demand thereof, both for Home Consumption and Expotation: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to give such Aid and Relief to the distress'ed State of the Linen Manufacture as shall be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to enquire further into thep elent State of the Linen Trade in Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Booksellers, Printers, and others. Copy Right whole Dependence is on the Trade of Bookselling and R , Printing, residing in the City of Edinburgh, was pre- 00 fented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the (Edinburgh.) Petitioners observe, from the Votes, that Leave has been given to bring in a Bill for Relief of the Booksellers in London, Westminster, and others, by veiling the Copies of printed Books in the Purchasers of such Copies from Authors, or their Assigns, for a Time to be therein limited; and being informed, that the Aim of the London Booksellers, since the Failure of their late

Attempt to gain a dangerous and perpetual Monopoly at Common Law, is now to obtain an Exercise, for a limited Time, of the same exclusive Privilege, beyond the Terms of the Act of Queen Aand to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, they think it their Duty to submit to the House, that the special Indulgence prayed for by the London Booksellers will, if granted, be highly injurious to the Rights of all who, in this Part of the Kingdom, are concerned in Bookselling, the Paper Manufacture, the Art of Printing, and other Branches therewith connected; and that, in the Paper Mills alone belonging to this City, there are many Hundreds of Perlqps employed; and the Booksellers,

Bookbinders,

666

Bookbinders, and Printers, there, are dill more numerous, who will all be moll materially affected, and some of them ruined, by the Consequences of the Bill, should it pats into a Law, and should it prevent them from re-p/inting English Books, when the Terms of the Act of Queen Anne are expired; few or no Competitions, even of Scotch Authors, are published originally in Scotland; and the Petitioners have hitherto lived chiefly by re-publishing, when permitted by the Act of Queen Anne; and their Bufinds must be given up altogether, if any further Monopoly is conferred upon the London Booksellers; and that, being at a Didance from the Capital, they have no Means of knowing with Certainty the Nature of the Relief which is prayed for by those who have applied for the Bill; but if, from the supposed Hardship of a particular Cafe, or the Confident ion of a lingle Inconvenience, the House should be led into a general Measure of enlarging the Terms of the Statute, such an Extension of the Monopoly will be the Ruin of many Families in , as well as preju-

dicial to the Community at large; and that Literary Property at Common Law never existed even in Idea in Scotland; the Attempt made feme Time ago to introduce it into Scotland was received with universal Difap-

probation; and, after a full Discussion of its Merits, was over-ruled by a Judgment of the Supreme Court; the Petitioners have, in consequence of the established Law of their Country, and inveterate Usage, expended large Sums of M >ney in the Printing of Books., which were not within the Protection granted by the 8th of Queen Anns, and in the Materials for Printing; they have Stocks of these Books upon Hand, and many are now printing'; and, if they-are to be exposed to Search and Seizure by the London Booksellers, and to vexatious Prosecutions before the Courts of Law, for exercising what they have all along considered to be their undoubted legal Right, and all in Consequence of a Law made ex post facto, they cannot but think their Situation extremely hard; and that the Petitioners know no Merit on the Part of the London Booksellers, to intitle them to such an undue Preference, and far lcfs are they con-feious of having committed any Crime, which should draw upon them those severe Forfeitures which will ensue upon the Law now proposed: And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may be heard, by Counsel, against the Bill; and that a reasonable Time may be allowed to fend their Witnesses to London, for proving all Fasts material to their Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for Relief of Booksellers and others, by veiling the Copies of printed Books in the Purchasers of such Copies from Authors or their Assigns, for a Time therein to be limited, be brought in.

Mr. Alderman Harley accordingly reported from the said Committee; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast- contained in the said Petition; and had directed a State thereof to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the 'Matter of Fast ntained in the said Petition is as follows:

An Act, made in the Twelfth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for regulating Buildings and Party Walls, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Liberties thereof, and other Places therein mentioned, was read. And, .

- Mr. John Jordan, a Builder, being examined, said. That , the said Act is in many Respects defective, and particularly in the Provisions relating to Party Walls being confined to Dwelling Houses only; so that the

feme is of no Effect for preventing the spreading <jf Fire from Offices, Storehouses, Warehouses, and other Buildings.

That some of the Provisions are contradictory; one Part thereof requiring the Walls of the Ground Story of every House to be Two Bricks and an Half in Thick-ness, and another Part, no more than Two Bricks; and that several Actions have been brought upon this Part of the Act for Penalties, to the Amount of £. 20,000, for Buildings not worth One Fifth Part of that Sum.

Vol. 34.

That there are several Terms made use of in the said Act, which Builders do not understand; and he instanced that of Flank or Side Walls.

That Builders are subject to many Penalties by the said Act, for Things that aTe either unavoidable or unne-ceflary; that he has known Actions brought against Builders for insignificant Projections of not more than Two Inches, for conveying Water from the Fronts of Houses, where it could not be done by Pipes, without great Inconvenience.

Mr. Charles Mills, a Builder, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Jordan.

Mr. Charles Groves, a Builder to His Majesty, being examined, laid, That a Prosecution was commenced against a Builder, for not Lime Whiting the Back of a Chimney, although it was absolutely unnecessary, as it was clear from the next House, and could not be deemed a Party Wall.

And all the Witnesses said, That the Meaning of the said Act is in many Places so doubtful, and the Penalties thereby inflicted lb numerous, that it is impossible for Builders to carry on their Business, without being subject to frivolous Ptofecutions brought against them by common Informers.

Your Committee then proceeded to enquire into the Prosecutions already commenced for Penalties imposed by the said Act. And,

Mr. John Jordan, being again examined, produced to your Committee an Account of Thirty-four Actions commenced upon the said Act, the Declarations upon which were for t-bi Sum of£. 39,600; and 161 Actions, upon which there are yet no Declarations; but supposing these to be in proportion to the other 34, they will amount to no less than £.187,517. 12J. ii.J And he informed your Committee, that the whole Value of the Buildings for which the said Penalties have been supposed to be incurred, does not amount to One Fifth of that Sum.

Mr. ‘John Pardon, an Attorney, being examined, said. That he is employed in defending a Builder in Three Actions brought against him upon the said Act, for Penalties amounting to T-3>95°» the Declarations upon which consist of 520 Sheets, though the Buildings for which these Actions are commenced, are only Six l’mall Houses, in the Parish of Saint John, which

the Owner has offered to fell for,£. 456.

Ordered, That Ixave be given to bring in a Bill for the further and better Regulation of Buildings and Party Walls, and for the morecffeftually preventing Mischiefs by Fire, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and other the Parishes, Precincts, and Places, within the Weekly Bills of Mortality, the Parishes of Saint Mary le Bon, Paddington, Saint Pancras, and Saint Luke at Chelsea, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. Alderman Harley and the Lord Mayor of London do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended:

That, after this Session of Parliament, before any Petition is presented to this House for making a Turnpike Road, or for the Renewal or Alteration of any Act of Parliament passed for that Purpose, Notice of such intended Application to Parliament be given, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, which shall be held for every and each County or District through which such Road pafles, or is intended to pass, at the Michaelmas immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented.

A Petition of Alexander Bookseller, in

Saint Pauf s Church Yard, London, was pretexted to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner has seen a Bill, brought in upon the Petition of certain Booksellers of London and for veiling the

Copies of Printed Books in the Purchasers of such Copies from Authors or their Assigns, for a Time therein to be limited; and, should the said Bill pass into a Law, a very dangerous Monopoly will be thrown into the Hands of a few wealthy Booksellers, to the great Detriment of the Public, to the Injury of Letters, and the utter Ruin of the inferior Booksellers both in Town and Country: And therefore praying, That the Statute of Queen Anne, which was expressly made for the Encouragement of Learning, may not now be altered, or suspended, for the Encouragement of the London Booksellers only; and that the Petitioner may be heard, by his Counsel, against the Bill now depending.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for Relief of Booksellers, and others, by vesting the Copies of printed Books in the Purchasers of such Copies from Authors or their Assigns, for a Time therein to be limited, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioner be then heard, by his Counsel, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Thames Mr. Dowdeswell reported from the Committee, to and Hi* whom the Petition of Mrs. Sarah of the Parish

Navigation. of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks-, and also the Petition of Morough O'Bryen, of Taplow Court, in the County of Bucks, Esquire, were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of Fact contained in the said Petitions, and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz. A State of the Matter of Fadl, contained in the First-mentioned Petition, is as follows An Act, made in the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for improving and completing the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and from the City of London, to the Town of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, was read:

And a Member present informed your Committee, That a New Cut has been made in the Parish of Great Marlow, between Marlow Mill, and , Bucks-, and

that a New Lock has been erected in the Weir near

low Mills, which is lower down than the Old Lock, and further from the said Bridge; and that the Barges and Vessels used, before the said Act was made, to pass through the Old Lock upon the other Branch of the River, on the South Side of the Eyet, at a Distance from Mrs. Winford's House.

Samuel Clarke, Servant to Mrs. Winford, informed your Committee, That the Barges now navigate close to the Garden Wall of Mrs. House, and moor

and lie there 2 or 3 Days together, close to the Wall; the Crews of such Barges commit great Indecencies, in-so much that Mrs. Winford has often been obliged to put up the Shutters of the Windows that look towards the River; and that the House being but Fourteen Yards from the Garden Wall, this Practice of mooring the Barges is a great Nuisance and Inconvenience.

The foregoing Evidence, with respect to the Alteration of the Locks, and of the Course of the Navigation of the River, was confirmed by a Plan, delivered in to your Committee by Mr. Broom-, who said, that the Barges never used to lie, for any Continuance, between the Lock, when in the old Place, and the Bridge; and it appeared by the said Plan, that the Distance from Marlow Bridge to the New Lock is only 266 Yards; which Plan, the Witness said he had examined, and it is an exact Plan.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained id the Second-mentioned Petition, is as followeth;

eferred; That the Committee had examined the Matter )f the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Greetham informed your Committee, That the Buildings and Inhabitants of the South Side of the Town of Liverpool, have of late Years greatly encreased; that there is at present only One Church in that Part of the Town, which is too small; that the Petitioners are erecting a new Church or Chapel within Toxteth Park, in the Parish of Walton, adjoining to the Boundaries of-Liverpool, and intend to fit it with proper Accommodations for Divine Service, but cannot establish it without Assistance of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for establishing a new Church, or Chapel, erecting at Toxteth Park, in the Parish of Walton, near ,in the County Palatine of Lancaster:And that Mr. Pennant, Mr. Comptroller of the Houshold, and the Earl S eft on, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Sir Cecil Wray reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Open Uninclosed Fields, and Parcels of Lands, within the Manor and Parish of Garton, in the East Riding of the County of York, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingossed.

whom the Bill for draining and preserving the Low Grounds and Carrs, within the Parillies, Townships, and Places, of Winejlead, Pattrington, South Frodingham, Hollym, Rimffwell, Owthorne, otherwise Seathorne, Wither-pea, Ingland Hill, and Walker Fields, in Holderness, in the Kaft Riding of the County of York, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee (except the Owners of about 90 Acres of Land, who refused to sign the Bill; and that the Lands to be drained consist of 1,550 Acres, or thereabouts; and that no Person appeared be-

fore the Committee to oppose the Bill) and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingossed.

Longitude. . Mr. Stephens, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Laws relating to the Discovery of the Longitude at Sea, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered Vol. 34.

in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same Were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all former Acts concerning the Longitude at Sea, except so much thereof as relates to the Appointment and Authority of the Commissioners thereby constituted, and also such ClaUfes as relate to the constructing, printing, publishing, vending, and licensing, of Nautical. Almanacks, and other useful Tables, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Provision be made, to enable the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, to pay, out of any Money in his Hands unapplied to the Use of tire Navy, the Sum of 5,000l. to any Person or Persons, who shall discover a Method of finding the Longitude at Sea, if such Method shall determine the same within one Degree of a great Circle, or Sixty Geographical Miles; the Sum of 7,500l. if such Method shall determine the same to Two.

Thirds of that Distance; and the Sum of 10,000l. if, such Method shall determine the same to One Half of the said Distance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Provision be made, to enable the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, to pay, out of any Money in his Hands unapplied to the Use of the Navy, a Sum not exceeding 5,000l. as an Encouragement and Reward for such Person or Persons as have already made, or shall make, useful Discoveries in Navigation, and for the making Experiments relating thereto.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Stephens, Sir Charles Hardy, and Sir Charles Whitworth, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Booksellers, Printers, and Bookbinders, of the City of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Leave has been given to bring in a Bill for the Relief of some Booksellers in London and Westminster, by giving them an exclusive Privilege, for a further limited Time, of re-printing Books not protected by the Act of the 8th. of Queen Anne; which Bill, if passed into a Law, will be highly detrimental to

the Community at large, as well as particularly injurious to the Petitioners, and to all Country Booksellers,

Printers, and others, dependant on those Branches of Business, who have heretofore been greatly hurt by the Monopoly of Books unlawfully exercised by the London Booksellers: And therefore praying. That the Statute of the 8th of Queen Anne, for veiling Copies in Authors, tdc. may Hand in full Force, as lately explained

by the House of Lords, and be neither amended or extended; and that the Petitioners be heard, by Counsel, against the said Bill being passed into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for Relief of Booksellers and others, by veiling the Copies of Printed Books in the Purchasers of such Copies from Authors or their Assigns, for a Time therein to be limited, be read a Second Time.

Lord Howe reported from the Committee, to whom Cotton the Petirioh of Richard Arkwright and Company, of Spinner*. Nottingham, Spinners of Cotton, and Manufacturers of Brhifk Cottcto Stuffy was referred'; That the Com-5 mi t tee

mittee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in d>e laid Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the lieport in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition is as follows:

It appeared by Letters Patent under the Great Seal, granted, in 17,69, to Rickard , That he had

invented a Machine, of a peculiar Construction, for {pinning Wool, Flax, and Cotton, in a better and more expeditious Method than heretofore, peculiarly adapted for spinning Cotton Yarn fit for Warps.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Jedidiah Strutt, who produced a Piece of plain white, and a Piece of printed. Cotton Stuffs (the Warp being Cotton, and tpun by the said Machine) manufactured from raw Materials, near Blackburn, in Lancash'tre, which he laid was better adapted for Printing than.any Thing of the.Kind heretofore used for that Purpose.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Stephen Williams, a Linen Draper, That there have been printed between 50 and 60 of the said Cotton Stuffs; and tlte Samples being approved of, he ordered about 300 Pieces more; but, upon the first Parcel being printed, the Officers of Excite demanded a Dury of Sixpence per Yard as Callicoes, being the same Duty that is paid upon Callicoes imported from the Indies; and thereupon the said Williams and Company preferred their Petition to the Commissioners of Excise (which Petition was produced) Setting forth. That the Petitioners having lately bought l'ome Cottons, the Warp and Shoot whereof were > all Cotton of the Growth of the Plantations, with an Intent to print them, but for the high Duty charged as aforesaid; and praying, as the Goods were the entire Manufacture of England, to be relieved from that Duty, and charged with the Duty of Three Pence per Yard only; which Petition being returned indorsed, u Charge with the Callicoe Duty; W.L." — That the Cottons, called

British Cottons, manufactured )n England (the Warps* whereof are moltly of foreign spun Yarn) pay only Three Pence per Yard; — that he countermanded his Orders in consequence of tire high Duty, as k would be an Advance upon them at Market of Three Pence per Yard.

Then Two Acts, pafi'ed in the Tenth and Twelfth Years of Queen Anne, were produced, and read; whereby it appeared. That upon Callicoes printed, painted, Itained, or dyed, in Great the ;Sum of Three Pence per Yard Duty is made payable by each Act; whereby such Goods being all Cotton, become liable to the Payment of a Duty of Sixpence Yard.

And also another Act, passed in the Seventh Year of King George the First, Cap. 7, S. 10, was read; whereby it appeared. That all Callicoes, printed, painted, Itained, or dyed, are prohibited to be worn, or used a* Furniture.

Then Mr. Strutt, being again examined, said, That the Petitioners had expended upwards of 13,000 in the said Manufacture; that if charged with the said Duty of Sixpence per Yard, it would totally hinder tire Growth, and obstruct the Sale, of this promising Manufacture, which, in all Probability, will begotbe a fkmrishing Trade, if encouraged, and be the Means of employing many Thousands of poor People, there being already upwards of 600 Persons of all Age^ employed in this Branch of Business; that Children of Seven Years oldyand upwards, are employed, and they prefer Children from Ten to Twelve Years old, for the preparing and spinning Cotton by the said Machine.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Cen-ijdera&aD of a Committee of the whole House*

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth. That the Improvement of the Navigation of the River Thames, Westward of London Bridge, within the Liberties of the Petitioners, will be a Work of great Public Utility; and that they are willing to apply the Sum of £. 10,000, if necessary, out of their Estates, towards carrying the said Work into Execution; which Sum, the Petitioners flatter themselves, will be sufficient for the said Purpose, without laying any Toll or Duty on Persons navigating the River Thames within the said Liberties; and that the Powers with which the Petitioners are at present invested, are not sufficient to enable them effectually to improve and complete the said Navigation; And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioners more effectually to improve and complete the Navigation of the River Thames, within the said Liberties, with such

Banker* A Petition of the Matter, Wardens', and Commonalty,

EiUtcs. of Society of Merchants Venturers of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making the Estates of such Persons as are Bankers only, within the Cities of London and and within a certain

Dittance thereof, liable to the Payment of their own and Partnership Debts; and for preventing certain Bankers from dealing in Goods, Wares, and Merchandize; and for regulating the Manner of ilfuing Bankers Promissory Notes; and for inflicting further Punishment on Clerks to Bankers who shall embezzle Money or Effects; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend, the said Bill is partial to a very great Degree, being calculated to favour and serve a particular Set of Men, who call themselves Bankers only, and that in Prejudice of the Merchant Bankers; and that the said Bill is framed on a Principle repugnant to Equity, which loves Equality; and that the Partiality of the said Bill, in Favour of the Persons who stile themselves Bankers only, is further evident, in that it lays no Restraint on the word Species of Trade in this Kingdom, which has injured Thousands, and mined many, and which is Chiefly exercised by a Set of Men dealing speculatively in the Public Funds: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Road*, whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Farmers, and Yeomen, Inhabitants of the County of Wilts, whose Names are thereunder signed; and also, the Petition of several of the Gentlemen, Fanners, and Traders, of the County of Middlesex; and also, the Petition of several Persons, being common Carriers, or otherways employed in carrying Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, on Turnpike Roads, were referred; and who were instructed to consider of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to explain, amend; and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the general Laws now " in being, for regulating the Turnpike Roads in that " Part of Great Britain called England; and for other " Purposes;" and to report their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had made a further Progress in the Matters to them referred; and had edme to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the.Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That it is proper and expedient that some Restriction ort Limitation should be put to the Weight of Merchandize, and other Loading of Carriages, which travel upon Turnpike Roads.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present additional Tolls dkefted to be taken on every Cart, Waggon, or Carriage, with its Loading, which shall, at any Weighing Engine, weigh One

Hundred Weight or more over and above the Weight allowed by Law, have, from Experience, in many Cafes* been found burthensome and oppressive, and require Alteration.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That instead of the additional Toll of Twenty Shillings per Hundred, directed to be taken by the said Act, for drawing greater Weight than are thereby allowed, it would be more equitable and convenient, if the following Tolls were to be taken; t the Sum of Three

Vol. 34.

Over Weight; and Sixpence for every Hundred of Over Weight, where the same shall exceed Two Hundred', and shall not exceed Five Hundred; and One Shilling for every Hundred Over Weight, where the Over Weight shall exceed Five Hundred, and shall not exceed Ten Hundred: and Five Shillings for every Hundred. Over Weight, when the Over Weight shall exceed Ten Hundred, and shall hot exceed Fifteen Hundred; and Twenty Shillings for every Hundred Over Weight, when the Over Weight shall exceed Fifteen Hundred.

Resolved, Thkt it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Waggons, Carts, or Carriages, employed only in Husbandry, or carrying only Manure or Lime for the Improvement of Land, Hay,-Straw, Fodder, or Corn unthrashed, shall not be weighed, Hay or Straw carried for Sale only excepted.

Resolved, That it is thh Opinion of this Committee,

That the Clause in the said Act, permitting an unlimited Number of Horses to be drawn upon any Turnpike Road where a Weighing Engine shall be erected, and the Carriage shall be weighed, should be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Trustees of the several Turnpike Roads, lying within Ten Miles of the Cities of London and Westmin-fler, and Borough of Southwark, ought, at their Quarterly Meetings, to be empowered to lower, at their Disc cretion, the several additional Tolls hereby authorized and directed to be paid for Over Weights.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of the Committee,

That the Exemption in the said Act, for Waggons,

Carts, or Carriages, moving upon Rollers of the Breadth of Sixteen Inches on each Side thereof, in hot paying the Toll now payable by any Turnpike Act for the Term of One Year* is found not to be a sufficient Encouragement to induce Persons to crest and make Use of the fame; and that it would be convenient that all such Waggons, Carts, or Carriages, should be exempted from paying any Toll, liable to be collected by any Turnpike Act, for a certain N umber of Years.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into jfutthet Consideration upon Wednesday Morning next.

Sir 'Thomas Claveringrepprted from the Committee, Durham to whom the Petition of the High Sheriff,' Grand Jury, County and Gentlemen, of the County Palatine of Durham, at the Assizes Holden at the City df Durham, on the Third Day of August 177 3, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter, of Fact contained in the said Petition-; and had directed hjm to reportVState thereof to the House; and he read the Import in his- Place and afterwards delivered it in-at the Clerk*s Table: Where the same was. read; and is as follotoeth i-yiz.

A State of the Matter of lflft.contained in the said Petition* is as follows:

Several Acts, passed in, the Fourth JYear of the Reign of William and Mary, the Sixth and- Seventh of William the Third, the Fifth of Queeh Anne, and the Third Year of King George the First, were read; whereby it appeared.

That certain Rewards were granted on the Apprehen-fion and Conviction of Highwaymen, Clippers, Coiners', and Housebreakers; and that Provision was made in the last mentioned Act of King George the First, for immediately re-paying to the Sheriffs, out of the Revenue of the Crown, all such Rewards as they shall have paid in pursuance of the said Acts. And,

' A Member present informed your Committee, That the Judges who have gone the Northern Circuit, upon being applied to for Certificates of the Conviction of Offenders, in the County Palatine of in Order

to entitle the Apprehenders and ConvictPrs of such Offenders to such Rewards, have always refused to give such Certificates, thinking that the said Acts do not extend to the said County Palatine of Durham, for that the Sheriff of the said County is not appointed by the Crown, but acts by Patent under the Bishop of Durham. Then,

An Opinion given by His Majesty’s Attorney and Solicitor General, in Answer to a Reference to them from the Commissioners of the Treasury, was produced to your Committee; which Opinion was. That the said Acts do not apply to the County Palatine of Durham; but that it did not seem unreasonable that the-Provisions of those Acts should be extended to that County. And,

The Member present proceeded to inform Your Committee, That the County of Durham is, in many Instances, become a Place of Resort for desperate Villains; .
