Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported Gold Coin, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to take into Confederation the State of the Gold Coin of this Kingdom; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Gold Coin of this Re^lm has been greatly diminished, by clipping, filing, and other evil Practices, particularly of late Years, in Violation of the Laws of this Realm, and to the great Detriment of the Public; so that the several Pieces of unlawful diminished Gold Coin, which have been received into the Bank at the Mint Price, in pursuance of the Directions from ' the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, of the Twenty-third Day of July 1773, amounting in Value to the Sum of £.3,418,960. 15 s.4 have been found

' to

y

i.4 Geo. III. 10° Mali.

to be deficient, upon an Average, at least Nine per Cent.

Resolved’, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Part of such of the Gold Coin now remaining in Circulation, as was coined before the Accession of His present Majesty, is deficient in Weight Five Pounds per Centum; and that a Part of so much thereof, as hath been coined during the Reign of His present Majesty, before the First Day of January is

deficient Two and an Half per Centum.

Resolved, That is is the Opinion of this Committee, That it has been a Practice to export and melt down the new and perfect Gold Coin, loon after it is issued, for private Advantage, to the great Detriment of the Public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That while Pieces of Gold Coin, differing so greatly in Weight, are allowed to be current under the same Denomination, and at the same Rate and Value, great Quantities of the new and perfect Pieces will continue to be exported and melted down; and, there is Reason to apprehend, will be re-coined into Pieces the most deficient that are allowed to be current.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, to prevent the.Mischiefs to which the Public are thus exposed, it is proper that all Guineas, weighing less than Five Penny-weights Fight Grains; and all Half Guineas, weighing less than Two Pennyweights Sixteen Grains; and all Quarter Guineas, weighing less than One Pennyweight Eight Grains, be called in, and be re-coined.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Guineas, Half Guineas, and Quarter Guineas, be called in by Degrees; and that it is proper to proceed therein as fail, as the Occasions of Circulation will allow, and as the Officers of the Mint are able to re-coin the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Purpose of calling in the said Guineas, Half Guineas, and Quarter Guineas,' it is proper that certain Days be appointed, after which they shall not be allowed in Payment, or to pass, except only to the Oolleftors and Receivers of the Public Revenues, or to such Persons as shall be appointed by His Majesty to receive and exchange the same; and that certain other Days be appointed, after which they be not allowed to pals in any Payment whatsoever, or to be exchanged in Manner before mentioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all such Guineas, Half Guineas, and Quarter Guineas, be re-coined according to the established Standard of the Mint, both as to Weight and Finenels.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Public bear the Loss arising from the Deficiency and Re-coinage of the said Guineas, Half Guineas, and Quarter Guineas; provided such Deficiency does not exceed the Rates settled by the Order of the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, of the 23d of July I a ft, and provided they be offered in Payment

to the Receivers or Collectors of the Public Revenue, or are brought to such Person or Persons, as shall be authorized to receive and exchange the fame, within the Times to be appointed according to the foregoing Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Methods of Coining hitherto invented, for the Purpose of preventing the unlawful diminishing of the Gold Coin of this Realm, by clipping, filing, and other evil Practices, and the Laws hitherto enacted for the Punishment of those that are guilty thereof, have been found to be ineffectual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the only effectual Method of preserving the Gold Coin from being unlawfully diminished, and of preventing the Mischiefs to which the Public is thereby exposed, is, that the said Coin should be current by w eight, as well as by Tale.

; VOL. 34-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the moll convenient Method of making the Gold Coin so current, is, that every Person who shall receive in Payment any Piece or Number of Pieces of such Coin deficient in Weight, shall be entitled- to receive a Commentation for the said Deficiency from the Persontendering the said Coin.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,-That such Compensation be at the Rate of One Half Guinea for every Sixty-five Grains, and in the like Proportion, as near as conveniently can be, for every Grain under Sixty-five, according to such Table or Tables as His Majesty shall cause to be publiftied, from Time ‘to Time, for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That considerable Quantities of the old Silver Coin of this Realm, or Silver Coin purporting to be such, greatly below the Standard of the Mint in Weight, has been lately imported into this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it be made unlawful to import into this Kingdom, or Ireland, from Foreign Countries, any of the Silver Coin of this Realm, or any Silver Coin puporting to be such, that is not of the established Standard of the Mint in Weight and Fineness; and that the fame, if fei2ed, be made subject to Confiscation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That for a limited Time, the Silver Coin of this Kingdom be not allowed to be legal Tender in the Payment of any Sum exceeding Fifty Pounds, but according to its Value by Weight, after the Rate of Five Shillings and Two-pence per Ounce.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there be made, under the Direction of the Officers of His Majesty’s Mint, One Weight of a Guinea, and One Weight of a Shilling; and also oilier Weights, being Parts and Multiples of the said Guinea Weight, and Shilling Weight, according to the established Standard of this Realm; which several Weights, after they have been ascertained by the Report of the said Officers, ' and approved by His Majesty in Council, shall be the Standard Weights for regulating and ascertaining all Weights to be made Use of for weighing the Gold and Silver Coin of this Realm, and shall be lodged in the Custody of an Officer, to be appointed for that Purpose, with a Salary, to be paid out of the Coinage Duties: And any Weights, which shall from thenceforth be rftade use of for weighing the Gold and Silver Coin of this Realm, shall not be reputed and taken to be true and perfect, unless they have been first compared with the said Slandard Weights; and, in Testimony thereof, marked by the Officer to whom the Custody of tire said Sfandard Weights shall be intruded.

Dr. Maty then informed your Committee, That at the Time he gave his Evidence, the whole Number of Tickets were engaged for a Week to Come, and Three hundred more Persons were waiting for an Opportunity to see the Museum; that, during last Summer, 2,000 Persons waited at the same Time for Admission, who, if they did all fee it, could not be admitted within Three Months after their Application; that the Institution has existed 20 Years, and there has hot been One vacant Day during that Time; that there are 6 Officers, besides himself, appointed to attend Persons tb fee the Museum, and another to attend the Reading Room, by the Establishment; that, by the Bye-Laws, Two Persons are to attend each Company; and Once in Three Years each under Librarian is obliged to act as Secretary to the Trustees. And being asked, What Inconveniences occurred to him in the present Mode of Admission ? he said. They might be referred to Four Heads; viz. The First with Regard to Persons applying to see the Museum; the Second with Regard to Persons while they are seeing it; the Third to the Officers who shew it; and the 'Fourth to the Houfo itfolf: That, in the first Place, the Number of People who apply every Year to see the , arc so confi-

derable as to cause great Difficulties and Delays tb those who wish to fee it, from a great Number of Persons being obliged to fend every Week, for a considerable Time, before they can be informed when they may have their Tickets, and from several Tickets often remaining useless, the Persons who sent for them being prevented from using them on the Day for which they are made out.

That, in the Second Place, the joining of Companies is often disagreeable, from Persons of different Ranks and Inclinations being admitted at the same Time, and obstructing one another.

That, in the Third Place, it is very disagreeable to the Officer to attend some of the lower kind of People, who, in many Instances, have behaved very improperly to them; that, by the Number of Applications constantly made to the Officers for Tickets, they are reduced to the disagreeable Necessity, either to disoblige, or to be accused of procuring Tickets sooner than they can be had in the usual Mode of obtaining the m; which often lays them under Difficulties, and the Imputation of Partiality.

That, in the Fourth Place, there is no Museum in Europe which is so constantly resorted to as this; no less than 10,000 Persons being admitted every Year, upon an Average; that all other MufeUms in Europe are (hut up some Months every Year, and that Re-eels is very necessary for the Collections; that every Branch of a Collection should be carefully examined at least Once a Year, to fee what Mischief may have been done, and to prevent or check Damages that may be doing by Decay or otherwise; that the Books should be dulled, and, if damp, dried; that -from the conti-Vot. 34.

Mali. 73$

nual Accession of Things, new Arrangements become necessary, which sometimes must be attended with considerable Labour; but from the constant coming of the Companies none of those Works can be done, though at present very necessary; that the only Vacant Day in each Week; is intirely taken up in dulling and cleaning the Rooms, and the Outsides of the Cafes; that the Officers have no Refcefs for their private Affairs, or for the Benefit of their Healths, except such as is allowed by the following Bye-Law; viz.

" That the said Committee have Power to give " Leave of Absence to the Officers, upon Application " from the said Officers, at such Times as they shall " judge proper; provided that such Leave of Absence do not exceed the Space of 30 Days in One Year, " unless the same should appear to be of such Importance as necessarily to require longer Absence; and " that the said Leave be not granted to more than 3 of " all the Officers at one and the same Time; nor to so " many, unless in Cafes of Necessity; it being understood, that there shall always remain One Officer, at " least, in each Department."

That though under the said Bye Law each Officer may obtain from the Trustees Leave of Absence for One Month in a Year, the Attendance falls the heavier on those who remain.

And being asked. What he knew of any Foreign Mufeufns ? he said, At Paris there are Two principal Royal Col left ions, The Lib, and A of

Natural Curiosities at the Jar din; that he Was in-

formed the former has 8 Officers, and the latter 6; that both are open only Two Days in a Week, Two Hours each Day, for the Admission of all Who come, besides which the Officers have a I*ower of‘admitting private Companies at all Times; that there is a Vacation at each of them of Four Months, in the Summer, as the Witness believed, from the Beginning of July to the Beginning of- November; that, besides the Collections above

mentioned, there is a Collection of Antiquities, but not publickly shewn; that, as he believed, the Collections at the Hague, Brujfells, Florence, and almost all Foreign

Museums, have no public Days; but there are Officers who have Salaries for shewing them to such proper Persons as apply, according to their Discretion,

Dr. Solander and the Reverend Mr. Harper confirmed the foregoing Evidence, as far sis Tame to their Knowledge. And,

Dr. Maty, being again examined, was asked. What Salaries the Officers have who shew the British Museum ? he said. The principal Librarian has £. a Year Salary, and £.12for Coals and Candles; that each <jf the Three under Librarians have 106 a Year Salary, and £. 8 for Coals and Candles; that the Three Assistants, and the Keeper of the Reading Room, have £. 50 a Year Salary, and £.6 for Coals and Candles'; that it is absolutely necessary that all the Officers should be Men of liberal Education and Men of Learning, and have considerable Knowledge in the modern as well as the antient Languages.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the chief Inconveniences which attend the present Mode of viewing the British Museum, arise from the Length of Time many Persons are obliged to wait for Admission, on Account of the great Number of Applications constantly made for that Purpose, and the general Admittance of Persons at all Times, Gratis.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the most probable Method of obviating those Inconveniences will be, by enabling the Trustees to demand and receive Money for the Admission of Persons' to see the said Museum, on certain Days in the Week, some Days and Hours being still allotted for receiving P'ersons Gratis.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

A Petition of David Hartley, Esquire, being offered Hartley’* to be presented to the House; c Fir?

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, Secar, T*-acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recom.-mends the same to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioner has invented a Method of securing Buildings and Ships against Fire, which, he apprehends, will prove of the greatest public Benefit; and that this Method has, by repeated Experiments, been found effectual, in the Judgment of a great Number of Persons who have been present at the making of such Experiments; and that the Petitioner has already expended a considerable Sum of Money in the Prosecution of such Experiments; but, conceiving it to be a Matter of great Importance, that the Efficacy

That the Petitioners Lave been informed, that there is an Intention. to restrain the Interest to be taken on Monies, to be lent on Lands in the India Islands, to Six per Cent, only; and that, however favourable this Re-striction might prove to some Proprietors in the few Islands where the Interest is so fixed, which are in the most advanced State of Cultivation, yet the Petitioners Vov, 34.

I6 Mail. 74!

are persuaded that such Limitation, or any Ihterest less than Eight per Cent, which has been established by their respective Legislatures in the greater Number of Islands, on the unanimous Sense of the Inhabitants, and after the most serious Consideration, would prove of the most pernicious and ruinous Consequences to those Islands where the legal Rate of Interest is fixed at Eight per Cent, many of which are still in an Infant , State of Settlement, and where the Inhabitants are consequently under the more prefiing Want of Assistance and Support: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed, to shew why it should not pass into a Law, with any other Limitation of Interest than has been fixed by the several Governors, Councils, and Assemblies, in the respective Islands.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Mr. Thomas Tdwnjhend, Junior, reported from the Hartley’* Committee, to whom the Petition of David Hartley,

Esquire, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, a State whereof they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place ;and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s 'l'able:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, is as follows 1

The Petitioner produced a Patent granted to him for his Invention of a Method of securing Buildings and Ships from Fire. And,

Francis Farr and Foljambe, Esquire, Mr. William Hammond, and Mr. William JeJJop, severally informed your Committee, That they had been present at the making Experiments of the Utility of the said Invention, which they described as follows: That thin Iron Plates were placed upon a Frame of Wood, over which were laid some Deal Boards, in the Nature, and of the Thickness, of a common Floor; and over this Model of the Floor, there was suspended a Model of a Ceiling, faced on the under Side with Plates of Iron, over which Plates of Iron and between the Joists, was laid about two Inches Depth of Rubbish, and upon the Top of the Joists was laid another Course of Plate, over which were laid Boards, in the Nature of an upper Floor; and between the Two Models, there was a Space of about a Foot and a Half, which was filled with Faggots and Combustibles, together with Laths nailed to the under Side of the Plates of the Cieling, in order that the Experiment might be as fully tried, and with as intense Heat of Fire, as the Place Would admit.

That all the Combustibles being consumed, they examined the Floor and Ceiling; and that they found the Flooring Boards considerably charr’d, but the Joists underneath not in the least affected; that as to the Ceiling, they found the under Side of the Joists charr’d to about the Eighth of an Inch, without any other Damage done to the fame, and that the upper Floor was not in the least affected: And the Witnesses said. That they thought the said Invention pradicable, and that.it would be of Public Utility.

And several Members present, who had seen the above Experiment, confirmed the Evidence of the said Witnesses.

And Mr. Hammond further informed your Committee,

That he had seen Two Houses built by the Marine Society, armed against Fire by the above Method, as had also a Member present at the Committee.

And Mr. Hartley informed your Committee, That he had expended a considerable Sum of Money in the Prosecution of the said Experiments, and said, That the Efficacy and Utility of the said Discovery, cannot be generally ascertained to the Benefit and Satisfaction of the Public, without fuller and more expensive Experiments:

And he produced a Floor and Ceiling, which had undergone the before mentioned Experiment; and likewise a Paper, containing the Nature and Process of the said Discovery; which Paper is hereunto annexed, N* 1.

APPENDIX, N’l.

An Account of the Method of securing Buildings and Ships against Fire.

The proposed Method of securing Buildings against Fire, is by the Application of thin Iron Plates under the Floors, and to the Ceilings: The Effect of these Fire Plates, depends partly upon their preventing the immediate Access of the Fire itself to the Timbers of the House, and partly upon their flopping the free Supply and Current of Air, without which no Fire can get to any great Height, or make any destructive Progress.

The mechanical Part of the Workmanship in the Application of the Fire Plates to any House, is very Ample, being no more than nailing them to the under Side

of

14 Geo. III. 130 Mail

of the Joists in each Storys in the Manner of a Ceiling, and upon the upper Side of the Joists, before the Floors are laid: A Quantity of dry llubbish of any Kind, should be put over the Ceiling Plates, somewhat in the Nature of a Counter Floor, which will deaden Sound between Floors, and at the same Time still farther stop the Progress of Fire.

The Efficacy of the Fire Plates applied in this Manner, to secure Houses against Fire, is not now a Matter of Speculation, but. of Experience: The Trials which have been made, have not been upon Models only, but upon Buildings erected for the Purpose; and I think I may say. That the proper Application of them would insure any Decree of Security that the same might require, whether it may be for a Magazine* a Merchant’s Warehouse, a Banker’s Shop, or a private Dwelling House; it will likewise make a material Difference in a common Dwelling House, whether the Rooms are to be finished with Stucco, or wainscotted Dado high, or wain-scotted to the Top of the Room, together with a Wooden Cornice: All these Circumstances being taketi into due Consideration, the Preservative against Fire is to be applied in Discretion, according to the Cafe. The Expe- timents which have been made, will justify me to say. That if the Floor be armed with the Fire Plates, any Fire will not penetrate through downwards, and if the Ceilings be properly armed, it will not communicate through to an upper Floor. But in the Course of these Experiments, we are infejifibly led into the Inconsistency of supposing an House thus armed, to be actually on Fire; whereas the Operation of the Fire Plates is to prevent any such House being liable to take Fire. What we have to deal with in the Beginning, is perhaps no more than a small Spark, which with the Addition of Air and Fuel, might in Time become an Hotife on Fire, but which, without the Concurrence of either, must die away. It i s an easier Talk to prevent Fire, than to extinguish it. Let the Beginning of Fire in any House be ever so secret, the preventive Effect of the Fire Plates is con-staritly in Force, as an obftmate unconquerable Negative to its Progress.

I ivery Fire, even the greatest, must arise from small Be§ {innings: A Difference of Reception to the first Pro* gress of the smallest Spark, may decide the whole. A sing ;le Fire Plate under a Crevice in a Floor, or over a Crack in the Ceiling, might have prevented the Fire of Lon don. Prevention, when one has hold of a found and app lying Principle, is not less certain, but, on the contrary, far more secure than any subsequent Remedy. Thi $ is a fundamental Point to keep in View, with respect to t he Fire Plates. In the Experiments which I have mad e, I have always put in an Heap of Faggots and Con lbuftibles to let the Fire going* which is not taking the Power of the Fire Plates to its greatest Advantage of b eing preventive against the Commencement of Fir?; To make an House burn, there must be a Body of Heat coll edted secretly till it comes to burst out all at once. It is known, and reasonably to be presumed* that this Bo dy of Heat cannot any where be collected so secretly, gr idually, and effectually, as under Floors, among the Ti tnbers of an House. This Spurce of F,iie would be ef fedtually prevented by tjic- Armour under the Floor. Ti lis Operation Of the fire Plates is not demonstrable, being a Negative, but to the Eye of Reason it will amount to a Demonstration* that if, the Fire Plates can re lift the Power of Fire, when Faggots and Combustibles h: ive given the Alcendant to its Fury, they will much more easily reGft it in its infant and commencing State. The Armour under the Floor being incombustible, will p Tevent any Fire from dropping through Chinks or Crevices in the Boards, to the Timbers of the House, and lurking the re till it forms a great -Body of Heat, and lourfts out all at once. In common Houses, a Floor on Fire is the House on Fire, but in an House that is armed, as the Floor will not take Fire to make a Body of Heat* liow is the House to be set on Fire ?

Hartley’s

Fire

Experiments.

It seems defirabie that a Set of methodical Experiments should be publicly made; in the first Place, to shew the utmost Power of these Fire Plates in thefevereft Trials, and afterwards satisfactorily to reduce the Application of them to practical Purposes. I imagine that the Addition of about Four per Cent, upon the Expences

of Building, would secure an House against the severest Trials. But as no Man builds an House with an Intention to set Fire to a Score of Faggots in any One Room, it is absurd to think it necessary to require Security against such extravagant Suppositions; more especially* as it is probable by pursuing a proper Line of Experiments, that every rational Degree of Security may be provided at an easier Rate, and an equal Quantity of Fire Plates might give Security to a greater Number of Houses, at less Expence to each. We are so accustomed to the frightful Idea of an House on Fire* that it requires some Courage of the Understanding to believe, that an House might be so provided, as that Fire should not be able to make any Progress beyond a certain limited and small Degree. If we had never seen the Effects of Fire in any House beyond the Degree of a Yard or Two square on the Floor, or Part of a Wainscot, without spreading or communicating beyond a single Apartment, it would have been considered as a flight Accident* which a Bafbn. of Water might put an End to, whenever it happened; I am inclined to believe, from the Experiments which I have seen, that Houses might be put into that Degree of Security without the Expence or Trouble of a complete Armour, and this upon the Principle of flopping the Fire in the Beginning; at which Moment it is as easily and certainly to be kept down, as it becomes tremendous, if it once gets the Ascendant.

The Principle in rhilofophy is flri&ly true* that no Fire can subsist without Air; but it does not therefore follow, that it is necessary totally to exclude the Air to effect the sufficient Security of Houses against Fire* Nothing less 1 It is known by constant Experience, that Fire will not bum under a common Boarded Floor to any Effect, till the Crevices begin to open, though there are always Crevices enough to let in such a Quantity of Air as a languishing Fire may just subsist upon; but when the Fire begins to widen the Crevices, acquiring fresh Fuel as well as Air, and when the Plaister of the Ceiling begins to drop, and leaves the Laths bare, like the most combustible Faggotting, to spread the Fire uni-verfally, and when a clear Current Or Air and Fire is opened through the Frame Work of Timbers, Joists, Laths, and Flooring Boards, then it is that the House is, properly speaking, on Fire; but if we have it in our Power to limit the possible Progress of any commencing Fire, so that it cannot open Access for Air beyond a very small Aperture, nor by any Means make a Communication or free Current between Two Stories, the utmost possible Magnitude of the Fireunder such Circumstances can never exceed what a limited Current of Air can supply: Witness every common Fire in a Grate, over Which you have a complete Power, to make it rife or to damp it, in Proportion as it is made to lie hollow, or stifled for want of a sufficient and liberal Currenj of Air. If the Plaister of the Ceiling would not drop, or if the Joints ,in the Floor would not widen> no Fire could gain any destructive Ascendant. With respect to the Fire Plates, they are no more Air-tight than a common Floor, but thqre is this essential Difference, that though there is a Perspiration of Air at every Doubling and Joint of the Plates, yet those Joints will never yield or widen by the Application of Fire, to give a free Current and additional Fuel to the beginning Flame.

Can there be any Construction of Combustibles so advantageously laid for burning, as in the Buildings of an House? The Laths as dry as Tinder undermost, the Timbers and Joists next, with Shavings and Saw Dust frequently between; then the Flooring over all adding Fuel as the Ceiling drops, and as the Edges of the Boards open to admit the Current of Air. Let the Dif-

fcrence of Construction of an armed House be compared with this-, Fire Plates nailed to the under Side of the Experiments. j0jfts instead Df Laths, with an Inch or two of Sand and Chalk between, instead of Saw-dufl and Shavings, and, over all, the Floors secured by Fire Plates against any Possibility of transmitting either Air or Flame, how is it possible, under these Circumstances, that any Materials, let them be ever so combustible, should conquer such Obstacles, and from the slighted Beginning rife, in Spite of them all, to an infinite Fury ? as certainly as Effect and Caui'e can in any same be connected, Fire Will languish till it dies, if oppressed from the Beginning; and nothing but a free Circulation of Air can raise a l’mall Fire to a large one.

After the repeated Trials that have been already made of these Fire Plates, I think it might' be safely laid, that an House armed in the most complete Manner, may be made Proof against any possible Casualty, or even Malice from Fire. Having the refore Pofiession of certain Conditions of Security at a small additional Expence, any subsequent Experiments may be tried and repeated, to ascertain that Degree of Provision which will be sufficient in Reason, in order to retrench needless Expence. This will be according to the same; an House, with a certain Quantity of Wainf-cot, may be secured in one Manner, another in another, and so for less or more; we have but to find out that Provision, which will not be sufficient in any Case, and when that is found out, to go to the next Degree for Safety.

It should seem not unreasonable that such Experiments, being for the Satisfaction of the Public, and to reduce the Price for their Use, should be tried by public Authority. The Expence in such a same would be very inconsiderable as a public Object. The main Question, whether the Fire Plates will secure Houses, may be determined by one House; which, if it cannot be let Fire to by any such Means as can possibly happen in common Life, the Ground Work will be so far decided upon: But when the Question comes to be split, to determine how much is necessary for reasonable Security, such Experiments should be repeatedly tried in the Presence of a Number of proper Persons, to observe and judge, that we may not be led to give up a full Security upon a fallacious Dependance. Unless these Points are ascertained by special Experiments, it might require an endless Term of Years for that Experience to come of itself, especially as every one would be disposed to the lafeft Side, until there were a sufficient Warrantry from actual and repeated Experiments to suit each particular Cafe. Such Trials might be publicly made and attested without Fear or Favour. There being no Doubt of the Efficacy of the Fire Plates at a moderate Expence, the remaining Question is a Point of (Economy; and yet it is not merely the (Economy of saving a few Shillings, where the utmost Expence is so trifling, that is the main ObjeCb The real Necessity is to forecast how we can make the Plates go the farthest; for if the Application of them should in any Measure become general, it would make such Consumption as could not easily be provided for. A Proposal on this Subject is in Agitation with where

the Devastations by Fire are infinitely b'eyond what, they are in this Country; and it would be desirable to have the Manufacture for Exportation encouraged in, our own Country.

This Invention is applicable to Ships as well as Houses; that is to say, to those Parts of Ships where there is the greate.ft Danger of Fire lurking unseen. I do not sufficiently know the Construction of Ships, to express this in proper Terms; but I have had this Opinion from several Gentlemen of the Navy.

Pitch, and Turpentine; to the encouraging the Growth of Coffee in His Majesty’s Plantations in America; to the free Importation of Cochineal and Indico; to the prohibiting the Importation of Books re-printed abroad, and first compol'ed, written, and printed, in Great Britain; to the Bounty on the Exportation of made Cordage; to the free Importation of certain Raw Hides and Skins from Ireland and the British Plantations in America; to the regulating the Fees of Officers of the -Customs and Naval Officers in America; and to the preventing the Spreading of the contagious Disorder among the.Horned Cattle in Great Britain.

towards defraying the extraordinary Expences of His Majesty’s Land Forces and other Services incurred, between the Twenty-fourth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-three, and the Twenty-second Day of April One thousancbSeven hundred and Seventy-four, and not provided for by Parliament.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported Great from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it Raisins. was referred to considerof the Duties now payable upon the Importation of Great Raisins, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read, and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duty, according to the Rate of One Pound Ten Shillings per Hundred Weight, now payable upon the Importation of Great Raisins, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That instead and in lieu of the Duty payable according to the said Rate, all Great Raisins imported into this Kingdom shall be rated to, and pay, the old Subsidy, granted by the Act of Tonnage and Poundage, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, according to the Rate and Value of Ten Shillings for every Hundred Weight.

The laid Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the said Resolutions: And that Sir Charles Whitworth and Mr.

Cooper, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

who, on or before the Twenty-eighth Day of this Instant May, and before the Sum subscribed shall amount to One Million, shall subscribe their Names, or signify their Consent to accept, in Lieu of their Interest: in any Part of the said Principal or Capital Stock standing in their Names, and in full Satisfaction and Discharge thereof, the Sum of Eighty-eight Pounds, in Money, for every One hundred Pounds, and in that Proportion for any greater or less Sum, or Sums, composing One or more entire Sum, or Sums, of One hundred Pounds, or Fifty Pounds, of such Principal or Capital Stock, One Moiety thereof to be paid on or before the Fifteenth Day of July next, and the other Moiety on or before the Twentieth day of October next, together with the Interest due on the Capital Stock so subscribed to the Fifth Day of July One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-four, shall, for every One hundred Pounds Principal or Capital Stock as aforesaid so subscribed, be entitled to receive Six Tickets, in a Lottery to consist of Sixty thousand Tickets, at the Rate of Twelve Pounds Ten Shillings each, and in that Proportion for any greater or less Sum, the said Tickets to be paid for in Manner following; that is to say; that every Person or Persons, Bodies Politic or Corporate, so subscribing, or signifying his, her, or their Consent as aforesaid, shall, on or before the Thirfy-first Day of this Instant May, make a Deposit of One Pound, in respect of the Money to be paid for each Ticket, as a Security for making the future Payments to the Cashiers of the Bank of England, on or before the Times herein after limited; that is to lay; for and in respect of every such Ticket, Two Pounds on or before the Thirtieth Day of June next, Three Pounds on or before the Second Day of August next. and Three Pounds Ten Shillings on or before the First Day of October next; that, upon such Payments being completed. Tickets shall be delivered as loon as the same can be prepared, to the Persons entitled thereto; that the Sum of Six hundred thousand Pounds shall be distributed into Prizes, for the Benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery, which Prizes shall be paid at the Bank of England, in Money, to such Proprietors, upon Demand, on the First Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five, or as soon after as Certificates can be prepared, without any Deduction whatsoever; and that all Monies to be received by the said Cashiers shall be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, to be applied, from Time to Time, to such Services as shall then have been voted by this House in this Session of Parliament; and every Person or Persons, Bodies Politic or Corporate, so possessed of, interested in, or entitled to any of the said Annuities, and so subscribing as aforesaid, shall have a Certificate from the said Cashiers of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, of the Amount of the Principal or Capital Stock by them respectively subscribed, and of all such Sum and Sums of Money as he, she, or they shall be entitled to receive in Consideration of such their Subscription, and in Lieu and in Discharge of his, her, or their Capital Stock so subscribed; and the Holders or Bearers of such Certificates shall be paid at the Bank of England, or at the South Sea House, the several Sums of Money expressed in such Certificates, together with Interest after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum on the Capital Stock so subscribed, in the Manner, and at the Times, herein before described; that, upon Payment of such Sum or Sums of Money, with such Interest, the Whole of the Principal or Capital Stock so subscribed shall Hand discharged, and be annihilated; and the Annuity payable in respect thereof shall, from the said Fifth Day of July, One thousand Seven hundred and-Seventy-four, cease and be extinguished.

That Books be opened, at the Bank of England, for receiving such Subscription and Consent; and that, during the Two First Days on which such Subscription and Consent are to be received, no One Person, Body Politic or Corporate, be admitted to subscribe or signify his, her, or their Consent, for any Sum or Sums, amounting in the Whole to more than Five thousand Pounds Principal or Capital Stock.

The Order made this Day, for the House to resolvi itself into a Committee of the whole House, at Three of the Clock this Afternoon, to consider further of the Bill for explaining an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act to " reduce the Rate of Interest, without any Prejudice to " Parliamentary Securities, being read; -

A Petition of the foveral Planters having Estates in Tob*ga the Island of Tobago, and of others concerned in the India Blands, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting‘forth.

That the Petitioners, as well as a great Majority of all who are interested in the Success of the India Islands, consider the Bill now depending, fof explaining the Act of the Twelfth of Queen Anne, as of the utmost Importance to their well-being, and to the 1‘rofpe-rity of Great Britain, as it promotes the Trade with those Hlands; and that Doubts having arisen, as to the Validity of Deeds executed in Great Britain, (or securing Loans made on Lands Abroad at the Rate of Interest allowed by Law where the Subject mortgaged lies, large Sums already lent both to the Colonies and to Ireland are thereby endangered; and while those Doubts subsist, no Man will lend Money on such Securities, whereby the further Cultivation and Improvement of the Islands will be prevented, -and' the large Sums already employed, particularly in the New Islands, will be in Danger of being loft; and that the Petitioners, sensible of the Importance of the Act of the Twelfth of Queen Anne, and that just Objections may occur to an unlimited Permission to raise Money in Britain for the Colonies, without fixing a Rate of Intpreft, are well satisfied that the same be limited to Six per Cent,; which, being only One per Cent.above the legal’ Interest in Great Britain, is no more than a moderate Compensation for taking Securities in drftaht Parts; where Loss of Time and Difficulties pi ay occur in recovering the Money, which is the Sense not only of the Petitioners, but of a great Majority of all the Islands where Eight per Cent.js allowed; and also the Sentiments of almost

all the Merchants in London trading to the West; and that, although a Petition has been jjirefented by. certain Dominica Planters, praying, that Eight per Cent.

Interest might be allowed; and although it may be the Wilh of many that the same Coialjl take place, without Prejudice to Great Britain, yet the Majority of the Dominica Planters are well satisfiid with the Bill at Six per Cent.; and there {land Minutes of the Dominica Society, repeatedly and recently confirmed, to that Effect, notwithstanding the Means that have been used by a Minority of the Society to have them cancelled; and that the Tobago Society, who belong to an Island still less cultivated than Dominica, and where Interest is also Eight per Cent, were, at a numerous Meeting, unanimous in approving the Bill at Six Cent.: And therefore praying the House to tike the Premises under Consideration, and to pals the Bill, confirming the Validity of Deeds to be executed in Britain on Property in any of His Majesty’s Colonies Abroad, at an Interest not exceeding Six per Cent.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for explaining an Act,.made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of Queen intituled,

" An Act to reduce the Rate of Interest, without " any Prejudice to Parliamentary Securities," is committed.

Then the House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House upon the said Bill.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Walpole took the Chair of the Committee.

A Message from His Majesty, by Sir Francis Moly-neux, Gentleman U flier of the Black Rod;

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty;

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended His Majesty, in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills following; viz.

An Act for the better regulating the Government of the Province of the Massachusets Bay, in New England:

An Act for the impartial Administration of Justice, in the Cafes of Persons questioned for any Acts done by them in the Execution of the Law, or for the Suppression of Riots and Tumults, in the Province of the Massachusets Bay, in New England:

An Act to prohibit the Importation of light Silver Coin of this Realm, from Foreign Countries into Great Britain or Ireland; and to restrain the Tender thereof beyond a certain Sum:

An Act to indemnify such Persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments; and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes; and to indemnify Members and Officers, in Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or, having been stamped, have been lost or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; and to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the Execution of Indentures of Clerks to Attornies and Solicitors:

An Act for regulating Insurances upon Lives; and for prohibiting all such Insurances, except in Cafes where the Persons insuring shall have an Interest in the Life or Death of the Persons insured:

An Act for further continuing so much of Two Acts, made in the Sixth and Thirteenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the opening and establishing certain Free Ports in the Island of Jamaica:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be applied the Sum of Thirty thousand Five hundred Sixty-one Pounds Nine Shillings and Three Pence, paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, in pursuance of Two Acts, made in the Second and Ninth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, by the Receivers General of the several Counties in England and Wales, that have not raised the Militia.

Another ingrafted Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Ryder, That after a Year the Owner may draw down the Water as low as he thinks proper.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with a Blank, which being filled up, the said Clause was read the Third Time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made Part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Three Pence Sterling Money Gallon be laid upon all Melasses and Syrups which shall be imported or brought into the said Province, in Ships or Vessels belonging to His Majesty’s Subjects in Great Britain, or to His Majesty’s Subjects in the said Province.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Six Pence Sterling Money per Gallon be laid upon all Melasses and Syrups, which shall be imported or brought into the said Province in any other Ships or Vessels in which the same may be legally imported.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duties be levied and paid, over and above all other Duties now payable in the said Province of Quebec, by virtue of any former Act or Acts of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Pound Sixteen Shillings Sterling Money be paid for every Licence which shall be granted, by the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, or Commander in Chief, of the said Province, to any Person or Persons, for keeping a House of Public Entertainment, or for felling or retailing Wine, Brandy, Rum, or any other Liquors, within the said Province.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duties to be raised in the said Province be applied, in the First Place, in making a more certain and adequate Provision for the Charge of the Administration of Justice, and the Support of Civil Government, in the said Province; and that the Residue of the said Duties be reserved for the Disposition of Parliament.

A Petition of the several Merchants of the City of London, trading to the Province of Quebec, in North America, whole respective Names are thereunder written, was presented to the House and read; also taking Notice of the said Bill; and letting forth. That thetre is a Claui'e in the said Bill, by which His Majesty’s Royal Proclamation, and the Grants and Commissions issued inconsequence thereof, will be revoked and made void; and that, by another Clausein the said Bill, all Matters' of Controversy, relative to the Property and Civil Rights of any of His Majesty’s Subjects of the said Province, are to be decided by the Laws of Canada, and by the Judges presiding in the Courts of Judicature of that Province, without the Interposition of a Jury; and representing to the House, that the System of Government and Administration of Justice in the said Province of Quebec, which have taken Place in consequence of His Majesty’s said Royal Proclamation, have been hitherto, as nearly as might be, according to the Laws of England, and such Government and Administration of Justice have been perfectly satisfactory to His Majesty’s Subjects residing' in the said Province of Canada-, and the Petitioners conceive, it will be highly injurious to H is Majesty’s said Subjects, and all other His Majesty’s Subjects trading to the said Province, to have the Laws of Canada substituted in the Place of the Laws of , England, and to have the Trial by Jury abolished: And therefore praying (in Behalf of themselves and others interested in the Prosperity of the said Province) That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, with the above-mentioned Clauses remaining in it; and that they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the fame.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petiticfn, if they think fit.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in thq said Petition is as follows;

Your Committee proceeded to examine Mr. John Hawkridge (a Linen Draper; at Pilton, near whose Name appears to be subscribed to the Petition of the Merchants, Tradesmen, Freeholders, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the Borough and Parish of Barnstaple, and its Neighbourhood, in the County of Dfvon (which was presented to the House upon , the Ninth Day of March last) who informed Y our Committee,

That he did not sign the said.Petition, nor authorize any Person to do it for him; and that ,his Name-Was pdt without his Privity or Consent.

Mr. George Burzacott '(a Mariner at Barnstaple, whose Name also appears to be subscribed to the said Petition) being, examined, said, That he did not. sign his Name to the said Petition, nor employed any Person to do it for him; that he failed ftentti>Barnstaple the Twenty-fecqnd of January last, and did not return till the Twenty-sixth of February; and that there is no other Person of the fame Name in Bartfafle.

Mr. John Darke (a Watchmaker at whose

Name also appears to be subscribed to the said Petition) being examined, said. That he did not sign the fame, or authorize any Person to do it for him; and does not know who put his Name to the Petition :.That he was applied to by Mr- Christopher Irwin, to sign the Petition’; who represented to -him, that therfe was a Thing smuggled up by the Mayor and Corporation, and signed by a Parcel of poor Mechanics, who would raise what Taxes they pleased upon the Inhabitants; and a/ked him if he would sign a Petition against-it; to which the Witness replied, That in that same he would sign it, if he had Ten Names; but that he did not sign it: That the Petition was not offered td him to sign, and he never saw it till he came to London: That when Mr. Irwin applied to him, he told the Witness, that Mr. Hole was going about with the Petition, and would have had him to have gone about with Mr. Hole, but he would not; and never saw Mr. Hole.mth the Petition; but was told by his Servant, that, the Petition had been brought to his House by Mr. Hole and Mr. Langdon, in his Absence.

Mr. Jacob Penbethey fa Joiner at Barnstaple, whose Name also appears to be subscribed to the said Petition) being examined, said. That he did not sign the fame,' nor authorized any Person to do it. for him, and that it was put without his Knowledge: That he did not know whose Writing it was, nor whether there is any other Person of the same Name in Barnstaple.

That his Daughter told him, Mr. Hole and Mr. Langdon had been.at his House witffa Petition, and had left Word for him to go to Mr. s House in order to sign it, but that he did not go; and that he had not seen Mr. Hole finef.

Mr. Humphry Burzacott (a Seaman at Ilfracombe, and whose Name likewise appears to be subscribed so the said Petition) being examined, said, That he did not sign his Name to it, nor authorized any Person- to do it for him, neither was he ever applied to by any Person for that Purpose; and knows no Person of the same Name as himself: — That he was not at

Barnstaple in February last, when the Petition was carried about to be signed, and does not think he has been there for Twelve Months past,

A Member present informed Your Committee, That he presented the Petition complained of, to the House, at the Request of Mr. William Hole.

Mr. Richard Coffin also informed Your Committee, That he introduced Mr. Hole to the said Member, at Mr. Hole's Request, who delivered the Petition to him as the County Member, in order to present it to the House.

Mr. James Martin, being examined, said, That he was employed by Mr. Hole and Mr. Irwin, as Agent for the Petition complained of; that they brought the Petition to him in March last, and desired he would do all that was necessary to get it presented to the House; that he advised them to apply to some Member to present it, and recommended one of the County Members as the proper Person; and that, a Day or Two afterwards, Mr. Hole told the Witness, he had got M#. Coffin to introduce him to one of the County Members.

That when the Petition was delivered to the Witness, it appeared to be signed; and that he acted under Mr. Hole and Mr. Irwin's Direction in this Business.

Your Committee then called Mr. William Hole; who laid. He was concerned in drawing the Petition complained of, at the Request of the Non-freemen of Barnstaple; that he penned it himself, signed his Name to it, and carried it about the Town of Barnstaple to get it signed, and believed he saw Sixty or Seventy People subscribe their Names to it; but did not fee John Darke, Jacob Penbethey, George John Hawkridge, or Humphry Burzacott sign it, nor knows who put their Names to the Petition.

That the Petition was begun to be signed at his House; that he carried it about the Town from Eight in the Morning till Three in the Afternoon, when he returned Home, accompanied by several Persons who had been round the Town with him; that he went into his Office, in order to get ready to let off for London, and left the Petition with the Company, desiring the y would finish going about with it, after they had taken some Refreshment; that about Eight of the Clock at Night, the Company sent for him, and told him they had been about with the Petition, and about Half an Hour afterwards he set off for London with it, being the Evening of the Twenty-first of February last.

That when he went into his Office, he believes about Sixty or Seventy Persons had signed the Petition; but when he returned, there appeared to be more Names to it; and that the Five Persons Names above-mentioned were not put to the Petition during the Time he went about with it: That he does not know their Handwriting, neither does he know the Hand-writing in which their Names are signed; and knows of no Person that authorized another to put his Name to the Petition, except Roger Manley, who requested Lewis Langdon to do it for him.

Mr. Christopher Irwin, being examined, laid, That he accompanied Mr. Hole to London with the Petition, but never had Possession of it himself; that he signed it at Mr. Hole's House, and went about with it for near an Hour to solicit Names; that he applied to Mr. John Darke to sign the Petition, who said he would sign it with both his Hands; that the Witness told him it was a Counter Petition against the Quay Dues, and that Mr. Hole was going about with it; but does not know whether Mr. Darke, or any of the Five Petitioners, signed the Petition; and that he applied to no Person, except Mr. Darke, to sign it.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That the Names of John Darke, Jacob Penbethey, Humphry Burzacott, John Hawkridge, and George Burzacott, which appeared to be subsenbed to the Petition presented to this House, upon the 9th Day of March last, were not sub-

Icribed by them to the said Petition, but were set thereto by others, without their Authority, Privity, or Consent.

The House was moved, That the Resolution of the House, of the 14th Day of November 1689, " That " all Petitions presented to the House ought to be signed " by the Petitioners, with their own Hands, by their " Names or Marks," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Resolved, That it is highly unwarrantable, and a Breach of the Privilege of this House, for any Person to set the Name of any other Person to any Petition to be presented to this House.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making more effectual Provision for the Government of the Province of Quebec, in North America; which Bill, the Petitioners alledge, will, in all Civil Cafes, take away the Exercise of the EngLaw', and that sacred Part of it the Trial'by Jury, and will substitute in its Stead the French Law of Canada, whereby the Freedom of the Person, and Security of the Property, of His Majesty’s Subjects will be rendered very precarious; and Setting forth. That, if the said Bill passes into a Law, the Roman Catholic will be the only legal established Religion, without any Provision being made for the free Exercise of the Protestant Religion, which may prove greatly injurious and oppressivef to His Majesty’s Protestant Subjects, who do now, or may hereafter, reside in the said Province; and that the Legislative Power is veiled solely in Persons appointed during Pleasure by the Crpwn, which is totally inconsistent with the Liberty and Principles of the English Constitution: And therefore praying, that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

appointed to inspect the Offices and Committee Rooms Offices and belonging to this House; and to consider the State Committee thereof; and how far it is necessary to make any, and Rooms' what, Alterations, or to erect additional Buildings for those Purpol'es; and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House, with a Plan and Estimate of such Alterations or Additions; that the Committee had inspected the same accordingly, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The most convenient Alterations to be immediately carried into Execution appear to your Committee to be as follow;

First, In the Offices belonging to the Four chief Clerks out of Doors, to throw the Room, now occupied by the Clerk of the Fees, into that Office, and to pull down the East Front Wall, and enlarge the whole Building at least Four Feet in Breadth, and to divide the whole into Four separate Seats, One for each Clerk.

Secondly, To widen the Passage between these Offices and the Room now occupied by the Clerk of the Journals, and to apply the said Room, and the adjoining Chamber, to the Use of the Clerk of the Fees.

Thirdly, To build an additional Chamber for a Committee Room, of the same Size of the intended Room below, over the Offices designed for the Four Committee Clerks.

Fourthly, To enlaige the Passage from the Lobby to these Offices, and to build a Staircase up to the pew Committee Room.

Fifthly, To turn the two long Rooms over the long Gallery into a Court of Wards, and a Room for the Clerk of the Journals; and to stop up the Communication between these Chambers and the Smoaking Room.

Sixthly, To convert the present Court of Wrards into a large Committee Room.

Seventhly, The Election Chamber to be converted into a Committee Room, with a Fire Place, and to make the Seats removable.

Eigjrthly, To alter the Secretary’s Room, and Vote

Office,

Swinburne’s

Estate.

Office, by enlarging the fame, railing the Ceiling, and giving it more Light.

Ninthly, To enlarge the Serjeartt's Room, by carrying it to the further Staircase, and lighten it by a Skylight.

Tenthly, To make such Improvements in the Lobby, and Approaches to it, as may be thought necessary and convenient for the Accommodation of Persons attending on the House.

Eleventhly, To heighten and make more commodious the Apartments now belonging to the House-"keeper.

These Alterations your Committee would recommend to be immediately carried into Execution; but they further beg Leave to represent to the House, That it would tend further to the Accommodation of the Committees of this House, if the Building, at present occupied by the Office of Ordnance, was appropriated to the Use of this House, other convenient Apartments being first provided for the Office of Ordnance.

And your Committee having taken the Opinion of Mr. Taylor, Architect, of what will be the Expence of the Alterations, which your Committee recommend to be immediately carried into Execution, he is of Opinion, that the same will not exceed the Sum of £. 1,200.

And your Committee further observe. That it may be proper to make use of Mr. Hartley % Fire Plates in such Parts of the Buildings adjoining to this House as they may be thought suitable to.

Mr. Burke also acquainted the House, that he was directed by the Committee to move the House, that an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Directions for the improving and enlarging the several Offices and Committee Rooms belonging to this House; and to allure His Majesty, that this House will make good the Expence attending the fame.

And Mr. Burke moved the House accordingly j Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, That He will be graciously pleased to give Directions for the improving and enlarging the several Offices and Committee Rooms belonging to this House; and to allure His Majesty, that this House will make good the Expence attending the fame.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Mr. Pownall reporteddrom the Committee, appointed

to consider of the Methods practised in making Flour from Wheat, the Prices thereof, and how far it may be expedient to put the same again under the Regulation* of an Assize; and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had examined the same accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereto, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That until the Statute, intituled, " Panis tff made in the 51st Year of the Reign of Henry the Third, was repealed by an Act, intituled*, " An Act to regulate f* tile Price and AlUze of Bread," passed in the 8th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, the Charge of the grinding and dressing the Corn into Meal and Flour was included in the Assize which was let Upon Bread from the Price of Wheat.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the letting any Assize on Bread, and the fixing a Rate upon the Labour, Pains, Livelihood, and Profit, of the Baker, so long as the Miller or Mealman is at Liberty to make what Sorts of Flour he shall please, and to affix thereunto whftt Prices he shall in like Manner please for his Labour, Pains, Livelihood, and Profit, is fcither impracticable, or must be injurious to the iBaker, or a great Burthen to the poor Labourer, Mechanic, Sind Manufacturer.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, the -Evils arifirtgfroin there being no Restraint, either with felpcft to thfc Sorts of Flour that are made, or to the Trices at which they are fold, may be remedied, by letting filth an Assize upon Flour as shall be found just and reasonable, with respect to the Average Market Price of Wheat.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That 4he whole Flour of Wheat is in general, as it hath always -proved to be, in Weight nearly Three-fourth Parts of the Weight of the middling Grain.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That according to the ancient Custom of the Land, every Twentieth Grain, or Five per Centum of the Weight of the Wheat, is full and sufficient Toll for the Miller’s Labour, Pains, Livelihood, and Profit.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That every Miller, if the Law does not at present oblige him so to do, should, under certain Restrictions, be obliged to grind and dress all such W heat as shall be brought to his Mill by any Person requiring the fame.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That -Forty-two Pounds avoirdupois of the whole Flour, when sold at the Mill, is equal in Value to the middling Price of a Winchester Bushel of middling Wheat at the same Time.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Magistrate, Magistrates, and others, who is and are, by the Laws now in being, authorized and impow--ered to set the Assize, and fix the Price, on Bread, should be authorized and impowered in like Manner to let the Assize, and fix the Price, of Flour.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That when the Magistrates who are, by the Laws now in being, authorized so to do, shall have prohibited any Bread, purporting to be of the superior Quality, or fold

at an higher Price, than the Standard Wheaten Bread, from being made for Sale, they be impowered, in like Manner, to prohibit, if they think proper, any Flour purporting to be of a superior Quality, and sold at an ' higher Price, than the whole Flour of Wheat, ftom being made for Sale, or fold, except for the Purposes of making such small Bread as may then be allowed (by

Licence under the Hand and Seal of such Magistrate) -or for the Purposes of Paltry and Confectionary.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the said Magistrates should, in order to inforce the Regulations made respecting the Standard Wheaten Bread, be impowered to order, if they think proper, that no Miller or Mealman shall use, during the Continuance of such their Order, any Bolting Cloth finer than herein described; that is to say, a Cloth 6 Feet in Length, and 6 Feet 7 Inches in Breadth at the Head, and 6 Feet Broad at the Tail, composed of Woollen Yarn, and weighing One Pound when new, having 32 Threads to the Inch in the Warp, and 28 Threads to an Inch in the Shoot, and what is at present known and commonly called a 13*. Cloth; nor any finer Wire Sieve or Machine than that which consists of 42 Wires to an Inch both Ways, and the Weight of 6 Inches Square of which is One Ounce and One Dram.

Ordered, That the said Report, with the Appendix, ' be printed.

N. B. A printed Copy is with the Original.

14 Geo. III. 22° Junii. — 40 Augujli — 150 Septembris. 821

gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as foU make a further Progress in the Reduction of the loweth; viz. National Debt.

My I^ords, and Gentlemen,

I have observed, with the utmost Satisfaction, the many eminent Proofs you have given of your zealous and prudent Attention to the public Service, during the Course of this very interesting Session of Parliament.

The Necessity of providing some effectual Remedy for the great and manifold Mischiefs, both public and private, arising from the impaired State of the Gold Coin, induced Me, at the Opening of this Session, to recommend that important Object to your Consideration: In the several Meal'ures you have taken for the Redrcls of those Evils, you have sufficiently manifested, as well your Regard to the general Credit, and Commercial Interelis, of the Kingdom, as to the immediate Ease and Accommodation of My People.

The very peculiar Circumstances of Embarrassment in which the Province of Quebec was involved, had rendered the proper Adjustment, and Regulation of the Government thereof, a Matter of no (mail Difficulty. The Bill which you prepared for that Purpose, and to which 1 have now given My Assent, is founded on the cleared. Principles of Justice and Humanity; and will, I doubt not, . have the best Effects in quieting the Minds, and promoting the Happiness, of My Canadian Subjects.

I have long seen, with Concern, a dangerous Spirit of Resistance to My Government, and to the Execution of the Laws, prevailing in the Province of Massachusets Bay, in New England. It proceeded, at length, to such an Extremity, as to render your immediate Interposition indispensably necessary; and you have, accordingly, made Provision, as well for the Suppression of the present Di (orders, as for the Prevention of the like in future. The Temper and Firmness with which you have conducted yourselves in this important Business, and the general Concurrence with which the Resolution of maintaining the Authority of the Laws, in every Part of My Dominions, hath been adopted, and supported, cannot foil of giving the greatest Weight to the Measures which have been the Result of your Deliberations. Nothing that depends on Me shall be wanting to render them effectual. It is My most anxious Delire to fee My deluded Subjects, in that Part of the World, returning to a Sense of their Duty, acquiescing in that just Subordination to the Authority, and maintaining that due Regard to the Commercial Interests, of this Country, which mult ever be inseparably connected with their own real Prosperity and Advantage.

Nothing material has happened, since your Meeting, with respect to the War between RuJ/ia and the Porte; and it is with Pleasure I can inform you, that the very friendly Assurances which 1 continue to receive from the Neighbouring Powers, give Me the strongest Reason to believe, that they have the same good Dispositions as Myself to preserve the Tranquillity of the rest of Europe.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

Ir

I thank you for the Supplies, which you have lo chearfully given; and I lee, with great Satisfaction, that, notwithstanding the ample Grants you have made for the several Establishments, and the Compensation which has been so properly provided for the Holders of the deficient Gold Coin, you have been able to

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have nothing to recommend to you, but, that you would carry into your respective Counties, the same affectionate Attachment to My Person and Government, and the same Zeal for the Maintenance of the Public Welfare, which have distinguished nil your Proceedings in this Session of Parliament.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the Fourth Day of August next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the Fourth Day of August next.

Jovis, 40 die Augujli;

Anno 14° Georgii III,a Regis, 1774.

THE House being met, pursuant to the last Prorogation; and Mr. Speaker being in the Country;

A Message was brought from the Lords, by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly the House, with the Clerk Assistant, went up to the House of Peers: Where the Commission was read, for the further proroguing of the Parliament, until Thursday the 15th Day of September next: And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until the x 5th Day of September next.
